Title: Statement regarding false claims made by two board members
text: 01.03.2019 Statement regarding false claims made by two board members With a report from the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland to the Prime Minister, Dated. On February 21, 2019, the protocol of two Board members followed the posting of two Board members making serious comments on a memorandum from the Bank's legal advice, Dated. 7 December 2018, on the subject matter of the Council's report with a reply to the Minister who was then available. The protocol calls it an indiscriminate interference in the work of the Board of Directors. It claims that the memorandum included an attempt by the Central Bank to prevent the Board of Directors from responding to the minister. This statement was a real surprise and is far from the truth. By law, I attend board meetings with the right to propose proposals and participate in discussions. However, I will leave the meeting if the Board of Directors decides. I did not attend the meetings where the Board of Directors worked on its report, but most meetings where the Bank provided evidence in the case or explained its views. Then I attended a meeting where I discussed the arrangements for the work and the involvement of the Bank's staff. In none of these meetings so much as I exaggerated that the Board of Directors should not respond to the Prime Minister. In fact, on the contrary. In addition, I instructed the Bank's staff to assist the Board of Directors as requested and to send quickly and readily requested information and opinions. It could, as the case may be, go directly and without my review, as the Board of Directors is part of the Central Bank. A large number of employees worked hard to assist the Board of Directors at the many additional meetings needed to complete the answer to the Minister. The Bank also hired an external employee to work with the Board of Directors on its report. On 5 December, the Chairman of the Board of Directors requested written comments from the Central Bank on a draft response to the ministers who were then available. The legal advice memorandum was part of the written comments and was received by the Council on 7 December 2018. Its contents were subject to the legal provisions applicable to the supervisory authority of ministers towards an institution such as the Central Bank of Iceland. The Bank's legal advice is on the board of directors as requested, as mentioned earlier, the Board of Directors is part of the Central Bank. The opinions thus given are then prepared with the best knowledge and conscience of the Bank's lawyers, but it is then up to the Board of Directors itself to what extent it agrees with such opinions. There is nothing wrong with checking that the Board of Directors or individual Board members make substantive comments on such opinions and that there is a logical substantive debate about them. In this case, it was not to be dispersed. The Bank and its employees provide information and opinions to the Board of Directors. However, it has no qualms about stopping the decision-making of the Board of Directors. The Board of Directors has its own chairman and can meet without the Governor and other employees of the Bank and make the decisions it wishes. Finally, it should be noted that the booking in question is a big surprise to me and those involved within the Bank. There was no opportunity to come to the point of view regarding the harsh allegations made in the protocol in question before it was published. M87r Gu?mundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland See here the Central Bank of Iceland's legal advice memorandum of 7 December 2018.

Title: Rebuilding the Icelandic economy
text: 31. March 2009 Rebuilding the Icelandic economy Icelandic economy has faced a lot of difficulties lately. I believe, however, that with actions taken or pending, the foundations for restoration have been laid. As I said in a speech I gave on February 27th, the day I took office, Iceland unfortunately has become an image of how serious the impact the global financial crisis can have, but also I believe that Iceland will be before long a model for other countries on how to achieve a rapid economic recovery. My experience of dealing with the banking crisis, currency crisis and debt crisis in Norway in the early 1990s, and in dealing with the Swedish government debt crisis in the mid-1990s is that a reversal of this kind is possible. The prerequisite for success in this regard is concerted and vigorous action. There are still a lot of things that need repair. The daily discussion focuses on individual factors and current events. Therefore, I think it is useful to outline the overall picture in order to promote a general debate on economic and monetary policy. In my opinion, the revival of the economy will be based on four important factors (see the accompanying figure): 1) Adaptation in the real economy, 2) monetary policy that promotes stability, 3) strengthening the state budget for the coming years, and 4) the restoration of an efficient financial system. As for the first point, inflation has plummeted rapidly. There has also been a turnaround in foreign trade that will boost the economy for the future. Inflationary pressures appear to have decreased significantly, and the Central Bank of Iceland predicts that inflation will be down to 2.5% in the first half of 2010. As for the second point, monetary policy aims to stabilize, while supporting economic recovery by lowering interest rates as far as the goal of stability allows. The first step in the interest rate cut process was taken on 19 March when the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee decided to cut interest rates by one percentage point. Furthermore, it was announced that the next interest rate decision would be taken on 8 April in light of the high debts of households and businesses, which are partially indexed and partially indexed, the Central Bank proposes the main focus is on bringing down inflation and ensuring a stable exchange rate of the krona. It is essential that efforts are made to reduce the deficit in the operation of the Treasury and to achieve a surplus. Similarly, work must be carried out according to the plan on various agreements relating to the financial sector, to restructure its restructuring and refinancing, because the economy needs to maintain solid financial institutions with good liquidity. The coming months will be crucial over the next few months can be challenging, but they are crucial for governments, businesses and organisations in achieving the above goals. However, the harvest will be the more generous when the necessary changes have been made and the processes and plans that are being worked out will be completed. It will turn out that government debt has increased significantly from before the banking crisis. However, the net debt position of the Treasury will likely be close to the average European country, so there should be no specific reason for the relatively high debt load on Icelandic bonds. At the same time, the foundations for the restoration of the banking system have been laid. These measures and changes are expected to be completed before some. Once this work is done, it's time to look to the future. Furthermore, a foundation has been laid for the revival of the economy, and economic growth must be focused on the means of increased exports, while a permanent surplus in trade with foreign countries is a priority. Foreign borrowing of companies, households and banking institutions has meant that the national debt as a whole has increased greatly and of these must be paid. Many positive signs of the positive in this for Icelanders are, as you know, one of the most working and tooled nations in Europe. She will enjoy creating good fishing grounds, and Iceland's fishing and fish industry are at the forefront of the world. This provides an excellent platform for the travel industry, renewable energy and the industry it is based on it, as well as a much wider range of economies than many foreigners realize. So with the right actions, we should be able to be confident that economic growth can be strengthened. These are certainly challenging times for everyone, and the others The global financial crisis does not make it easier for us to cope, but greatly adds to the uncertainty. The Central Bank of Iceland is responsible for some of the policies described here. This is especially true of money policy. In addition, as we build on the Central Bank's defined role and its independence as described in the Bank Act, we will cooperate as closely as possible with other public institutions, organisations and companies in order to create a solid foundation for renewed interest rates and stability. Svein Harald oygard, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland

Title: Article by Chief Economist at the Central Bank of Iceland: The Question of the Krna
text: 02.03.2013 Article by orarinn G. Petursson, Chief Economist at the Central Bank of Iceland: The Question of the Krona orarinn G. Petursson, chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland, wrote an article published in Frettablaoio and on visir.is 2 March 2013. The article discussed the pros and cons of keeping your own currency. The Question of the Crown Increased discipline in economic management is a common refrain in public debate at the moment, as the demand to restrain inflation and reduce economic volatility is noisy. Awareness of the need for increased discipline should be welcomed and is hopefully an indicator of reform in this area, as disciplined economic management could be one of the greatest boons for Icelandic households and businesses if successful in this regard. The debate now in the run-up to the upcoming election, however, gives rise to moderate optimism, as few seem willing to outline what exactly is meant by increased economic discipline. Moderate optimism also seems appropriate in the face of the monetary policy debate, with few actually seemingly willing to take the steps needed to get inflation permanently down. Following the Central Bank of Iceland's extensive assessment of Iceland's options in currency and exchange rates (see Special Publication No. 7 and a general summary of its findings in issue 38 and 39 of Indicators, September 2012), some have also put a call for greater discipline in economic management in the context of the question of the most appropriate currency arrangements in Iceland and seem to believe that with improved economic management, the debate over membership of a larger currency area will actually be unnecessary. Improved economic management, however, will not solve all the problems associated with an independent currency in a small currency area. Still, it will be an intrusive question of whether it is suitable for a country with as little national economy as Iceland to have its own currency. The main reasons for this will be traced below. Its own currency in such a small economy comes with a variety of costs.... As attributed to the Central Bank's report, it comes with various direct and indirect costs of having their own currency, especially in a small open economy. For example, the direct cost of having to switch from one currency to another in international trade could amount to about 5-15 ma.kr. each year, or up to more than a tenth of last year's trade and services surplus. The macroeconomic costs associated with making it harder to use the feasibility of size in a small currency area, e.g. when operating your own payment processor, is not taken into account. Icelandic financial system is also extremely small and expensive to operate. Market participants are few, turnover is relatively low, and the cost of doing business is relatively high. Thus, for example, only three market participants in the foreign exchange market and the difference between buy and sell offers (the traditional measure of market efficiency) is roughly two- to three times higher than among other developed countries. This is reflected in higher exchange rate fluctuations in this country and higher domestic interest rates. Research published in the Bank's report thus indicates that the burden on domestic real interest rates could fall by 11/2 percentage points on becoming part of a larger currency area. This could otherwise lead to an increase in domestic capital stocks and gdp per capita rising permanently by 2%. Exchange rate fluctuations can be part of the normal adjustment of relative prices following economic fluctuations (e.g. when the exchange rate falls following an economic shock). They are therefore not necessarily harmful in themselves and even desirable insofar as they reflect changes in economic conditions. However, fluctuations in the exchange rate appear to be greater than can be explained by changes in the economic conditions of the economy and appear to be largely spontaneous, as attributable to the Bank's report. Such volatility is intended to foster instability instead of facilitating the national adaptation to economic slumps. What's more, research suggests that such exchange rate fluctuations make it harder for companies, especially small and medium-sized ones, to hash out international markets, for example, where there is a long build-up to such access that requires investment and market activity that high exchange rate fluctuations can sooner than last to pull the foundations away. This matters in a small economy such as the Icelandic where the small size of the home market puts sizeables in manufacturing, operations and marketing narrow constraints that participation in international trade can lift. McKinsey's recent report points to just relatively low productivity levels as one of the main drags of economic progress in this country. Other research suggests that its own currency may act as an obstacle to the influx of direct foreign investment. They show, for example, that following the adoption of the euro, direct foreign investment between eurozone countries increased by 30%, corporate mergers across eurozone borders increased, and more international companies chose to use the eurozone as their establishment. Membership of a larger currency area also appears to lead to increased trade with other countries. The Bank's report details a number of studies suggesting that membership of the eurozone has normally led to a permanent increase in foreign trade. Based on the median of these studies, the increase in iceland could be 70 ma.kr. per year, which corresponds to more than 60% of last year's goods and services surplus. Other research suggests that increased foreign trade is accompanied by a permanent increase in domestic income levels, and given the above increase in foreign trade and the results of these studies, GDP per capita could rise permanently by 3%. .. which must be offset by vague gains As attributed above, it comes with some of the costs of operating your own currency system in as little national economy as those Icelandic. These costs need to be offset by possible gains in their own currency that can be used in response to specific Icelandic economic slumps, but as attributed in the Central Bank's report, Icelandic economic volatility seems to be little associated with the economic volatility of other developed countries, suggesting that flexible exchange rate policies are suitable for Icelandic national economy. In many ways, this exchange rate flexibility can be thought of as a guarantee that can be activated when it comes to national economy. Therefore, the costs described above can be regarded as the premium of the insurance. Everyone agrees that it makes sense to buy a deposit against trauma. However, it may not cost too much, especially considering one of the central bank's main findings that increased exchange rate fluctuations do not appear to have reduced economic fluctuations in small states and that fluctuations in the exchange rate reflect only a small degree of adjustment to domestic economic slumps. The crown seems to have not been enough to perform the volatility of the role that is bought at expensive prices. Improved economic management will allow us to make better use of the advantages of flexible exchange rates of our own currency and reduce the cost of operating such a small currency system. That doesn't change, however, because it will continue to come with some costs, and although there will certainly be a period in which flexible exchange rates can facilitate adjustments following a shock, the long-term gains are not obvious. So the question of the crown will remain in place. The writer is chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland and a member of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee. The views expressed herein do not have to reflect the views of the Bank or other members of the Monetary Policy Committee.

Title: Monetary policy and Icelandic krona
text: 02.04.2003 Monetary policy and Icelandic krona Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson, CEO and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, gave a speech published here at the Annual General Meeting of the Icelandic Tourism Association on 2 April 2003. Good attendees. I would like to start by thanking you for the invitation here to the Annual General Meeting of the Icelandic Travel Industry Association and for the opportunity to speak to the attendees about monetary policy and Icelandic the krona. If you look back in time, you can see major changes in the economic environment and its management. Previously, economic policy was highly arbitrary and sometimes took a stake without much notice. Struggling with inflation was an ongoing economic challenge, and often prices got significantly out of hand. Foreign exchange controls were regulated and exchange rates were determined by the government in consultation with the Central Bank of Iceland, but often the government intervened in developments with devaluations determined at a political level. Interest rates did not work as a control instrument except to a very limited extent and the Central Bank's role as defined in the Act on the Bank was multifaceted and some of its objectives were contradicted by others. Gradually, major changes have been made to the structure of the economy. The transfer of capital between Iceland and other countries is now unrestricted, but the last remnants of restrictions were abolished in 1995 when short-term capital was allowed to be transferred between countries. The foreign exchange market was established in 1993 and has intensified significantly since then and the exchange rate is now determined by supply and demand in the market. When the inflation boom burned to its happiest, it was often tried to rectify the imbalance in the economy through devaluation. The role of the devaluations was to increase export revenues and thereby overtime negative domestic cost trends. The benefits were usually short-lived, and sooner than that, the situation was in the same way as before, high inflation and imbalances. Interest rates were determined by the Central Bank of Iceland and usually by heavy interference from politicians. This, on the one hand, led to the burning of capital assets, often at an alarming rate and on the other hand to an unreasonable allocation of credit that was scarce, and many remember long queues at the banks' front doors that began to form in the early hours of the morning. The indexation of capital was the first successful attempt to break out of this vicious circle. Change took a long time, however, and was often painful. The national reconciliation between the social partners and the public sector in the late 1980s marked the beginning of a greater economic balance. The national reconciliation was based on a temporary cut in purchasing power and a rate fix that led to price stability and enabled companies in the country to achieve a better balance of operations. Despite the uptick in the young capital market, unemployment and the cut in power, defence was successfully turned on the offensive and in recent years economic growth in Iceland has been well and better than in many other places and stronger support has been strengthened in the economy in Iceland, both in the arena of large-scale business operations and smaller operations. Purchasing power has also grown considerably, with few examples of as much as long-lasting growth in purchasing power among developed countries. Along with this development, there was also significant progress in the capital market and in the management of monetary policy. Progress in this area began in earnest at the beginning of the last decade. The legal framework for monetary institutions and capital transactions was substantially improved as a result of Iceland's accession to the European Economic Area and further changes have since been made to it. The stock market gradually gained strong root and various capital markets were established, such as the domestic foreign exchange market and then the interbank market with kronur. Controls on the transfer of capital between countries were gradually abolished as much as I could before, reducing public interference in the operation of companies in the capital market. In May 2001, the Althing passed by the votes of all present members of the Althingi a new Act on central banks Iceland, which entailed major changes from previous laws. The act took into account innovations in central bank legislation in other countries and, among other things, strengthened the new policy that had been decided two months earlier when the inflation target was adopted. The most important change from the previous law was that the Central Bank was set one main objective, namely to promote stable prices. He was granted independence to use his controls to achieve this goal. In addition, the Bank was entrusted with preserving foreign exchange reserves and promoting an active and secure financial system, i.e. the stability of the financial system. The act also stipulated that the Treasury was not allowed to borrow from the Central Bank, but a few years earlier it had been decided by agreement between the Central Bank and the Minister of Finance. In addition, they made certain demands for transparency and financial statements towards the government and the public. For example, the Bank was obliged to publicly outline its monetary policy and the progress of monetary and exchange rates and its actions in those areas no less frequently than quarterly. In March 2001, the monetary policy in Iceland was changed. The government and the Central Bank then issued a joint statement that the so-called inflation targets would be adopted as the ballast and framework of monetary policy. At the same time, it was proposed by a fixed-rate policy that had been followed for over a decade. In the beginning, the exchange rate policy was such that there were relatively narrow tolerances for the reference rate or the central exchange rate of the krona of 21/4% in each direction. They were expanded in two phases, reaching 9% in each direction in early 2000. So there was a huge deflection in the development of the gang. During this period, stable prices were the main objectives of monetary policy and the intermediate target was a stable exchange rate. The inflation target is that the Central Bank should contribute to inflation as close as possible to 21/2%. If inflation variances exceed 11/2% each direction, the Bank shall submit a report to the Government clarifying what causes this deviation, how the Bank intends to respond to it and how long it considers it will take to regain inflation to the inflation target. The Central Bank has only one control to achieve this goal. It is the interest rates that apply in the Central Bank's dealings with credit institutions, sometimes called the Central Bank's policy rate. The banks then decide on their own interest rates, taking into account the Central Bank's interest rates and short-term market interest rates change in line with the Central Bank's interest rates. The Central Bank's interest rate changes also affect long-term interest rates, but other factors also affect them. The reaction to the Central Bank's interest rate changes in the long-term market is therefore not always predictable and will often have some delay. When the domestic foreign exchange market was established in 1993, there were significant changes in the exchange rate decision. The exchange rate of the krona against foreign currencies was determined on the market and depended on supply and demand. Up front, the Central Bank had significant interference in the foreign exchange market, as domestic banking institutions were not equipped to carry the torch initially. Although the exchange rate policy arrangement allowed fluctuations in exchange rates, the Central Bank was obliged to intervene in developments if there was a chance that the exchange rate would go beyond the tolerance. At first, the Central Bank was a member of most foreign exchange trading, but as other banking institutions grew, the Bank withdrew and eventually largely disappeared from the market. The great period of economic growth that lasted here between 1995 and 2001 ended in overheating. There was a lot of optimism, wages rose sharply and private consumption increased. All of this had the effect of making trade balances with other countries very unfavourable and the trade deficit reaching just over 10% of GDP in 2000. This resulted in high inflationary pressures, and the Central Bank responded to it by raising interest rates already in 1998 and then further in 1999 and 2000. The increase in interest rates resulted in surplus demand in the economy and the exchange rate rising, holding back an increase in the consumer price index as the overvaluation of the economy was in turmoil. The exchange rate of the krona reached its highest level in the spring of 2000. Expectations in the market changed in the spring of 2000 and the exchange rate began to fall. Undoubtedly there are a number of explanations for this, but the heaviest is most likely to be concerned about the huge trade deficit and the massive foreign funding needs caused by it and Iceland's investments in foreign securities during that year, not least pension funds. The rate reduction process lasted until the end of November 2001. Several times between mid-2000 and late 2001, the Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market in an attempt to prevent a decline in the exchange rate. In particular, there was an intervention when it appeared that a decline spiral was on the rise or when the Bank assessed that its intervention may have an impact in order to change market expectations. This was based, among other things, on the Bank's position that the exchange rate had already fallen more than was compatible with the long-term balance in the economy. The Central Bank spent large sums of money on interventions in the foreign exchange market, totalling over ISK 40 billion. This, however, could not prevent the exchange rate cut in the krona. At best, this delayed the decline until the economy had slowed somewhat, but it also caused the inflation effect of the rate cut to be lower than it would otherwise be. Observations that have now been made and published in the Monetary Bulletin of the Central Bank show that the interventions have at best had a very short-lived impact at any given time and the market has traditionally sought its previous outlook again. In other words, the assumption is that intervening in the foreign exchange market has had very little effect against a heavy underflow. It comes home to the experiences of other countries. The Central Bank has limited influence on the real exchange rate in the long run. In the intense discussions about the exchange rate of the Icelandic of the krona, voices have often been heard that its exchange rate is less stable than the exchange rate of other currencies and that the krona behaves in some way differently than other currencies. There is little evidence, however, that it is. If you compare the development of the exchange rate with the development of other currencies, large and small, it can be seen that in principle it behaves the same way. Indeed, the development of the krona in the long run takes the most account of domestic economic development, and often economic development in Iceland is not in line with economic development in other countries, but it is precisely one of the main advantages of having its own currency. The exchange rate can take the pressure off other economic tools, including interest rates and measures in the state budget. I'm going to give you a picture showing the exchange rate of several currencies against the U.S. dollar. The currencies are Icelandic the krona, the British pound, the Norwegian krona, the Swedish the krona and the euro. Exchange rates of several currencies against the US dollar (Figure in pdf file) As shown in the figure spanning more than five years, the krona has essentially behaved in the same way as other major currencies. The weakening of the krona against the US dollar from the beginning of 2000 to the end of 2001 is very similar to the weakening of the euro against the US dollar in mid-2000 to the end of 2001. The main difference is that the weakening of the krona lasted longer. It started to weaken earlier than the euro, but both of these currencies began to strengthen around the same time. After the turnaround at the end of 2001, the rise in the Icelandic the krona became much faster and greater than the euro,as the economic situation in Iceland has been much more robust than the eurozone's economic situation, for example. The figure does not show that the main movements of the krona (i.e. its trends) are in good harmony with the trends of other currencies. Another point that has often been criticized is that the short-term volatility of the krona, or its volatility, is far greater than that of other currencies. This criticism also does not add up to closer scrutiny. In this picture you can see the day-to-day changes in foreign exchange rates against the US dollar. It can be seen that the volatility of currencies is normally 1%, but from time to time there will be larger fluctuations. The picture has been marked on which currencies have the main spikes on individual days. It is far from clear that the Icelandic krona will stand out in the picture if it is left with a short period from March to June of 2001, immediately after the new exchange rate arrangements were adopted and the krona left floating. During this time, the effects of a prolonged seamen's strike were observed. Date changes in exchange rates against the US dollar (Picture in pdf file) Changing rates call for a change in working practices. Because it has been relatively short since fluctuations in the exchange rate of the Icelandic the krona began to emerge in the current way, many smaller companies have not yet learned to respond to this trend. I suspect that many travel companies are in that group. In most countries, import and export companies have used certain methods, called exchange rate hedging, to reduce exchange rate risk. The exchange rate hedging includes the use of futures currency contracts, swaps and option agreements to lock in changes to exchange rate. It seems that if conversations with parties in the banking system are to be believed, that iceland exporters take advantage of exchange rate hedging to a much greater extent than immigrants, as exporters rarely have the opportunity to transfer the cost of unfavourable exchange rate developments to the price level in the same way as immigrants. For smaller companies, futures contracts for the purchase or sale of foreign currencies are a relatively simple option and it can be assumed that local banks are prepared to provide these services. An example of such a deal could be a company that has to pay a certain amount in U.S. dollars after six months. The company enters into a futures contract with a bank which ensures that it receives the agreed amount in foreign currency on a given day after six months at a certain exchange rate. For this, the company pays far more domestic and foreign interest rates as well as a surcharge related to the size and position of the company towards the relevant bank. In addition, the company must provide 8 - 10% of the total amount as collateral initially. With futures contracts, the company can fix exchange rates for a certain period of time and erase exchange rate uncertainty. It doesn't matter how much money the banks are willing to negotiate. Some go down below 1,000. It doesn't matter who the individual banks are. It depends on whether the company is trading with the relevant banking institution, how big it is and how big its foreign exchange transactions are. Swap agreements are also useful for companies that, for example, own foreign exchange but do not need to take advantage of it immediately. Thus, the company can borrow kronur against a kind of mortgage in the currency without waiving it with the associated exchange rate risk. Option agreements are yet another type of exchange rate hedging. The main difference between futures contracts and option contracts is that a party that owns an option is not obliged to exercise it. It can be more advantageous for him to let the contract expire without its fullness. Option agreements are only available for higher amounts and the cost of them exceeds the extent that favorable exchange rate movements can often be benefited from favorable exchange rate movements. It is probable that the use of exchange rate hedges will continue to grow substantially in Iceland, as the development of foreign exchange transactions is relatively short-lived so far. A lot of companies in the travel industry trade in foreign currency. I wanted to draw particular attention to this here because information obtained from the banking system suggests that these companies have only to a small extent taken advantage of exchange rate hedging, but exchange rate risk must be very high in the operations of travel companies. Good attendees. I mentioned earlier that the Central Bank publishes a quarterly report on the state and outlook for the economy and the inflation forecast for two years. The last time the Bank issued such a forecast was in early February. Since that forecast was published, there have been a number of important changes, which include the decision to accelerate various public projects and begin the expansion of Noroural's smelter in Grundartangi. In addition, there will be more weight in the construction of the Karahnjukar power plant this year than previously anticipated. These three, together with the reduction in the Central Bank's policy rate in February, lead to higher demand in 2003 and 2004 than expected in the macroeconomic forecast, and this will unchanged increase economic growth. State and local governments have decided to accelerate construction totals of approximately ISK 10 billion, with an estimated fall of approximately ISK 51/2 billion in 2003 and about ISK 41/2 billion in 2004. The council will be expanding noroural's smelter in two phases. Production capacity per year will be increased by 90 thousand tonnes in 2005 and by an additional 60 thousand tonnes in 2008 and 2009. In connection with this expansion, work will be carried out for energy generation at Norolingaoldu, Nesjavellir and Reykjanes. Total construction is due to noroural's expansion of ISK 21/2 billion in 2003 and isk 14 billion in 2004. Landsvirkjun's new plans for construction of the Karahnjukar power plant envisage an increase of ISK 5 billion in 2003 and just over ISK 1/2 billion in 2004. The combined total is therefore a direct increase in investment of ISK 13 billion in the current year and approximately ISK 19 billion next in excess of what was expected when the Central Bank's macroeconomic forecast and inflation forecast were issued in February. Due to changing assumptions, observations suggest that economic growth this year could easily be between 2 - 21/2% and well above 3% next year. This is up to 1% higher in gdp each year than previously expected. Employment prospects also improve considerably. Given that production slack was never high and the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in February was 3.2% and had not changed much since September, it is clear that it is much shorter now than previously thought that tensions may start to recede. Inflation this year is likely to be close to the Bank's 21/2% inflation target, but may unchangeably rise next year. It is predictable that these major projects will collapse to some extent in 2004 and 2005, with the greatest weight coming in 2005 and 2006. The economic crisis will therefore be greater than thought when the smelter in Reyoarfjorour and related power plants were calculated only. This outlook calls for a response in favour of both monetary and fiscal policy management. The scale of the reaction will depend on exchange rate developments, but it is clear that preventing overheating and inflation will be a very important task in the near term. Realistic fiscal measures are necessary so that the pressures are not primarily on monetary policy, thereby increasingly affecting export and competitive sectors. The more robust fiscal restraint measures will be at the top of the construction, the smaller the increase in real exchange rates they will inevitably follow, and the better the current export and competitive sectors will fare. Good attendees. Comparing economic developments in Iceland and the eurozone, that comparison is well represented in the Iceland. In the eurozone, people should struggle with economic stagnation and unemployment. It is therefore very natural that there is a difference between interest rates in Iceland and the eurozone, as the challenges are completely different in the economy. The European Central Bank, for example, has recently revised its growth forecast for the eurozone as a whole and forecasts growth of 1% this year. This means that in key countries such as Germany, there will be no economic growth during the year because it is higher in various marginal regions of Europe. In Iceland, economic growth is forecast to be between 2 and 21/2% as I mentioned earlier. Unemployment in the eurozone is projected this year at 8.5%. In this country, unemployment is forecast to be 3% and that it will decrease next year. Compared to the eurozone, we Icelanders can therefore hold our heads high. In the past, there has been considerable debate about whether Iceland should apply for membership of the European Union and subsequently become a member of the European Economic and Monetary Union and adopt the euro as its currency. In fact, there has sometimes been a debate that Icelanders should adopt the euro as a currency, either unilaterally or through some kind of agreement or secondary membership of the Monetary Union. Those advantages are undoubtedly unrealistic and there is no chance that neither the European Central Bank nor the rest of the European Union leadership are prepared to agree to such an arrangement that could set an example for nations to cut their way into the Monetary Union. Although we stand outside the Monetary Union, we in our economic and monetary policy have dedicated ourselves to much of what European Union nations have adopted with them. Iceland has adapted its legislation on financial markets to EU legislation, and the Central Bank of Iceland has greatly adapted monetary policy to the methods used by the European Central Bank. The Central Bank of Iceland has not taken any position on whether it is appropriate to join the European Union and the Economic and Monetary Union, as it is not in its job. However, the Central Bank has been closely monitoring the developments of these issues, has a good relationship with the European Central Bank and made a detailed assessment of the advantages and disadvantages of becoming a member of the Monetary Union. I think it is clear that if the minds of the people were headed to adopt the euro as a currency, it would be most immediate to join the European Union with all the obligations and advantages that come with it, including membership of the Monetary Union. However, the decision to do so depends on more factors than merely concerning the nation's currency, and the process would take several years. It's first and foremost a big political question that I won't be discussing in detail here. We therefore need to continue to peddle the international community as a nation with its own currency, but under the conditions of free movement of capital it requires very disciplined economic management.

Hagstjrnarvandinn verur v meiri en tali var egar eingngu var reikna me lverinu  Reyarfiri og tengdum raforkuverum. essar horfur kalla  vibrg  hagstjrn bi vi stjrn peningamla og rkisfjrmla. Umfang vibraganna mun rast af gengisrun en ljst er a a verur mjg mikilvgt verkefni nstu misserin a koma  veg fyrir ofenslu og verblgu. Raunhfar agerir  rkisfjrmlum eru nausynlegar til a lagi veri ekki fyrst og fremst  peningastefnuna og bitni annig  of miklum mli  tflutnings- og samkeppnisgreinum. v flugri sem ahaldsagerir  rkisfjrmlum vera  htoppi framkvmdanna, v minni verur s hkkun raungengis sem eim mun hjkvmilega fylgja og v betur mun nverandi tflutnings- og samkeppnisgreinum farnast. Gir fundarmenn. Ef borin er saman run efnahagsmla  slandi og evrusvinu kemur s samanburur vel t fyrir sland.  evrusvinu eiga menn a glma vi efnahagslega stnun og atvinnuleysi. a er v mjg elilegt a munur s  vxtum  slandi og  evrusvinu, enda vifangsefnin allt nnur  efnahagslfinu. Selabanki Evrpu hefur t.d. nlega endurskoa hagvaxtarsp sna fyrir evrusvi  heild og spir um 1% hagvexti  essu ri. a ir a  lykillndum eins og skalandi verur enginn hagvxtur  rinu v hann er meiri  msum jaarsvum  Evrpu. Hr  slandi er sp hagvexti  bilinu 2 - 2% eins og g gat um an. Atvinnuleysi  evrusvinu er tla  essu ri 8,5%. Hr  landi er sp 3% atvinnuleysi og a a fari minnkandi  nsta ri.  samanburi vi evrusvi getum vi slendingar v bori hfui htt. A undanfrnu hefur allmikil umra ori um a hvort sland eigi a skja um aild a Evrpusambandinu og  framhaldi af v a gerast aili a Efnahags- og myntbandlagi Evrpu og taka upp evru sem gjaldmiil. Reyndar hefur s umra stundum komi upp a slendingar ttu a taka evru upp sem gjaldmiil, anna hvort einhlia ea me einhvers konar samningum ea aukaaild a Myntbandlaginu. eir kostir eru vafalaust raunsir og engar lkur  a hvorki Evrpski selabankinn n arir  forustu Evrpusambandsins su reiubnir til a fallast  slkt fyrirkomulag sem gti gefi fordmi fyrir v a jir styttu sr lei inn  Myntbandalagi. tt vi stndum utan vi Myntbandalagi hfum vi  efnahagsmlum okkar og peningastjrn tileinka okkur margt af v sem Evrpusambandsjir hafa teki upp hj sr. slendingar hafa laga lggjf sna um fjrmlamarkai a lggjf Evrpusambandinu og Selabanki slands hefur laga stjrn peningamla mjg a eim aferum sem Evrpski selabankinn beitir. Selabanki slands hefur ekki teki neina afstu til ess hvort rtt s a ganga  Evrpusambandi og Efnahags- og myntbandlagi, enda er a ekki  hans verkahring. Selabankinn hefur hins vegar fylgst mjg vel me run essara mla,  gott samband vi Evrpska selabankann og geri fyrir nokkrum rum tarlega ttekt  kostum ess og gllum a gerast aili a Myntbandalaginu. g held a s ljst a ef hugur jarinnar stefndi til ess a taka evru upp sem gjaldmiil vri nrtkast a ganga  Evrpusambandi me llum skyldum og kostum sem v fylgja, ar me tali aild a Myntbandalaginu. kvrun um slkt rst  af fleiri ttum en eingngu vara gjaldmiil jarinnar og ferli myndi taka allmrg r. a er auvita fyrst og fremst str plitsk spurning sem g mun ekki fjalla nnar um hr. Title: Governor's introductory remarks at a meeting of the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi 27 March 2019
text: 02.04.2019 Governor's introductory remarks at a meeting of the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi 27 March 2019 Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, met with the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi on Wednesday 27 March 2019 to discuss the administration of the Central Bank of Iceland in the implementation of foreign exchange controls. Attached are the governor's introductory remarks at the meeting. The Governor's introductory remarks at a meeting of the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi on Wednesday 27 March 2019. I would like to start by thanking us for this opportunity to comment on this forum on the topics you have had under consideration. In preparing and deciding who should attend the meeting, we assumed that the topic was the Foreign Exchange Act and the Central Bank's administration in the investigation of foreign exchange violations, and in particular the recent opinion of the Ombudsman of the Althingi and what was stated at your meeting with him on 6 March. That doesn't preclude us from answering questions on other issues, but as you're aware, there's a limit to how much we can comment on individual cases at an open meeting. It seems to me that we are facing two important questions after the committee's meeting on March 6th, first, whether the Central Bank may have been clear after it received the attorney general's position since May 2014 that there were no valid sanctions in rules issued on the basis of the Foreign Exchange Act before the time that the rules were incorporated into the law in 2011? Second, whether the Bank has, even deliberately, concealed this knowledge from the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, the Institute of Law at the University of Iceland and the Ombudsman? We will now answer these questions but will also, if given time, enter more details in this introduction that have been under consideration. Otherwise, we can answer questions. The implementation of capital controls was formulated in legislation passed by the Althingi in such a way that the legislature delimited the main points which the Central Bank was entrusted with the authority to provide for in the rules on foreign exchange. That's the kind of material that the Central Bank was required to work with under the law. Investigative powers were first held by the Financial Supervisory Authority but were transferred to the Central Bank by amending the Law in the summer of 2010, among other things, to increase the effectiveness of the sector as set out in a report by that bill. It is not an uncommon phrase for expert authorities to be entrusted with the authority of the law for regulation, and the courts have considered that this does not conflict with the Constitution or the European Convention on Human Rights as long as the main subject of the authority is provided for in law. Considerations on the validity of sanctions in such cases have often been brought to court, and most recently in the recent district court ruling in the case of Arctica Finance ehf. against the Financial Supervisory Authority. Considerations on the validity of foreign exchange rules in particular as sanctions have been debated since the introduction of restrictions, i.e. whether there were adequate authorisations to impose administrative penalties or otherwise punish for violations of capital controls until the Foreign Exchange Act was amended in late 2011. The Central Bank has, among other things, since 2010 requested external legal opinions that have been harmonious that guilty decisions can be based on the penalties of the Rules on Foreign Exchange and thus the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Act, at least until the courts have not provided otherwise. At the same time, the position of the Ministry of Foreign Exchange in 2011, which was re-established in 2015, on the validity of the rules, is also available. It clearly states that the rules are valid as a criminal offence and that the main points of the rules have been delimited in the act and therefore the delegation of the legislature was not too accommodating. In addition, 2 meetings were held in 2011 on investigations and complaints for alleged violations of the rules on foreign exchange in housing the Ministry of the Interior, as stated in a letter written by the Central Bank to the Director of Public Prosecutions in 2012 and delivered to the Committee. The first meeting was attended by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, representatives of the Central Bank's foreign exchange controls, the National Commissioner of Police, the Prosecutor of Economic Crimes and the Director of Public Prosecutions. At that meeting, according to the letter, the state prosecutor's position was that it was the courts to decide, on the basis of each case as it were, whether criminal sanctions were clear enough to punish men for violations of the rules. The second meeting was attended by the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Economic Affairs and Trade with his assistants, the Governor and the Deputy Governor, along with representatives of the Central Bank's Foreign Exchange Supervisory Authority, the National Commissioner of Police and the Prosecutor of Economic Crimes. At that meeting, the prosecutor specifically mentioned economic crimes that the notion of inadequate sanctions for alleged violations of foreign exchange rules did not delay the progress of those cases. The positions of the Director of Public Prosecutions of 20 May 2014, addressed by the Ombudsman, concern the confirmation by the Director of Public Prosecutions of the repeal of cases dropped by the Special Prosecutor's Office due to rules that had not received the formal approval of the Minister. The Central Bank's first response to the Prosecutor's handling of 20 May 2014 was that the position would give rise to whether all cases against foreign exchange rules should be dropped, and such matters were put on hold immediately. A legal opinion was obtained, concluding that there was sufficient authority to impose fines for violations of foreign exchange rules. But it was primarily communications with the special prosecutor's office in the summer of 2014 and the prosecution's implementation of the handling of cases related to foreign exchange rules that took place after the state attorney general's handling of May 20, 2014, that ultimately led to the failure of the investigation of these cases. These communications with the special prosecutor's office indicated undoubtedly on the part of the Central Bank that the office's understanding was that the Director of Public Prosecutions had dealt only with the general validity of all rules on foreign exchange as a possible subject and not as the final outcome of the case, as the governor's conclusion concerned not all the rules on foreign exchange, but only those that lacked the formal approval of the Minister. Confirmed the subsequent implementation of the special prosecutor's office for the foregoing understanding of the Central Bank. Specifically, the handling was in such a way that violations of the rules that lacked consent were dismissed, but the alleged violation of other rules was returned to the Central Bank for treatment and decision. There was no mention that other foreign exchange rules could not be considered a valid sanction. If it had been the attorney general's explicit position that no rules on foreign exchange were valid as a criminal offence, then the special prosecutor's office should have dropped the cases, or, as the case may be, cease their investigation, but not returned them to the SI for treatment, provided there would be no basis for an ongoing investigation. Despite this practice by a special prosecutor, the Central Bank sought ways to get a definitive out of this issue cut by the Attorney General. The Central Bank therefore appealed a similar return of a case from a special prosecutor, which also concerned other rules on foreign exchange than those that lacked the formal approval of the minister. With the Director of Public Prosecutions' position of 31 August 2014, the Director of Public Prosecutions confirmed the implementation of a special prosecutor and specifically instructed the Central Bank that the Bank could appeal violations of other rules, which had received formal approval from the Minister, to the special prosecutor for re-processing. In the Central Bank's view, this position of the Director of Public Prosecutions was confirmation that its previous handling of 20 May 2014 only applies to rules that lacked formal approval, as it was difficult to see what the purpose would be by instructing that the Central Bank may sue for conduct if the rules were not a valid sanction. The Central Bank felt that it was capable of nothing more than following the prosecution's actions and guidance. Subsequently, the Central Bank dropped all cases relating to alleged violations of the rules that lacked formal approval in accordance with the conclusion of the special prosecutor's office, which the Attorney General confirmed on May 20, 2014. In view of the opinion of the Ombudsman of the Althingi of 22 January 2019 and as part of the Central Bank's decision on its own initiative to take a substantive position on the arguments made in its submission to the Central Bank, the Bank requested by letter on 15 February 2014, the Director of Public Prosecutions regarding its consideration of the general validity of the rules on foreign exchange in its handling of 20 May 2014. The Central Bank received a response on 19 February stating that the Office's conclusion is that the rules on foreign exchange did not have sufficiently clear legal support to build on that penalty, until the rules were legislated in the autumn of 2011. The position is clear and the Central Bank has begun reviewing all fines due to foreign exchange rules and it is hoped that this review will be completed as soon as possible and that the parties concerned will be refunded imposed fines. Admittedly, the Bank would have preferred that such an outcome had been reached much earlier, or as early as 2012, when the Central Bank first sought it for a discussion that had taken place in the media about the validity of foreign exchange rules, citing the governor's comments in that context. The Central Bank requested a letter for information on whether the Attorney General actually considered that legal authority was insufficient to indict men for alleged violations of the Foreign Exchange Act and whether it had confirmed that position with reporters. The Attorney General's office did not respond to the letter at the time, but the attorney general's recent explanation said it was that it could have caused the Attorney General to become incompetent in other cases that were being handled by the prosecution at the time. I think this review shows that the Fed had a variety of interactions with other governments and prosecutions on the question of whether rules were a valid sanction and that it did not ignore other people's suggestions. On the contrary, the Bank believed that it needed to take into account the legal interpretations of the prosecution as it could not get far with a case otherwise. The problem was that the message in the summer of 2014 was not clear and stemmed to some extent. The Bank is compiling evidence of its contacts with the prosecution in the summer of 2014 in response to the Prime Minister's letter. The bank is ready to share that data with the committee when it is ready which should be early next week. So I turn to the second question, namely whether the Fed has concealed the governor's position and even deliberately. At least it is clear that the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland was informed of the matter at a meeting of the Council on 19 June 2014. As far as the Legal Authority is concerned, it should be reiterated that the directors had no involvement in that audit and did not know what data the Law Institute received. The Chairman of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor were in charge and also towards the Foreign Exchange Supervisory Authority. I have been informed now afterwards that the Icelandic Legislative Authority has been informed of these dispensaries and was handed a legal opinion written on the occasion of the result and discussed in a memorandum to the Law Institute. So the law enforcement agency knew about their existence and would have received them if they had been sought. As far as an agent is concerned, perhaps the issue is something more complicated. As I have said before, it was the Central Bank's view that the handling in question did not deter the final conclusion so that all foreign exchange rules could not be considered valid sanctions. Communications with the ombudsman on the eve of his letter of 2 October 2015 did not give the Central Bank any reason to conclude that the ombudsman was examining whether the transfer of legislative powers was unlawful or whether the criminal provisions of the Act were satisfactory. Nevertheless, the Bank may have handed over these positions to the Ombudsman on its own initiative, but would not wish to assert too much without further scrutiny. I think the issue is partly that after the conclusion in the autumn of 2014, the matter will plainly go back to being dealt with. The person sitting here, at least, wasn't mindful of these positions when it was a long time coming in 2014. I know I'm probably starting to sin uptime, but at the end I'd like to say a few words about the questions that come in the Parliamentary Ombudsman's letter to the Prime Minister of 4 March and appeared at a meeting of the Committee on 6 March regarding what was the role of employees of the Central Bank's foreign exchange controls in informing the employees of the Icelandic National Broadcasting Service about the proposed search and whether the Bank's supervisory board authorized it. It is understood that data was handed over from a news outlet to the Central Bank, which was used in the investigation. I was not present at that data delivery and therefore cannot comment on what was going on there. Whether and what communications took place after it is now under review within the Bank in relation to a response to the Prime Minister. I do not recognise that the Bank's supervisory board has authorized the delivery of confidential documents to the media and there is currently no evidence that this has happened. I have asked internal auditors to check my emails in the lead-up to the search and see if there is anything to be found that sheds light on this issue and also examine what is contained in the foreign exchange control documents. However, when examining the media in connection with the case, it was recalled that a special prosecutor conducted a search of the Central Bank some months before the search and the media was outside. Bloomberg published a story about the case, which was then picked up in various foreign media outlets. It also seems from the media from those years that it was relatively common for the media to quickly be on the brink of searches.

Inngangsor selabankastjra  fundi stjrnskipunar- og eftirlitsnefndar Alingis mivikudaginn 27. mars 2019. g vil byrja  v a akka fyrir a vi hfum fengi etta tkifri a tj okkur  essum vettvangi um a efni sem i hafi haft til umfjllunar. Vi munum n svara essum spurningum en koma einnig, ef tmi gefst til, inn  fleiri atrii  essum inngangi sem hafa veri til umfjllunar. Annars getum vi svara spurningum ar a ltandi. Framkvmd fjrmagnshafta var mtu  lggjf sem samykkt var af Alingi me eim htti a lggjafinn afmarkai au meginatrii sem Selabankanum var falin heimild til a kvea  um  reglum um gjaldeyrisml. a er s efniviur sem Selabankanum var gert a vinna me samkvmt lgum. Rannsknarheimildir voru fyrst um sinn  hndum Fjrmlaeftirlitsins en voru fluttar til Selabankans me breytingu  lgum sumari 2010, m.a. til a auka skilvirkni mlaflokksins eins og fram kom  greinarger me v frumvarpi. a er ekki algengur setningarmti a srfristjrnvldum s falin heimild  lgum til reglusetningar og dmstlar hafa tali a slkt stangist ekki  vi stjrnarskr ea mannrttindasttmla Evrpu svo lengi sem kvei er  um meginefni heimildarinnar  lgum. litaefni um gildi refsiheimilda  slkum tilvikum hafa oft komi til kasta dmstla og nna sast  nlegum dmi Hrasdms  mli Arctica Finance ehf. gegn Fjrmlaeftirlitinu. litaefni um gildi reglna um gjaldeyrisml srstaklega sem refsiheimilda hefur veri til umru fr v a hftum var komi , .e. hvort til staar hafi veri fullngjandi heimildir til ess a leggja  stjrnvaldssektir ea refsa me rum htti fyrir brot gegn fjrmagnshftum ar til lgum um gjaldeyrisml var breytt sla rs 2011. Jafnframt liggur fyrir afstaa ess runeytis sem fer me gjaldeyrisml fr 2011, sem aftur var stafest  rinu 2015, um gildi reglnanna. Kemur ar skrt fram a reglurnar su gildar sem refsiheimild og a meginefni reglnanna hafi veri afmarka  lgunum og v hafi framsal lggjafans ekki veri of rmt. Auk ess voru 2 fundir haldnir ri 2011 um rannsknir og krur vegna meintra brota  reglum um gjaldeyrisml  hsakynnum innanrkisruneytisins, eins og fram kemur  brfi sem Selabankinn ritai rkissaksknara ri 2012 og afhent var nefndinni. Fyrri fundinn stu, auk runeytisstjra, fulltrar gjaldeyriseftirlits Selabankans, rkislgreglustjri, saksknari efnahagsbrota og rkissaksknari.  eim fundi kom samkvmt brfinu fram s afdrttarlausa afstaa rkissaksknara a a vri dmstla a skera r um,  grundvelli hvers mls fyrir sig eins og a lgi fyrir, hvort refsiheimildir vru ngilega skrar til a unnt vri a gera mnnum refsingu fyrir brot gegn reglunum. Seinni fundinn stu innanrkisrherra og efnahags-og viskiptarherra samt astoarmnnum snum, selabankastjri og astoarselabankastjri samt fulltrum gjaldeyriseftirlits Selabankans, rkislgreglustjri og saksknari efnahagsbrota.  eim fundi nefndi saksknari efnahagsbrota srstaklega a hugmyndir um fullngjandi refsiheimildir vegna meintra brota gegn reglum um gjaldeyrisml tefu ekki framgang eirra mla. Afstur rkissaksknara fr 20. ma 2014, sem umbosmaur fjallar um, vara stafestingu rkissaksknara  niurfellingu mla sem embtti srstaks saksknara felldi niur vegna reglna sem ekki hfu hloti formlegt samykki rherra. Fyrstu vibrg Selabankans vegna afgreislu rkissaksknara fr 20. ma 2014 voru au a afstaan gfi tilefni til ess athuga hvort fella tti niur ll ml gegn reglum um gjaldeyrisml og voru slk ml sett  bi egar  sta. Afla var lgfrilits og var a niurstaa ess a fullngjandi heimild vri til staar til a leggja  sektir fyrir brot gegn reglum um gjaldeyrisml. En a voru fyrst og fremst samskipti vi embtti srstaks saksknara sumari 2014 og framkvmd kruvaldsins  mefer mla tengdum reglum um gjaldeyrisml sem ttu sr sta eftir afgreislur rkissaksknara fr 20. ma 2014 sem leiddu a lokum til ess a rannskn essara mla var ekki htt. essi samskipti vi embtti srstaks saksknara gfu til kynna n nokkurs vafa af hlfu Selabankans a skilningur embttisins vri s a rkissaksknari hefi einungis fjalla um almennt gildi allra reglna um gjaldeyrisml sem hugsanleg litaefni en ekki sem endanlega niurstu mlsins, enda varai niurstaa rkissaksknara ekki allar reglur um gjaldeyrisml, heldur einungis r sem skorti formlegt samykki rherra. Stafesti sari framkvmd embttis srstaks saksknara framangreindan skilning Selabankans. Nnar tilteki var afgreislan me eim htti a brotum gegn reglunum sem skorti samykki var vsa fr en meint brot  rum reglum voru endursend Selabankanum til meferar og kvrunar. Hvergi var minnst  a arar reglur um gjaldeyrisml gtu ekki talist gild refsiheimild. Ef a hefi veri afdrttarlaus afstaa rkissaksknara a engar reglur um gjaldeyrisml vru gildar sem refsiheimild  hefi embtti srstaks saksknara tt a fella niur mlin, ea eftir atvikum htta rannskn eirra, en ekki endursenda au til S til meferar, enda vri  enginn grundvllur fyrir framhaldandi rannskn. rtt fyrir essa framkvmd srstaks saksknara leitai Selabankinn leia til a f endanlega r essu litaefni skori hj rkissaksknara. Selabankinn kri v sambrilega endursendingu mls fr srstkum saksknara, sem varai einnig arar reglur um gjaldeyrisml en r sem skorti formlegt samykki rherra. Me afstu rkissaksknara fr 31. gst 2014 stafesti rkissaksknari framkvmd srstaks saksknara og leibeindi Selabankanum srstaklega um a bankinn gti krt brot gegn rum reglum, sem hloti hfu formlegt samykki rherra, til srstaks saksknara til afgreislu  n. A mati Selabankans var essi afstaa rkissaksknara stafesting  v a fyrri afgreisla hans fr 20. ma 2014 tti einungis vi um r reglur sem skorti formlegt samykki, enda vands hver tilgangurinn vri me v a leibeina um a Selabankanum s heimilt a kra httsemi ef a fyrir lgi a reglurnar vru ekki gild refsiheimild. Taldi Selabankinn sr ekki frt um anna en a fylgja eirri framkvmd og leibeiningu kruvaldsins.  framhaldinu felldi Selabankinn niur ll ml sem vruu meint brot gegn eim reglum sem skorti formlegt samykki  samrmi vi niurstu embttis srstaks saksknara sem rkissaksknari stafesti 20. ma 2014.  ljsi lits umbosmanns Alingis fr 22. janar 2019 og sem li  v a Selabankinn tki a eigin frumkvi efnislega afstu til eirra rksemda aila sem gerar voru  erindi hans til Selabankans skai bankinn eftir me brfi hinn 15. febrar sl. skringum rkissaksknara vegna umfjllunar hans um almennt gildi reglna um gjaldeyrisml  afgreislum hans fr 20. ma 2014. Svar barst Selabankanum hinn 19. febrar sl. ar sem fram kemur a niurstaa embttisins s s a reglur um gjaldeyrisml hafi ekki haft ngjanlega skra lagasto svo byggja mtti  eim refsingu, ar til reglurnar voru lgfestar um hausti 2011. Afstaan er skr og hefur Selabankinn hafi yfirfer allra sektarmla vegna reglna um gjaldeyrisml og vonir standa til a eirri yfirfer ljki sem allra fyrst og a hlutaeigandi ailum veri endurgreiddar lagar sektir. neitanlega hefi bankinn kosi a slk niurstaa hefi legi fyrir miklu fyrr, ea strax ri 2012 egar Selabankinn leitai eftir henni fyrst vegna umru sem hafi tt sr sta  fjlmilum um gildi reglna um gjaldeyrisml og vitna var til ummla rkissaksknara  v samhengi. skai Selabankinn me brfi eftir upplsingum um hvort rkissaksknari liti  raun svo  a lagaheimild vri ekki ngileg til a unnt vri a kra menn fyrir meint brot  lgum um gjaldeyrisml og hvort hann hefi stafest  afstu vi frttamenn. Rkissaksknari svarai ekki brfinu  eim tma, en  nlegum skringum rkissaksknara var sta ess sg hafa veri s a a hefi geta valdi v a rkissaksknari yri vanhfur  rum mlum sem voru til meferar hj kruvaldinu  eim tma. g held a essi yfirfer sni a Selabankinn tti  margvslegum samskiptum vi nnur stjrnvld og kruvald um  spurningu hvort reglur vru gild refsiheimild og a hann hafi ekki hundsa bendingar annarra. vert  mti taldi bankinn a hann yrfti a taka mi a lagatlkunum kruvalds enda kmist hann ekki langt me ml ella. Vandinn var s a skilaboin sumari 2014 voru ekki skr og stnguust  einhverjum mli . Bankinn er a taka saman ggn um samskipti sn vi kruvaldi sumari 2014  tengslum vi svar vi brfi forstisrherra. Bankinn er tilbinn a deila eim ggnum me nefndinni egar au eru tilbin sem tti a vera snemma  nstu viku. Sn g mr  a seinni spurningunni, .e. hvort Selabankinn hafi leynt afstu rkissaksknara og a jafnvel vsvitandi. a liggur alla vega fyrir a bankari Selabanka slands var greint fr mlinu  fundi rsins 19. jn 2014. Hvaa Lagastofnun varar  er rtt a treka a bankastjrar hfu enga akomu a eirri ttekt og vissu ekki hvaa ggn Lagastofnun fkk. Bankarsformaur og innri endurskoandi voru  forsvari og einnig gagnvart gjaldeyriseftirlitinu. Mr hefur veri tj n eftir  a Lagastofnun hafi veri upplst um essar afgreislur og var afhent lgfrilit sem rita var  tilefni af niurstunni og um r fjalla  minnisblai til Lagastofnunar. Lagastofnun vissi v af tilvist eirra og hefi fengi r ef eftir hefi veri leita. Hva umbosmann varar er mli kannski eitthva flknara. Eins og g hef ur sagt, var a mat Selabankans a umrddar afgreislur flu ekki  sr endanlega niurstu til ess a allar reglur um gjaldeyrisml gtu ekki talist gildar refsiheimildir. Samskipti vi umbosmann  adraganda brfs hans fr 2. oktber 2015 gfu Selabankanum ekki tilefni til ess a lykta a umbosmaur vri a kanna hvort a me eim hafi framsal lagasetningarvalds veri lgmtt ea hvort refsikvi laganna vru fullngjandi. Eigi a sur kann a vera a bankinn hefi tt a afhenda umbosmanni essar afstur a eigin frumkvi en vil  ekki fullyra of miki n frekari athugunar. g held a mli s a hluta til a a eftir a niurstaa liggur fyrir hausti 2014 fer mli hreinlega aftur fyrir sem afgreitt. S sem hr situr var alla vega ekki me hugann vi essar afstur egar langt var lii  ri 2014. g veit a g er lklega farinn a syndga upp  tmann en g vil  lokin segja nokkur or um r spurningar sem koma  brfi umbosmanns Alingis til forstisrherra fr 4. mars sl. og komu fram  fundi nefndarinnar hinn 6. mars sl. varandi a hver hafi veri hlutur starfsmanna gjaldeyriseftirlits Selabankans  a upplsa starfsmenn Rkistvarpsins um hina fyrirhuguu hsleit og hvort yfirstjrn bankans hafi heimila a. Ljst er a ggn voru afhent fr frttamili til Selabankans, sem notu voru vi rannskn mlsins. g var ekki vistaddur  gagnaafhendingu og get ar af leiandi ekki tj mig um hva ar fr fram. Hvort og  hvaa samskipti ttu sr sta eftir hana er n  skoun innan bankans  tengslum vi svar til forstisrherra. g kannast ekki vi a yfirstjrn bankans hafi heimila afhendingu trnaargagna til fjlmiilsins og ekkert liggur n fyrir um a slkt hafi gerst. g hef bei innri endurskoenda a skoa tlvupst minn  adraganda hsleitarinnar og kanna hvort ar s eitthva a finna sem varpar ljsi  etta ml og kanna jafnframt hva s a finna  ggnum gjaldeyriseftirlitsins. Vi skoun  fjlmilum  tengslum vi mli rifjaist hins vegar upp a srstakur saksknari geri hsleit  Selabankanum einhverjum mnuum fyrir hsleitina og fjlmilar voru fyrir utan. Bloomberg birti frtt um mli sem var san tekin upp  msum erlendum fjlmilum.  virist einnig af fjlmilum fr essum rum a a hafi veri tiltlulega algengt a fjlmilar voru komnir fljtt  spori vi hsleitir.

Title: Introduction to Chairman of the Board of Directors, at a meeting with the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi 27 March 2019
text: 02.04.2019 Introduction to Gylfi Magnusson, Chairman of the Board of Directors, at a meeting with the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi 27 March 2019 Gylfi Magnusson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, attended a meeting of the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi on 27 March 2019 where the Central Bank of Iceland discussed the administration of the Central Bank of Iceland in the implementation of foreign exchange controls. Gylfi's introductory remarks at the beginning of the meeting are included here. Introductory remarks of Gylfi Magnusson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at a meeting with the Constitutional and Supervisory Committee of the Althingi on 27 March 2019 on foreign exchange controls of the Central Bank of Iceland. I would like to thank you for this opportunity to follow up on the work of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland for its reporting on the so-called Samherji affairs and other work by the Central Bank in enforcing the restrictions known as either capital controls or capital controls. The latter name is probably more accurate, but the first is tamara to me. It is clear that the Central Bank was by no means prepared to enforce capital controls when they were imposed almost without warning in the autumn of 2008. The work had to be done by the Bank based on an unbearable regulatory framework that had not been tested in practice or by the legal system. In that respect, the Central Bank was in a much worse position than other national regulators, which can normally base their work on a number of precedents, both in Iceland and abroad, especially in Europe, and laws, regulations, methods and norms that have passed repeated court tests. There was no such thing as 2008. There appear to have been no usable sanctions for violations of the caps for almost three years or from their inception until Act No. 127/2011 came into force in September 2011. The flaws in the sanctions were not initially blighted by the hammering, of which it is not disputed, although it is disputed to some extent about the causes and seriousness of them and explanations and when central bank executives might have been aware of them. The legal arguments for this are long and complex, and probably many people are better suited to tracing and explaining them than the economist sitting here. Although the Bank's staff and management have done their best to deal with this extremely difficult task, I have no doubt about that and have not seen anything to suggest otherwise, it is now faced with the fact that it was not wholly successful and inexplicably in some ways very badly. The bank managed to get the controls to work in an economic sense. It was of paramount importance to the national economy. In this way, normal payment processing and transactions between Iceland and other countries were successfully secured. It was almost life or death to play for the Icelandic the economy, as its recession and cuts in living standards would have been much more serious if the necessary trade between Iceland and other countries had not been secured. This obviously requires foreign exchange trading. When evaluating how this was done, it is necessary to keep this in mind. Those who stood in the line of fire defending capital controls felt - and were in fact - working on a project that was crucial to the national interest. It explains decisions and scenarios to some extent, but of course does not excuse everything that was done. Mistakes were made and had serious consequences. However, it managed to get the controls to work, of course not perfectly, they undoubtedly lashed out, but well enough to pursue as normal foreign trade as possible and also to settle and settle the enormous debts that rested on a number of domestic companies, especially the fallen banks, without the market for the Icelandic kronor going sideways. However, it was not even possible with the enforcement and sentence of the seas in various other ways. In particular, it is worth noting that litigation and charges relating to alleged violations of the doping have almost wholly been rejected by the courts or prosecutors. Furthermore, the administrative penalties imposed by the Bank have been overturned by the courts once they have been tried. The Bank's management of capital controls has also been heavily criticised. This is especially true of the so-called Confederacy. In the aforementioned report, the history of that case is traced and draws conclusions from it. I'm not going to trace the whole story here, but the report is public, so anyone can study it as indeed numerous other documents, including the judgments and opinions of the Ombudsman of the Althingi. In view of all this, the Board of Directors has concluded that it is normal for the Central Bank to take its work on the capital controls all under careful consideration and draw from it natural lessons. The Council also considers it appropriate to examine whether the Bank's progress towards those under investigation for possible breaches of the restrictions was sued by the Bank or fined was normal. This includes measures against samherji. In such an examination, of course, a number of serious suggestions from the Ombudsman of the Althingi, as well as the conclusions of judges and prosecutors in cases relating to the capital controls, should be taken into account. In view of the experience of recent years, the Board of Directors believes that the Central Bank needs to prepare in advance for measures such as capital controls and other emergency measures. It should be a natural part of his efforts to preserve financial stability and respond to shocks. In this context, it should be remembered that financial crises are unfortunately almost inevitable folly of modern financial systems. There has been no magic solution, although of course the systems can be made more stable in various ways, preparing financial institutions and especially central banks to deal with them. The Central Bank of Iceland, like other such institutions, needs to do so. Such preparation, however, is not just a central bank project, but also of the legislature, ministries and commercial banks. Part of the explanation for the embarrassment of capital controls is that such work had not been carried out in the lead-up to the 2008 crash or at least not well enough. It is worth bearing in mind, however, that even with extremely good preparation, capital controls would always have been very difficult to implement in an open economy with a financial system that was interwoven with the financial systems of neighbouring countries like the Icelandic. The proposed merger of the Central Bank and the FME moves a variety of activities which are inherently similar to those undertaken by the Bank as a result of the capital controls to the Bank. The experience of the Central Bank's work in monitoring capital controls strongly suggests that this may be accompanied by significant disadvantages. They need to pay close attention to these changes. It is a very intrinsic activity to operate a regulatory authority and to exercise sanctions and to be on the other hand the "bank of the banks", and to formulate monetary policy, thereby contributing to stable prices. A unified organization needs to be able to play both roles  and indeed others  well and without one role becoming entangled in the other. A new management system needs to take that into account. Similarly, it is undesirable that the Board of Directors of the Central Bank plays a role in such criminal matters as further explained in the report. The Board of Directors has a statutory supervisory role and should of course perform  and does  but it should not in any way control the Bank's progress in individual criminal proceedings or be some kind of appeals committee. 27 March 2019 Gylfi Magnusson Chairman of the Board of Directors
