Title: Historical papers from the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 1 Mr. President of Iceland Ministers Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland Governor Other good members Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 2 1. go (First sign of the Central Bank) The Central Bank of Iceland began operations as an independent institution on 7 April 1961. The Central Bank is the central bank of the financial system, currency and monetary policy, the state bank and the bank of other banks, and it handles issuing banknotes and coins. The central bank is affected by the economy through interest rate decisions and other controls. It plays a key role in shaping financial stability. The Central Bank is the centre of payment and settlement systems, which are the foundation of the business world. The Central Bank of Iceland has been a formative and forceful force for financial institutions, financial markets and monetary and foreign exchange transactions. The Central Bank of Iceland's operations were rapidly intensifying. In 1962 he took over foreign government loans, and in 1967 he fully assumed the management of mints in addition to the issue of banknotes. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 3 Photo 2 (Photos from the front desk and office) In the spring of 1961, the Central Bank of Iceland's employees were 61. At first, there was a lot of work done on banking supervision, securities transactions and settlements of check transactions. The Central Bank was a member of the Economic Institute and was responsible for product loans, the Government Guarantee Fund and the Founding Loans Department of the Fisheries Sector. Employees of the Central Bank of Iceland were in front of participants in landsbanki easlands employees' associations, but the Central Bank of Iceland Employees' Association has long been in charge of social life and interests. In 1977, bankers were granted contractual rights. Stability characterizes the Central Bank's workforce, and many have had their seniority in the Institution. Currently, about 60% of employees have a university education. In the Central Bank of Iceland's workforce, the gender share is now almost equal to that of management positions in general. At the end of 2010, 144 people were employed by the Central Bank. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 4 3. go (Bank house on Austurstrbeti) In front of the central bank's history, the country's leading commercial banks were owned by the State. The financial system was shaped by state custody and specialized publicly owned investment funds. Efforts were made to boost savings, but savings are community investment and development funds. The value of money and interest rate development are the main tasks and have a decisive impact on all savings. For a long time the Central Bank and Landsbanki easlands were jointly operated, as Landsbankinn had been in charge of central bank projects since 1927. The role of the banks was separated in 1957 and to the fullest in 1961. But the Central Bank continued to work on business issues, such as product loans and foreign exchange remittances. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 5 4. go (A?alst9a?var IMF) The Central Bank has many projects in multinational cooperation. He is approached for currency exchange and information for collateral transactions. The Central Bank of Iceland handles communications with foreign banking institutions, international funds and international organisations in the fields of trade, investment, credit and foreign exchange. These include the Nordic central banks, the European Central Bank, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the International Payment Bank. The Central Bank of Iceland has the role of promoting and clarifying Icelandic cause and interests in relations with foreign trading partners, banks and international organisations. The Central Bank is also an advisory body for governments in the field of foreign exchange and monetary policy. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 6 5. go (First Bank of England) In 1986, the Central Bank of Iceland act was passed and again in 2001. Then the Bank's mission and its relationship with the government changed. The Central Bank of Iceland's divisions work in international affairs, marketing, financial systems, statistical processing, monetary and economics, as well as the Bank's operations, its collections and treasuries. J97n G. Mar92asson was the first Chairman of the Board of Directors. Next to him was Dr. J97hannes Nordal, who led the institute for a long time and made a mark on it, followed by J97n Sigur?sson, Birgir easleifur Gunnarsson and Dav92? Oddsson. In 2009, it was decided that the governor would be alone, but before that the three were together. Svein Harald afygard was Governor of the Central Bank in the first half of 2009, after which M87r Gu?mundsson took over as Governor of the Central Bank. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 7 6. go (Picture of banknote safety features) Money is a unit of measure, value storage, and payment method. Today's standard of living and way of life are unthinkable without business, and money makes business possible as a unit of measure in all transactions with value, goods and services. Mints and banknote printing are important tasks, and security features are highly elaborate. The safety of payment systems is a prerequisite for the economy and living standards of the people. Security in the value of money is also important, as Icelanders know well. In this country, the safe value of the krona has often been sacrificed. The result has been chronically high inflation and imbalances. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 8 7. go (Old and new notes and coins) Traditional land farming was in the 18th century, but money became more common than before. In 1776 a royal letter was issued on the trade in money, and in 1778, curry banknotes were legislated. The Althing asked the king in 1853 for a banking institution. In 1873, the time of the crown began. Landsbanki easlands was founded in 1886, but previously several savings banks operated. easlandsbanki senior began operations in 1904 and worked until 1930. The National Trust of Iceland issued the first series of banknotes in 1886. easlandsbanki the Elder issued two banknotes. Landsbanki easlands issued banknotes from 1929. The National Trust issued Icelandic coins from 1922. Currency exchanges occurred in Iceland in 1948 and again in 1981. The Central Bank of Iceland issued the first series of banknotes in 1966 and two later. The Central Bank of Iceland's first series of currencies was published in 1969. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 9 Image 8 (Picture of various old publications) Economic and monetary policy developments became volatile in the 1960s and 1970s. Catch records were broken during the herring years. Then the imbalance was still exacerbated by inflation, exchange rate changes and labour market conflicts. The Central Bank was responsible for checking transactions, changes in reserve requirements, product bills of exchange, measures for lending expansion and responses to catch failures and Heimaey eruption. Price stops, credit programs and agreements on restraint on the lending of the banking system were taken. The Central Bank of Iceland interfered with the fish industry's price matching fund, the insurance department of export loans and the Industrial Development Fund, and the Bank also worked on fisheries issues. In 1971, international exchange rates changed when the U.S. abandoned that structure with a fixed but convertible exchange rate identified as Bretton Woods. The Banks' Data Centre began operations in 1974, and in the same year the publication of statistics for the month began. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 10 9. go (Se?labankah9csi?) In the 1980s, great progress was made towards an open financial system. In 1979, the Financial Obligation Indexation Act was passed, which laid the foundations for further development. The new crown was introduced at the beginning of 1981. Inflation in the early 1980s beat all previous records. The Central Bank emphasized restraint measures through agreements with commercial banks. The aim was to ensure freer trading practices in the banking system regarding interest rate and foreign exchange decisions. Special deposit binding was applied in addition to general reserve requirements. The stock exchange began operations in 1986. Interest rate liberalisation came into force and a new act on the Central Bank of Iceland. A cornerstone was laid at the Central Bank's house in May 1986, and in the spring of 1987 the bank opened the building. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 11 10. go (Overview: page on controls) At the beginning of the final years of the last century, a national consensus was successful in action against high inflation. There were changes in the banking system when four banks merged in 1990. There have been a lot of changes in the professional system. Credit cards charged instead of checks and liquidity. The open currency market began in 1993. Rules in the interbank market were cleared, reserve requirements and interest rates were reduced. In 1994, Iceland joined the European Economic Area. In 1998, the Central Bank of Iceland's controls were changed in accordance with developments abroad and general open market measures were aimed at general open market measures. In 1999, the Financial Supervisory Authority began operations, where banking supervision was transferred from the Central Bank. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 12 Image 11 (Picture of the modern computer studio of the Algorithm) The technology of payment processing was thrown out at the turn of the century. The Central Bank of Iceland established new rules on the Large Payment System and the Equalisation System, while the Icelandic Banks' Data Centre was responsible for the operation of the systems. The use of credit cards increased and they took over as the dominant payment method. The Central Bank reduced the weight of indexation and withdrew from the roles of market makers with savings certificates. Tolerance within which exchange rates could fluctuate were changed and a continuous foreign exchange market began. State banks were converted into limited liability companies. The development of interest rates continued. The Central Bank of Iceland's research projects were greatly strengthened, and in 1999 the Bank began publishing the journal Monetary Bulletin. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 13 12. go (Image showing computers of marketing) There have been many changes in attitudes towards economic policy, monetary policy and central bank policy. Previously, the central bank's main role was to finance the Treasury and be a backbone of the financial system. Over the years, new monetary policy was formulated with macroeconomic objectives as a guiding light. It was agreed that inflation is a monetary phenomenon and can only be affected by the Bank's general market actions and the impact on expectations. The main task had to seek to ensure price stability. The importance of general financial stability has become clearer than before. In addition, it is generally agreed that in order for central banks to succeed, they need independence towards political governments to use their controls. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 14 13. go (Going: Peningam87logFj87rm87last9a?ugl) A new law was introduced in 2001. The Central Bank and the Prime Minister's Office agreed on inflation targets and on the Central Bank's response if inflation seeks from a set target. The constitutional independence of the Central Bank was confirmed. In 2005, the publication of a new financial stability magazine began. The state-owned commercial banks were fully privatised in 2003 and took initiatives in the financial market, in lending and expansion to other countries. Expansion was exacerbated by large-scale economic activity, major energy projects and a transition to the mortgage market. The Central Bank of Iceland met this progress with conventional instruments but failed to ensure stability and low inflation alone. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 15 Figure 14 (Photo of central bank press conference) In 2002, the Central Bank of Iceland published rules of procedure for preparing and promoting monetary policy decisions. In the same year, the harmonisation of the rules on reserve requirements with European rules ended. A record-breaking year was held on the Iceland Stock Exchange in 2003. Payment and settlement systems were harmonised with international monetary fund rules. In the interbank market, developments were underway in the registration of letters and conditions for mortgage eligibility. The exchange rate of the kr97na rose and there was a large flow of capital in the country, including in exchange rate and interest rate differences. An expansion adventure made an impression on all financial activities. The Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority achieved limited results, but the credit rating of Icelandic financial undertakings was considered to be excellent. Inflation and trade deficits continued to increase. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 16 15. go (Current Bank logo) In 2008, the financial system collapsed. International credit markets almost stopped and financial institutions were closed. Reasons were also domestic, excessive growth and risk-taking. Construction collapsed. The crown's exchange rate collapsed. Debt amounts skyrocketed. The central bank was overridden, but domestic payment services passed. A new law was passed in 2009, the Board of Directors abolished, but appointed one governor and monetary policy committee. Criticism appears in a report by the Parliamentary Investigation Committee. The Bank's controls were reviewed and currency controls taken. The Central Bank undertook tasks in foreign exchange control and asset management. The Central Bank of Iceland now follows monetary policy with a long-term inflation target, but short-term exchange rate stability is taken into account. The loosening of the capital controls and the formulation of monetary policy is proposed ahead. The Central Bank of Iceland has gained important experience for the future. Agenda 7 April 2011: Experience of the Central Bank of Iceland /JS 17 I thank the audience.

Title: Statement by CEO
text: Ingimundur Frioriksson CEO: Address to a meeting of the Nordic and Baltic countries on payment processing and securities settlement in Reykjavik 25  26 August 2008 I welcome you to Reykjavik and the Central Bank of Iceland. The Central Bank of Iceland is young in years. It was established by law in 1961 and carries out all the traditional tasks belonging to the central bank's operations. The bank's employees number about 115, which is not considered much. The Central Bank of Iceland has inflation targets and performs all the tasks it requires. The Bank plays a clearly defined role in the field of financial stability, overseeing government loans, managing foreign exchange reserves, issuing banknotes and coins, and so on. We are delighted to hold this meeting. No doubt we can learn a lot from each other at the level of payment processing. As a result, it is important that we compare our books for the purpose of ensuring continued security and efficiency in the operation of payment and settlement systems in our countries. The Nordic countries have long collaborated in this area and now the Baltic countries have joined us as active partners. It has been said that the role of central banks is essentially threefold: (1) Ensuring price stability; (2) maintaining financial stability; and (3) to ensure the seamless and secure operation of payment, and settlement systems. Secure and efficient payment processing is among the cornerstones of financial stability, and payment and settlement systems are the basis on which payment processing is based. As a result, there are strict requirements for these systems of safety and efficiency. Your daily tasks include monitoring developments in this area and formulating policies and promoting progress in line with international recommendations and policies of your central banks. The operation of payment systems is also important, although in their eyes they are little known, they may be rather unforgiving. Some believe that they are characterized by right-wing development and even stagnation. Of course it is true that payment processing and basic payment systems are highly specialised, but if you look closely, it is actually extremely interesting. The fact is also that payment services have evolved rapidly in recent years. Increasingly stringent requirements are being made for safety, efficiency, efficiency and transparency. Turnover in payment systems has multiplied, cooperation within countries and internationally has grown strongly, and stock exchanges and securities exchanges have merged or established formal cooperation. Payment systems have evolved from tailored or regional solutions in each country to standardised systems, however, which need to be adapted to a certain extent to the historical and technical environment of each market or state. The basis of payment processing in Iceland is in some ways unique and domestic payment services are based on long and successful cooperation between the Central Bank of Iceland, commercial banks and the country's savings banks, as will be further described at tomorrow's meeting. The Central Bank of Iceland foreshadowed this cooperation, which began in 1973. The operations of the Icelandic payment and settlement systems in its current form date from 2001 and 2002, but their roots and foundations lie in the cooperation that began 35 years ago. In the beginning  and indeed for a long time  the operations of the Icelandic payment processing system were more or less limited to Iceland. The system was extremely efficient, cost-effective and user-friendly, but did not necessarily apply models to foreign systems. After the middle of the last decade, the Central Bank of Iceland initiated the development of the system in accordance with internationally recognised requirements. After years of structure and improvement, Icelandic payment systems meet these requirements. However, there is always scope for further improvement as markets and infrastructure are in rapid development. In recent years, the Central Bank has described these systemic changes in detail in its annual report and other regular publications, including the Bank's annual publication, Financial Stability. Payment systems currently in use in Iceland are good and efficient. Serious problems have been rare and the "uptime" of the system relatively very high. The environment is changing rapidly and the trend is scarce. Therefore, we must be well alert to change and be prepared to make changes in line with global trends, rapidly growing turnover and increased the importance of payment services for the economy and financial stability in general. If we look back, we can see that we have accomplished a lot in this area, such as:  Formal external assessment of payment systems  Internal assessment of specific aspects of the system  System development, new updates and various improvements 2  Improve regulation and legal framework  Increased transparency in system management  Updated tariffs and increased transparency  Advanced statistical analysis  Increased consultation among participants  Effective activities and services of the system  Improved contingency processes However, many changes are still in sight. These include:  Increased cross-border communication  Increased emphasis on financial stability and increased awareness of its importance  Increased differentiation and independence of individual payment systems Many important projects are in the works or in the future. These include:  Audit of the securities settlement system, including settlements in ISK and the proposed settlement of securities transactions in euros  In-depth assessment of the large payment system  Design of an internal valuation system within the Bank to ensure that systemically important systems meet national and international requirements  Further improvements in the regulatory and legal frameworks, especially regarding the securities settlement system The current structure Icelandic payment processing involves certain operational risk factors that were identified by experts Swedish the Central Bank in an audit conducted several years ago. The audit conducted at the request of the Central Bank of Iceland was not least focused on assessing how well the Bank's bulk payment system met Rule No. 7 of the Core Rules 10 from the World Bank in Basel. Since that time, various improvements have been made in accordance with the recommendations of the Swedish experts. All of the changes aim to increase efficiency and define and manage the underlying risk factors as far as possible, based on current system structures and operating arrangements. As I mentioned earlier, the Bank intends to conduct a thorough review of the bulk payment system and how well it meets the 10 core rules. In addition, it will assess whether the Bank should continue to develop the existing system or invest in a new system, as it has done in Sweden and Norway. It will be important for the Central Bank of Iceland to have the opportunity to learn from the norwegian and Swedish experiences of the new systems. 3 In June of this year, the International Monetary Fund conducted a secondary review of the Icelandic financial system as part of the so-called Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). Among the topics was the evaluation of systemically important payment systems. However, the audit was not a comprehensive assessment of whether or to what extent Icelandic the financial system meets the 10 core rules, but an assessment of whether Iceland had complied with the Fund's recommendations and recommendations in previous FSAP audits. The result was that it had been done. In addition, the Fund pointed to certain aspects of regulation and implementation in Iceland that may require change. We will take these tips into consideration. The International Monetary Fund's assessment focused not only on the bulk payment system and the settlement system, but also on the securities settlement system. In this context, it is necessary to also consider some of the factors under consideration at present by the Central Bank of Iceland and the Financial Supervisory Authority, in their joint assessment of the systems of the Icelandic Securities Depository. The Bank and the FME intend to complete that audit before examining the bulk payment system. Several Icelandic companies have expressed interest in listing their shares in euros. Legally, there is nothing to prevent. If shares are listed in euros, it must be ensured that the settlement of transactions with them meets the legal requirements, domestic and foreign. At present, the Icelandic Securities Depository is preparing for the arrangements for such a settlement in cooperation with the Central Bank of Finland so that a monetary settlement Icelandic securities transactions in euros can be carried out through the eurozone's large payment system, Target2. The Central Bank of Iceland has nothing against such an arrangement. The Bank would not be a direct operator of such a solution although it will have an overview of the settlement arrangements in euros in cooperation with the Central Bank of Finland. As you are aware, the European Central Bank has decided to begin preparing for the design and development of a new securities settlement system under the name Target2  Securities, which will be based on the Target2 bulk payment system. The new securities settlement system is expected to contribute to increased coordination and efficiency. However, this remains to be seen, especially in relation to the settlement of securities transactions in currencies other than the euro. Securities depositors outside the eurozone are available to participate in the proposed scheme and the possibility of settling securities transactions in currencies other than the euro has been opened up and provided that a central bank 4 The country in question supports that solution so that settlements can be made in its currency. Neither the Icelandic Securities Depository nor the Central Bank of Iceland has taken a formal position on this matter. I see that many issues are on your agenda at the level of payment and settlement systems. It is my sincere hope that your meeting will be the most successful. Over and over again, I welcome you all. 5

Karen e7slaug Vignisd97ttir1 Monetary Policy Committee for seven years The Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Iceland has been in operation for more than seven years. When the monetary framework was amended by a legislative amendment in 2009 that stipulated the monetary policy committee's structure, the results were taken into account, parishes investigated the best arrangements for monetary policy decision-making. At the same time, changes were made aimed at increasing transparency and credibility of monetary policy. An examination of the monetary policy committee's votes in the period 2009-2015 reveals that there were different views within the Committee. A full consensus could not be reached in nearly half of the votes, in a third of the cases one committee member voted against the majority, and in nearly a sixth of the cases, two members were in the minority. In the case of disagreements in the Committee, the majority consists more often of both internal and external members than merely internal members. The composition of the minority in interest rate decision meetings has also varied somewhat over the period. The monetary policy committee's voting structure seems to be similar to that of our neighbouring countries, which have similar arrangements. Changing monetary policy decisions seems to have been successful. The economy has recovered in the wake of the financial crisis and has been more balanced. Inflation has been below the Bank of England's inflation target for two and a half years and long-term inflation expectations have blurred downwards. It can be assumed that the success of the policy's money in recent years has contributed to the creation of a more solid ballast than before. Other different factors, however, have also played an important role in the economic recovery in recent years. Entrance There have been major changes in the world's monetary framework in recent decades, and central banks, where monetary policy decisions are made by multi-appointed monetary policy committees rather than one individual or a small number of banking executives have increased. Research suggests that such arrangements are more suitable for monetary decision-making. Decisions tend to be more thoughtful when a committee composed of experts combines its powers, knowledge and different experiences in order to reach the best outcome through critical and constructive dialogue. If the background of the decision-making process is communicated to the public through notifications and publication of minutes, it also facilitates the dissemination of monetary policy. But what kind of monetary policy structure is best suited? They differ in type, e.g. regarding the arrangements for decision-making, the size and composition of the Committee and the position of governor within it as Chairman. The changes made in early 2009 came after the financial crisis in the autumn of 2008 and took into account the experience in the lead-up to the crisis. Monetary Policy Board with monetary policy committee In recent decades, the number of central banks where monetary decisions are made by a multi-appointed committee rather than one individual has increased. This development took place while increasing emphasis was placed on central banks being independent, providing a logical requirement that the decisions of an independent institution are taken by a multi-agency body where different viewpoints are allowed to be enjoyed and that transparency prevails on those decisions. According to Maier (2010), more than 80 central banks in the world had a monetary policy committee in charge of monetary policy at the beginning of this year dozens, and nowhere has it happened that a central bank has changed the monetary policy framework in a way that has disappeared from a multi-appointed decision-making body into an arrangement in which one person makes monetary policy decisions. As Blinder (2009) runs, most research suggests that a multi-appointed monetary policy committee is more suited to monetary policy decisions than an individual, regardless of the results of academic research or international experience. If monetary policy decisions are solely at the discretion of an individual, there is a greater risk that his interests and ideas will prevail. By entrusting a committee with the role of making important decisions under conditions of uncertainty, it is possible to ensure that circumstances do not arise where the potential failure of judgment of one individual prevails (see Qvigstad et al., 2013). The results of Blinder and Morgan's experiments (2005, 2008a, b) in which individuals were asked to solve certain tasks, including making monetary policy decisions using simulations, suggest that groups make better decisions than individuals. Furthermore, their findings show that there did not appear to be more inertia in decision-making in groups than in one person. The experiments of Lombardelli, Proudman and Talbot (2005) lead to the same findings that committees make better decisions than individuals in particular because a group of individuals combine different information and their opinions as well as learning from each other. Sibert (2006), however, makes a number of arguments that committees could make worse decisions than an individual. Committee members, for example, could act like a free rider and rely on others on a committee inside to do all the work without contributing. Similarly, there may be a risk of a certain "groupthink" as the committee tries to reach consensus on specific issues but does not take sufficient account of other options. Such herding behavior could lead to worse decisions than an individual would take. Different types of monetary policy committees Most often, monetary policy committees are separated by two types prior to arrival. On the one hand, there are committees where committees still vote based on their own assessments and the results are obtained by a majority of individualistic committees. Such committees do not place particular emphasis on achieving unity on the decision, and each member of the committee is simply responsible for his or her vote. The money policy committees of the Bank of England and the Central Bank of Sweden, and the US Federal Reserve since the middle of the last decade, are examples of such committees. In public debate, members of committees of this kind can even express their differing views and make it clear to market participants, for example, that the Committee is not always unanimous on monetary policy decisions. In this context, Sibert (2006) mentions that the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee is an example of how to avoid potential problems related to groupthink. It encourages committee members to take an individual position, as well as the transparency of the decision-making process in the form of minutes and public disclosure of the members' votes creates external restraint. However, there are committees emphasizing that unity prevails on the decision, at least publicly, and the Monetary Policy Committee is all behind the decision (collegial committees). A formal vote does not always take place and it is not publicly clear how the votes fell when that happens. The European Central Bank (ECB) and the Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Norway are examples of this ECONOMY 5 ECONOMICS NO. 8 ECONOMICS NO. 8 ECONOMY 6 arrangement. In such committees, the position of governor as chairman of the Committee may differ depending on the manner in which consensus is reached. It can be extremely strong in such a way that the governor is almost one of the councils on the policy and other members of the committee are expected to follow him. An example of such a committee is the Monetary Policy Committee of the Us Federal Reserve when Alan Greenspan was governor of the Federal Reserve. On the other hand, members of the committee may exchange opinions behind closed doors and thus influence the decision, but are then ultimately consensual about the outcome when it is announced and in public debate. The ECB is an example of such an arrangement (Blinder, 2007).3 But what is the structure of monetary policy committees best suited? Blinder (2007) concluded that a committee in which named men vote based on their own opinions is probably best suited to exercise the qualities that committee arrangements have beyond when a person makes decisions. However, he noted that the main disadvantage was potential problems related if the committee was in some cases deeply inconsistent and expressed differing views publicly, but this could reduce the clarity of the committee's message and complicate the speech on monetary policy instead of explaining the arguments for specific decisions. According to Maier (2010), the most appropriate arrangement is actually what reflects both advantages of the above methods i.e. the Monetary Policy Committee where individuals vote based on their own convictions and opinions, but that it is still sufficiently co-ordinated and disciplined for the message to be both clear and transparent. Gerlach-Kristen (2005) looks at whether there is a risk that the money-raising policies that focus on achieving unity on the decision respond too late and too little to changing conditions in the economy. Its findings suggest that in the committees where down positions are obtained by a majority of votes, changing m conditions in the national economy are dealt with more quickly than in committees where consensus on the decision needs to be reached. Committees seeking to achieve a consensus position are also less likely to change interest rates, however, changing them in larger steps than committees where decisions are made with a simple majority. The size of monetary policy committees Various studies have been conducted on what is the most appropriate size of monetary policy committees. Sibert (2006) concludes that the most suitable number of committee members is approximately five and that more numerous committees are likely to be less effective. Her research suggests that as the number of members increased in excess of seven to nine, there is a risk of reducing the participation of individual members and that mutual relations are worse in groups with more than a dozen members.6 Maier's summary (2010) shows that the most common number of members of the MPC committees is between five and ten. His findings suggest that the more people on the committee, the more likely it is that a committee member will dodge responsibility as it becomes less obvious if a particular person does not participate in the decision or does not prepare for a meeting. Similarly, the findings of Erhart et al. (2007) indicate that inflation is traditionally more volatile in countries where there are fewer than five members. New Monetary Policy Framework in Iceland Changes to the monetary policy framework following the financial crisis In early 2009, fundamental changes were made to the framework of the Pen inga policy in Iceland and the current structure of the management of money eels was established. The Act on the Central Bank of Iceland was amended in such a way that the formulation of monetary policy and decisions on the application of bank notes' controls would in future be in the hands of a special monetary committee that would be composed of five members instead of a three-member board of directors previously. The Committee shall consist of three representatives from the Central Bank, namely the Ceo, Deputy Governor and One of the Bank's Heads in the Field of Monetary Policy, and two external experts in the field of economic and monetary policy.7 The Governor of the Central Bank is chairman of the Committee. In changing the monetary policy framework, international experience of monetary policy decision-making arrangements was taken into account. Efforts were made to ensure that the structure and practices of the Monetary Policy Committee were in line with the results of research on how best to formulate the framework around decision-making powers in penal matters. The change also aimed to further strengthen the professional basis of the Central Bank's monetary policy decisions. As discussed in the Central Bank's publications, there are a number of reasons for this, including the international conditions of liquidity and low interest rates, the deterioration in the monetary policy trading process and failures in its implementation and the unfavourable interaction between monetary policy and the financial emission of public policy. This contributed to the failure to ensure sufficient credibility for monetary policy and to create inflation-friendly ballast in the inflation target (Central Bank of Iceland, 2010, 2012). Therefore, it was important that the changing monetary structure take into account the views on increasing the credibility of monetary policy and at the same time further ensuring the central bank's independence. The current act stipulates that the Monetary Policy Committee holds meetings at least eight times a year and that the Committee's decisions are based on a careful assessment of the state and outlook of economic and monetary policy and financial stability. The act also provides for the Committee to establish rules of procedure for the preparation, justification and presentation of its monetary decisions. For each interest rate decision, detailed 1-2 day meetings are held where experts within the Central Bank present recent developments and prospects in economic and financial markets before the Committee, as well as specific topics when appropriate. It is sometimes also called for external presentations on various issues under consideration within the Committee. The goal is for all viewpoints to be established and to ensure that decisions are based on a professional and solid basis and as transparent and predictable as realistic as possible. The Committee's practices in respect of the interest rate decision have evolved in the period since it began work. In principle, they involve the Governor proposing an interest rate decision that he believes will gain a majority after hearing the positions of the other members. A vote on the proposal will then take place and a majority will decide the result. The organization of the meeting also means that members of the Committee do not always express their position or vote in the same order. The monetary policy committee's practices are similar to those of the monetary policy committee, e.g. Bank of England and Central Bank of Sweden. Their results show that transparency increased in the vast majority of central banks between 1998 and 2010.8 This result includes developed countries, emerging markets and developing countries. The global financial crisis does not seem to have reversed that trend. The main reason for greater transparency, they believe, is that it is an effective way to strengthen the credibility of central banks and their commitments. The commitment to ensure low and stable inflation will be more convincing if the Central Bank explains exactly how its decisions lead to the Bank's objectives being met. However, the proportion of cases where at least a quarter of the committee members are in the minority is rather lower here than in the UK, but in turn somewhat higher than in Sweden. At the same time, the average number of members who are in the minority is rather higher here than in the US and Sweden but lower than in the UK. The results of a study by Gerlach-Kristen (2009) on the voting patterns of the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee also indicate that external committee members tend to prefer lower interest rates than internal committee members, as is the case in Iceland as previously attributed, particularly during recession periods. Monetary policy committees can be of a different nature, and international experience of the arrangements for decision-making in money matters was taken into account when the Committee was established here. Monetary Policy Committee votes in the period 2009-2015 show that there is no evidence of block formation within the Committee. The results show that a full consensus could not be reached in nearly half of the votes, and that in a third of the cases one committee member voted against the majority, and in nearly a sixth of the cases, two members were in the minority. Different views have therefore been present within the Committee for the past seven years, as the aim of the multi-appointed Pen inga policy committee is for different opinions to be addressed, which increases the likelihood of making an informed decision. In the case of disagreements in the Committee, the majority consists more often of both internal and external committee members than merely internal members. On occasions where two named arms are still in the minority, internal committee members have only formed a majority in a quarter of cases. The composition of the minority has therefore varied somewhat over the period. However, there appears to be a difference between the electoral behaviour of internal and external committee members when the minority votes are examined in more detail. When internal members were in the minority, they voted more often for higher interest rates than the governor's proposal sounded rather than lower interest rates. The same is not true of the external committee members, as the number of their minority votes is divided equally between wanting higher or lower interest rates than the majority voted for. The monetary policy committee's voting division and differences in the electoral behaviour of internal and external committee members also appear to have been similar to that of our neighbouring countries, which have similar arrangements. text: Jon Sigurosson, Governor of the Central Bank Communications delivered to islandsbanki hf. Thursday, February 3, 2005 Good belongings Now people use the euro in many parts of continental Europe, and many national currencies are gone, including the German sights and the French franc. This includes new circumstances, including the Icelandic crown. The euro's progress increases interest in research into economy mergers. Globalization in manufacturing, services and trade usually aims to the same extent. It also focuses on assessing what can be considered a suitable and cost-effective currency area. The measuring parameters highlighted by Robert Mundell in article 1961 in assessing a viable common currency area, and many others have targeted since, are these: * The importance of the business relation internally in the area; * Convergence in economic fluctuations and development; * Related or similar sensitivity to trauma; * Flexibility, especially in the labour market; * Potential for common oscillation. Surveys do not suggest that Icelandic circumstances are compatible with these conditions now. Here are at least the arguments and causes that know in other directions. In Iceland, there has been a consensus that the euro will hardly be adopted except as part of Iceland's full membership of the European Union. Unilateral adoption of the euro without membership of the European Union, people believe that the equivalent of taking on commitments and inconveniences without guaranteeing rights and opportunities in return. Many people think it is advantageous for Icelanders to adopt the euro as a legal currency. It is also wise to keep the probable costs of membership of the European Union in mind as well. Surveys indicate that Iceland's cost of membership will range from at least 2.5 - 4.0 ma.kr. annually, but the government's expenditure will be higher than this amounts to. 2 People don't agree on this any more than hope. However, everyone agrees that our direct payments will be greater than instalments from the European Union here. A closer look at the indicators of the common currency area adds some elements to the overview in Mundell's study. These include the position of a marginal area within a larger total, the impact on sectors, on the state of the Treasury, the development of competitive conditions, the prevention of economic fluctuations not related to this periphery, and the last development of transaction costs in general. It is very difficult to assess these factors to inexperience. The business sector must not least focus attention on the last point mentioned, business expenses. Important aspects of business expenses include these: * Shipping costs - zooms - chemical products - energy costs of service costs; * Cost and price decisions arising from market size, risk and distance; * Marketing costs of any kind - cultural differences - differences in circumstances; * Uncertainty as an obstacle and cost to trade between regions; * Capital expenditure - interest - currency costs; * Taxes - actual actual taxes - tax comparison; * Human resources - employee expenses - employment terms; * Various provisions in collective agreements - difficulties in communication of the labour market; * Effort in communicating with authorities -delays - various surcharges; * Regulatory system - blockade - the surveillance industry - regulatory burden. It's a difficult comparison and a lot of things that can be stretched in a number of ways. Conditions shaping a common larger area have several characteristics, including these: * Common regulatory system - same service system - billing factors - legal aspects; * Production capacity - market size - investments  service market, e.g. tourism; * Specialization increases  integration and optimization can increase convergence increases; * Competition - general pricing - price comparison - the same competition rules; * Not in the area of exchange rate risk - not currency risk - not border costs; 3 * Not its own monetary policy - not its own exchange rate policy or foreign exchange policy; * The role of public finances changes - tax revenue from increased transactions; * Labour market rules - increased unemployment - mutual funds are added. The general price of everyday goods matters in this. Some time ago, the difference between prices in Iceland and in the nearest neighbouring countries ranged from about 9 % higher prices here to just over 30%, depending on which types of grocery stores were compared. But here are also reasons for the history of unrelated to the merger of economies. Various studies have been conducted on the effects of consolidation of economies, trading systems and markets. A 2002 study by Jeffrey Frankel and Andrew Rose shows that in a common trading area, exports of land into the common area will triple and economic growth will increase permanently. In a report compiled by orsteinn orgeirsson for the Icelandic Industry Association in the summer of 2002, the adoption of the euro is estimated to reduce the general transaction cost by 44 ma.kr. per year and economic growth will increase by up to 0.4 % per year permanently. In a new study by the Central Bank of Iceland: Out in the cold? Iceland's trade performance outside the EU (Working Paper No. 26, Dec 2004) by Francis Breedon and orarin G. Petursson are the main findings: * Significant and clear trade increase - the economy is changing; * Trade with eurozone nations increases by 60%; * The weight of trade in GDP increases by 12 %; * The assumptions of economic growth are strengthened permanently; * Increase will be two-thirds greater if Danes, Swedes and Britons take up the euro. A 2002 report by the Confederation of Icelandic Industry provides examples similar to this: * Cost reduction in memory gjaldmiolaskipti by 0.5 % af vlf. * Decrease in general transaction costs by 3.0 % af vlf. * Hagvaxtarauki by 0.4 % per year 4,4 ma.kr. 26,4 ma.kr. In addition, the report, and taken from the Globalisation Committee's report, states that in the long term interest rate cuts will be 1.5 - 2.0 4 %, but updated, it is equivalent to at least 17.0 ma.kr. But this must be assessed in each company individually, and in fact impossible to inexperience. Most things have changed in Iceland since Iceland became members of the European Economic Area. These findings point to even greater changes in the potential adoption of the euro. Some of the most important factors are these: * Prices will be more transparent - competition changes  significant price cuts for consumer goods; * Common business environment  integrating economies into one common whole; * Growth base strengthens  becomes part of a much larger economy and business world; * Trading in the common area greatly increased; * Integration in the economy increases - specialization, optimization and cooperation increases; But we also have to keep in mind - that channels will be longer - the advantages of the small community are dwindling; - that government priorities are at least partially removed; - that local fluctuations will be exposed - new ways against local trauma. There have been a number of windfalls about the exchange rate of the Icelandic the krona in recent years, and a rate hike has raised concerns in recent months. According to the average exchange rate between 2000 and 2004, the krona had risen in the face of the US dollar but declined in the face of the euro, pound and Danish krona. The real exchange rate of the krona has recently increased on both the scale of prices and wages. Most people consider Icelandic the krona to be vulnerable for many reasons, although this trend is not one-sided and it cannot be explained by merely pointing out the central bank's actions. Financial markets, the foreign exchange market and the interbank market have evolved and matured greatly in Iceland in recent years. Great progress has been made in this development of the financial and banking system. The Central Bank's actions and regulations are aimed at strengthening these autonomous markets that aim for efficiency. These include reserve requirements, foreign exchange reserves and payment systems etc. The exchange rate Icelandic the krona attacks the market in the context of various market assumptions. Expectations of sudden intervention, hand control or political snares provoke temptation and raise irresponsibility. All of this involves a return to previous circumstances that people agree had completed their role. 5 The Central Bank does not regulate the economy or the standard of living of the public except to a very limited extent. It can have a defined effect on progress by lowering waves and promoting stability. The main influences in the economic development of works in the manufacturing, service and labour markets and they are in charge along with decisions on public finances, the Treasury and municipal funds. The main aspects of economic development at the moment are known to everyone: * The trade deficit is high, amounting to about 7 % of GDP last year, and overall consumption is more beneficial than a third of the trade deficit. * Large-scale practical projects are ongoing and amount to about 30 % of one year's GDP, but are distributed over a longer period of time. Over the next two years, this investment will be close to 11 % of GDP each year. * Economic growth is high. Production voltage is generated. Inflation is at a tolerance point. * Commercial banks have provided the households with around 120m. Mortgages in a short period of time, but it is estimated that 10-12% of this goes into general consumption. This has resulted in very large price increases in housing, although the net increase in loans does not amount to these amounts to these amounts. * The state of state and local finances is not a simple matter, but as a whole these parties have not responded with an appropriate recession. In this respect, people look not only at the Treasury or the largest municipalities, but also the Housing Financing Fund. People try to find a way to sail between the cutters and the boars. Central bank actions are attempts to respond to the prediction of future developments, but economic assumptions are shaped by, among other things, previous scenarios and decisions by the parties to the economy. Everyone sees what the consequences will be if a central bank starts nothing wrong, in hyperinflation, labor disputes, balance loss and dissolution. But actions are also badly affected. The increase in control rates is accompanied by an effect that, among other things, works poorly on the status of exports and competition sectors. In fact, the effect is not one-sided, as you can read, for example, in the Business Journal of Morgunblaoio on January 27th. It describes, among other things, the price movements that have occurred in the markets and changes in foreign debt amounts during rate hikes. This is by no means mentioned here to belittle the extreme difficulties of the export sectors at the moment. 6 Central bank measures on monetary policy are brokered across the economy phase before the phase, taking the trading process up to two years. The Central Bank must therefore maintain high-quality professional practices and be forward-looking in the power of research, modelling and forecasting. Exchange rate changes play a part in this trading process and matter. The Central Bank of Iceland cannot control the trading process by means of authority or manual control. The experience is unappealing that it is detrimental to try to intervene in the development of the foreign exchange market. This prevents people from analyzing the problem, delays success, and brings the nation to a head of multiplication of powers later. It is important to distinguish between nominal and real exchange rates. There is no reason to cast a scrap on the Icelandic the krona because it plays an important role in the monetary trading process. It's the real exchange rate that matters most in your professional life. The real exchange rate will not be managed by hand-wringing, but will determine, among other things, deep currents in the development of the economy, as described in, for example, the publications of the analysis departments of islandsbanki and Landsbanki this week. The Central Bank of Iceland has responded to the economic progress with an increase in the policy rate six times in the past year. At the same time, the Central Bank has also changed the ratios between individual interest rate types by narrowing the so-called interest rate hike and, among other things, making changes to the rules on trading accounts and agreements on arrangements for payment systems. These measures aim to lower waves and promote stability in the economy and business, while strengthening autonomous markets aiming for efficiency continue to be strengthened. It is the Central Bank's view that, for example, changes in reserve requirements are not suitable as an active control device. Indeed, they pull market liquidity together and raise the market interest rates, but they come with more that are not applicable. It is more successful to continue to target the free interaction of self-responsible entities in a market that operates in all eyes. This does not mean that Icelandic money markets are perfect or exemplary in all or most respects. Here are and will be endless projects that call for. And, of course, the forces in the markets are only human beings. But comparisons of options seem to show that Icelanders follow policies that lead to success better than other well-known ways, at least these years. Market participants are forward-looking at activities and their expectations are crucial. The Central Bank explains its inflation target publicly and how it intends to approach it. He assesses market expectations and tries to shape them in line with the inflation target. Expectations, trust and results are watching. 7 The Central Bank of Iceland seeks to formulate and implement independent, transparent and predictable monetary policy in autonomous and efficient markets. As a central bank in the monetary, foreign exchange and interbank markets, the Central Bank is also a kind of security hub in the financial system. Looking at the interaction and mutual impact of these markets in the manufacturing, service and labour markets, you can see how the Central Bank is designed to work toward stability and strengthen by doing so indirectly strengthen both commercial enterprises and businesses  and thus also stabilizes the purchasing power of the public. The Central Bank is thus, after all, ultimately a service institution for the whole public. By enforcing an independent publicly known monetary policy in a professional and transparent manner, the Central Bank of Iceland can best fulfil its service obligations. In the same way, the Bank is generally known as measuring parameters of actions and achievements in all eyes. In this way, the Central Bank strengthens its credibility and represents its case against the financial system, the government and the whole nation. I thank the audience.

Title: Talk at the Central Bank of Cyprus on lessons from debt restructuring in Iceland
text: 03.02.2014 orvarour Tjorvi olafsson: Talk at the Central Bank of Cyprus on lessons from debt restructuring in Iceland orvarour Tjorvi olafsson, economist at the Central Bank of Iceland, recently gave a talk at a conference at the Central Bank of Cyprus on handling default loans and restructuring household and corporate debt. Defaults have increased rapidly in Cyprus following last year's financial crisis, with 46% of all loans now overdue and work on debt restructuring is just beginning. The Central Bank of Cyprus held an international conference on this occasion and invited representatives from Iceland and Ireland to the island to share the experiences of these countries, while also giving talks to representatives from the International Monetary Fund, the European Commission and the European Central Bank, as well as domestic parties. The conference took place in Nicosia, cyprus' capital, from 27-28 January. In his talk orvarour Tjorvi discussed how the scale of the problem had been assessed in Iceland, the institutional framework that was set up around the restructuring of household and corporate debt and the measures introduced. Finally, he discussed the lessons that could be learned from Iceland's experience in dealing with defaults and restructuring loans. The accompanying document shows images and texts that orvarour Tjorvi supported in the paper: orvarour Tjorvi olafsson: Quantification of troubled debt and policy responses. Lessons from Iceland. Title: Interview with the Governor at a Meeting of the World Bank
text: 03.03.2014 Interview with the Governor at a Meeting of the World Bank Due to the wishes of representatives of financial undertakings, this is a full interview conducted by a foreign subscription media outlet, MNI, at a meeting of the World Bank of England recently held in Sydney. Iceland Gov: Govt's Plans Mustn't Hurt Centbank's Credibility 04:20 EST / Feb 28 By David Barwick SYDNEY (MNI) - It is important that the credibility of monetary policy not be negatively affected by potential changes to the governance structure of the Central Bank of Iceland in order to avoid an impact on inflation expectations, Governor Mar Gudmundsson told MNI Monday. Independent of the communication of possible changes, the real monetary policy stance of the central bank will tighten if economic slack turns into a positive output gap next year as forecast, he said. Gudmundsson, speaking on the margins of a meeting of central bankers taking place in conjunction with the G20 gathering of finance ministers and monetary authorities, said nevertheless that nominal interest rates in Iceland might possibly decline in the near term. "On the one hand, inflation is coming down closer to the target, and hopefully inflation expectations will follow suit," he said, which given current nominal interest rates would imply a real tightening. "And that might happen too fast for the kind of situation we're in, and therefore it is conceivable that nominal rates might even go down in the near term," he said. "It depends on the exchange rate, it depends on inflation." Gudmundsson continued: "But looking a little further ahead, you have these prospects of all the slack disappearing and turning into a positive output gap, which will call for a tightening of the real policy stance." Although the mix of relevant elements makes the overall situation "more than a bit uncertain," he said, "what is for sure is that given current forecasts, the real stance is unlikely to be reduced and will, if the forecasts materialize, become higher going forward as the slack in the economy disappears." The Icelandic government informed Gudmundsson on February 20 - hours before the expiry of the relevant legal deadline and six months before the end of his current five-year term - that it would advertise the position of central bank chief. "This is a decision that the Finance Minister on behalf of the government has a right to take, according to the rules of the game," Gudmundsson told MNI. "The Minister has been adamant, and said so in public, that this is not because of any lack of confidence or trust in me. The reason given for this decision is that the government is contemplating potential changes to the management structure of the central bank." It is important that communication regarding the process and its objectives maintain the credibility of the central bank's monetary policy in order to avoid negatively affecting inflation expectations and in turn the stance of monetary policy, said Gudmundsson. "Depending on the communication in the next few days and weeks, if the markets begin to draw the conclusion that there is some implicit change to either the inflation target or the de facto willingness to use the instruments of monetary policy to achieve the target, then that might affect inflation expectations and market expectations, and that in turn will always have an effect on monetary policy, " he said. " There is speculation to that effect but there are no statements that I am aware of from the Finance Minister that support that." The Icelandic central bank since 2009 has had a governor and a deputy governor, with monetary policy decisions taken by an MPC that includes both these officials as well as the chief economist of the bank and two external members. According to Gudmundsson, the government may elect to return to the previous system of three governors, or introduce some other model. In any case, he said, "they felt that their degree of freedom in making such changes would be reduced if my term was extended automatically." To be sure, he noted, the government and in particular the Finance Minister have denied any intention to curtail the central bank's independence. Nonetheless, there is now some uncertainty about what will take place and the implications for the central bank's inflation-fighting mandate and its willingness to use the tools at its disposal to fulfil that, he said. "I have no quarrel with the government contemplating different models for the governance of the central bank. But that has to be a good process, a well prepared process, and at the end of the day it is the parliament that has the final word," Gudmundsson said. "But I think it's important to find ways to relieve the kind of short-term uncertainty associated with this and to make an effort to avoid negatively affecting the credibility of and trust in the central bank and its monetary policy process." Asked whether he would potentially be willing to remain at the bank as one of several governors, Gudmundsson, who had been willing to start a second term under the current set-up, replied: "The question for me is not whether I would be willing to be a governor, but rather, will I be willing to apply for the position of governor or possibly of chairman of the board of governors if there is a change to the system? That is something that is impossible for me to say at this point and will depend on the credibility of the process and any potential new framework." Still, he added, "if the process is credible, if I can believe in it, then I might consider doing that." Turning again to the economy, Gudmundsson noted that despite the fact that the central bank has been bulking up its foreign reserves, the krona continues to appreciate on the back of strong net exports including tourism, bringing inflation down "rather rapidly recently," he noted. "We are hoping that we will be very near to our inflation target or even hit it this month," he said. "And our prediction is that we will then stay near the target towards the end of this year. But then, inflationary pressures might begin to increase again because of the slack in the economy turning into a positive output gap. But there are uncertainties about that, for sure." Title: Is there a need for changes to the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee?
text: 03.04.2014 Thorvardur Tjorvi olafsson: Is there a need for changes to the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee? There appear to be plans to review the central bank's (Si) oversight and even the arrangements for monetary policy decision-making. Concerns seem to include the fact that different opinions do not have enough runway within the Monetary Policy Committee and that the Governor has too much weight in the current structure. It is important that such a review looks at the results of research on the desired arrangements for monetary policy decision-making and the five years of experience gained from the current structure. There are two types of monetary policy committees. On the one hand, those who do not place particular emphasis on achieving unity on the decision, each member is in particular responsible for their vote and the results are obtained by vote. The chairmen of such committees may be caught in a minority, and it is common for different viewpoints of committee members to appear publicly. The UK and Sweden monetary policy committees, as well as the US after Ben Bernanke took over in 2006, are examples of such committees. However, there are committees that emphasize that unity prevails over the decision (at least publicly) and the committee as a whole is responsible for it. The position of the Chairman varies where such an order is in place. In some cases, it is very strong, either according to law or tradition, and he is almost unanimous about the policy. This has most often been the case in the United States and famously the way Alan Greenspan spoke and voted before other members, who then had to walk in tandem. In other cases, the position of the chairman is weaker. The European Central Bank is an example of such an arrangement. Since early 2009, the five-member Monetary Policy Committee has exercised monetary policy decision-making powers in Iceland. The committee's structure and practices are essentially in line with the specifications of research (see e.g. A. Blinder, "Making monetary policy by committee", International Finance, 2009:12) and international experience in monetary decision-making arrangements. The committee consists of three representatives from si and two external experts. The Committee has established clear rules of procedure to ensure careful preparation and the greatest transparency of decisions. At the same time, different viewpoints are allowed to enjoy themselves at the same time as it is ensured that there is a consensus on the official presentation of the decision. Furthermore, the Rules of Procedure specify that the Governor does not propose a decision until after the committee members have had the opportunity to outline their position. Is there any reason to fear that the exchange of views within the Committee is too homogeneous and the governor's position too strong in the power of the majority of the committee being appointed by representatives of the SI? The results of voting in 2009-2013 can be found in the annual reports of si, so it is natural to look at the statistics and see if the electoral behaviour bears the characteristics of such blockbuster formations. Since the committee began work, it has in half of its positions chosen to keep interest rates unchanged, in 37% of cases it has reduced them and in 15% of cases they have been raised. The results of the vote show that in about half of the cases, one member of the committee has voted against the majority, and in 17% of cases the vote has gone 3:2. It is not to be seen that one opinion is always prevalent. It is also not to be seen that votes are divided by fixed blocks of internal and external members: in 11% of cases, the internal member has been in the minority, while an external member in 16% of cases (see attached image). Of the individual members, the internal member who applies his mandate to the Governor has most often been in a minority (24% of cases) and voted against his boss, who has himself landed in a minority for once. The deputy governor, who is applying his mandate to ministers and not the governor, has twice been in the minority. If you look only at the cases where there has been a dispute the decision then the majority consists more often of internal and external members than the internal ones alone. In the time votes have fallen 3:2, internal members have only formed the majority in 29% of cases. The division of votes in Iceland seems to be in good harmony with what is common abroad (see, for example, M. King, "The MPC ten years on", speech from 2 May 2007). In view of the above, it will therefore not be seen that different opinions will not be enjoyed within the Committee and that the governor's position is too strong in the current structure. Reassessment of monetary policy frameworks is natural and desirable. However, it matters what reason it takes place and by what means. In Canada, such reassessments are carried out on a regular basis, in good cooperation between the authorities and the Central Bank, and on the basis of in-depth research. It is important to ensure that a review of the SI Act, including possible changes to the structure of the Monetary Policy Committee, is based on the results of international research and the experience gained in Iceland. Let's work and fix the price stability that has now been achieved. orvarour Tjorvi olafsson, economist at the Central Bank of Iceland. The opinions expressed in the article are the authors and do not have to reflect the views of the Central Bank of Iceland.
