Title: Statement at the Breakfast Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce today
text: Birgir isl. Gunnarsson Speech at a meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce Friday 3 December 2004 Good attendees The Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland decided yesterday to increase the Bank's policy rate by one percentage point from 7.25% to 8.25%. I'm going to use my time here today to clarify that decision and then of course discuss the state and outlook for economic and monetary policy, and thus the Bank's new macroeconomic forecast and inflation forecast. Since the Fed last published an inflation forecast in June, the long-term inflation outlook has deteriorated considerably. This can be attributed mainly to higher growth in domestic demand than previously expected. Let me mention a few things that I'll be getting more detailed about below. Economic growth is and will be higher than predicted in June. Increased competition in the credit market has resulted in public access to credit becoming much more favourable than before, and interest rates on long-term mortgage-backed mortgages have fallen. This has led to a sharp increase in lending to individuals and this in turn led to an increase in house prices. The heavy industry plans have still grown and compressed more over the next two years than previously the outlook. Statements on tax cuts have been confirmed and plans for restraint in public spending over the next two years are somewhat unclear. The prospect is that all of these factors will lead to much higher production tensions than previously thought and torched under inflation, particularly in 2006 if nothing is done. Then 2 increase the likelihood that wage items of collective agreements will be reviewed in the year if inflation is not controlled. Let us then deviate from price trends, but stable prices are one of the Bank's main tasks by law, and the inflation target of 21/2% is calculated as an increase in the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX in 12 months. In recent months, inflation has been on the rise, reaching 3.8% in November. This was the seventh consecutive month that inflation measured more than 3.5%. The Office for National Statistics publishes two indices that give an indication of underlying inflation. The annual increase in core Index I, a consumer price index without volatile subs, farms, vegetables, fruits and gasoline, was 3.3% in November and had been around or above 3% over the past seven months. Core Index II, which also excludes public service prices, rose by 3.1% in the 12 months to November, with an annual increase fluctuating around 3% over the past seven months. Inflation is still tied to relatively few subs. Their rise is largely attributable to rising demand, but partly to direct cost pressures. The clearest indicator of demand pressures is the rapid rise in house prices in recent months and years. Of the index's 3.8% rise over the past twelve months, 1.3% is explained by the increase in housing stock. Another 0.6% of the increase in the consumer price index is explained by the price increase in gasoline, but changes in gasoline prices in the global market are quickly reflected in gasoline prices in this country. In addition, the price of public services has risen more than the index as a whole. In this way, more than 4/5 of the inflation rate over the past twelve months is explained by the price increase in housing, gasoline and public services. Except for the above, price increases have been modest. The price of services on the general market had at the beginning of November increased by 2.3% in twelve months, the price of imported goods without alcohol and tobacco by 2.5% and domestic goods without farms and vegetables by 1.6%. 3 There has been little let-up in the increase in the market price of residential housing, and as the impact of increased competition in the mortgage market and the decline in interest rates on mortgages began to take hold in the autumn, residential property prices rose rapidly. In November, the housing stock index had risen by 8.8% in 12 months, resulting in a 1.6% rise in the consumer price index as previously reported. The increase in residential prices over the past twelve months has been the fastest in the capital area but has also been considerable in rural areas. The fastest prices of single-family homes and larger properties in the capital area have risen, or by over 20% over the past twelve months, while the price increase for apartments in residential areas has at the same time been 12%. Over the past four months, the increase in larger assets has been particularly rapid, normally 2-3.5% per month. The macroeconomic forecast, which the Central Bank has now published, forecasts considerably higher growth in demand and economic growth over the next two years than previously done. Let's take a look at each team individually. In June, the Central Bank forecast a 51/2% interest rate on private consumption in 2004. Now it looks like the growth will be considerably higher. Private consumption increased in the first half of 2004 by 7.2% from the same time last year and is forecast to grow at 7% for the year as a whole. Looking to the next two years, it seems one-sided that private consumption will continue to grow rapidly. It is forecast to grow by 91/2% next year and by just under 7% in 2006. There's a lot going on there. Households' response to banks' mortgages has been rapid, with most indications that they will continue to refinance their debts in the coming years, extending the life of outstanding debt at the same time. The payment burden of outgoing loans will therefore lose considerably. Households will therefore have more money at their disposal after interest rates and installments than before, and likely spend the bulk of it on private consumption. Tax cuts will likely have the same effect. In addition, households are likely to respond to a lighter payload with increased borrowing. 4 Consumption growth this year looks set to be approximately 11/2% or similar to what was expected in the Treasury Department's macroeconomic budget published in early October. The impact of the teacher strike, which reduces intergenerational spending in 2004, has also been taken into account and increased in 2005. The Central Bank's forecast estimates the 2.5% growth rate on consumption, but rather more than the budget expected, which accounted for its 2% growth rate. Of these, 3% are in municipalities and 2.3% in the state. The reason for the budget's assumptions about underlying consumption growth is firstly because this year's spending figures appear to indicate that both spending and revenue exceed autumn estimates. In this regard, it can be pointed out that consumption growth has traditionally been underestimated around this time of year in recent years, or an average of 11/2% between 1998 and 2003. However, if the ministry's plans go ahead that we must hope, economic growth would presumably be 1/2% lower in 2005, but the impact of 2006 would not be as great. It would be expected that annual inflation over the next 2 years would be 0.2 - 0.3 percent lower than it would otherwise be. The growth in capital formation is marked by the growing weight of construction of power plants and heavy industry. In June, the Central Bank predicted that capital formation would grow by 17% in 2004, and that forecast appears to be able to go ahead. Capital generation in the first half of the year increased by 19% from the previous year. The growth has most likely been similar in the third quarter of the year, although growth in imported investment products has also declined. It is clear that the government's investments have decreased as the year has progressed and here it is expected to decrease in the latter part of the year. Business investment, however, is growing very rapidly due to power plant construction. Most of the evidence also suggests that residential investment will increase at least as much as last year. The Central Bank forecasts that investment will increase by over 20% next year and by just under 3% in 2006. This is a much higher investment next year than expected in June, but somewhat lower growth in 2006 than predicted. More funding next year is largely explained by changing timings and new plans for 5 heavy industry projects and from increased housing investment, partly attributable to new conditions in the domestic mortgage market and their impact on house prices, which further encourages residential investment. Lower capital formation in 2006 than the last forecast is primarily explained by the fact that investment next year will be higher than previously planned and the growth between 2005 and 2006 is therefore lower. According to the Central Bank's forecast, economic growth will be 5.4% this year and 6.1% next, but will only reduce economic growth in 2006 or to 4.9%. Next year is looking at the highest level of economic growth here since 1987. This macroeconomic forecast for the years 2004 to 2006 indicates a large and growing trade deficit. It is projected to grow from 61/2% of GDP in 2004 to 10% in 2005 and just over 11% in 2006. This, of course, is accompanied by a large amount of debt collection and foreign debt is expected to be around 112% of GDP by the end of 2006. Part of this trade deficit can be attributed to the heavy industry construction, or 40 - 50% during the period. New aluminium smelters will lead to a very high growth in aluminium exports. In 2008, when all projects taken into account in the Central Bank's forecast will be completed, aluminium exports will be about 160% higher than they will be this year. It can be roughly estimated that the value of exported aluminum will be almost ISK 100 billion in 2008, an increase of ISK 60 billion from what it likely will be this year. This will of course help reduce trade deficits once the construction of factories and power plants is completed. It is clear that production over the next two years will far exceed the production capacity of the economy. Based on the revaluation of demand and production capacity in recent years, the estimate of the production voltage in 2001 drops to 11/2% and the slack in 2002 is now estimated to have been around 11/2%. As before, it is believed that the slack has disappeared as early as last year. This year, a new era began. Given the assumptions of the macroeconomic forecast, 6 Among other things, unchanged exchange rates and unchanged control rates from November, in the coming years there will be a significant production voltage of just under 2% this year, just under 4% next year and approximately 5% in 2006. The purpose of forecasting production tensions for two years is to assess the impact of demand on inflation. Given the high level of construction at the same time as much more favourable public access to credit, there is as much production voltage as shown here is not improbable. If economic restraint is increased from what is expected in the forecast, as the Central Bank has already done with the increase in the policy rate announced yesterday, it will reduce production tensions and thus reduce inflationary pressures. I will then deviate from the Central Bank's inflation forecast. I would like to emphasize that, as always, it is based on the unchanged exchange rate, which was now relative to the index 120, and on the Central Bank's unchanged policy rate, i.e. those that were valid this November. This forecast shows first and foremost what inflation would be if the Fed did not act. The inflation forecast is therefore a tool the Fed uses to determine its interest rates. According to the forecast, inflation would be above the Central Bank's inflation target throughout the forecast period and above the upper tolerance of 4% at the end of it. The outlook is for this year's average inflation to be 3.2%, which is in line with the Bank's forecast from June. Next year's average inflation would be according to the forecast of 3.4%. In 2006, the average inflation rate is forecast to be 3.5% and just under 4.5% over the year. The main driving force for the next two years is the growing domestic demand, leading to rising production tensions, i.e. production beyond the long-term production capacity of the national economy. However, I would like to reiterate once again that the Central Bank's decision on an interest rate hike yesterday is intended to prevent the developments that the forecast suggests will actually occur. It is intended to contribute to the re-reaching of the inflation target. I'm going to give a few words to the great lending expansion that has been here in recent times, but the growth in lending has been much higher but can be compatible with stable prices in the long run. Lending as a whole increased by 15.4% in the 12 months to the end of June. 7 Figures on the loan system as a whole until the end of September are not available, but growth can be close by adding up lending by credit institutions, the Housing Financing Fund and pension funds. By the end of September, the lending of these entities had increased by 22% in 12 months. Commercial lending had increased particularly rapidly. By the end of June, lending to the business sector had increased by over a fifth, and by the end of September, lending by depositors to the business sector had increased by almost a third. Lending to individuals has also grown significantly in the past two quarters. The annual growth rate on aggregate lending by depositors, pension funds and the Housing Financing Fund to individuals at the end of September was 14%. Figures on lending by depositors and the Housing Financing Fund are available until the end of October. Domestic lending by depositors increased by just over 7% in that month and had increased by a third in one year. The lending growth at deposit institutions is in some ways at the expense of the Housing Financing Fund and perhaps pension funds, but no information is available on pension fund lending in October. By the end of October, lending by depositors and the Housing Financing Fund had increased by almost 23% in one year. I will then slightly deviate from the Central Bank's changing policy on foreign exchange purchases. Since the beginning of September 2002, the Central Bank of Iceland has regularly purchased foreign exchange in the domestic foreign exchange market for the sole purpose of strengthening its foreign exchange reserves, but the Bank's foreign position had been significantly diminished, mainly due to its interventions in the foreign exchange market in 2000 and 2001. From September 2002 to next year, the total amount of foreign exchange purchases will probably be around ISK 75 billion and the foreign exchange reserves will likely be around ISK 70 billion by the end of the year. The Central Bank does not consider it material to further strengthen the reserves as it stands. It has therefore been decided that at the beginning of 2005 regular foreign exchange purchases will be discontinued to strengthen the Bank's foreign exchange reserves. From that time on, the Central Bank will only buy foreign currency in the domestic foreign exchange market to meet the needs of the Treasury for payments on foreign loans. Accordingly, the Bank will in 2005 buy US2.5 million once a week on the market. The Central Bank will buy foreign currency on behalf of 8 the Treasury if the repayments of foreign loans exceed the capacity within these plans and notify market makers in the foreign exchange market of the arrangement of the purchase in advance. Finally, I want to say a few words about the monetary policy. The interest rate hike now is truly unusual. It must be examined in light of how rapidly conditions in the credit market have changed in the past, that the main weight of investment in power plants and aluminium smelters is short and that the activities associated with them will increase faster than previously thought. It should be noted that although the policy rate has been raised five times by a total of less than 2 percentage points between May and November, real control rates at the end of November, based on the inflation rate of non-indexed government bonds were only slightly if somewhat higher than the estimated natural real interest rates in Iceland, i.e. real interest rates that, on average, above the economic cycle, can be expected to conform to the balance of the economy. Inflation expectations have been higher than desirable, resulting in the Central Bank's interest rate hikes so far not biting as expected. It may again have played a part in keeping inflation expectations high. By raising interest rates more in one step now than has been customary, the Central Bank seeks, among other things, to ensure that the Bank's expected real operating interest rates rise, both through higher nominal interest rates and lower inflation expectations. This reflects the Bank's intention that monetary policy provides sufficient restraint to keep inflation in check when the construction weight reaches an even higher level. Speculation that has been raised in the public debate that the Central Bank's controls are no longer biting are based on misunderstandings. The monetary policy trading process may have changed, but it is there and monetary policy will have the desired effect. Given the Bank's unchanged policy rate from what it was in November, the prospect of inflation would be significantly higher than the 21/2% inflation target when collective bargaining wage items can be reviewed in November next year. The inflation outlook for that period has deteriorated considerably since the last forecast. Leading high inflation to further 9 Wage increases would worsen the inflation outlook in 2006. This could lead to more interest rate hikes in 2006. In order to have a sufficiently rapid impact on inflation during this period, we need to act quickly and in a timely manner. As we now see, the Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates further in coming months. In the coming years, monetary policy will have to deal with situations that will greatly test the resilience of the national economy. It is very important that monetary policy and fiscal policy work together under these conditions. The heavier the burdens placed on the monetary policy during this period, the greater the negative side effect of adherent monetary policy. The Central Bank has placed great emphasis on relieving monetary policy with strict fiscal restraint and the public sector as a whole. The budget bill for 2005 entails a somewhat increased restraint compared to the previous year. Nevertheless, the economic volatility-adjusted performance of the Treasury in 2005 and 2006 looks to be considerably poorer than in the overheating years of 1999 and 2000. The restraint then proved inadequate given that significant repercussions of the overheating occurred in 2001 and 2002. In order to offset the stimulus of tax cuts in the coming years, a very drastic cut in government spending is needed that will no doubt face resistance. Therefore, it is a real concern how vague the plans for cuts are. Most years, public spending has tended to exceed budgets. In making monetary policy decisions, it is therefore wary of relying on ambitious plans for spending cuts to go ahead fully, because if it does not happen, it may not be too late to respond to its consequences in the circumstances ahead. The Central Bank must target monetary policy actions on the progress it considers most likely. On the basis of this, the Bank raised interest rates now and is prepared to raise them further in order to direct inflation as soon as possible to the 21/2% inflation target.

Title: Talks about errors in economic forecasts
text: With accuracy in economic forecasts e7sgeir Dan92elsson The core addressed the distortions in growth forecasts in an article published on 26 February under the heading "The Central Bank's growth forecasts and Statistics Iceland are almost always wrong" ( /). The article states that the Central Bank's forecast for economic growth in 2006 of 4.2% was the Bank's only forecast that has proved to be just up to one decimal point. All other forecasts for economic growth between 2000 and 20013 were incorrect based on this accuracy. This method of measuring the quality of economic forecasts is somewhat unusual but let it be. One of the most important but also difficult things about the presentation of economic forecasts is to explain the uncertainty in them. Sometimes the reaction to such an explanation goes something like this: "I hear that friend that you just don't know anything about this." Famously, former President Harry Truman's remarks asked for a one-armed economist because he was tired of listening to economists discuss that "on the one hand" this could happen but "on the other hand" something else. While there is uncertainty in forecasts d0 and it is often important to understand how great it is and specifically address certain anomalies that are considered likely d0 it does not diminish the importance of the information inherent in the (basic) forecasts. Forecasts for growth in 2006 The history of the error in the forecast for economic growth in 2006 is a good example of the tensions that come with the work of macroeconomic forecasters. As stated in the article in Kjarnainn, the Central Bank predicted the first issue of Monetary Bulletin of 2006, published in March of that year, that the year's economic growth would be 4.2%. The Office for National Statistics' first official figure on economic growth for the year was published in March 2007, a volume of 2.6%, which meant the Bank had overstated economic growth by 1.6 percentage points. Later, the Office for National Statistics raised the estimate of economic growth, and since 2011, its estimate was that 2006 economic growth had been 4.7%, which meant that the Central Bank had underestimated economic growth for the year by 0.5 percentage points. This was the case until 19 September 2014, when statistics published revised figures on economic growth from 1998, when it was revealed that economic growth in 2006 was 4.2% and d0 bingo! d0 The forecast from March 2006 turned out to be right up to one decimal place! A few weeks ago, Danish economist Lars Christensen was interviewed on national television. It described him as the man who predicted the crisis in 2006 in the fall of 2008. In the spring of 2006, Christensen came to Iceland and recently presented Danske Bank's report on the Icelandic economy ( ) at a famous meeting at the Grand Hotel. In this report, it is likely that there will be an economic recession of 5-10% in Iceland over the next two years. At the meeting, Christensen waved a copy of the Fed's Monetary Bulletin, saying it had a similar forecast. While both sides predicted that economic growth would decline, neither predicted that all three big Icelandic banks would fall. If it had been added to the forecasts, they would have been much darker than they were. 2004-2006 was a good year for the Icelandic economy. Growth was 8.2% in 2004, 6.0% in 2005 and 4.2% in 2006, all according to the latest statistics. Unemployment was very low, but inflation shot upwards in 2006 as a result of the rate decline. Whether people were looking to make sure that the economy of a developed economy is unlikely to grow at this pace for years in a row or were concerned about the consequences of overheating, such as inflation, and wanted the government to use its controls to reduce it, it was reasonable to expect economic growth to decline. But the growth rate of 2007 surprised many prophets uncomfortably, but those inconveniences came in stages. In March 2007, the Central Bank forecast a 0.8% interest rate. In March 2008, when the Office for National Statistics published the first figures for the year's economic growth of 3.8%, this forecast looked nothing derisive, although it might not exactly be good. The Office for National Statistics soon raised the estimate of economic growth in 2007, accounting for 6.0% between 2010 and 2013, but in the revision published on 19 September, the growth rate for the year had reached 9.7% and the skew in the Central Bank's forecast was 8.9 percent, which is of course derivative. Different methods of measuring economic growth At the bottom of the article in Kjarnainn, an educational material on the concepts of GDP and economic growth is referred to as part of an educational material originally published on national television under the heading "Journey to Money", but The Essence has published excerpts from these factors. The stated objective of this educational material is very respectful, to educate Icelandic the public about finances. Much is done there very well, but somehow it has reproduced so that many key concepts in economics are incorrectly explained, including a respected and serious TV presenter being given a false definition of trade balance and misrepresenting the context of trade balance with the national debt position in an episode aired on Rf2V on January 22nd. to measure GDP. GDP can be measured in three ways: It is possible to measure how people and businesses allocate their money for the purchase of newly produced goods and services (disposition settlement); the added value can be measured in all companies in the country (production settlement) and it is possible to measure the income from production in the form of wages, interest, profits and rent (income splitting settlement). If everything is correctly calculated and all the information based on the correctness, these three methods should give the exact same result. But that's not the case, either in this country or abroad. Statistics Iceland published its first revenue splitting results in November, but the calculation of GDP is still based on calculations from the disposition side and from the production side. There was a time when the National Statistics Agency, which handled national accounts until it was shut down in 2002 and statistics took over this project, specifically published what came out of the settlement of national accounts from the production side as well as the result received from the disposable side. Differences in GDP measurements from the disposition side and from the production side were shown in tables and referred to as "differences in settlement methods". The largest was this difference in 1990, when it was 8.0% of GDP according to disposable results and in 1983 when it was 7.9%. The lowest value was also in 1990 when GDP according to production results was calculated again according to a new basis. Since 1998, the National Statistical Institute/Statistics Iceland has not published the results of production results and disposition statements separately, but the figures are streamlined so that the outcome is as close as possible to what is believed to be the correct value. Statistics from other countries use most of this method, thereby using information from all three methods to measure GDP. Sometimes the average is calculated, but most of the time we try to assess the reliability of this different information and the final value of GDP and economic growth is calculated from that. It was once mentioned here as a job tasked with examining tax evasion, and she used the differences in settlement methods to measure the extent of such evasion. The disposition statement was expected to measure GDP correctly, but that the production settlement lacked the added value of those working black. While the idea behind this plan is not entirely out of the question, it is probable that the difference in settlement methods is a poor measure of the extent of tax evasion. However, its magnitude and variability provide clues to the uncertainty in gdp measurements. The importance of analyzing predictive errors The analysis of errors in forecasts is very important. Therefore, the Central Bank regularly publishes an overview of errors in the Bank's forecasts. A few in recent years, the coverage of the errors in the forecasts has appeared in the last issue of Monetary Bulletin of each year, most recently in Monetary Bulletin 2014-4 ( ) discussing errors in the Bank's forecasts in 2013. Table 4 shows that the Bank underestimated economic growth in 2013 in all Monetary Bulletin issued in 2013 and in the first issue issued in 2014. When this staple was released, the office for National Statistics' first gdp figures for the first three quarters of 2013 were low. The average forecast error in these five forecasts was 1.3 percent, and the skew in the first forecast was 1.4 percent. Some aspects of the processing of macroeconomic forecasts are easy to foresee. Others are more difficult. A few weeks ago, for example, it was decided to increase the capelin quota during the current season by 320,000 tonnes. Its impact on this year's GDP is probably in the range of 1/2 - 1%. The price of oil has fallen sharply in recent months with a significant impact on inflation and the balance of trade. When assessing uncertainty in forecasts for economic growth in iceland, a skew of 1 percentage point is not a large size. There is probably uncertainty in the Office for National Statistics' measurements of economic growth at least 1 percent. When the uncertainty is this high, it is unwarranted to give up measurements and forecasts with decimal places. When the Office for National Statistics released its first figure on economic growth in 2007 of 3.8%, it indicates that the accuracy in the measure is 0.1 percent, i.e. that the correct figure lies in the range of 3.75-3.85%. The cancellation to the next full number, 4% in this case, would be closer, but it would indicate that the accuracy in the measurement was up to 1 percentage point. The same goes for predictions of economic growth. In doing so, I am not suggesting that the Office for National Statistics stop publishing figures for economic growth of one decimal point or that the Central Bank stop publishing forecasts specifying the forecast for economic growth by a single decimal point. There are international traditions in these matters that are difficult to violate, and GDP is not just an economic concept but part of a tax return that state contributions to international organizations take into account. However, it is appropriate to keep this size of uncertainty in mind when reading statistics and economic forecasts. The difference between a forecast of 3.2% and another of 3.3%, or even up to 3.6% is within all normal margins of error, at least in this country and probably in many other states as well. e7sgeir Dan92elsson The writer is director of research and forecasting at the Economic and Monetary Policy Department of the Central Bank of Iceland. The opinions expressed in this article are the authors.

Title: The release of controls and the path to stability
text: 4 December 2015 Arnor Sighvatsson, Deputy Governor The release of capital controls and the path to permanent stability speech delivered at a symposium of the Association of Certified Public Accountants Good attendees It has been almost seven years since capital controls were introduced following the collapse of all of Iceland's major banks and the sharp fall in the krona. It is now understood that the restrictions that were bound can be resolved before the 8th anniversary of the oceans. It is therefore appropriate to look back and ask what we have learned from the events that caused capital controls to become inevitable for a while, from the implementation of the controls, of the government's efforts to prepare for the release of capital controls and from the events that shook the financial and economy of the whole world at the same time. If we can learn the right lessons from these events, we can hope to avoid major shocks of the kind we have faced in recent years, even though the economy will still go through hills and lows. The modern market system is built on trust. Auditors are reliably clear, other professions rather, as it can be argued that the essence of the auditor's day-to-day work is to make sure that information published by companies and institutions about their activities provides a true and correct picture of their position, which is a prerequisite for customers, investors and governments to have confidence in the company in question. The stability of financial institutions and currencies is particularly sensitive to events that can affect the trust that is being borne to them, and when trust fails without warning, the consequences can become serious. From overbelief to distrust A precursor to cross-border trust, however, is often a period of over-belief that turns out to be based on sand, as happened in the run-up to the banking collapse in 2008. Economic success for many years and long-standing stability had dulled the judgment of many investors who underestimated the risks of the financial imbalance that was gradually building and pumped it money into risky investments around the world. Some of this capital was sought in Iceland, where major events, external conditions and domestic economic management pushed up expectations that proved unrealistic. Obvious warning signs, in the form of massive lending growth, an asset price bubble, an unsustainable trade deficit and persistent tensions in the national economy, long did not degrade many people's belief in the Icelandic economic wonder, fueled by several fairytale banks. Hesitation hit some lenders in the autumn of 2005, more in March 2006, and after several foreign banks had lost confidence, and thus life in 2008, over-belief had turned into total distrust. The precipice was largely financed by foreign credit in the short term. The banks therefore communicated to households and businesses, and indirectly to the public sector, as opposed to the hedging of foreign bond issuers in isk Icelandic. The bonds had sold to investors in search of better returns than the one offered in the bond markets of low-interest rates. With the collapse of the banks, trust in the banks collapsed not only, but also in the Treasury, the economy as a whole and thus the country's currency. As a result, all capital was abandoned, whether it was claims against the fallen banks, the Treasury or other parties, which were not stopped anytime soon except by capital controls. Foreign credit markets closed almost entirely at the same time. Once the capital controls were introduced, short-term foreign demands on domestic entities that were expected to be dynamic (especially so-called "offshore krona") amounted to approximately a third of GDP. There was also considerable uncertainty about possible outflows from domestic sources, as expectations of the escape of certain capital are likely to cause the instability of other capital that would otherwise be stable. The combination of the claims and assets of the winding-up of fallen financial institutions was at the time an irrational size, but it was later estimated that the indirect requirements of foreign entities on domestic assets of the trustees amounted to almost 40% of GDP, although the net impact on foreign exchange markets had likely been somewhat smaller, or between 20-25% of GDP. When this problem became fully apparent in 2012, it was decided to move the winding-up estates also under the capital controls for the most part. Capital controls were in these circumstances a prerequisite for ensuring adequate stability of the currency, thereby reducing uncertainty about the economy of the Treasury, financial institutions, households and businesses during the restructuring of their economy. It was unclear how much the Treasury would actually owe, i.e. taking into account costs that might fall on the Treasury because of the financial crash. It was clear that the budget deficit would be huge in the first few years and debt collection depending on it. The balance sheet of the new banks was extremely fragile, both because of foreign exchange risk because their liabilities were almost exclusively in isk but assets largely tied to foreign currencies, and because a large proportion of lending was overdue, reflecting devalued households and businesses. The foreign exchange reserves controlled by the Central Bank were totally inadequate in light of the balance of payments problem. Capital controls provided scope The capital controls imposed on 28 November 2008 and the borrowing of the International Monetary Fund and neighbouring countries, in conjunction with the relevant economic plan, gave scope to solve the balance of payments faced by the national economy, build a new financial system, restructure household and corporate debt, and master public finances so that the Treasury could refinance foreign debt. At the same time, the capital controls reduced the need for an increase in interest rates to overcome the inflation that followed the fall of the krona and made it possible to lower them again faster than otherwise after inflation began to rebound, accelerating the economic recovery. The capitals also supported the economic recovery by tempering the decline in domestic asset prices. The benefits of this policy have been unequivocal. First, the exchange rate of the krona has been relatively stable in relation to the circumstances and contributed to the stability of prices. The current period of low inflation is the longest since the inflation target was adopted. Second, one of the longest periods of economic growth in recent economic history has been ongoing since 2010 with associated job creation and unemployment falling low. Third, in a relatively short period of time, it was sufficiently successful in the state budget so that the Treasury could refinance debt in the general market. The yield on foreign treasury bonds has fallen and the terms offered to the Treasury at the moment are well acceptable. Fourth, government market access abroad has now paved the way for market access for commercial banks, which have also restructured their own economies in ways that make them more credible borrowers in international markets. They have reduced their own foreign exchange risk as their customers' unprotected foreign exchange risk has diminished and recovery has improved after the restructuring of the loan portfolio. It has returned them to a strong equity position in international comparison and the liquidity position is strong enough to withstand significant pressures on the disposal of capital controls. The strong position of the Treasury and the banking system is an important prerequisite for loosening the capital controls without much risk. Fifth, the economy has been characterised by a better external balance than has prevailed for a long time, and the economic recovery has at least not so far been at the expense of that balance as is often the case, although blinkers are now in the air. It can be assumed that the above results would have been much more torrid without the capital controls. While the economic policies carried out under the cover of capital controls have proved effective, the controls have also created a new problem, resulting in them not being released without the risk of instability unless 2 Special actions are taken. I do not mean the long-term cost of capital controls in the form of lost job opportunities, many of which have become frequent, but rather the short-term problems that were achieved in the shelters of the seas. Nevertheless, it is best to know the moderation of rejoicing over this situation. Newly acquired balance can be easily disrupted again by an unfortunate mix of external circumstances, an unrealistic response from the private sector and unscrupulous economic management. It is already possible to discern the first signs that an old-fashioned event is about to begin, which if the likelihood of a new recession eventually ends. A number of reforms aim to increase the resilience of the financial system, thereby reducing the likelihood of its effectiveness being disrupted by the downturn, costs falling on taxpayers or, at worst, the vicious cycle of government debt problems and financial institutions' capital problems forming as happened in some European countries a few years ago and to a certain extent also in Iceland. The most important reforms are likely to involve substantially increased capital requirements to be made to banks in Europe and around the world given the state of prevailing before the financial crisis. The capital requirements consist, among other things, of several capital buffer laws that include different penalties if a financial undertaking does not meet the requirements. The increases are divided into "protection buffers", "systemic risk buffers", "increase on systemically important financial institutions" and "countercyclical capital buffers". They come in addition to capital requirements that the Financial Supervisory Authority can make, under another pillar of the so-called Basel Rules, that individual financial undertakings bind equity in order to meet specific risks on their balance sheet. These increased demands should lead to the fact that if losses occur in the operations, they will be dealt with sooner to approach financial institutions risk limits. At the same time, clearer international standards are being set up for the implementation of supervision of financial institutions that should give them greater restraint and reduce the risk of latent risks being generated, which will not appear on their balance sheet in a timely manner. Among the issues that need to be taken into account is whether the ratios should vary in terms of the economic cycle and thus be a direct countercyclical instrument or whether the ratios will be kept unchanged, thus having only indirect implicit effects on volatility. It added that their application concerns equality between generations, which could raise questions about the proxy problems of regulators tasked with applying the devices. It adds to the problem that the experience of their application is further limited. Before the banking collapse, monetary policy faced the problem of restraining inflation under the conditions of domestic overheating but low interest rates abroad. The capital inflows that followed increased interest rates countered monetary policy efforts to restrain domestic demand growth, reduced the bite of policy during the boom and intensified the downturn as huge inflows turned into capital exodus. There is some evidence that monetary policy may face similar problems in coming years in the low-interest rate environment that now characterizes the rest of the world, although the scale of the influx is still laid off from the heights it reached then. If a trade deficit financed by foreign credit and weaknesses in the financial system is generated, the transition could be earlier and faster than it would otherwise be because Iceland has previously imposed capital controls in such a position. Lenders and investors may therefore expect it to happen again with detrimental effects for them. There are several ways to temper capital inflows and thereby reduce the risk of capital exodus, with the associated adverse effects on the implementation of monetary policy and financial stability. First, a fiscal policy aimed at reducing domestic demand could be run and thus the need for adhering to monetary policy. The Public Finances Bill contains provisions relating to long-term policy formulation in the public finances and should contribute to improved economic management, but experience must determine how well its objectives will be achieved in implementation. Government revenues are highly susceptible to economic volatility, and there is a risk of easing fiscal restraints as tensions begin to develop in the national economy, as already shows signs. Second, to some extent, the volatility can be softened by a more active interventionist policy in the foreign exchange market, as the Central Bank has pursued in recent years. However, it should be avoided to use the Central Bank's foreign exchange reserves to erase fluctuations in exchange rates altogether, as they are an important monetary policy trading route in a small open economy. An active intervention policy also comes with significant costs, especially if the difference between resource returns on the one hand and interest on domestic funding of the interventions on the other will be great. Third, it is considered to curb the influx by direct measures (so-called cash flow instruments), e.g. a tax on inflows, a general tax on all capital transactions (so-called Tobin tax) or a special reserve requirement on foreign funding. Measures aimed at tempering inflows, along with narrower rules on foreign exchange balances and restrictions on loans to unprotected parties could by imposing other macroprudential instruments supported by monetary policy, thus reducing the problems associated with independent monetary policy under the conditions of unrestricted capital movements and helping to preserve the stability of the financial system. However, it is not entirely clear how far this can go within the framework of the Agreement on European Union 8 the Economic Area. It can also be assumed that with such measures, some of the feasibility benefits that free movements of capital movements are considered to result in will be lost. Little experience has yet been gained in the application of macroprudential and financial flow instruments that I mentioned above, and uncertainty about their effectiveness is considerable. The government's reliance on monetary policy and macroprudential policies to be solely responsible for softening volatility in the national economy, the undesirable side effect will be greater. However, if policy is improved in the state budget or at least to reduce its tendency to be enraged by economic volatility, it can be hoped that the application of macroprudential tools will be a useful aid. However, the above macroprudential cautions may also prove to be an inadequate tool to prevent excessive capital inflows when monetary conditions in Iceland become very different from conditions in the outside world. Therefore, it would be helpful, as long as there is a willingness to run an independent monetary policy, to be able to take special action in order to slow the influx of capital during the boom. The temperation of capital inflows involves varying degrees of efforts to isolate monetary conditions in Iceland from prevailing conditions in the rest of the world. It also includes vague costs and possibilities of circumvention. The alternative is to move in the opposite direction: abandon independent monetary policy while seeking greater co-insurance through participation in the Currency Union and the European Banking Union. Instead of seeking to reduce risks by isolating monetary conditions in Iceland from those in the outside world, it would focus on co-insurance through increased integration of Icelandic economy and monetary and financial systems with the European. I hope I've been able to show that some useful lessons have been drawn. It will become clear in the coming years whether the improvements that have been undertaken or will be undertaken in the near term will be enough to prevent similar events from recurring. I think the likelihood of such a serious event has at least decreased considerably. The second thing is that history is not a cycle. Measures aimed at preventing risk from forming in ways that caused the last crisis do not necessarily prevent the formation of same-sex risks in new ways, which will cause many to say, "This time it's different," cf. Title: The Governor's article on the success and exchange rate of the krna
text: 05.01.2017 The Governor's article on the success and exchange rate of the krona It's going very well in the icelandic economy at the moment. It's full employment and perhaps a good thing better, as evidenced by the massive immigration of foreign labour and the fact that about 40% of businesses complain of a shortage of labour. In addition to this, the purchasing power of wages is at historic highs, and household assets in excess of debt have not for a long time been greater. We have previously been through high-spiked employment and purchasing power along with rising tensions in the national economy. It has often ended badly as the many imbalances in the national economy intensified to the point that snap adaptations did not escape. Now, however, the balance of the economy is, after all, much better than before. Measured inflation is below the inflation target, but people and businesses' expectations of future inflation are at that. The savings of households and households are much higher now than usual at this stage of the economic cycle, and for this reason there is a significant surplus on our trade with foreign countries. It can also soften the impact of crises that may become the resilience of the national economy is greater than often because the leverage of households, businesses and the public sector has decreased considerably in recent years and the foreign position of the economy is good. Foreign exchange reserves have not been relatively larger since the end of World War II. Banks have a lot of equity and have good liquidity. In particular, there are three factors that play the most part in a relatively good position. First, a huge improvement in business rates in recent times. Second, the growth of travel. Third, economic management, including monetary policy, and precautionary policies regarding the financial system that have jointly contributed to low inflation, created incentives for savings, and strengthened the resilience of the national economy and the financial system. In the year leading up to last year, export revenues (the purchasing power of exports of goods and services towards imports) increased by nearly a third, mainly due to improved trading conditions and the growth of tourism. This sharp increase is the main reason for strong economic growth, and it, together with monetary policy, plays a major role in the fact that large wage increases have primarily resulted in increased purchasing power and not in increased inflation. The same factors explain the large trade surplus that has contributed to the strengthening of the krona. What's the risk? Is there no possible woe? Yes, of course. The risk of severe overheating of the national economy is obvious. Trade conditions could deteriorate again. Then there could be a backlash to travel. It is important that the relevant parties are alert to these risks and try where possible to reduce the likelihood that the risks will be realised. The government must also seek to preserve and strengthen the resilience of the national economy. In this way, the trauma and its consequences can be softened. In the short term at least, we can have little impact on the terms of trade determined in foreign markets. However, too much demand can be reduced by adhering economic management, thereby reducing the likelihood of swift adjustments later on. The significant easing of monetary policy restraint aimed at a swift reduction in real interest rates contradicts the current circumstances of that target. Long-term real interest rates, however, may continue to subside if savings levels remain high, and the balance in the national economy will not be too disrupted anytime soon. But then someone may ask: What about the great strengthening of the crown? Isn't that the biggest risk? To answer that question, you need to be aware of the reasons for the higher exchange rate. It seems obvious that it is primarily the result of the developments I have made here as a topic of discussion, especially in the second half of the year. Thus, in the third quarter there was a record trade surplus, primarily rooted in the surplus in services trade. At the same time, the capital inflows were very low. Overall, the Central Bank's actions during the year have counteracted the strengthening of the exchange rate. Designated reserve requirement on capital inflows into the bond market and into deposits has almost stopped interest-only trading. Last Tuesday, the bank had purchased foreign exchange for the year for 385 ma.kr. That's about 40% more than in 2015. The krona can certainly override, however, and it supports the cautiousness inherent in heavy foreign exchange purchases, although it is not conclusively possible to assert that the exchange rate is much above balance given the prevailing circumstances. Despite the above, some believe the Fed should simply buy much more and cut interest rates significantly in charm. But it is not expendable as the internal balance of the national economy and price stability are then compromised. After all, the increase in the exchange rate partly entails the national adjustment to the growth of the tourism sector after full employment is reached. It can therefore be seen as the market's way of directing development on a more sustainable path. To mitigate the risks certainly inherent in this development, it is therefore most effective to cut to the root causes of the problem that at present lies in too much competition for the workforce, housing and various other savers of this country. Travel is so important that it can't be excluded. Article published in Frettablaoio, December 30, 2016.

Title: Address at the Bank's annual meeting
text: April 5, 2018 Address orunnar Guomundsdottir, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the 57th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 5 April 2018. Supreme President of Iceland, Prime Minister, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, Minister of Education, Science and Culture, Minister of Transport and Local Government, President of the Althingi, Governors, Delegates of Foreign Countries and other good guests. I welcome you and present here with the 50th and seventh annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. As previously stated on this occasion, the statutory role of the Board of Directors is to monitor that the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with the laws applicable to its operations. In addition, the Board of Directors confirms various decisions and rules set by the Governor. The Council consists of seven members elected after the election to the Althingi. At the beginning of 2017, the Board of Directors was appointed so that the chairman was orunn Guomundsdottir. Other members were Jon Helgi Egilsson, Ingibjorg Ingvadottir, Ragnar arnason, agust olafur agustsson, Bjorn Valur Gislason and Auour Hermannsdottir. The Board of Directors was elected on 25 April 2017, but the members of the Board of Directors were orunn Guomundsdottir, who was elected chairman at the first meeting of the newly elected Council, Bjorn Valur Gislason, Sigurour Kari Kristjansson, or Saari, Sveinn Agnarsson, Frosti Sigurjonsson and Auour Hermannsdottir. The Board of Directors held 13 meetings during the year. As stated in the annual report presented here, the Central Bank carries out regular tasks in relation to the Bank's objectives as well as various initiatives. In March of last year, the historic milestone was reached that capital controls were largely loosened. However, important projects related to the final release of the capital controls and a new foreign exchange framework are still underway after the controls are gone. During the year, extensive improvements to in-house IT were carried out and a new business system was put into use after considerable preparation. At the same time, a great deal of work was carried out on the renewal of the Bank's interbank systems, the so-called balancing system and a large payment system. This work continues this year, but work must be distributed on the implementation of the current financial infrastructure in the banking system to reduce risks to it and pressures on IT departments and the Banks' Data Centre. According to the law, the central bank's main objective is to promote stable prices. At the same time, the Central Bank shall promote financial stability. Inflation remained below the inflation target throughout last year. The Monetary Policy Committee kept the Bank's main interest rate unchanged ahead of the year, falling in May, June and October by a total of 0.75 percentage points. This is further explained in the second chapter of the Bank's annual report. In 2017, economic conditions were essentially favourable to the financial system. As a year ago, the leverage of households and businesses was relatively modest in historical terms and their scope to meet shocks more than for a long time. The position of the big commercial banks at the end of the year was solid; capital ratios were high and liquidity was well above the minimum. This is discussed in the third chapter of the annual report. One of the main functions of the Central Bank is to preserve the foreign exchange reserves of the population. The stock market has been quite large in recent years. Last year it decreased by almost ISK 130 billion and amounted to ISK 687 billion at year-end. His reduction was mainly due to settlements with offshore krona holders and repayment of foreign debt by the Treasury. However, the reserves were still large by the end of the year on most scales. According to the income statement, losses from the Bank's operations amounted to just over ISK 23 billion in 2017, while the previous year the loss was just under ISK 35 billion. The Bank's negative performance is mainly due to the foreign exchange reserves and is explained by negative exchange rate and interest rates as can be seen in the accounts that are available here. Wages and related expenses decreased by 3% between years after increasing by 9% in the previous year. The Bank's assets amounted to ISK 764 billion at the end of the year, while equity decreased from ISK 44 billion to ISK 22 billion. The Bank's capital ratio was 2.9% at year-end, compared with 5% at year-end 2016 and 8.6% at year-end 2015. Profits are not available and the Bank considers it not time to decide on the withdrawal of equity on the basis of Article 34 of Act No. 36/2001, as set out in the annual report. Last year, a milestone in the operation of companies owned by the Bank was established when a winding-up process was started at the Central Bank of Iceland ehf., or ESi. A resolution committee was appointed over the company in October and completed a recall to it in December. The winding-up process of ESi-owned companies, i.e. Hilda and the SPB, also started last year and completed a recall to those clubs in July. The plan is to end these partnerships this year. ESi was established at the end of 2009 and had the role of preserving, processing and collecting the requirements that the Central Bank had in the wake of the banking collapse. When the company was founded, its balance sheet amounted to ISK 491 billion, while equity was ISK 1 million. At the end of last year, the size of the balance sheet was down to more than ISK 8 billion and a large part of that was bank deposits. In the eight years since its establishment, ESi has fully settled its loan with the Central Bank, paid about ISK 69 billion in interest and the same amount in dividends to the Central Bank, as well as almost ISK 20 billion in taxes paid to the Treasury. The company has Therefore, a total of ISK 157 billion was returned to the Central Bank and the Treasury. With the dissolution of the ESi, a complex settlement project is completed which the Bank's subsidiary was entrusted with solving and a significant period following the banking collapse has ended. An important final step was taken in capital controls emissions in March last year without any disruption to any financial or economic stability. Emissions may have taken longer than many hoped, but the process was well planned and was always guided by the impact on the economy. It happened, and the case. The capital controls were a considerable intervention, but there was also some work to be done to loosen them, as the Central Bank's foreign exchange controls have played a major role in both the regulation and the resolution of various issues. A nearly decade has passed since a severe currency crisis hit and the banking system ran out of money. These events made a mark on national life and in a way still do so. At this juncture, there will be no reason to pause and look back and evaluate how things have turned out. Indeed, it took longer than originally planned to resolve the shock and the complications caused by the crash. We can say, however, that on the whole, it has been a success and that the national interest now stands firmer than anyone dared hope or anyone ever dreamed of. Undoubtedly, events will continue to be disputed in the lead-up to the crisis and subsequent responses. However, it will be barely disputed that within these walls there was an ordeal to save what was saved, including securing financial services and payment services in the country and abroad when the breaker of the crisis raged on and in its wake. At the end of 2017, there were a total of 185 employees at the Central Bank. The gender ratio remained fairly even, with 92 men and 93 women at the end of the year. The executive group consisted of six men and five women before the end of the year, but that changed after the new year, so that women in that position had grown to six and the five men. Although the main objectives of the Central Bank's work were simplified by a change in the law in 2001 in promoting stable prices, there are more targets and many projects. The Bank conducts high-quality research activities in the Bank's field, as published publications and essays testify. Data collection and information processing must meet the strict international requirements set by our participation in international co-operation and everywhere we need to be most careful whether it is in the regulation, handling of funds or in dealings with other authorities, other domestic entities or foreign entities. In order to do the work and achieve the objectives set by the operation, qualified employees are required and the Bank must have a grant to fulfil its statutory role. I would therefore like to finally take this opportunity to thank the Bank's employees for their exceptionally good cooperation in 2017. In particular, I would like to thank the members of the Board of Directors, the Governor, the Deputy Governor, the Secretary of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their good cooperation. We are now listening to prime minister Katrin Jakobsdottir's address, and after that Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, will speak.

Title: Interview with the Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland on the IMF website
text: Search ABOUT RESEARCH COUNTRIES CAPACITY DEVELOPMENT NEWS VIDEOS IMF NEWS DATA PUBLICATIONS COVID-19 Mar Guomundsson has been Governor of Icelands Central Bank since 2009 (photo: IMF) IMF COUNTRY FOCUS (/EN/NEWS/COUNTRY-FOCUS?KICKERTRUE) IMF and Iceland: Candid Discussions May 3, 2017 Iceland, a Nordic country with a population of 340,000, has staged a spectacular turnaround of its economic fortunes. In 2008, its banks and currency collapsed in a financial meltdown that led to capital controls, austerity, and a 2.1 billion IMF-supported program. But today, Iceland is booming, with a growth rate of 7.2 percent of GDP in 2016. 1/3 RELATED LINKS Preliminary economic findings Iceland and the IMF 2017 Spring Meetings In a wide-ranging interview, Governor of Icelands central bank Mar Guomundsson talked about how Iceland turned its economy around. In mid-March, most of Icelands remaining capital controls were lifted, closing another chapter in the book on Icelands financial crisis. What do you expect from this move, and how much do you worry about dangers posed by yield-starved foreign investors? For all intents and purposes, capital flows are now free for businesses, households, pension funds, and financial institutions. There are a few things left to change and legislation to remove, but the process has gone very well. We preserved stability in the process. The original imposition of capital controls was, in fact, a proposal that came from the IMF at the height of the crisis. We had good and helpful discussions with the Fund on how to proceed with removing capital controls. We may be entering rougher seas now that capital controls have been mostly removed. But we are very well prepared. First, we have a relatively well-balanced economy, a current account surplus, and debt levels are much lower than they were prior to the crisis. Second, from being net borrowers abroad, we now have more assets abroad than liabilities for the first time in the history of compiled data. Third, we have a high level of foreign exchange reserves of around a third of GDP, unlike prior to the crisis. And finally, our banks are well prepared with regulations that can mitigate and reduce the risks associated with free capital flows and foreign exchange positions. In addition, we are not yet at the point where the inflow of hot money would be a major issue. That is because we still have in place our special reserve requirement on capital flows into the bond market and high yielding deposits. Tourism has become Icelands number one industry, overtaking fishing. Do you expect tourists to keep coming, or will they move elsewhere as the herring once did? The experience is that if you have a tourism boom of this magnitude, it is there to stay. There might be some ebb and flow, but tourism will, to my mind, continue to be one of the main pillars of the economy. That means we need to manage it well. What are the implications for economic policy making? Is overheating an inevitable consequence? Yes, it is quite clear that there is a risk of overheating in the Icelandic economy. We are importing labor on a significant scale. The tourism industry is hiring people, and is competing with other industries. That has contributed to rising wages. We are ator abovefull employment. There are also pressures in the housing market. Home building collapsed during the crisis. Then the construction industry was so busy building hotels that they did not have the resources to build enough homes. So now there is excess demand in the housing market but supply has begun to increase. The tourism industry is, of course, a generator of a lot of foreign exchange, which explains the current account surplus. That has put upward pressure on the exchange rate. To a significant degree it is a benign part of the adjustment but there is always the risk that the currency will become overvalued. We are very vigilant in this regard. Dealing with this is challenging. But it is better to deal with challenges in good times than being at the other end of the scale, as we were during the crisis. 2/3 The latest IMF concluding statement on Iceland suggests improving financial sector oversight should be the top priority. Would you welcome a new architecture where banking regulation and supervision are unified under the roof of the central bank? The Central Bank does not have an institutional view on it. But we have done a lot to improve both regulation and the supervision. We have a relatively new architecture of financial stability oversight. Whether that is the best arrangement remains to be seen. I think what the IMF proposes is in many ways good. But ultimately, this is an issue for Parliament as a change in the architecture requires change in legislation. You spent the early years of your governorship steering the country out from the aftermath of the financial meltdown in 2008. That period followed a collapse of the banks and of the krona, and brought capital controls, austerity, and a 2.1 billion IMF-supported program. Looking back, how do you evaluate the IMFs role? In fact, crisis management in Iceland had already started, and very important decisions had been taken before we agreed on our program supported by the IMF. These were crucial decisions on how to handle failing banks which, to my mind, played a big role in the success that we have had so far. Remember, these were private banks that held assets amounting to 10 times Icelands GDP, and their balance sheets were primarily denominated in foreign currencies. The Icelandic authorities didnt have the resources to bail out these banks, so they allowed them to go into resolution. Three, smaller, domestically-oriented banks were carved out of these failing internationally active banks. But now they have been turned into strong financial institutions that are still domestically oriented. To keep it that way, we strictly regulate them on the international asset side, with specific liquidity and funding requirements in foreign currencies. The banks are strong with capital adequacy rates in the range of 25 to 30 percent and with high liquidity buffers. The percentage of bad loans has also been dramatically reduced. And the IMFs role? The IMF came in 2008 to help us deal with the balance of payments crisis, the markdown in currency, and stabilizing the macroeconomy. Creating the conditions for recovery is the IMFs forte, in addition to dealing with crisis management in a banking crisis. I think our cooperation has been good. We have always had candid discussions, and sometimes disagreed. And then we did what we thought was right. The IMF had a big role in prompting us and challenging us. Sometimes during these discussions, it was not the initial view of the IMF that prevailed and we met in the middle. I find that the process, and the discussions, showed a relationship of equals between the Central Bank and the IMF. I found this helpful and I still do. 3/3

Title: Speech on the state and outlook of economic and monetary policy
text: Birgir easl. Gunnarsson State and outlook for economic and monetary policy Speech at a meeting of the Representative Council of the National Union of Pension Funds Thursday 4 December 2003 I thank you for the invitation to this meeting of the National Union of Pension Funds to discuss the state and prospects of economic and monetary policy. At the beginning of November, the Central Bank published its quarterly monetary bulletin, which published a new macroeconomic forecast and inflation forecast. What I have to offer here today is of course very much based on that subject, but I will then add to it as the occasion arises and new information has emerged. I will start by discussing price trends, but price stability is the Central Bank's main objective under the Act passed on the Bank in May 2001. Inflation has been close to 2% for the longest time this year. The Central Bank's inflation target is 21/2% according to a joint statement between the Government and the Bank and the price level therefore remain below the target. According to a November price measure, the index has risen by 2.5% over 12 months, with the exception of housing costs by 1.1%. Statistics Iceland publishes 2 in addition to so-called core indices I and II, which are taken from the index, were volatile items, and the rise in the core indices was found to be somewhat higher in the past 12 months, 3.1% and 2.8%, or slightly above the inflation target. The housing stock of the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX explains the bulk of the increase in the index over the past 12 months, as shown in this figure, where the index is analyzed by nature and origin. By the beginning of November, the housing stock had risen by 9.7% in one year, down from its increase since August by just over 1%. The exchange rate development of the kr97na has played a major role in the deflation of inflation since the beginning of 2002. Since the summer months of 2002, the price of imported goods has generally fallen. The exchange rate continued to rise until the middle of this year, but after a near-continuous increase since November 2001, it weakened somewhat again this summer but has remained relatively stable ever since. It is likely that the impact of the exchange rate increase on the kr97na on prices is likely to be reduced. I will now deviate from a number of factors relating to the development of the economy. The external conditions of the national economy have deteriorated somewhat this year. Seafood export prices have fallen and catches have been more diminished, but have been sparked in recent weeks. This has led to 3 that exports have proved to be weaker than expected. However, the price of aluminum has risen somewhat but remains low historically. Oil prices have risen somewhat this year Macroeconomic accounts for the 2nd quarter of the year confirm somewhat robust growth in domestic demand, as had been expected. However, slumped exports held back economic growth, which was similar or embedded more sluggish than in the 1st quarter, although the growth in national spending was much higher. The growth of private consumption was particularly powerful. The growth in consumption and capital formation was also high. From the national accounts for the first half of the year, it can be concluded that domestic demand has increased considerably faster than expected in the first forecast. National expenditure in the first half of the year was 51/2% higher than a year ago. The most important thing is the increase in private consumption. In contrast, the growth in capital formation was somewhat lower than expected. Consumption growth in the first half of the year, particularly in the 2nd quarter, was also considerably higher than previously expected. The growth of private consumption should come as no surprise. The growing purchasing power of disposable income, stability in prices, lower interest rates and an increase in asset prices are among the factors that are conducive to stimulating demand. The purchasing power of wages has recently been approximately 31/2% higher than a year ago, and households have 4 responded to lower interest rates with increased offensive credit, although this is actually the most for housing purchases. Other demand indicators suggest that growth was also rapid in the 3rd quarter of the year. Goods imports in the first ten months of the year increased by 8%, of which general imports increased by 121/2%. In fact, the growth in private consumption this year is likely to emerge unusually strongly in imports due to a decline in imports of durable consumer goods in the years ahead. Sales tax-related turnover has increased in most areas so far this year. According to data available until the end of August, real growth in wholesale sales and service sectors has increased particularly sharply. Day-to-day turnover in the 3rd quarter of the year was approximately 4% higher in real terms than a year ago, and credit card turnover in the first ten months of the year was 10% higher. The underlying aspects of demand therefore most point to the continued growth of private consumption. The value of goods exports for the first ten months of the year was 7% less at a fixed rate than at the same time the previous year. Information on the lending of the loan system as a whole is available until the end of June and for the banking system until the end of October. These figures clearly confirm the boom in lending that began last spring. The 12-month growth in the lending system amounted to just under 10% if the impact of exchange rate changes is kept aside. Snaking has 5 There has been a boom in lending to companies. They had grown by 15% in 12 months, while lending to households by just under 7%. The growth in lending to households is primarily explained by the lending of the Housing Financing Fund and pension funds, which increased by approximately 12% for each party. At the end of October, domestic lending by deposit institutions had increased by 15% in one year and the index and exchange rate update there has not had a significant impact. In addition to domestic lending, depositors have continued to increase their lending to foreign entities. The amount of money and savings recommended by M 3 has increased rapidly so far this year, but growth remained relatively high last year at the same time as the growth in lending stopped. The real growth rate of M 3 was higher than in March 1999 when it last peaked. From this it is clear that the increase in lending of deposit institutions is fully restored and therefore there is every reason to encourage them to be cautious, particularly in the loan repayments of foreign loans to borrowers who do not have income in foreign currency. It should be noted that in the reports of the rating agencies assessing the government's creditworthiness, it has been considered one of the greatest weaknesses Icelandic the economy of how high its foreign debt is, and in particular foreign short-term debt. There is therefore every reason to encourage the depositors to be cautious in this regard. If they 6 Failing can have serious consequences for the economy as a whole. As I mentioned earlier, a large part of inflation over the past 12 months has been caused by an increase in the price of housing. Apartment prices in the capital area rose steadily since the middle of last year, after several lows that began in the spring of 2001. This increase has now stopped. The price increase in real estate can be both the cause and result of increased demand. Studies have shown that the impact of property prices on private consumption is significant. This can be explained in general by so-called wealth effect, i.e. that as the value of household assets increases, they are more willing to increase consumption and less afraid to increase their debts on an equal basis with the increased value of assets. The increase in property prices further increases the mortgage space of a property, thereby making it easier for its owner to provide credit. In addition, the lending will of financial institutions may increase as credit risk decreases otherwise unchanged with the increased net worth of households. It is believed that the concentration of private consumption in recent years around the world, despite the decline in other areas, can be attributed considerably to the use of increased mortgage capacity of assets to finance consumption. It is likely that the same is true in this country. That property prices in the capital area should at present be about 45% higher in real terms than at the beginning of the year 7 1996 strongly indicates that it may decline in the long term. That's not to say that prices can't go up even further for a while. However, as tensions between property prices and underlying construction costs become greater, however, the risk of drastic adjustments to long-term balance increases. Therefore, it is important not to do anything in times of turmoil that could further intensify this tension. It is likely that the increase in maximum loans, the removal of mortgage allowances and changes to the social housing system have significantly pushed up demand in recent years. Plans to go even further in this direction could push for further increases and increase the risk of drastic adjustments later. Although domestic demand has increased significantly this year, there has not yet been a clear uptick in the labour market. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate currently 3.5% has increased continuously since the autumn of 2001, excluding November and December, when it remained in place. However, the increase over the past year has been lower than the previous year and has now stopped. The trend in unemployment suggests that increased activity in the national economy is still not beginning to take hold in job creation. This is normal because after a period of economic downturns, there is traditionally some surplus production capacity, which companies try to take advantage of before taking new hires.
