Title: Speech at IIEA in Dublin
text: 27 April 2015 Icelands crisis and recovery: facts, comparisons, and the lessons learned Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, speech at the Institute of International and European Affairs, 27 April 2015, Dublin Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, It gives me great pleasure to speak here at the Institute of International and European Affairs in Dublin about Icelands crisis and recovery and some of the lessons that could be learned from this experience. This is not least because of our historical bonds and the affinity that I feel exists between our people, to which we can now add the common experience of being hard hit by the Great Financial Crisis. It is well known that Iceland was the first advanced country to experience a full-scale banking crisis during the autumn of 2008, when its three big cross-border banks failed. It was also the first advanced country to go on an IMF programme. What is probably less well known is that at that point, Iceland was already on its way into a recession after an unsustainable boom and serious overheating during 2005-2007 and a currency crisis in the first half of 2008. The banking collapse and the associated wealth loss and further currency depreciation made the recession significantly worse, of course, as did the recession that hit the global economy in the fourth quarter of 2008. That autumn, two separate but interrelated sub-stories of the recent Icelandic saga converged in a tragic grand finale. The first story was related to Icelands boom-bust cycle and problems with macroeconomic management in small, open, and financially integrated economies. This is a story that has played out many times around the globe, and many of its elements have been seen before in Iceland. It might have been somewhat more extreme this time around, but it wasnt fundamentally different. 1 The second story was the rise and fall of three cross-border banks operating on the basis of EU legislation (the European passport). This story was much more unique, as it involved the first banking crisis in Europe since the EU single market was formed in the early 1990s. Figure 1 Let me turn first to the banking story. In a few years prior to the crisis, the banking system had expanded very rapidly, as you can see from Figure 1, making it one of the biggest in Europe relative to GDP. Most of this expansion was cross-border, and a significant part of it was really off-border, having little to do with Iceland, as both financing and investment took place abroad. 2 Figure 2 Towards the end, around two-thirds of the combined balance sheet of the three cross-border banks was denominated in foreign currency. On the liabilities side, the share of FX-denominated debt was actually higher, as can be seen from Figure 2, with almost half of the financing in the form of FX deposits and other short-term FX financing. The FX part of the balance sheet therefore had a significant maturity mismatch. However, there was no safety net of the type we have in a national setting, in the form of liquidity provision and lender-of-last-resort (LOLR) to back it up. It was an accident waiting to happen, and happen it did, with a vengeance, at the peak of the international financial crisis in autumn 2008, when there was a wholesale run on the FX financing of internationally active banks. When the Icelandic authorities were dealing with the failing banks, they assumed, based on published CAD ratios and stress tests, that the banks were solvent. Now, however, we know that this was probably not truly the case, as there were hidden vulnerabilities in their capital positions. Be that as it may, with the solvency assumption in mind, the authorities tried to build defences against potential foreign currency liquidity problems at the banks by negotiating swap lines and tapping foreign capital markets  in both cases, with limited success. Given the lack of international co-operation, the Icelandic authorities were forced to consider radical solutions. Although they were not necessarily articulated in full at the time, these solutions entailed several goals: to preserve a functioning domestic payment system, ring-fence the state in the case of bank failures, limit the socialisation of private sector losses, and create the conditions for rebuilding a domestic banking system. 3 The adopted solution was embedded in the so-called Emergency Act, which was passed by Parliament on 6 October 2008. The Emergency Act saved the domestic operations of the banking system by creating new banks, which involved carving domestic assets and liabilities out of the old, failing banks. The rest  and the much larger part  went into a resolution process. In order to reverse the ongoing run on domestic deposits, a declaration was made that all deposits in Iceland were safe, but this did not include deposits in foreign branches. Furthermore, all deposits in Icelandicheadquartered banks were given priority over other unsecured claims, including in foreign branches. As regards the blanket guarantee, the distinction made between domestic deposits and foreign currency deposits in the banks foreign branches added fuel to the fire of the socalled Icesave dispute about the settlement of deposit guarantees in the Dutch and British branches of one of the banks. But guaranteeing those deposits would never have been credible and might have bankrupted the Government had it been attempted. The deposits in question were in foreign currencies and amounted to 11 billion euros  far in excess of Icelands available FX liquidity at that time, as the sovereign was completely closed off from foreign capital markets. Furthermore, in economic terms, given that these deposits were used to a significant degree to finance illiquid assets outside Iceland, such a payment, if it had been possible, would have amounted to a net transfer of resources from Iceland to other countries  where the United Kingdom would have been prominent  at a time when Iceland was going through its deepest financial and economic crisis in the post-war period. That made no sense whatsoever! However, the preference given to deposits under the Emergency Act is a key element in the fact that recoveries on the failed banks estates will cover deposit claims from the foreign branches in full. In international discussion, there have been a number of misconceptions about this process. There have been claims that Iceland allowed its banking system to collapse, with what now seem reasonable results, and that others should consider doing the same. The fact is that Iceland kept the domestic part of its banking system running throughout, and at significant expense; otherwise, the consequences would have been dire. Some have claimed that the banks were nationalised. They were not. The failed private banks are private companies in winding-up proceedings governed by law. The Government fully recapitalised one of the new banks. The other two are private banks owned primarily by the estates of the old banks. Others have claimed that Iceland defaulted and got away with it. The opposite is true. The credit of the sovereign was preserved, and all debt obligations have been paid on time. Moreover, Icelands investment- 4 grade credit ratings from Moodys and S&P were preserved throughout the crisis. This is why the sovereign has been able to tap international capital markets twice so far since the crisis struck. You can see from this that the key characteristics of crisis management and bank resolution in Iceland were that shareholders lost all their equity, unsecured bond holders were bailed in, vital infrastructure elements of the domestic banking system were preserved, and deposits were given preference over other unsecured claims. Today this seems in many ways a standard approach, but it was not universally well received at the time. On the whole, these measures were successful, which mitigated the effect of the banks failure on the economy. The domestic payment system functioned more or less seamlessly throughout, and there was continuous access to deposits and basic banking services in Iceland. International payment flows were seriously affected, however, not least because of the freezing order imposed by the British authorities on Icelandic banks, but also because of general distrust among foreign counterparties. Let me now turn to the macroeconomic part of the story. I will paint with a rather broad brush here, both because time is limited and because the issues are somewhat better understood. All the usual suspects were present during the build-up to the Icelandic crisis: very strong capital inflows fuelling a credit and asset price boom that subsequently turned into a bubble at the same time as the economy overheated and an unsustainable external position developed, as could be seen in a double-digit current account deficit. And macroeconomic and prudential policies were not up to the task. Quite the contrary: there was a policy conflict between monetary policy and the demand levers pulled by the Government, and the risks inherent in capital flows, FX balance sheets, and credit and asset price booms were left under-regulated and insufficiently supervised. At a deeper level, the macroeconomic part of the story was related to three factors. The first factor centres on the complications that tend to arise with macroeconomic management as very small, open economies become more and more financially integrated. The second relates to the specific conditions of abundant, cheap credit at the global level. Third, major policy mistakes were made in Iceland, both of the type that would be deemed to be such in any book (such as giving an already overheated economy a demand stimulus), and those more closely related to the orthodoxy prevailing at the time: freely floating exchange rates, interest rate policy focusing mainly on low inflation in terms of goods and services, and good micro-supervision; and let the 5 markets do the rest. In the wake of the crisis, it is better appreciated that this view is deeply flawed. The imbalances in the Icelandic economy in the years leading up to the crisis were in many ways enormous. The clearest manifestation is perhaps the current account deficit that averaged over 17% of GDP during the years 2005-2008. Both it and the large positive output gap were bound to correct  a process that was likely to be associated with a significant slowing of growth, if not an outright recession. As a matter of fact, the Central Bank of Iceland predicted more or less consistently from 2007 onwards that there would be a recession in Iceland in 2009. This projection had nothing to do with the collapse of the banks but everything to do with the known investment profile of big projects in the energy and aluminium sectors and the accumulating signs of a grossly overheated economy. This belies the common statement that forecasters never predict recessions! The shocks that hit Iceland in 2008 and the imminent correction of unsustainable balances shaped macroeconomic developments in Iceland in the years that followed. But so did the policy responses, which took two main forms. The first was the crisis management regarding the failing banks, which I have already mentioned. The second was the economic programme developed by the Icelandic authorities in co-operation with the IMF. The IMF programme had three key goals: stabilisation of the exchange rate, fiscal sustainability, and reconstruction of the financial sector. Figure 3 6 Comprehensive capital controls were an important element in the programme, but their rationale was to help to stabilise the exchange rate in a situation where the currency had fallen more than 50% in 2008, where foreign krona positions that were a legacy of carry trade and capital inflows amounted to around 40% of GDP, and where a large fiscal deficit that had to be financed in the domestic market had developed. In this situation, the capital controls gave monetary policy more scope to focus on the domestic economy, as is demonstrated in Figure 3, which compares developments in short-term real interest rates during and after the currency and banking crises in Korea in 1997 and Iceland in 2008. Figure 4 Icelands recession was deep. But it was probably not as deep as many might have thought when they entertained the image of the total collapse of an entire banking sector, plus a major currency crisis. But then we should bear in mind the nature of the shocks. A significant part of the impact of the banking collapse was felt in other countries. Furthermore, the economic shocks disproportionally affected overblown sectors (banking and construction). Most of the export base was intact, however, and was subsequently boosted by the low real exchange rate. The real depreciation (see Figure 4) and the negative confidence effects of the crisis also contributed to lifting the saving 7 rate and compressing imports. The resultant adjustment in the current account can be seen in Figure 5. The double-digit deficits in the years before the crisis have been replaced by sizeable surpluses from 2009 to this day. Figure 5 Iceland had significant fiscal surpluses in the years leading up to the crisis. As expected, the crisis had a big impact on government finances: through the direct fiscal costs of the banking crisis, the loss of tax revenue, and higher unemployment expenditures as the economy went into recession. This impact was big as can be seen on Figure 6 showing the direct and indirect impact of selected banking crises on government debt and fiscal balance. But yours was bigger! 8 Figure 6 A deficit on the central government amounting to 8% of GDP opened up in 2009. It had to be financed domestically. Capital controls helped in that respect. To build confidence and open external market access, a medium-term fiscal consolidation plan was implemented as a part of the programme with the IMF. In 2009, automatic stabilisers were mostly allowed to do their work, but in 2010 a phased deficit reduction plan set in, with a primary surplus targeted for 2012 and an overall surplus for 2014. This fiscal consolidation was sizeable in international comparison, as can be seen from Figure 7, but it did not derail the recovery that began around the middle of 2010. It helped that monetary policy could be relaxed over the course of 2010, as the closure of loopholes in the capital controls in late 2009 contributed to the stabilisation of the exchange rate. 9 Figure 7 Figure 8 10 Figure 8 and 9 show developments in GDP and employment during the recession and subsequent recovery in Iceland, with predictions extending into 2017 for GDP and 2016 for employment. For comparison, it shows the distribution of the same for 30 other European countries, with Ireland highlighted. It shows that Icelands recession, as well as Irelands, was deeper than the median in Europe, but both countries have been doing better than the average during the recovery, especially lately and in the forecasts. Actually, there is relatively little difference between Iceland and Ireland by both measures, except that Iceland seems to be doing somewhat better lately in terms of employment growth. Icelands performance would be even better if we looked at the unemployment rate, as labour supply is rather elastic, both internally and because of cross-border mobility. Iceland lost just over 11% of output during the recession that ended in the first quarter of 2010. It will have probably more than gained that back by the first quarter of this year. Given developments in the supply side of the economy, the Central Banks assessment is that almost all of the slack in the economy has been absorbed. Unlike the pre-crisis peak, the current level of output is therefore associated with a relatively well-balanced economy both internally and externally. In recent months, inflation has been below the target because of international developments, and there is a current account surplus, which allows the Central Bank to accumulate reserves without undermining the exchange rate. Figure 9 11 So is Iceland out of the woods? The answer is no. The financial crisis casts a long shadow. Both household and corporate debt levels have declined significantly, with the household debt-to-income ratio around the 2005 level and the corporate debt-to-GDP ratio at its lowest since mid-2004. But there are significant pockets of financial fragility, with some of the households that bought and borrowed at the peak of the market still facing very heavy debt service burdens. And even though public debt is now on a declining path relative to GDP, it is very high in historical terms, which remains a vulnerability. The biggest legacy problem, though, is the capital controls. During the early stages of the crisis, the controls were helpful in stabilising the economy and providing the shelter needed to repair balance sheets and rebalance the economy. But over time  and increasingly, as the economy and the rest of the world recover  they begin to turn into obstacles to economic growth. Figure 10 The problem is that there are big obstacles to speedy removal of the capital controls. First, we have short-term krona assets in the hands of foreign residents, so-called offshore kronur, which currently amount to 15% of GDP, after having been reduced by more than half since the capital controls were introduced (see Figure 10). But more importantly, we have domestic assets held by the estates of the old banks. This is a balance of payments problem, as 94% of the claims on these banks are foreign and only 6% domestic, whereas 41% of the assets are domestic, including 21% in kronur (See Figure 11). Taking into 12 account the part of these assets that are already financed in foreign currency, we get the result that unfinanced domestic assets that could revert to foreign residents with the unwinding of these estates will amount to 25% of GDP (see Figure 12). When considering the complication that this creates for Iceland, you should bear in mind that it is partly because the resolution of the third-largest bankruptcy in the history of mankind is taking place in one of the smallest countries in Europe. Figure 11 Therefore, potential outflows amounting to 40% of GDP might seek a speedy exit if we were to lift the capital controls tomorrow. If our relatively large FX reserves (30% of GDP) were our first line of defence, they would be wiped out completely, and then the exchange rate would give way, with potentially serious consequences for economic and financial stability in Iceland. We are currently working hard on solutions to this problem, and such solutions do exist. From a logical standpoint, the solution must take the form of either a significant reduction before early exit or a secure longer-term holding period before the controls are lifted. 13 Figure 12 I am coming towards the end of my talk and will have to leave discussion of the lessons learned for the Q&A session. The list is long and includes the need to avoid policy conflicts in small, open, and financially integrated economies, to better regulate FX risk in domestic banking systems, to give up the dream of financial centres in small countries if they do not have access to credible and comprehensive international or regional safety nets, and to improve policy frameworks and tools in light of the experience that we have been through. In Iceland, this process has gone past the talking stage: frameworks for monetary and financial stability policies have been improved, new prudential rules have been introduced, financial sector legislation has been amended, and supervision has been improved and strengthened. And there is more to come. Thank you very much 14

Title: Statement by Chief Economist at the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Arn97r Sighvatsson, Chief Economist at the Central Bank of Iceland:1 Can the central bank handle inflation? At the end of March 2001, the Board of Directors of Monetary Policy in Iceland became a turning point when the exchange rate was floated, the Central Bank set inflation targets and at the same time given independence to determine the policy rate in order to achieve this goal. In a joint statement, the Central Bank and the government further defined the inflation target as a 2.5% increase in the consumer price index in 12 months as a rule. In the period since this juncture, inflation has averaged 4.9% and fluctuated between 1-12%. The exchange rate of the krona has also fluctuated significantly. Inflation is still far above target, has increased in recent months and the inflation outlook is sluggish in the near future, but in Monetary Bulletin issued in April, it was predicted that the inflation target would be reached in 2010. This cannot be considered satisfactory results seven years after the inflation target was adopted. There is therefore every reason to look back and ask what went wrong and what lessons can be learned from Iceland's attempt to run independent monetary policy in an economy the size of a small city in Europe. Before turning to our seven years of experience with an inflation target, however, it's right to look at how it came to Iceland ended up in the position of running the world's smallest floating currency. The beginning can be traced back to 1993, when Iceland became a member of the European Economic Area (EEA). With the advent of the EEA, the EFT Countries became members of the European Union (EU) common market. They underwent the four freedoms, i.e. the free flow of goods, services, labour and capital. However, they did not take part in one of the most important final steps towards an unrestricted internal market, namely the monetary merger that involved the establishment of the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999. Iceland's membership of the EEA meant that in 1995 all controls on short-term flows of capital were abolished. The abolition of capital movements without participation in currency integration in Europe included greater 1 Talk delivered at a seminar of the Faculty of Business and Economics at the University of Iceland 2 June 2008. Diagrams are included in a special Power Point document. It is available in the same place on the Central Bank of Iceland's website as this appointment. The opinions expressed in this paper are the authors and do not necessarily reflect the central bank's position. a fundamental change in the premises of monetary management in Iceland than most people were aware of at the time. In this context, it is useful to recall the incompatible trinity, i.e. the conclusion of the Mundell-Fleming model that it is not possible at the same time to operate independent monetary policy, keep currency exchange rates stable and capital movements unrestricted. Bound by the provisions of the EEA Agreement on the unrestricted flow of cross-border capital, Iceland was therefore two choices, namely to completely abandon self-sized monetary policy with a much firmer connection to the euro than previously known, e.g. by at least a monetary council, or to allow the kr97na to float and find independent monetary policy other than exchange rate. These are sometimes called corner solutions. Neither gold foot nor money volume control seemed realistic options, but in the years ahead a number of countries had adopted inflation targets, seemingly with excellent results. Some of them were small open economies, such as entrepreneur New Zealand. None of them were as small as Iceland. Of course, reality is not quite as explicit as the models of economics. In the end, the Central Bank's initial response to the new situation was not to immediately disappear from corner solutions, but to take advantage of the scope devoted to the incomplete markets in order to drive monetary policy with limited independence within a certain framework, as the exchange rate remained an important ballast, but not entirely fixed. It worked well for a few years. However, it did not have to wait many years for the failures of that policy to try to keep the exchange rate stable while utilizing the limited scope of monetary policy to hold back rising inflationary pressures. The first reaction was to increase the scope, allow the exchange rate to strengthen more. This helped in the short term, but soon capital inflows that for some time had pushed for a rate increase began to turn into outflows. A larger trade deficit than had long been known formed between 1998 and 2000. The Central Bank therefore soon had to sell foreign currency in order to prevent the exchange rate from falling below the set tolerance level. By March 2001, it was clear that this policy had come to an end. The central bank's foreign exchange position had been severely diminished. Such conditions give capital fugitives and speculators a burden under both wings. Iceland was on the verge of a currency crisis when the exchange rate was allowed to float on 27 March 2001. Of course, a traditional exchange rate cut would have come to the fore. However, this was not the case in light of experience. With the tensions that prevailed in the labour market, a rate cut would soon have led to a new cavity of wage increases. The experience of currency crises in Asia also suggested that the foreign exchange market would soon have new benchmarks tested in exchange rate issues, especially given how much the currency position had been scrapped. 2 The result was to allow the exchange rate to float but instruct the Fed to work to get a grip on inflation by November 2003 and to keep it as close as possible to 21/2% from that time. I believe that the decision was not necessarily taken on the assumption that the floating exchange rate was the most appropriate exchange rate arrangement in Iceland, but was based on the fact that it was shown that a fixed-rate policy had prompted shipwreck and that the political assumptions that such a policy might succeed in the future were not available. Without Iceland's membership of the EU, EMU membership was excluded and a weaker form of fixed-rate policy was not likely to meet the conditions of unrestricted capital movements. It can therefore be said that the inflation target was chosen because other options were excluded, although it was also seen that asymmetric economic fluctuations seemed to suggest that the gains of independent monetary policy could be considerable, according to the theory of the most efficient currency area, as economic fluctuations in Iceland are often marked by specific demand or supply slumps. Unlike many countries that adopted inflation targets in the wake of the currency crisis, inflation targets were adopted in Iceland on the brink of a currency crisis. The period of inflation target therefore began with a significant devaluation of the kr97na, which resulted in inflation removing the inflation target instead of approaching it, as was aimed at. It can be said that initially the repercussions of the imbalance that had been built up under the fixed-rate system had to be dealt with, so it is not justified to judge the results of the first year on the basis of that short experience, as the inflation target was reached despite a poor start roughly a year earlier than it was planned, or in November 2002. However, I am of the opinion that the rate cut and the inflation gust that followed were greater than inevitable due to inadequate monetary restraint. Although the kr97na was under pressure and inflation significantly above target, the Central Bank began its career as an independent central bank with an interest rate cut. You have to make mistakes when looking back. Instead of responding to the decrease in the kr97na with an interest rate increase, thereby creating increased incentives for investors to own kr97nur, the Central Bank continued to hike the foreign exchange position in order to counteract the decline in the kr97na. This proved to be a useless action at the end of the day. The inflation period that began in 2004 and still stands is in that respect a more serious setback for monetary policy than the first that the anomaly will not be explained in reference to the aftermath of a fixed-rate policy that failed. It has also lasted longer and the anomaly has been larger. Since May 2004, inflation has been 5.4% on average and higher if you overlook the impact of the reduction in consumption taxes. Inflation expectations have almost all along been above the inflation target and never more so than in the last week. One of the main objectives of monetary policy, i.e. to create ballast inflation expectations, has therefore not been achieved. 3 The ineffectiveness is reflected in ruthless purchase requirements and collective bargaining agreements where purchasing power is protected by special inflation and purchasing power provisions. What went wrong? Naturally, the criticism is largely directed at the Central Bank, as the Bank has been set a goal of keeping inflation under control. It is claimed that the Bank has made a mistake. Title: Article by Chief Economist on the economic outlook in the midst of the financial crisis in Frttablai 6 October 2012
text: 06.10.2012 Article by orarinn G. Petursson on the economic outlook in the midst of the financial crisis in Frettablaoio 6 October 2012 Economic outlook in the midst of financial crisis Banks are not like ordinary businesses. Banks are not like ordinary businesses. In a sense, they are like the vascular system of the economy, where about them the lifeblood of savings flows to households, businesses and institutions. At the same time, they are more leveraged and dependent on short-term financing than traditional businesses. They are both important and sensitive. It's never as clear as during a banking crisis: then the banking system stops being able to perform its function, the payment processor of the economy is disrupted, businesses lack the resources for traditional business, and for investment, and household finances deteriorate. This is followed by an equally significant economic recession in which output declines and jobs are lost. Icelandic the banking collapse will likely be considered one of the most serious banking crises in world history, as it is extraordinary that almost all banks in a particular country will go bankrupt at roughly the same time. The problem we faced in early October 2008 was therefore serious and there was a possibility that there would be no operating banking system. However, the financial crisis began earlier, as at the beginning of the year there had been a jolt in the currency crisis in which the influx of foreign exchange to domestic private sector employers stopped and turned into a massive outflow that resulted in a half-fall in the exchange rate. In the autumn, confidence in everything Icelandic was broken, and companies suddenly faced the prospect of having to pre-or-cash goods that had previously been obtained through normal payment terms. Payment services towards foreign countries were therefore upsetting and there was a real risk of a shortage of essentials and supplies from abroad. The problem in the winter of 2008 was terrifying. Fortunately, however, the worst was able to be averted, including with help from the international community. Although foreign payment services had been lashed, the operations of a rebuilt domestic banking system were successfully secured, and payment processing and the fall of the krona were halted. Gradually, the public finances (which the financial crisis had played badly) were able to come to grips with the rebound of inflation. However, it was impossible to prevent a subsequent great recession, as it inevitably reflected the national adjustment following the overheating years ahead, as the Central Bank had indeed repeatedly predicted in the years ahead. In the beginning, it was not easy to realize how severe the economic recession would be, with few to be built given the scale of the banking and currency crisis. However, a number of studies indicated that a drastic economic recession could be expected in the wake of such a "twin crisis." As early as November 2008, the Central Bank calculated that GDP would contract by a total of 10% in 2009 and 2010, but that there would be a turnaround in mid-2010 and 2011 economic growth would be just above 3%. Despite the great uncertainty of the winter of 2008 and the fact that global economic developments have proved far less favourable than they were then expected and worse than in many previous crises, the Central Bank's assessment of the economic progress following the crisis appears to have gone ahead: based on the latest statistics from Statistics Iceland, the recession in 2009 and 2010 totalled just above 10%, the economic recovery began in mid-2010 and last year's economic growth was just under 3%. This development is in good harmony with the experience of other countries of serious financial crises. Iceland's experience has become the subject of some international coverage in light of the magnitude of the shock. However, the outlook remains unclear, not least because of the situation in Europe. The most important thing is to continue to underpin the economic recovery through disciplined economic management, so that past results will not be glued down. This article was a post by orarinn G. Petursson in a summary of Frettablaoio on the occasion of four years since the economic collapse. This article appeared on page 24 of the newspaper.

Title: Statement by Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland at Bifrst University of Business Administration
text: Jon Sigurdsson, Governor of the Central Bank: YES-21447 Talk at a seminar at Bifrost Business School held on 3 March 2005 Good belongings As is well known, the economy is divided into distinct markets. The markets need to be able to operate as freely as possible and be efficient and self-employed to the greatest extent possible. The economy's markets are interrelated, but mismatched and misguided. The main markets are firstly the commodity and services markets, secondly the labour market, thirdly the real estate market, fourthly the securities and capital markets, and fifthly the money markets, the foreign exchange market, the foreign exchange market, the krona market, which are also referred to as interbank markets. The last time the markets have matured well in recent years in this country. Now competition and equality rules, interest rate liberalisation, free movements of capital and the exchange rate of the krona are free on the market. And here regulatory bodies operate in accordance with European regulations. There has been a revolution in Icelandic financial system over the last decade and a half. In the 1990s, there were 13 banks and investment funds, as well as the Institute of Regional Development and the Housing Authority, which was then called, and the state was dominant in this area. Since then, fusion crawling has erupted in colorful phases. Now here are three handsome commercial banks and a joint banking institution of the savings banks. Over the same period of years, the state has withdrawn from the operations of commercial banks and the vast majority of investment funds, a torrential downturn in Icelandic economic and business history. The privatisation has occurred in recent years and on its terms the banks have strengthened and intensified by half, starting to expand to other countries and into new areas, both in investment, participation in risk management and in real estate mortgages. The Central Bank operates closely with financial and money markets, foreign exchange markets, the krona market, i.e. the interbank markets. As a central bank or central bank, it can be said that a central bank is, among other things, a supervisory and security centre at this level. The Central Bank of Iceland has the main objective of promoting stability in the development of prices. He is a state bank - but may not grant loans to the Treasury -- and he is the bank of the banks, watching over payment systems in Icelandic financial system and over the security of the financial system, taking care of 2 The Foreign Exchange Reserve Fund is involved in the formulation of foreign exchange policy, is responsible for cooperation with international financial institutions, has exclusive rights to monetary issuance in Iceland and holds treasuries, and also works on a variety of analyses, research, and publications. Markets are important sources of information and, among other things, they must have scope for efficiency and autonomy. Attempts at hand control obstruct the information sharing that society needs to receive from the markets and can mislead people's view of problems and resolutions. And expectations of political snares are illusions. The main currents of society are in the commodity and service markets and the labour market. It displays value creation, living wage development, economic growth and economic strength or weakness. Banking and money markets work more indirectly, and they do not dictate everything about the progress of the national economy and living standards in Iceland. The Central Bank has an important role in the security and stability of the interaction between markets and the institutions that work there. Not least, it is the central bank's task to watch over the common unit of measure of the markets, which is here Icelandic the krona. Price developments and inflation are actually synonymous with changes in the equity's own value. It is important to distinguish between trends in different markets. It's not the same thing that happens, for example, in the goods and services markets or in the money markets. There is also a difference between short-term waves and long-term currents. Across the markets, various temporary waves are moving, varying whether or how they touch the permanent currents. The effect runs between both directly and indirectly and varyingly strongly. Some decisions in the markets are on the periphery, because the optimization of them is small or heedless in it and that time. The awareness of marginal position shapes everyone's actions. Banks, governments and central banks aim to influence marginal decisions and marginal measures, push or reduce them as appropriate. Changing marginal conditions may, among other things, affect overall activity in the market, for an increase or contraction. Such changes also affect all trends in prices in the market. It is worth bearing in mind that in the economy, everywhere the so-called trading effect, and even multiplication effect, so that limited action, touching on the periphery, can continue to work progressively level by level and multiply across the markets and the economy. A key element for understanding central bank operations is the awareness of the interaction between different markets, of differences in short-term waves and long-term currents, and of marginalisation and mediation and multiplication effects. Central banks touch the money markets with short-term measures that directly and indirectly affect the economy. 3 Financial systems and markets need to be safe and stable, and trust must prevail over the strategies and tools used in the markets. Market progress and prospects, particularly in an efficient and secure market, shape future forecasts and so-called economic expectations in society. Human assessments and predictions of the situation after, for example, a year or two shape expectations and estimates of the value of secular objects both after this time and also already. That's how your expectations are determined every time. Inflation is a reflection of the currency's own value. With the interaction of the markets in mind, it can be seen that price development is a monetary phenomenon. Monetary measures do not dictate everything about price developments in the economy in individual terms, but they have a defined impact on it and can shape it in the overall draw. This effect is mediated by short-term marginal measures in money markets. Central bank monetary measures then spread across the economy through a trading process level by level and phase of phase. It is believed that the Central Bank of Iceland's interest rate changes will take up to two years to achieve the full expected effect. The trading process, for example, begins with the central bank changing its interest rates. They affect market growth in the business world, thereby continuing on lending volume and money volume, on asset prices, and directly and indirectly at the exchange rate of the krona. At the same time, this scenario affects expectations and credibility in the system. The next phase of the trading process shows the impact and changes in domestic demand and in imports and exports. Thus, there will be changes in overall demand and activity in the economy. It improves or reduces. Exchange rate changes will include changes in import prices. A rate cut is causing price increases, but price increases in imports begin to rebound after a rate hike. Finally, this outcry appears with changes in the inflation trend. Due to these effects of central bank actions, its main interest rates are referred to as controlling interest rates. But they act not directly or immediately, but first as a short-term marginal operation in the money markets. In Icelandic economy, the impact appears first with changing short-term interest rates and indirectly through exchange rate changes, but without the Fed controlling the exchange rate in any way or trying to control it. Traditionally, a variety of effects work simultaneously on the development of the exchange rate. Exchange rate developments, for the taste of an elder, are unpredictable. It is clear that rate hikes, which may, among other things, be linked to an increase in controlling interest rates, can come down heavily on Iceland's export and competitive sectors. But it's hard to know for sure what determines the outcome at any given time. The competitive position of Icelandic companies is sensitive due to comparisons including wage and operating expenses in other countries. The competitive position of Icelandic companies in the single market may not be vulnerable to currency changes in other markets. They also have to have 4 Note that exchange rate changes affect debt payments Icelandic companies abroad. Exchange rate hikes, for example, have reduced debt levels and installments. Often the options in favour usually seem to be in it, and that time either an interest rate hike and a rate hike or on the other hand, inflation, labor disputes and instability that come down even worse and heavier in the business sector. It is often necessary to seek a shipping route between cutters and barrels, and the Central Bank has a defining role in this. In autonomous markets aiming for efficiency, market participants dominate the move. Market participants in the markets mentioned here in particular are commercial banks and savings banks, investment banks and holding companies, pension funds and other similar companies and institutions. The market participants are forward-looking at activities and their expectations for progress are crucial. The Central Bank publishes and explains its objectives and focuses, thereby trying to shape the market participants' expectations. In this case, the credibility of the central bank is very important. The Central Bank of Iceland is among many central banks that adhere to the so-called inflation target. In addition, the Central Bank seeks in line with its official objective of ensuring stable long-term pricing developments through its monetary measures. Static or deflation in prices is not considered desirable, and neither is high inflation or volatility. The Central Bank of Iceland aims for an annual inflation rate of 2.5%, and if annual inflation exceeds 1.0 - 4.0%, i.e. past deviations of 1.5 % in each direction, the Bank shall make the Government publicly aware of, among other things, how and during how long the development will be steered back to the target. But the Central Bank of Iceland's target is not the scope between 1.0 and 4.0 % but the annual inflation rate of 2.5%. Monetary policy decisions are made in risk and uncertainty. Other forces also work at the same time, dividing the state's finances by far. The trading process needs to be open and visible. It is important, for example, that the exchange rate of the currency is free on the market, but the exchange rate is an important link in the trading process. Short-term fluctuations in the exchange rate communicate effects and provide information that is wary of trying to hide,  as experience has shown. Indeed, in discussions about interest rates and exchange rates, there is a reason to remind you that its own is what nominal interest rates and real interest rates, nominal exchange rates, or the development of real exchange rates. Decisions on changes in control rates are based on many factors and careful intelligence and academic processing. Controlling interest rates are often changed when it is available to forecast expected inflation trends 5 clearly deviating from the inflation target and economic developments seem to deviate from equilibrium with consequences in the expected price trends. Also, forecasts and estimates of expectations are of great importance. Interest rates in interbank markets are the central bank's main instruments. Most importantly, interest rates are in so-called reversible business, the so-called control rates. Reversible trading is a chain of periodic trading in the interbank market where the central bank lends funds for several days at a time in order to secure liquidity in the economy and is called "reversible" because the securities set as collateral are reversible after the agreed period. It also matters what the difference is between the individual interest rate types of the Central Bank, i.e. how wide or narrow the so-called interest rate hike is. Central banks have used a number of other tools and methods, such as exchange rate decisions, control of interest rates in the business world, and decisions designed to shape the amount of money in circulation, such as the so-called reserve requirement, in which case banks are obliged to have funds in central bank accounts. As mentioned earlier, the exchange rate of the Icelandic of the krona is now free on the market, and interest rate liberalisation prevails and capital movements are free. It is not believed that a reserve requirement is suitable as an active control device to have a short-term impact on activity in the markets. All measures and decisions of the Central Bank of Iceland are aimed at, among other things, strengthening and strengthening autonomous and efficient markets. Thus, the Central Bank of Iceland must meet other market participants, at least in part, according to the terms of the market and not always by unilateral authority, although the Central Bank actually has a role in regulation. A great deal of work is put into preparation and reasoning regarding decisions on control rates. Scientists have done a lot of research in this area. But circumstances are, of course, endlessly underpinned by change, and one is an examination of the past and another a responsible decision about the future. It is important to find a usable definition of so-called balanced interest rates and the balancing use of production factors, for example, because the economy is an ever-changing platform for living people. There are several examples of influences and indicators. Collective bargaining usually promotes consumer demand. Major projects increase, among other things, demand for capital and labour. House price rises have proved to be a leading indicator of inflation ahead. The ratios between state and local income and expenditure have a dominant effect on the entire economic situation. The public finances are so extensive that their development is determined, and presumably the public in a democratic society wants it to be. Major projects and the state of the state of the state budget have so-called rugby effects throughout the economy, because their strength shapes the terms and facilities of other parties. In general economic management, many parties must be summed up. Often people say that the more the government, local authorities and other public sectors 6 the parties take on volatility management and volatility responses, the less hits the central bank and its monetary policy. In practice, this is usually the opposite, - that the less dealt with in the public finances, the more weight hits the central bank on concentrated monetary policy measures. The Central Bank of Iceland puts a lot of effort into its models and economic forecasts. Of particular importance, the Central Bank's inflation forecasts are important, as they are the basis for monetary policy measures. Through this work, the Central Bank seeks to identify the most likely prospects for economic and pricing progress two years ahead, but monetary policy measures, in particular changes in the policy rate, are aimed at influencing the progress at that time. In order to approach the subjects, many central banks do not suffice to publish a single forecast at any given time, but they also publish anomalous forecasts to show different probability and possibilities. This applies, among other things, to the forecasting of the Central Bank of Iceland. In order for a central bank to succeed, it needs to maintain professional practices and meaningful transparency. His actions need to be predictable under a policy that is publicly promoted and known. Credibility is a prerequisite for success. In a free economy and business, credibility and trust make all the difference. You can't play with the trust and expectations of free people. Similarly, central banks must adhere to permanently publicly known long-term sentiments and avoid instant anomalies that do not pertain to them. On this basis, the Central Bank of Iceland thus has alkaline measurements of the effectiveness of its operations. By virtue of them, he has independence in the face of government and can take responsibility. This independence is part of the development of a democratic system of government. Political struggles have their normal scope and area of society, but the Central Bank is outside this area according to normal division of labour. The Central Bank of Iceland was established as an independent institution in 1961, having previously been part of Landsbanki islands. On 27 March 2001, the Government and the Central Bank of Iceland published a joint statement on the Central Bank's inflation targets and independence in work, and now the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with Act No. 36 of 22 May 2001. With these changes in 2001, the Central Bank of Iceland formulated a position and policy in accordance with the best in this area. The Bank's main objectives are determined by law and some policy decisions are taken by the accession of the Prime Minister, but otherwise the Central Bank of Iceland has independence and its own responsibility for activities and actions. Autonomy and self-liability, for example, apply to monetary decisions and actions. 7 By aiming for its inflation target, the Central Bank of Iceland seeks to strengthen and strengthen the nation's business and economy and to formulate business and public expectations on progress and then to validate them successfully in practice. In this way, the Central Bank works, among other things, to approach a balance that contributes to the stability of household purchasing power. As a central bank or central bank, the Central Bank of Iceland is thus not least a service institution for the general public. Thank you to the audience

Title: Governor with a talk at the International Monetary Fund conference on economic and economic growth policies after the banking collapse
text: 8 March 2011 Mar Guomundsson: Panel comments in Session 6: The international monetary system The implications of cross-border banking and foreign currency swap lines for the international monetary system The financial crisis in Iceland throws light on one of the more important fault lines at the intersection between the international monetary system and the international financial system.1 This fault line was the operation of cross-border banks with large foreign currency balance sheets featuring significant maturity mismatches, but without an effective lender of last resort in terms of foreign currency.2 1 There are many definitions of the terms international monetary system and the international financial system and their relationship to each other. I construe the former to consist of exchange rate arrangements, payments and settlement systems across borders, and other international factors that would be included in the definition of a domestic monetary system, including liquidity provision by a LOLR, and the institutions and the rules that apply to all of these. The international financial system then consists of the operations of financial institutions and markets across borders as shaped by market forces and domestic and international regulations. In some sense, capital flows belong to both, as they go through markets and institutions but are conditioned by factors like exchange rate regimes and exchange rate restrictions. 2 See Gudmundsson and Thorsteinsson (2011). On the financial crisis in Iceland more generally, see Gudmundsson (2010) and references therein and Report of the Special Investigation Commission (SIC) / 3 Bernanke (2011) and Carney (2010) provide interesting recent analysis of one of the important omitted issues; i.e., the functioning of the adjustment mechanism. 4 See, for instance, Baba and Shim (2010); CGFS/MC (2010 a-c); Fender and McGuire (2010); McGuire and von Peter (2009); and Moessner and Allen (2010 a and b). Professors Obstfeld and Shin have developed this theme during this conference. See also Obstfeld (2010). For the Korean case, see Park (2010). In these brief remarks, I would like to concentrate mostly on this fault line, its implications for the international monetary system, and potential remedies, although, due to lack of time, I will leave aside many other important issues regarding the international monetary system.3 However, my topic will lead us into other key issues, such as the reserve currency, a global lender of last resort, and the role of foreign exchange reserves. Back to cross-border banking and the international monetary system. My former colleagues at the BIS and others have described in several articles and reports how foreign exchange risk in cross-border banking (currency mismatches and maturity mismatches in foreign currency) accumulated prior to the crisis, how that risk materialised in a forceful way after the collapse of Lehman, and how the ensuing dollar shortage was prevented from triggering widespread failure of banks to deliver on their foreign currency payments by LOLR operations in foreign exchange, using countries reserves and the dollar swap lines that were granted on a large scale.4 The same episode played out in the case of the Icelandic banks, but with a less happy ending, although there was much more to that story that I cannot expand on here, such as hidden vulnerabilities in the capital positions of the banks. Maturity mismatches are, of course, the bread and butter of modern banking, although they make banks vulnerable to runs. In the case of solvent institutions, we have known theoretically since Thornton (1802)  and probably over a century, as a practical policy  how to deal with that vulnerability in a domestic setting: with central bank LOLR operations, later complemented by deposit insurance. This process is facilitated by two factors. First, the funds withdrawn from banks during a domestic run flow in one form or another to the central bank, which can then redirect them back to the banks. Second, central banks have a very large short-run capacity to expand their balance sheets. In the current setting, it is far from guaranteed that this process can be replicated at the international level. In normal times, of course, managing liquidity across currencies from countries with free movement of capital and relatively developed capital markets is not much of an issue. In these conditions, foreign exchange swap markets can speedily be used to convert liquidity from one currency to another at spreads that closely reflect the differences in domestic money market rates in the two countries concerned. In other words, the covered interest parity condition broadly holds. But in any case, runs are less likely in normal times, and during the peak of the crisis, this process broke down almost completely in many cases, and FX swap spreads skyrocketed afterwards. It became extremely costly, and in some cases almost impossible, to convert domestic liquidity into dollar liquidity. The same scenario played out vis-a-vis the euro for several European countries outside the euro area. In a situation like this, the home central banks ability to help banks refinance the foreign liquidity denied them on the market is limited by the size of its reserves or the willingness of its larger neighbours to help. The Icelandic case brought this into sharp relief. Just before their failure, the three cross-border banks had foreign currency balance sheets amounting to almost 7 times GDP. In comparison, the reserves of the Central Bank, including swap lines with Nordic countries and committed credit lines, amounted to around 35% of GDP. Even if some of the foreign currency liabilities were long-term, the reserves were no match for the bleeding balance sheets of the banks. The issue here is one of the ebb and flow of international liquidity, which is a monetary issue. Although the provision of foreign currency liquidity through reserves was clearly important during the crisis, most studies seem to support the conclusion that it was the dollar swap lines that made the key difference, especially when they were uncapped vis-a-vis some key central banks. It was to a significant degree the domestic LOLR process replicated at the international level. Does this mean that we have the solution? At the conceptual level, yes, but at the practical level, no. The swap lines are not a permanent and reliable feature of the international monetary system. Will they be resurrected if similar circumstances arise in the future? Excellent central bank co-operation and strong leadership were involved on this occasion. However, we have seen their existence challenged in political discussion in the US. And remember that, although this time it was dollar liquidity that was needed around the globe, next time it might be other currencies. And then there is the issue of access criteria. Who gets a swap line and who does not? Should the provision of international liquidity be subject to the decision of one national central bank? It is also possible to turn the question around and ask whether it would ever work for an international process to decide on a major expansion of the balance sheet of a national central bank. After all, the FX swaps amounted to over a quarter of the balance sheet of the Fed at the peak,5 and then there was the promise of an uncapped expansion vis-a-vis a few key central banks. 5 Moessner and Allen (2010b). 6 Moessner and Allen (2010a) report sizeable increases in reserves in the case of Denmark, Sweden, Hungary, and Brazil. 7 On a much-discussed proposal, see Zhou (2009). IMF (2011) provides an interesting analysis of the issues involved. 8 See Keynes (1980). What are the alternatives? Certainly, one of them is that the international financial system would change as a result of the problems revealed in the international monetary system. This would entail the contraction of cross-border banking through market processes, with subsidiarisation and local funding being part of it, but also as countries adopt measures to deal with risks by restricting international activities of home banks and placing more strict prudential limits on currency mismatches and foreign currency maturity mismatches. For example, when Iceland lifts its current capital controls on outflows, it will probably impose restrictions on both size and composition of the foreign currency balance sheets of home-headquartered banks. Some might see such restrictions as capital controls in another form, but I see them as prudential rules. These developments might result in the restriction of significant cross-border banking to larger countries with international currencies. This need not be all bad, as the structure of cross-border banking would then be adjusting to the real risks involved, but I suspect that some smaller countries might not like it. In Europe, at least, smaller countries have the option of joining the EU and the euro area, which would make it safer to be a home base to cross-border banks, not to mention if EU- or EMU-wide supervision, deposit insurance, and crisis management and resolution were put in place for such banks in the future. This might even entail two types of bank licences, one for domestic banks and another for those wanting to have substantial operations across borders. Increased self-insurance by countries building foreign exchange reserves is also an alternative, and we have seen this happening after the crisis.6 However, there are well-known drawbacks and limitations to this option. Another currently discussed alternative is to strengthen the IMF as an international LOLR and, in the process, enhance the role of the SDR as a reserve asset. It would involve making the supply of SDR more elastic and the process more conducive to managing international liquidity. In the grander visions, the SDR would run parallel to the USD as a reserve currency and potentially replace it.7 Such an arrangement would be a move in the direction of Keynes original idea of an international clearing union and its currency, the Bancor.8 This idea merits further research and full discussion, and I note that the IMF is doing substantial work in this area. At this point, however, I see several obstacles. First, we should make the distinction between lending to sovereigns and lending to banks. The IMF has focused on lending to sovereigns, whereas swap lines were actually a form of lending to banks because, from a liquidity standpoint, the foreign central banks were simply intermediaries of the Feds global liquidity operations, although the counterparty risk was borne by the foreign central banks. In the initial stages of a financial crisis, banks can encounter foreign currency liquidity problems even if the finances of the sovereign are in good shape and there is no balance of payments crisis. Even solid Norway struggled on this point for a few days post-Lehman. The central bank was able to manage with its own reserves, but to be on the safe side, and probably in order to contain the liquidation of US dollar assets, a swap arrangement was swiftly negotiated with the Fed, at the same time that the Fed made comparable agreements with several other central banks. However, as we saw in several cases during this last episode, a banking crisis in a small, open economy will affect the sovereign in due course and may ultimately result in a full-scale fiscal crisis. Second, the SDR itself is not at present a currency in its own right, but a claim to use other members currencies or foreign exchange reserves. For the SDR to become a truly international currency on a par with the US dollar, it needs robust payment and settlement systems, and the private sector will have to be induced to use it on a large scale. In addition, if alterations in the supply of SDR are going to be an important tool for managing international liquidity, not to mention using it for LOLR operations vis-a-vis international banks, then the IMF needs to be able to create liquidity or swiftly tap into those that can. Furthermore, speed and scale are of the essence if such an option is to be a viable alternative to the swap lines. Third, the governance mechanisms for such a new global reserve currency do not exist. It is hard to envision the current IMF Executive Board taking decisions that are more akin to what central banks do, such as setting SDR interest rates if and when it gets a life of its own, or acting quickly to decide on LOLR operations that are basically directed at banks, although probably through national central banks. What is needed is possibly some kind of International Liquidity Committee composed of central bank governors  and perhaps full-time executive directors. Maybe it should meet at the BIS! At least, it seems to me that the arguments for central bank independence that apply to monetary policy carry over to affecting global monetary conditions. Let me conclude by saying that the expansion of cross-border banking that we witnessed before the crisis was part of the ongoing and at least partly beneficial process of financial globalisation. However, if we do not deal with the risks involved, we face the danger of a major reversal. It is fine to elaborate on grand schemes, and one day they might be realised. In the meantime, what we can expect is some combination of a partial retreat of cross-border banking, increased self-insurance, expansion of regional arrangements, and some partial reforms to the international monetary and financial systems. Speedier and more flexible credit lines at the IMF are certainly a welcome part of the latter. Let us hope that the reforms will dominate the retreat. Title: Capital controls and claims in the estates of fallen financial institutions
text: Capital controls and claims in the estates of fallen financial institutions It is sometimes argued that the capital controls disposal plan has been unsuccessful, they must be released immediately, but in the same breath it is claimed that the demands of creditors/hedge funds must be written into the estates of fallen financial institutions significantly down. An example of this kind of speech is an article written by Heioar Guojonsson in Frettablaoio on March 5th, which states: "Fortunately, the signing of a nebulous agreement last autumn was successfully averted, but there was little to remember, because the Central Bank allowed creditors to move over 300 billion, about 2,500 million, out of the country in September and planned to release multiples of that amount by the end of the year. It was prevented from a catastrophe." These claims by Honest go on to contradict the facts of the case and the logical context of events. It is therefore appropriate to state the following: 1. It was at the initiative of the Central Bank that the estates of fallen financial undertakings were further brought under the Foreign Exchange Act (hereinafter the Foreign Exchange Act) in March 2012. Had this not been done, the national authorities would now have little control over payments from the out-of-pocket payments of the old banks, which could cause considerable instability in the foreign exchange and financial markets if it is not properly handled. 2. In the co-operation of the Althingi, under pressure from the winding-up boards of the old banks, exemption clauses were put in place regarding certain foreign currency deposits of the central bank of Iceland (the 300 billion that HG speaks of) and the obligation was placed on the Central Bank of Iceland to set general rules that would allow the disbursement of recovered foreign currency from foreign assets of the estates. 3. Formulated ideas for ending the dissolution of fallen financial undertakings through a nebulous agreement did not emerge until after the aforementioned changes to the Foreign Exchange Act became a reality, although this possibility was certainly discussed by creditors. However, it is clear that the vast majority of creditors are now interested in ending the dissolution of the estates through a forced deal. 4. It is up to the courts and not the Central Bank to accept compulsory agreements. However, a composition agreement has no relevance to creditors unless the Central Bank grants exemptions from the Foreign Exchange Act. That and the willingness of creditors to end the dissolution with a forced agreement provides an opportunity to ensure that the dissolution occurs in ways that do not cause currency instability and could thus accelerate the disposal of currency controls. 5. When the Central Bank grants exemptions, the Bank shall, pursuant to law, look at two main considerations, one of the interests of the person requesting the exemption and, on the other hand, the effect that an exemption may have on the stability of exchange rate and monetary policy. The Bank, in other words, should look at meaningful moisture when processing exemptions. 6. The aforementioned interests do not need to be reproduced, but it is clear that the stability of foreign exchange can be guaranteed by one of two, very long repayment periods of claims made on domestic parties or a significant reduction in those claims in foreign currency measured. A combination of both is also eligible. The Central Bank will not accept any exemption that jeopardizes foreign exchange stability or financial stability in ambiguity. This is well known to the creditors' representatives. 7. It is clear that the most valuable domestic assets of the estates are two commercial banks, islandsbanki and Arion, and bonds between old and new Landsbanki. Ownership of banks concerns an important public interest that calls for the involvement of political government. The Central Bank will therefore not grant an exemption for forced contracts except after consultation with the Government. The Act on Financial Undertakings contains provisions on active holdings in financial undertakings, which stipulates that the Financial Supervisory Authority assesses the eligibility of parties to exercise active holdings. Those who consider there is a risk that the banks may, despite the aforementioned provisions of the Act, fall into the hands of unsafe parties who do not have long-term considerations should consider whether there is reason to sharpen the provisions of Act No. 161/2002 on the Ownership of Financial Undertakings. 8. That foreign hedge funds (or financial undertakings that could to some extent be considered of this kind) have acquired approximately half of the claims in the estates of fallen financial undertakings have no legal significance and therefore make little difference to the progress of the case. These are claims on Icelandic out-of-state estates subject to Icelandic law, including the Bankruptcy Act and the Foreign Exchange Act, to the extent that foreign exchange transactions or foreign exchange movements are involved. Demands can be made to purchase and sell. Some buyers of claims have already cashed in on profits, others are hoping for such a move, and yet other creditors are from among the original creditors who have suffered significant damage but are hoping to minimise the losses by waiting for the recovery to end rather than delegate claims. All of this, however, has limited implications for resolving the issue. The objective considerations that prevail over the possible granting of an exemption from the Foreign Exchange Act primarily concern the impact of the dissolution on foreign exchange and financial stability. The Central Bank will protect the national interest and call for all the expertise, whether inside or outside the Bank, that it is necessary to have in its power in order for the objectives to be achieved. In the debate over the dissolution of fallen financial institutions, it is important not to lose sight of the main points and facts of an issue. Otherwise, the debate is prone to secondary issues that appeal more to people's feelings than to logic. It is therefore important that those involved in the discussion examine the facts of the matter carefully before they advance to the writing field. In this way, they promote moderate and meaningful debate and a broad consensus and reconciliation of Iceland's interests. Arnor Sighvatsson Deputy Governor.
