Title: Address at the Annual General Meeting 2011
text: Saturday, 7 April 2011 Address Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, at the 50th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 7 April 2011 The President of Iceland, the Prime Minister and other ministers, the President of the Althing, the Chairman of the Board of Directors, the chairmen of political parties, governors, directors of institutions, ambassadors of foreign countries and other good guests! The Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland is held on the Bank's 50th anniversary. It would be overstated to say that calm and quiet prevail around the birthday boy. On the contrary, the season is stormy. We are also at a crossroads in our nation's economy and monetary policy. Policies that will be taken at these crossroads can have a significant impact on developments in the future. This may not be similar to the circumstances that prevailed when the bank was established. More about that later. So what are these crossroads? The first is that the economy has been changing. Instability and recession are vying for better balance and economic recovery. The trade deficit of the overheating period has been turned into an underlying trade surplus that has supported the exchange rate. The exchange rate is now 71/2% higher than at the beginning of last year. At the same time, the Central Bank has bought foreign exchange on the market for ISK 33 billion, as part of the plan to build uncommitted foreign exchange reserves. The Central Bank's inflation target was reached towards the end of last year, which involved higher rates, a sluggish pace in the economy and that inflation expectations had fallen towards the inflation target. Of course, this trend is not independent of the development of monetary policy restraint, as underutilised production capacity can coincide with a vicious cycle of falling exchange rates and rising inflation expectations if confidence is lacking. There are indications that a weak economic recovery began in the third quarter of last year and forecasters expect it to continue this year. However, the recovery is still weak, not least given the extreme slack in place. In this regard, it is not least worrying that business investment is still low historically and the growth in exports is rather low in light of the low real exchange rate of the krona and the robust recovery of international trade. It is important here that the main export sectors are subject to production restrictions and increased exports will therefore not be in any way considered without investment. However 1 there is good growth in the sectors that do not have such restrictions, but their share is still low. The next crossroads are due to the fact that the foreign liquidity of the economy has greatly improved along with increased foreign exchange reserves. At the end of February, the reserve amounted to ISK 719 billion, which corresponds to 46% of GDP. It has never been greater on this scale, even at the end of World War II. Increased resources, greater stability, the progress of a budget for a surplus on the Treasury in coming years, and the purchase of foreign government debt in the secondary market have since led to voices about government liquidation. This is important for the fact that it is now considered safe to work on the disposal of currency controls and that the conditions for foreign borrowing by the Treasury have improved significantly, but it could pave the way for other domestic parties. The referendum on the Icesave agreement next weekend could, of course, put a line in this account. If the result is yes, the government's control and borrowing will go ahead as planned. If the Icesave agreement is rejected, however, there is evidence that the two big U.S. rating agencies will decide to put the Treasury's credit rating down to a speculative category. Furthermore, the foreign borrowing of the Treasury will be heavier, and the progress of the programme to abolish the capital controls would therefore be slower. However, there is uncertainty about how strong and long-lasting these effects would be. The financial system is also approaching crossroads. The first phase of the restoration of the financial system is largely behind us. Banks are operating with a defined balance sheet, restructuring household and corporate debt is being restructured, and changes have been made to some of the most obvious flaws in the regulatory framework of domestic financial institutions. However, there are many hard work to be done in establishing an active and stable financial system. It is not yet possible to state that it can securely fund itself without the support of currency controls and declarations of universal deposit guarantees. In this regard, it is important to improve the functioning of financial markets that are important for trading, financing and risk distribution, especially the foreign exchange market and the stock market. It is also important to reopen access by financial institutions and other entities to foreign credit markets. The task is then to develop a policy on the nature, size and international relationship of Icelandic financial system. It is no less important to formulate a policy on instruments and organisation of financial stability, but the financial crisis teaches us that assessing systemic risk is a key factor, along with solid arrangements for the application of devices to counteract it. Lastly, economic policy and economic policy are at a crossroads because of the changes I have attributed here. In the shortest case scenario, the projects are moving from achieving stability and decent balance to economic growth and, moreover, from crisis response to long-term reconstruction. As far as monetary policy is concerned, this shows, among other things, that the Monetary Policy Committee has changed its propensity from falling interest rates to neutral 2 Status. That doesn't mean that interest rates can't fall further, but rather the other that since inflation seems to have reached a low, an economic recovery has begun and active control rates have come closer to balanced interest rates than before, it's less obvious in which direction the next interest rate changes will be. The future is therefore more determined than ever by what the latest evidence suggests on the state and outlook of the economy. The Monetary Policy Committee is expected at its next meeting to assess whether and how the outcome of the Icesave vote and the newly published plan to abolish capital controls will affect monetary policy in the near future. The plan is based on dividing the project into two main phases. The first will work to lower the status of so-called offshore krona by, among other things, allowing their owners out through tendering or into investment in Icelandic economy. It is the first after satisfactory progress has been made in this material that controls will be released from domestic capital outflows. If the conditions are right, the second phase could go relatively quickly, but otherwise in smaller steps. It is difficult to say how long the first phase lasts, as it depends on a wide range of uncertainties such as adequate access by the Treasury and other parties to foreign credit markets. It is important, however, regarding monetary policy in the near future that the first phase is thus designed at the front of at least a small amount of exchange rates and foreign exchange reserves. It is the first in the second phase that interest rates against foreign countries begin to matter much more in terms of the development of the exchange rate, than it is now. Monetary policy has in the past been part of a larger government economic plan in cooperation with the International Monetary Fund. Key elements of that plan have been stable exchange rates, sustainable fiscal policy and the reconstruction of the financial system. Despite delays in implementing the plan, overall, significant progress has been made. The partnership with the International Monetary Fund on the current economic plan ends in August. Of course, decades of cooperation with the International Monetary Fund are not over. On the part of the Central Bank, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the International Monetary Fund and its employees for their cooperation in the past. The end of a programme with the International Monetary Fund and the implementation of a programme of deregulation of the capital controls set the agenda for shaping monetary policy in the coming years and in practice the framework of economic policy as a whole. This work has begun, including a report published by the Central Bank on the subject in December, called Monetary Policy after a restraint. Let's go back to 1961 when the Central Bank of Iceland began its operations. As will be explained in the following errands, Icelandic national economy then went through a lot of changes. A number of structural changes were well under way, changes that we still live in. Work was carried out under an economic plan aimed at stabilising the national economy on market assumptions. Trade in goods and services became freer and the multi-exchange rate had been replaced by exchange rate listings that took into account the underlying economic conditions. As it was now, Iceland with 3 economic plan in cooperation with the International Monetary Fund. Then, as it is now, the economic ties between Iceland and the rest of the world were in the doldrums. The establishment of the Central Bank was part of these changes and the Central Bank's work was part of a broader set of measures. The central bank's position was strong from the start. It is of course remarkable that here in this hall sit today various of those who were both important thinkers and perpetrators of these changes. Good attendees! As I have mentioned earlier in my speech, there is now a need to formulate both monetary policy and a policy on financial stability for the future. The revision of the Act on the Central Bank of Iceland will presumably be part of that process. The Central Bank will endeavour as a participant in all of these policies, with many more involved, with which the Bank expects good cooperation. In the end, however, it is parliament and in some cases the nation itself that has the last word. Finally, I would like to thank the many partners of the Central Bank for their cooperation over the past year. No less would I like to thank the Central Bank's employees for their good work, but without it, little progress would be made from the Bank's work. This time, I would like to finally thank you for the contribution of the many people who over the past fifty years have put their hands up on the Central Bank and it is nice to see how many of them are here today. 4

Title: Speech at the Bank's annual meeting
text: April 7, 2021 Statement by asgeir Jonsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland at the 60th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 7 April 2021. The Prime Minister, the Chairman of the Board of Directors and others who hear from me. 2021 is a great year for the Central Bank of Iceland. These are the anniversary  measured by three figures  1961, 1981 and 2001  each marking a turning point in the Bank's history. It should first be believed that the Central Bank became an independent institution on this day  7 April  1961. We are celebrating our 60th anniversary today. Until then, central bank operations had been in the hands of two commercial banks; First islandsbanki and then Landsbanki islands. The establishment of the Central Bank was part of extensive economic reforms at the start of the Reform Regime  reforms that freed the country from the woods of capital, commodity rationing and multiple exchange rate listings. But 60 years is not an advanced age - if we think that the sovereignty of the country will be 103 this year. The sovereignty of 1918 meant that the Icelandic krona became an independent currency. Iceland had therefore been sovereign for 43 years without a special central bank to stand behind independent monetary control. No one should be surprised that the economy has failed at this time. Title: Address at the annual meeting
text: April 7, 2021 Address by Gylfi Magnusson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at the Bank's 60th Annual General Meeting on 7 April 2021. The Prime Minister, the Governor and other members of the Central Bank. I'm here with the 60th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. As a year ago, the COVID-19 virus is setting its sights on the meeting. There are a handful of guests on site, but the meeting is broadcast online. The Central Bank of Iceland was established by Act No. 10/1961 and celebrates its 60th anniversary this year. The central bank is now very different from the one established in 1961. The Bank's operations and the legislation on which it is based have thus undergone many changes over the past six decades. Significant changes were made to the Act on the Bank in the 1980s when interest rates were voluntary and also in 2001 when the Bank's independence to use its instruments was ratified as well as other important changes. Most recently, there were major changes with the act, which came into force at the beginning of last year when the Financial Supervisory Authority was merged with the Bank and thereby entrusted with supervision of all financial activities in the country. The Bank's operations are now divided into three main pillars: the formulation and implementation of monetary policy, financial stability and supervision of financial activities. Over the past year, the Bank's work has been characterised to a large extent by the response to the virus. The Central Bank's main actions have been aimed at responding to the resulting problem and the situation has had a considerable impact on where and how the bank's work is carried out. In addition, there was a strong emphasis on integrating the Central Bank's operations on the basis of the aforementioned legislative changes. According to the New Act on the Bank, the Governor is responsible for the Bank's activities and exercises decision-making powers in all matters not entrusted to others by law. asgeir Jonsson has served as Governor of the Central Bank since August 2019. Three deputy governors began work at the beginning of last year. Rannveig Siguroardottir is deputy governor of monetary policy, Gunnar Jakobsson deputy governor of financial stability and Unnur Gunnarsdottir deputy governor of the Financial Supervisory Authority. The Governor and the Deputy Governors make joint decisions on specific matters, as compared to the Governor. 3 article of the Act on the Bank. Three committees are currently making decisions on the application of the Central Bank's powers and controls regarding monetary policy, financial stability and financial supervision, i.e. pen- 1 inga policy committee, Financial Stability Committee and Financial Supervisory Committee. In addition to the Governors and the Deputy Governors who sit on the committees in accordance with their responsibilities, they sit on external representatives. The Bank's new structure came into force at the beginning of 2020 following the entry into force of new laws. The Bank's core divisions are seven and the four support divisions, as well as the Central Office of the CEO. Information on the Bank's operations and results can be found in its annual report published today. According to the income statement, profit from the Bank's operations amounted to just over ISK 68 billion in 2020, while the previous year the profit was just over ISK 22 billion. The Bank's profits can largely be attributed to positive exchange rate differences, but assets in foreign currencies are significantly greater than liabilities, and value changes in assets. The Bank's operating expenses amounted to just over ISK 7.4 billion. They increased year-on-year as a result of the merger with the Financial Supervisory Authority, but in 2019 the Bank's operating expenses amounted to more than ISK 4.7 billion. Net interest income during the year was ISK 75 million, but the previous year it was negative by more than ISK 9 billion. The Bank's assets amounted to just under ISK 843 billion at the end of the year, about ISK 3 billion more than the previous year, but about 97% of the Bank's assets were foreign. Equity increased from ISK 82 billion to ISK 150.8 billion, which is ISK 800 million more than the Bank's capital objective confirmed by the Board of Directors. Profits in excess of the Bank's capital objectives were paid to the Treasury as dividends. At the end of 2020, there were 303 employees at the Central Bank, an increase from 177 from the previous year as a result of the merger with the Financial Supervisory Authority. The gender ratio remained fairly even and equal pay analysis continued to show that there was no significant, unexplained pay gap between the sexes. During the year, construction work was started on the Bank's premises at Kalkofnsvegur 1. It needed renewal after decades of use, but a parallel effort was made to redesign working facilities in order for more workers to be accommodated. After construction, all main activities of the Central Bank will be able to be placed in the Bank's house. In 2020, the Central Bank, its management and its staff were severely tested. For many corners, we looked at the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority. As a result, heavy tasks were added in the wake of the COVID-19 epidemic. Normally, the staff, who had to do most of their jobs at home, were very much involved in the year. The Central Bank responded to these challenges and can only be said that it has well lived up to the expectations set for it and that the first year of operation after the merger went well given the circumstances. The role of the Board of Directors is to monitor that the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with the laws applicable to its operations and to confirm various decisions and rules established by the Bank. In the past year, the Board of Directors was appointed by orunni Guomundsdottir, Sigurour Kara Kristjansson, Frosti Sigurjonsson, Bolla Heoinsson, Una Maria oskarsdottir and Jacqueline Clare Mallett, along with me, who served as Chairman of the Board of Directors. The Board of Directors held 14 meetings during the year. I thank the Bank's employees for their good work and cooperation in 2020. I would also like to thank the members of the Board of Directors, deputy governors, secretaries of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their good cooperation. I would like to extend a special thanks to the Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, asgeir Jonsson, for the cooperation. asgeir will give his annual meeting speech hereafter, but first we will listen to the address of Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir. In the end, we will see a video about the design of the Icelandic banknote series, but 40 years have passed since the current order of banknotes was put into circulation during a coin change. Finally, I congratulate the Central Bank of Iceland and its employees on their 60th birthday. The Bank is doing well at this juncture and there are all the prerequisites to believe that it will succeed in carrying out its important statutory role in the future.

Title: Speech at the French-Icelandic Chamber of Commerce conference in Paris
text: 28 February 2013 Icelands crisis and recovery and current challenges Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Speech at a Conference organised by the French-Icelandic Chamber of Commerce; Islande, La Renaissance, Paris, 28 February 2013. President of Iceland, Ambassadors, Ladies and Gentlemen Nearly all of you probably know that almost 90% of Icelands banking sector failed in the first week of October 2008. This fact is well established in the minds of scholars of the international financial crisis. What is probably less well known is that at that point, Iceland was already on its way into a recession after an unsustainable boom and serious overheating during 2005-2007 and a currency crisis in the first half of 2008. The banking collapse and the associated wealth loss and further currency depreciation made the recession worse, of course, but so did the recession that hit the global economy in the fourth quarter of 2008. That autumn, two separate but interrelated sub-stories of the recent Icelandic saga converged in a tragic grand finale. These are: 1. Icelands boom-bust cycle and problems with macroeconomic management in small, open, and financially integrated economies. This is a story that has played out many times around the globe, and many of its elements have been seen before in Iceland. It might have been somewhat more extreme this time around, but it wasnt fundamentally different. 2. The rise and fall of three cross-border banks operating on the basis of EU legislation (the European passport). This story was much more unique, as involved the first banking crisis in Europe since the EU single market was formed in the early 1990s. Today I am not going to talk about the build-up to these events, and I will have little to say about the second story. I have expanded on both in various publications and speeches that I can refer you to. Instead, I am going to talk about what happened to the Icelandic economy afterward  its deep recession and its recovery  and then reflect on some of the policy challenges that still face us. 1 But let us first reflect on the distance that has been travelled since that fateful autumn of 2008. Icelands financial sector was crumbling, and the authorities had to take extraordinary measures to keep basic domestic banking services up and running, including letting the international part of the banking system go into resolution, wiping out all equity in the banks, and removing their managers. Many expected the sovereign to default on its obligations, which would have left Iceland shut out of international capital markets for years. A key aspect of crisis management was therefore to ring-fence the sovereign from the failing banks and minimise the socialisation of private sector losses. And Iceland was well on its way into its deepest post-war recession, where GDP contracted by 12.5% from its peak in the fourth quarter of 2007 to its trough nine quarters later, in the first quarter of 2010. It fell from an unsustainable peak, of course, but the drop was spectacular nonetheless. Where are we now, almost five years later? First, there is hardly any talk of a potential sovereign default any more: the public sector has a primary surplus, the overall deficit is estimated to have been around 2% of GDP last year, government debt as a share of GDP is on a downward trajectory, and Iceland has investment-grade ratings from all three major rating agencies. Second, we are far advanced in rebuilding a domestically oriented financial sector. The new domestic banks, which were built on the ashes of the three failing cross-border banks, are profitable, well capitalised, liquid, and with non-performing loan ratios that, although still high due the crisis, are falling to normal levels as private sector debt restructuring progresses and the economy recovers. Fig. 1a Fig. 1b 2 Third, the economy has indeed recovered, as can been seen on Figure 1a. The economy has been growing since the second quarter of 2010, and unemployment has fallen from a peak of over 9% to around 5%. And as Figure 1b shows, this year Iceland is projected to be among the worlds five fastest-growing advanced economies, with growth estimated at 2.1%, although that is due in part to the recent slowdown in many other advanced countries. And the prediction is that Iceland will grow even faster during the next two years, or in the range of 3-4% per annum, causing the slack in the economy to disappear and the unemployment rate to fall to around 4%. Fig. 2a Fig. 2b So how did we get here? In answering this question, we need to remember that subsequent developments were not only a function of the negative shocks hitting the economy in 2008 but also a function of the policy responses. In addition to crisis management vis-a-vis the failing banks, which I have already mentioned, the economic programme that the Icelandic authorities developed in cooperation with the IMF played a key role. It provided financing amounting to 5.1 billion US dollars, which helped to build FX reserves. The programme had three key goals: stabilisation of the exchange rate, fiscal sustainability, and reconstruction of the financial sector. Comprehensive capital controls were a key element in the programme. 3 Fig. 3 The policy responses mitigated the recession but could not stop it from becoming the deepest in Icelands post-war history and a severe one in international comparison as can be seen from Figure 2. Iceland was not the hardest hit, however, as can be seen from this slide. Furthermore, developments were more or less in line with previous Central Bank of Iceland predictions (see Figure 3). The result was that Iceland fell significantly down the League of Nations. Fig. 4a Fig. 4b The currency played a significant role, both in the build-up to the crisis and during subsequent stabilisation and recovery. The currency crisis materialised in an over 50% depreciation of the krona over the course of 2008. It hit highly indebted corporate and household sectors, a large share of whose debt was either denominated in or linked directly to foreign currency, or linked indirectly to it through price indexation at a time of strong and rapid exchange 4 rate pass-through. The contractionary balance sheet effects of the currency depreciation were therefore substantial. Hence the need to stabilise the exchange rate, which was achieved in the middle of 2009. But the real depreciation  which took the real exchange rate to around 30% below its historical average for a time and left it at the current level of around 20% below that average  compressed imports and provided some stimulus to exports, thus helping to turn a double-digit current account deficit into an underlying surplus. But the stimulus to exports is limited by the fact that Icelands major export industries, such as fisheries and energy-intensive metal smelters, face capacity constraints that can only be lifted through investments that have been rather limited so far. Fig. 5a Fig. 5b Fig. 6a Fig. 6b 5 A very important and somewhat novel element of the successful policy response was the interplay of fiscal consolidation, monetary policy, and capital controls. The crisis dealt a heavy blow to government finances in Iceland, as can be seen from Figure 5. The resulting deficit  10% of GDP in 2009  would have been much more difficult to finance in the absence of the capital controls that locked in both foreign financing from before the crisis and new domestic saving. However, there was no escaping the fiscal consolidation needed to put government finances on a sustainable path, as Iceland lacked external confidence and market access. It was a big effort, as can be seen from Figure 6a, and it started in the middle of an economic crisis, which is far from optimal. But monetary policy was increasingly able to give support to the economy after the exchange rate had been stabilised and inflation came down (see Figure 6b). And the scope for monetary policy to support the domestic economy in spite of the balance of payments crisis was in turn enhanced by the capital controls, as can be seen from this slide, which compares short-term real interest rates during the recent financial crisis in Iceland with short-term real rates in Korea during the Asian financial crisis. Fig. 7 Finally, let me say something about Icelands current challenges. I will mention three. The first is to bring inflation back to the 2% target. It is currently running at 4.8% and is fuelled by the weak currency and wage increases in excess of productivity growth, which in turn are driven by good conditions in an export sector that benefits from the low exchange rate. Inflation is predicted to fall back to the target around the middle of next year, although this will depend on exchange rate developments. 6 Fig. 8a Fig. 8b The second relates to deleveraging, or reduction of debt levels. Public and private debt levels are on a declining path, as can be seen from Figure 8. In the case of businesses in particular, a significant part of this takes the form of debt restructuring and write-downs. That, along with the resolution process of the failed banks, will reduce Icelands net external debt to a sustainable level over time (see Figure 9). This is a good thing, of course, but the deleveraging process has two short- to medium-term side effects that must be managed. The first one relates the negative effect of deleveraging on domestic demand. The second relates to its negative effect on the exchange rate, as economic entities with foreign debt, little or no foreign-currency income, and no access to foreign credit are forced to repay foreign debt faster than is optimal for them and the economy. This is part of our balance of payments problem. Fig. 9a Fig. 9b 7 That brings me to the third challenge, which is to break out of Icelands balance of payments crisis and lift the capital controls. Through fiscal consolidation and reinforcement of its FX reserves (see Figure 10a), Iceland has seen a steep drop in the perceived risk of the sovereign as reflected in CDS spreads. Furthermore, the sovereign has been able to tap foreign capital markets twice, for a total of 2 billion US dollars, and use part of the proceeds to repay a significant part of the loans associated with the IMF programme ahead of schedule. FX reserves and other Central Bank FX assets currently cover scheduled sovereign foreign debt repayments beyond 2022 (see Figure 10b). Fig. 10a Fig. 10b The balance of payments problem that the current controls on capital outflows are intended to address therefore lies elsewhere. It is best demonstrated by Figure 11, which shows, on the one hand, liquid ISK assets held by nonresidents, which amount to 22% of GDP, and the old banks ISK assets, which will, in the absence of other action, accrue mostly to foreign residents and may be added to the overhang of potentially liquid offshore kronur. Given that the underlying current account surplus is in the region of 3-4% of GDP and that there are a lot of other debt repayments laying claims to it, it is clear that if these amounts were to be released overnight, we would be at risk of another currency crisis, with potentially significant financial stability implications. That is why these assets must be released after significantly reduced valuations in terms of foreign currency or must flow out over a much longer period. The more their value is reduced in terms of foreign currency, the faster can the controls be lifted. 8 Fig. 11a Fig. 11b The Icelandic authorities have a strategy in place to lift the capital controls gradually, as conditions permit, without unduly undermining exchange rate and financial stability. The strategy is currently under review. It is clear that the process will be significantly affected by how the krona problem associated the winding up of the old banks is dealt with, as an amicable solution could greatly expedite the removal of the controls. But the basic thinking will remain the same. The first element is to secure the framework conditions for lifting the controls, such as at least balanced public sector finances, an underlying current account surplus, and adequate FX reserves. All of this is either in place or well on its way. The second element is to put in place the economic policy frameworks and prudential rules that will make it possible for Iceland to deal with the risks associated with free and volatile capital movements. That is also underway. The third element is to reduce the overhang of liquid offshore kronur to a safer level, either through release at a discount or by tying the offshore kronur up in longer maturities and real investments. That is underway as well, although some are of the view that the process is too slow. The fourth element is to open market access and, through other means, generate longer-term inflows to replace the capital that wants to leave. History shows that those who jump early on such a bandwagon have a lot to gain. Let me conclude by saying that Iceland has made great strides since the autumn of 2008. The next major task is to re-integrate Iceland financially into the global economy, but hopefully in a safer way this time. Thank you very much. 9

Title: Position of the Krna - article written for Economic Affairs in December 2001
text: 08.05.2002 Governor Eirikur Guonason: Position of the Krona - article written for Economic Affairs in December 2001 Much of the debate about the Icelandic the krona at the moment stems both from its massive rate hike in the past and the fact that there has been an interest in shutting it down and adopting the euro. I'm going to talk a little bit about this stuff here. All I can say is that we've done well in the economy lately. For most of the last decade, inflation was low, economic growth was high and unemployment was low. We benefited from ratings from foreign credit rating agencies. If it is added that in Iceland, income distribution is more equal than in many countries, it can be said that no further wish can be made for a single economy. It should be noted that such a success can be achieved even though the currency is Icelandic the krona, which is certainly a small currency in international comparison. But last year, the outlook changed somewhat for the worse when the catch was reduced on the advice of fisheries scientists. Some other news was also negative, especially the decline in the price of shares here and abroad. Both of these events were surprising, as often happens when there is a torrential downpour. It seems to have had a huge impact on expectations for the future. This year we added more reasons to reduce human optimism, as power sources in Iceland and abroad are still forecasting lower economic growth in the near future than they have been, particularly in the United States. Somewhat since the recession of symptoms emerged in the United States, but the September terror attacks add black on top of gray, if at all, and will likely deepen the downturn that had begun. In just under two years, the outlook for the economy has changed dramatically. However, there is no reason to think that the situation is serious, even if it only reduces economic growth for the time being. We just need to get a little out of it, too. The exchange rate of the krona has fallen so much so that the real exchange rate has reached a historic low. The reasons include the negative news that has been mentioned, but also the large trade deficit against foreign countries, the excessive availability of credit, foreign securities purchases by pension funds and others, rising inflation as well as the fact that the exchange rate had risen considerably shortly before the negative news spawned. It would be too much simplification to mention one of these points, as is sometimes done, and say that is the reason for the rate cut. I believe that the main reason is how great the trade deficit became, but it does not have to lead to a rate cut if the prospect of its decline is differently, i.e. by the growth of exports or the decline in imports. The rate's decline curve in 2000 began when it was shown that exports would not continue to grow as expected. And unchanged rates, there was no reason to expect a decline in imports, as wage increases and tax cuts had greatly increased public purchasing capacity. From what had come, the economy, which now resides in the market listing of the exchange rate, was bound to adapt to the changing outlook with the exchange rate cut of the krona. It reduces imports and improves the balance of trade as well as increasing the revenues of export companies. But a rate cut is not flawless, especially when it gets as high as it has now become. It can threaten financial stability, due to the debt burden on those who have taken foreign loans, and it has now for a while fed our primary enemy, inflation. This has given rise to debate about whether the krona should be abandoned as a currency in Iceland. There have been claims such as those that the krona is ruined and it is best for us to adopt the euro. Therefore, there are both advantages and disadvantages of having an independent currency, and the same applies of course to having a different currency. The drawbacks of having our own currency and free trade with foreign countries with goods, services and capital, for example, are that interest rates will likely be higher than in neighbouring countries, and so the other that when the outlook changes for the worse in economic terms, it is prone to a reduction in the exchange rate of the currency, whether the reason is a homemade problem or an external one. Newly acquired experience shows that problems, mostly homemade, yielded large-scale a rate cut, which for the time being causes a different kind of problem. We still don't see the end of how we fare from the consequences of the exchange rate change. From this, it can be clear that large exchange rate fluctuations are undesirable. What, then, is there' let's consider three options. First of all, in this country, another currency is introduced. The euro is most underwhelming because of our high levels of trade with other European countries. The advantages of joining the European Economic and Monetary Union would be, for example, that interest rates would be lower here than they would otherwise be and that economic failures here would not lead to a decrease in the exchange rate of the currency. But the mistake could cause other inconveniences such as increased unemployment, at least temporarily. In addition to membership of the European Union, there would have to have been low inflation and a stable exchange rate for several years before the monetary union could be joined. There are more conditions, but these are cited as examples of our important challenges. We would have to be very careful with economic management, even though we had a currency other than the krona. It should also point out the main flaw in the way that the exchange rate of the euro against the dollar and other currencies will reliably fluctuate, and those changes would not always be favorable in our trade with American or Asian countries. Secondly, the option shall be to go to previous corporate governance, i.e. to centralise the exchange rate listing of the krona and to block free relations with foreign countries, e.g. by prohibiting Icelanders from buying foreign securities and reviving more bans in relation to foreign currency. This meant that homemade economic problems did not necessarily have to lead to devaluation, at least not simultaneously. Due to increasing relations between countries, this is probably an unrealistic option, but it is necessary to keep it in mind because some restrictions are possible and may become inevitable if satisfactory results are not achieved in other ways. Third, I mention the most immediate option under the prevailing circumstances, namely that we learn from the mistakes and manage to maintain stability in economic development in the long run. In short, this means we need to save more than we do and strive to have low inflation here permanently. Whether the future holds a different currency in this country or not, this is an urgent challenge. It is therefore appropriate to remind you of a report on the promotion of macroeconomic savings issued by the Ministry of Finance in late 1998, which highlighted four proposals. The first proposal was to trust the performance of the public sector, as it was considered the fastest and safest way to increase macroeconomic savings. The next two were about increased pension savings and home share purchases. The fourth was on the verge of checking whether various systems, such as the interest rate compensation system, were out of debt. These proposals are still relevant. My assumption of these reflections is that it is absurd to judge Icelandic crown as a disused currency. One of the main problems that our economy has had for a long time, too little macroeconomic savings, will not be attributed to the fact that the currency is the krona and not the euro. However, discussion of joining the European Monetary Union is normal and necessary. However, those who participate in it should not judge one path of almighty and another incapable, but should pay attention to the pros and cons of each individual, as well as to realistically assess the conditions of participation. And whether our currency will be Icelandic krona in the future or not, it is clear that the proportions of consumption and savings need to be changed here. It is, in my opinion, the most urgent subject of the present moment. Written in December 2001. About the author Education: Matriculation examination from ML 1965. Title: A few points on monetary policy
text: A few things about money submitted at the visit of the Oddfellows box of the Central Bank of Iceland. May 7, 2008: 7 May 2008 Gizur White in Here we will briefly discuss some of the current challenges as they face us at the Central Bank. There will also be issues that are somewhat debated at the moment, namely the indexation of loans and the use of the euro in Iceland. There have been a lot of unsecurity clouds in the sky of the economy lately. However, there is no reason to despair. We have work to do and Icelandic economy has previously shown the flexibility necessary to work its way out of trouble. But it is essential that we realize the problem and try to learn from experience. Inflation, which measures by double digits, is reminiscent of an unpleasant chapter of economic history that young people only know from demand. The exchange rate of the krona in recent weeks is causing an inflation shot now, but the subversion is intricate. It is very important that we do not lose track of inflation, but rather to establish a better balance in the economy. The imbalance is characterised by inflation and a large trade deficit with foreign countries, which is explained by high demand, not least because of consumption. We've spent on stuff forward and based our spending partly on loans. Due to high demand, asset prices rose sharply for a time, but there has already been a change in its development. The purchasing power of homes and businesses has for some time been much greater than the likely future growth in export earnings can sustain. Trade deficits and foreign debt, among other things, cause the Icelandic krona to become a target for investors. High interest rates and exchange rates also play a part. But the interest rates would not have had to be as high as they are if there had been more calm over waters and not the huge excess spending that has characterised the last few years. "Better is less and more equal" is an expression that truly applies here. Proposals have been heard for the Central Bank to cut interest rates even though inflation is high and the outlook is bad. This directly involves a request for surrender to inflation that would be dangerous to deal with. It would have been desirable that demand had been reduced earlier by increasing national savings tendencies. Therefore, it is not to be greeted and unfortunately looks like the necessary adjustments in the economy will be quite drastic. Holding back inflation is not an easy-to-understand problem. In recent years, various forces have been swayed by the expansion forces and thus the inflation risk. The construction in East Iceland is often referred to as they were unusually large. However, they were not surprised and would not alone have caused significant inflationary pressures. Immigrant labor helped. Another issue was about a large increase in general demand. Keeping inflation close 1 2.5% would have been an easier subject had demand been lower. It was large due to an increase in wages, a reduction in taxes, a lot of optimism, including high levels of employment and, most importantly, easy access to long-term loans with interest rates that for a time began to fall. Once the Housing Financing Fund's credit rules had been announced, banks felt weighed in and began to compete in the mortgage market known. Both were unfortunate that the rules of the Housing Financing Fund should be cleared when tensions had developed in the economy and that banks should go overboard in the provision of housing loans that were largely flowing for consumption. The weaker the approach in other areas, the tougher the Fed needs to provide because it should strive to keep inflation close to the target of 2.5%. It would also have helped if earlier information had been revealed about how vigorously the national yacht sailed out of the wave valley it encountered at the turn of the century. The Central Bank, like others, always faces uncertainty about future trends, the assessment of the current situation and unfortunately also on the developments of recent years. Hopefully we can find ways to improve indicators of economic development. I guess everyone wants to have a small price. The objective that the Central Bank has been entrusted with is that it is normally around 2.5%, as in our major trading countries. Sometimes it can be concluded from the debate that this is too strict a goal or even that it can be set aside for the time being. If this is the case, higher inflation than otherwise will be established, even if an old-fashioned swathe of purchase fees and prices will be re-formed, causing even higher inflation than it is now. When many forces counteract the low inflation target, the Central Bank's devices need to be used so that it has an unpleasant side effect. Therefore, it is desirable that more people than the Central Bank take responsibility for the inflation target. Large-scale wage increases are, for example, undesirable if they are cancelled to flow throughout the pay ladder, although at first they are intended to reach only a small group. Banks are obliged to take moderation in lending, and workers and borrowers should treat funds well. The national savings rate could be higher than it is. It is strange that interest rates in this country are higher than in neighbouring countries even at a time when the economy is not overexcited. There are two obvious reasons for this. On the one hand, we have a bad inflation history behind us and on the other hand that savings are low, or, among other things, consumption is high. To bring interest rates down to a similar level to those in neighbouring countries, there are other things that need to resemble what it is, such as low inflation in the long run and sufficient states instead of spending. Due to the inflation experience, the general indexation of financial obligations was adopted almost thirty years ago. Previously, indexation had been used to a limited extent, including on government savings certificates. It is sometimes argued that it is necessary to abolish indexation here, but the arguments are not always the same. One is that insurance needs to be abolished in order to bring down inflation. It has also been mentioned that if indexation was out of the question, the loan cost of the borrower would be lower than it would otherwise be. Finally, the abolition of the price- 2 insurance is considered capable of improving monetary policy trading in such a way that interest rate changes at the Central Bank are spreading earlier throughout the economy than otherwise. The first two arguments are based on misunderstandings. While there is a lot in the third, it is absurd to try to abolish indexation here by law. However, the work of reducing the use of indexation may well be continued. Developments in the market are best suited to contribute to this, but it is expected that a long time will pass before indexation is completely out of the question if ever. The Treasury has gone ahead by example by issuing unsecured bonds for a fairly long time. The experience of the last few decades shows that inflation here can be low, although the indexation of financial obligations is used to a large extent. Inflation in the 1990s was much lower than in the previous decades, although indexation was widespread. This experience shows that there is a misconception that inflation cannot be brought down even if indexation is used. There is also a misconception that borrowers' costs are reduced to the sole point of eliminating indexation. The indexed loans, on the contrary, are cheaper, as can be argued and shown by comparing statistics. The argument is that the lender does not need to add a risk load to its interest rate requirement in the face of uncertainty over inflation. By striking a indexed loan agreement, the borrower is basically taking a new loan every time the price index rises. This dictates that the remaining amount will decrease late even if the loan is paid off. This also causes the payload to remain in real terms fairly stable throughout the loan period, but decreases as a percentage of wages if the borrower enjoys increased purchasing power. The increase in the remaining amount can be avoided by paying the price compensation as an additional installment each due date. It would dilute the payload ahead of the loan period compared to the traditional treatment of indexed loans. This option is probably suitable for banks as they finance the loans in part with short-term capital. Banks also find it easy to provide unsecured long-term loans if interest rates are kept variable. Thus, the borrower would be free of the indexation, but would have a heavy payload in front of the loan period. There is every reason to complete as soon as possible a review of how housing loans will be handled in the future. As an example, it seems fortunate that the Housing Financing Fund can provide banks with the long-term capital it receives through the sale of indexed housing bonds and that banks continue to develop a complex of mortgages, including in the way mentioned here. The weight of indexation could also be reduced by providing housing loans in two parts, on the one hand indexed loans and, on the other, unsecured with variable interest rates. Perhaps further development of housing loans may become a collaborative project between the Housing Financing Fund and banking institutions. Exchange rate-based loans carry lower interest rates than krona-denominated loans, but the Central Bank has repeatedly warned against such loans to those who do not have income in the same kind of currency. In light of what has happened in recent weeks, it is interesting to recall one paragraph from the Central Bank's publication published in early November on 3 last year (Monetary Bulletin 3/2007, p. 25): "Foreign borrowing has increased greatly in recent times, and the proportion of exchange-linked loans from total household loans has increased. The currency composition of these loans has also changed in recent months. The share of low-interest currencies such as swiss francs and Japanese yen has increased. Such borrowing comes with both interest rate and currency risk. Despite the strong exchange rate, the share of foreign exchange-linked loans has continued to increase. As the real exchange rate of the krona deviates further from its equilibrium value, the likelihood of a decrease in the krona increases in the long term, thus increasing the risk of new exchange-linked loans. Given the exchange rate trends in recent times, however, the payment burden on foreign exchange-linked loans has arguably been lighter than that of indexed domestic loans, but this can change in a short period of time." A lot of things are said about the central bank, some understandable, otherwise not. It has been said that the Bank has lost credibility because of the policies it has followed in monetary policy. Therefore, he should be given a more qualified supervisory board, including foreign experts. It would be wishful that the solution to economic problems would be so simple. Foreign experts are interested in the economy here. Both the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD, and the International Monetary Fund have strongly urged that monetary policy continues to be followed. It's not good to be hit by misogynistic journalists. Recently, I got caught between quotation marks with a Danish journalist. What I told her gave no reason to certain conclusions that appeared outside quotation marks and in the headline of the article. The responsibility of journalists is huge and fortunately they usually treat it well. But if they have decided to move their coverage in a worse way than is warranted, either because of their own indoctrination or the orders from above, the game is uneven because they have final authority over what happens to the public. Sometimes prejudice towards the Central Bank can be discerned, which in my judgment is based on misunderstandings. For example, it has been argued that the Central Bank is entirely against the adoption of the euro here because the Central Bank may then be shut down. Of course, there should be a considered debate about possible membership of the European Union and the Monetary Union. But it is a long-term issue that must first be settled on a political level. Eurozone is not a solution to today's problems, and the debate over it must not overshadow the debate about the necessary measures to achieve a better balance here. The unilateral adoption of the euro, which has been mentioned, is much delirious especially because financial institutions in this country do not have access to a central bank issuing euros. Least of all, financial institutions should be involved in such an irresponsible measure. They have to realize that this is a long-term issue and it remains unfinished. The fact is that we live in a small economy and use Icelandic krona. Both can change, but it takes a long time. Misconceptions about this can cause harm. 4 Recently, the chairman of a financial undertaking was quoted as saying that he believes there are political reasons why the Central Bank does not grant it permission for a company to register its share capital in the euro. This has caused damage to the company's shareholders. This is a veritable misunderstanding because the Central Bank does not have the power to approve or reject an application on this matter. If shareholders have been harmed by the fact that the shares were not listed in the euro, this harm is entirely the responsibility of the company's supervisory board. Companies listed here on a regulated market (stock exchange) have the legal authority to transfer their share capital to a currency other than a krona whether it makes sense or not. To obtain them registered electronically, they can be registered abroad. In the meantime, I understand that the Icelandic Securities Depository can also provide such services, and this is a good thing. There is a misconception that joining the European Union and the European Economic and Monetary Union is sure to shut down the Central Bank. Central banks in the monetary union countries play an important role within the countries' central bank system and were of course actively involved in the preparation of the entry process. But it should be reiterated here that the issue needs to be settled on a political level and that it is a long-term issue. If any financial institution in Iceland believes that they can force the adoption of the euro by transferring their accounting in euros or converting the share capital into euros, they are misleading, leading only to misfortune. Regarding possible accession negotiations with the European Union, it is also advisable to note that our negotiating position would not be strong if we are forced to apply for membership. This shall not diminish the economics that may be derived from membership of the Monetary Union. But it must not be overestimated, nor should it be overestimated, and least of all people should believe that it solves all problems. Neither trade deficits nor inflation disappear at the point of Iceland take the course of joining the European Economic and Monetary Union. In a report published by the Prime Minister's Office in 19981, Ma. on the benefits of the Alliance: "The common currency eliminates currency risks and uncertainty in the internal trade of Member States, thereby contributing to increased efficiency in trade." Furthermore: "The common currency reduces direct currency costs in cross-border transactions." But of the shortcomings, Ms. McCarthy says: "The risk of rising unemployment during the recession of the economy is one of the main risks, taken by participating in the monetary union." The report claims that only the countries that are members of the European Union can participate in the European Economic and Monetary Union. This kind of talk implies a statement that there is a despair that we can behave fairly on economic issues without having instructions from others. There is some evidence that the framework of the financial system here is narrow, it is considered necessary that Icelandic financial undertakings have high levels of activity abroad. But is it necessary? An experienced figure from the banking world recently said in a radio interview that banks should tailor growth by stake. Isn't it advisable to wait until it's done differently, if you do? The banks have become too big for Iceland or are Iceland too small for the banks. Conditions in financial markets around the world have changed in a short period of time, so it is more difficult now than before for banks to acquire credit. They grew rapidly in times of favorable conditions in foreign markets. That business model must change. Of course, the solution to the problems that banks face depends primarily on themselves. Perhaps the solution is, among other things, that they are somewhat winding down their position, i.e. selling assets and paying liabilities. The Central Bank will do what it can to support the efforts of financial undertakings to strengthen confidence in their operations, including through the expansion of the foreign exchange reserves. The timing or scope of such actions cannot be mentioned at this time. The other thing to keep in mind is that it is costly to keep a large amount of foreign exchange reserves. It is also absurd that the Central Bank of Iceland is a lender for devaluation in any currency. He issues Icelandic kronor and provides the services that central banks traditionally do with their home currency. From the foregoing, it can be clear that the urgent challenges now are that banks are able to navigate their emulsion continuously through the current waves of global financial markets, and on the other hand that it succeeds in reducing inflation and trade deficits handsomely. In this case, everyone has work to do. 6

Title: Comments on writing about the implementation of foreign exchange controls
text: 10.09.2014 Comments on writing about the implementation of foreign exchange controls Arn97r Sighvatsson, Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, writes an article published by Fr8ettabla?i? today, where he comments on a guide writing in Fr8ettabla?i? on the implementation of foreign exchange controls. The article is accompanying here: COMMENTS ON THE NEWSPAPER'S CONDUCTOR On September 5th Fanney Birna J97nsd97ttir wrote a lead article in Fr8ettabla?i? under the heading Third World Iceland, stating that Iceland is in many ways similar to Third World countries, at least regarding the effectiveness of the business environment. I'm not going to take a position on that statement, but Fanney seems somewhat late in terms of the example she's taking to support her case. "When the restrictions were originally established, many feared a return to the time when party certificates or gangs were a prerequisite for getting currency allocated," says Fanney, noting that the Chamber of Commerce's letter to the Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs fully confirms that the mentioned fears should be supported. Fanney asserts that "opacity and inequality are characteristic of the decision-making of the Central Bank's foreign exchange controls and certain "advisers" receive, through their relationship with the Bank, a quicker and more favourable resolution of their cases". She finally asks whether this description of the Bank's practices is more related to central banks in another Western country or in the Third World. The false and unfair claim of Fanney is both unfair and untrue. First, it is unfair and misleading to assume that central bank practices in the Third World are generally bad. Second, a statement that such a description applies to the Central Bank of Iceland is unfair, untrue and unfounded. The author cites the Chamber of Commerce's letter, citing anonymous sources, but does not appear to assume that their claims may be false or based on misunderstandings, nor does the author appear to have tried to dig into their truthfulness. The Central Bank itself has tried to obtain information on cases that could shed light on the motive for these claims, including those at the Chamber of Commerce, but there were few answers. The Central Bank is keen to improve governance where there is a downside, but without information on the case, the Bank has a problem. The Central Bank has the obligation to grant exemptions from capital controls on the basis of views provided for by law. When granting an exemption, the interests of the exemption requester must be weighed and assessed on the one hand and the national interest on the other, as the unprecedented value of an exemption can weigh heavily. The Foreign Exchange Supervisory Authority therefore keeps a detailed accounting of exemptions, as administrative law imposes obligations on the Shoulders of the Central Bank that parties in a comparable position receive a comparable resolution of matters. A large part of the matter is now handled according to clear precedents. Whether a case falls under a specific precedent is, indeed, sometimes an appraisal decision. In the case of difficult matters, more than the foreign exchange regulator is traditionally involved in that case, and finally a special ruling committee composed of three experts, as well as the Governor and deputy governor. This should be considered a high-quality administration, although unfortunately it sometimes leads to longer turnaround times than would be desirable from other points of view. The Central Bank will continue to work high-quality administrative practices and improve them if possible. I expect the editors of The Associated Press to also make every effort to make sure in the future to elaborate on news and lead writing. Arn97r Sighvatsson Deputy Governor

Title: Deputy Governor's introductory remarks at the Nordic Central Bank Conference on Cybersecurity
text: Rannveig Sigurdardottir Deputy Governor, Central Bank of Iceland Introductory remarks Third Annual Nordic Cyber in Finance Conference 28 November 2019 Stockholm Panel  Cyber-Risk Governance (morning session) I welcome the opportunity to be here today and participate in this conference on Cyber in Finance, and I am especially delighted to have a chance to participate in this panel on Cyber Risk Governance. Unfortunately, figures show that cyberattacks are on the rise, and consequently, so is our awareness of how threatening cyber-risk is to institutions, markets, and society as a whole. Cyberattacks are difficult to foresee; indeed, some say that we are always behind the curve when it comes to cyberattacks. But one thing we can do is have a proper framework in place when they do occur, so as to prevent them from escalating to a systemic level. It is widely accepted that sound governance is a key factor in in countering cyberattacks. And this is consistent with other forms of risk management. But what are the ingredients for good cyber-governance? Good cyber-governance entails ensuring that a proper cyber-resilience framework is available and endorsed by an institutions board or equivalent body  a framework consisting of policies, procedures, and controls aiming to identify, protect, detect, respond to, and recover from a cyberattack. The framework should accord high priority to the safety and efficiency of the institutions operations while supporting broader financial stability objectives. The framework should also be guided by a cyber-resilience strategy that defines how cyber-resilience objectives are determined and identifies the people, processes, and technology requirements for managing cyber-risks. The fact that cybercrime is a relatively new category of operational risk  one that is driven by highly innovative criminals  means that an event like this one is of vital importance in raising awareness and sharing information and best practices. We still have much to learn when it comes to cyber-risks and how to manage them. And in the spirit of information sharing, I would like to share with you some of what is happening on the small island of Iceland, a country with 350,000 inhabitants that operates one of the worlds smallest central banks. The Parliament of Iceland has just recently passed a law that implements the NIS Directive (Net- and Information Security Directive). That law will enter into force in September 2020. Until then, a constructive mapping of who may fall under the scope of the new law is to take place. With respect to the banking sector and financial market infrastructure, the new law entrusts the Financial Supervisory Authority with deciding this. At the same time, the Central Bank of Iceland has both an oversight role to play and the duty to promote a sound and efficient financial system  a role it can only fulfil by promoting proper cyber-risk governance. And to conclude, these are also interesting times for the aforementioned institutions: on 1 January 2020, the Central Bank of Iceland and the Financial Supervisory Authority will merge into a single institution under the name of the Central Bank of Iceland. For a nation of 350,000, the merger will give us the opportunity to perform more effectively in the field of cyber-resilience for the financial market and to promote the importance of proper cyber-risk governance. Furthermore, the Central Bank of Iceland plans to launch a Financial Sector Forum for Operational Robustness in 2020, with emphasis on enhancing the sectors resilience against cyberattacks. Having said this, I look forward to fruitful discussions and to this afternoons session on how to increase cyber-resilience in finance.

Title: Joint conference between SUERF and the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 2 July 2014 Post-Crisis Recovery and the Reconstruction of the Financial Sector Opening address at a SUERF/Central Bank of Iceland conference in Harpa, Reykjavik, entitled Post-Crisis Recovery and the Reconstruction of the Financial Sector, 2 July 2014. Distinguished speakers, excellencies and other dear guests, On behalf of the Central Bank of Iceland, I am pleased to welcome you here in Harpa Concert and Conference Centre to this conference that we are hosting and have organised with SUERF. This applies especially to those of you that have come from abroad to participate in the conference. The Harpa is interesting but I do hope that many of you will be able to see some more of Iceland during your visit. It is a special feeling for me to be playing this role today as it has been ten years since we last hosted a SUERF event in Iceland. I was then the Chief Economist of the Central Bank and was scheduled to leave later that month to become the Deputy Head of the monetary and economic department of the Bank for International Settlements in Basel. In that role I later became a member of the Council of Management of SUERF. I have fond memories of these involvements with SUERF. Ten years ago, the topic of the conference was the interaction of monetary policy and financial stability in small open economies. Some of us at the Central Bank were worrying about the build-up of risks to financial stability and we felt we needed more instruments. We were groping around for what is now-a-days called macro-prudential policy. But the outcome turned out much worse than we expected and even worse than we feared. The risks did indeed accumulate on a massive scale in the years following the conference, both internationally and here in Iceland. In this country, we both experienced the most unsustainable boom in our history and developed a relatively huge cross-border banking system with a risk profile that was very vulnerable to the kind of shocks that hit the financial sector during the panic state of the international financial crisis. We have since been through what is currently called the Great Financial Crisis and the Great Recession. We, however, avoided the Great Depression. It is still not clear how much of a risk it was but much clearer that a forceful crisis management by central banks played a big role in averting it. Still, we have not had the Great Recovery. On the contrary the recovery has, in general, been slow and uneven and, in a number of crisis countries, unemployment is still at dramatic levels. Recent discussion has come up with many candidate explanations such as secular stagnation due to sustained lack of aggregate demand; slowing innovation; adverse demographics; lingering uncertainty; political risk; and policy mistakes. Even if some of these factors are contributing to slower growth, I think the main causes for weak recovery are financial and economic imbalances that built up prior to the crisis and the disruption of the crisis itself. Therefore, there are big legacy issues to deal with, such as high debt levels and still fragile banking systems. And the problems surmount when debt crisis and banking fragility interact in a vicious circle, as they have done in many countries in Europe. We know from several studies that recoveries from recessions that are associated with financial crisis are weaker than recoveries of traditional business cycles. One reason is that it takes a while to take down a mountain of debt. Another reason is that credit booms tend to create economic imbalances and sectoral misallocations that cannot be undone overnight. Yet another is that the financial crisis can partly be caused or accentuated by a flawed institutional set-up. Some of these explanations and related issues are dealt with in the first session of the conference. The financial sector was the epicentre of the crisis. It is on the mend both through its own efforts and regulatory initiatives. Banks have adapted business models in light of the crisis and the new environment. Capital levels have been increased, mostly through retained earnings. Basel-III rules on capital and liquidity are being phased in. However; there is a widespread perception that the task of creating a resilient and reliable financial system that serves the real economy is far from complete. The too-big-to-fail problem is, to a significant degree, unsolved. The framework for cross-border banking that turned out to be deeply flawed before the crisis is still to be satisfactorily reformed, both at the global and European level. There are still deep questions about the design of the financial system and its interplay with regulation and the safety net that need to be addressed. Some of these issues will be discussed in the second session after lunch. This conference is not about Iceland; although it features in some cases as an interesting example. Let me therefore use the rest of my remarks to say a few words about Icelands crisis and recovery. Icelands crisis was actually two crises wrapped in one. First, it was a traditional macroeconomic boom bust crisis where capital inflows, a credit and asset price boom followed by a sudden stop played the main role. Second, it was a collapse of three cross-border banks that amounted to 10 times GDP where over 2/3 of their balance sheet was in foreign currency, featuring the traditional maturity mismatch of banking but with no lender-of-last-resort to back it up. Icelands recession was deep. But it was probably not as deep as many expected when they had in mind the image of a total collapse of a banking sector, a huge balance of payments crisis, and currency crisis where the value of the krona fell by 50% in the course of 2008. But then we need to bear in mind the nature of the shocks. A significant part of the impact of the banking collapse was felt in other countries. The economic shock affected overblown sectors (banking and construction); however, a significant part of the export base was intact and was subsequently boosted by the low real exchange rate. Iceland has been recovering at around twice the rate of trading partners since 2011 and last year it was the fastest growing advanced country, where the prospects for this year and next are good. The slack in the economy is disappearing with unemployment already just under 5%. Moreover, inflation has fallen slightly below our inflation target of 2%. However, Iceland is still dealing with its legacy problems from the financial crisis. Debt levels are high, as they are in many other countries, but as a share of GDP public, household, corporate and external debt are all on a falling trend. The biggest challenge facing economic policy makers in Iceland at this juncture is, however, the task of lifting comprehensive capital controls on outflows that were introduced after the collapse of the banking system in the autumn of 2008. These were helpful in stabilising the economy after the financial crisis but are increasingly detrimental as the domestic and international economic situation normalises. A resolution of the failed banks that is consistent with balance of payments equilibrium and financial stability in Iceland is a key element in the process of lifting the capital controls. In the interest of time and in order to keep my powder dry let me stop here. Dear guests. We have brought to together top academics, senior policy makers and financial industry leaders to address the topics of the conference and we have an interesting programme ahead of us.
