text: 27. september 2012 Arnor Sighvatsson, Deputy Governor Iceland's currency options 27 September 2012: 27 September 2012. Good attendees! Discussions on the structure of currency issues in Iceland have escalated in recent times. There are many reasons for this. First, Iceland's experience of flexible exchange rate policy with an inflation target has not been the result that was hoped for. Second, the financial and currency crisis in recent years, which led to currency controls and closed Iceland's access to foreign credit markets, has raised questions about the role of an unstable currency in amplifying the boom before the banking crash and then the downturn in its wake. Third, talks on Iceland's possible membership of the European Union (EU) are now well underway and could lead to drastic changes in the arrangement of the country's currency, not only after the adoption of the euro but also in the lead-up to it. Finally, the financial crisis has shaken the eurozone in recent times, raising doubts among some about the sustainability of the monetary union and thus the gains of adopting the euro. On the 17th of this month, the Central Bank published a report addressing various aspects of this intricate issue. It is not the job of the report to bring the truth of the matter to the public and the rulers of the matter on a silver platter, but rather to make available material for research and analysis that could benefit readers in reaching their own conclusions. I will not make the contents of this extensive assessment relevant to this forum, but I will be able to draw some conclusions from the material contained in the report. It should be noted that these conclusions do not necessarily have to reflect the positions of the Central Bank or other officers of the Bank. A tool for adaptation or ballast? An independent currency and the exchange rate policy that is followed can play a dual role: on the one hand, being a tool for integration and on the other being a monetary ballast. There can be tension between these roles and sometimes they can come across badly. 1 The role of the currency as a tool for adaptation has traditionally had the upper hand and in some respects explains why the krona has lost almost all of its original value against the Danish maternal krona. The ballast arguments generally get stronger as countries are smaller. It is no wonder that most small states are supported by some kind of fixed-rate. See Figure 1 Should exchange rate policy be a ballast economic policy aimed at stable prices, as in Denmark and the Baltic countries, it cannot occur unless the role of the currency as a tool for adaptation is sacrificed, at least to a large extent. The question facing Icelandic the nation is therefore twofold: How much is the role of the krona worth as a tool for integration, and how much could the ballast of the ultimate fixed rate be valued against the source currency, e.g. the euro, if it is chosen? Most small states have a hard fixed-rate policy or alternative currency The benefits and costs of flexible exchange rates first turn to the previous question. The main argument that countries affected by special external clashes, such as Iceland, have some gains in flexible exchange rates are that with exchange rate adjustments, the impact of the shocks on employment levels and production in the country can be softened. This means that when the exchange rate of the currency falls, the competitiveness of exports and domestic production in competition with imported goods, exports and domestic market shares will therefore be greater and 2 import memory. In this way, production and employment can remain greater than otherwise. The potential benefits of the mitigating effects of exchange rate adjustments need to then offset the benefits of efficiency inherent in monetary mergers. The benefits lie, among other things, in lower transaction costs and risks in trade that stimulate foreign trade and the ability to use stable exchange rates as the ballast of monetary policy and stable prices. The smaller countries, the greater these benefits should in any case be, and research confirms that it is.1 Iceland's experience shows that the high cost comes with the need for large foreign exchange reserves. The impact on foreign trade is discussed in the Central Bank's report and I do not discuss them further here, but regarding the ballast argument, I would like to mention the following: When the currency exchange rate falls, the impact in a small, open economy is rapidly reflected in prices, relative price changes and wage levels. If prices and wage formations are asymmetrical, this reduces the likelihood of the exchange rate strengthening again, i.e. the nominal increase in prices and wages is reluctantly reversible even if the exchange rate rises again. As a result, a rate cut lasting several months or more is prone to not fully reversible. Inflation will therefore be high and unstable, and inflation expectations have difficulty gaining ballast at low inflation targets. The objectives of monetary policy are therefore difficult to achieve in small open economies unless we succeed in restraining exchange rate movements. Why does the flexible exchange rate amplify economic fluctuations? The arguments for gains in flexible exchange rates and independent currency seem to make sense. The problem is the facts. In theory, countries with flexible exchange rate policies should have more balanced economic growth and lower volatility than countries that run tougher exchange rate policies or belong to a currency union. It doesn't seem to be, and even the opposite applies when it comes to smaller countries. This is especially true of Iceland. There may be some explanations. First, currencies tend to fluctuate more than the underlying economic trends give rise to. These overarchases lead to real exchange rates fluctuating sharply, without being fully attributed to fluctuations in trading conditions and exports. See figure 2 The exchange rate is that the second strand of asset prices, which is determined, like other asset prices, is determined by expectations of an uncertain future. Foreign exchange markets under the conditions of free movement of capital can 1 On the impact on foreign trade, see section 8 of Iceland's Options for Currency and Exchange Rates, Special Publication No. 7, Central Bank of Iceland, September 2012. 3 swinging momentarily, as we have seen, from super-belief in the country's future revenue creation, to despair and distrust. Fluctuations in real exchange rates are greater than can be explained by fluctuations in trading conditions and exports Under certain conditions, e.g. a severe financial crisis, a country's currency may be raided in a parallel manner and a bank's deposits may be raided. When such a raid occurs, the exchange rate of the relevant currency traditionally decreases far more than the underlying economic development requires in the long term. Currency exchange rate movements have a much broader impact on the economy than other asset price changes. Currency not only preserves value, like various assets in which people invest their money. A currency is also a transaction account unit and not least a trade medium. His stability is a prerequisite for making sensible contracts in the long term. Currency fluctuations change relative prices throughout the national economy, particularly in small "dollar-denominated" economies, and increase trade risks. Violent changes in currency exchange rates twitch the foundations away from financial agreements and obligations that are a prerequisite for free trade. In the deep markets of large international avoidance currencies, this risk can be protected in some ways at a relatively modest cost. It's the last thing about 4 in the case of small currency areas, where few large parties can have a significant impact on price formation. Shallow markets and few trading partners cause companies in a small currency area to have difficulty guarding against currency risk, except perhaps in the very short term. Under certain circumstances, it can even become impossible, as the executives of many domestic companies know of their own. Exchange rate instability is therefore disastrous for companies in small currency areas that do not have the option of entering into agreements with foreign trading partners in their own currency. It poses risks that have a macroeconomic impact, and the greater the currency area is less. Direct and indirect foreign exchange risk can have a major impact on the conduct of businesses and households, which amplifies the economic volatility, especially where leverage is high. High leverage of households and companies in foreign currency or in the form of indexed loans promotes the co-indexed value of the exchange rate, i.e. stimulates demand during the boom, when the increase in the exchange rate eases the debt gap, while deepening the contraction of demand during recession, as the recession following the banking collapse is an example. The macroeconomic impact appears in the fact that Iceland, which has a uniqueness towards other states regarding the small size of the currency area, has a corresponding uniqueness in terms of the volatility of private consumption, even taking into account size. See figure 3 That's not where Iceland stands out. It seems obvious, therefore, that fluctuations in private consumption and national expenditure are mainly related to the exchange rate fluctuations of the krona, as shown in the accompanying figure. Therefore, fluctuations in private consumption will be reduced unless exchange rate fluctuations decrease. From the above, it can be clear that although theoretical arguments can be made that flexible exchange rates soften economic fluctuations, Iceland's experience suggests the opposite: that exchange rate fluctuations amount to volatility rather than leniency. Furthermore, research suggests that the same is generally true in small states. As a result, the benefits of flexible exchange rates, offset by the feasibility and ballast benefits of monetary mergers, appear to be less than nonexistent. An evil necessity? The rate cut after the 2008 banking collapse has resulted in a massive asset fire and displacement, more or less random. One may ask whether the violent adjustments after the banking collapse were not yet necessary to fix 5 national expenditure to the production capacity of the national economy. That's why eloquent people have argued. It is certainly true that the rate hike contributed to private consumption decreasing by about a quarter and investment by three-quarters.2 A significant aspect of this adjustment was necessary and inevitable and would have taken place in some way regardless of the arrangements of exchange rates and currency issues. Fluctuations in private consumption appear to be driven by exchange rate movements, not unstable exports However, you need to be careful about three. First, the imbalance that the crown corrected by its fall was in some ways the result of it itself; overcrowding, which is an inevitable accompaniment to overheating that occurred in the years before the crash and the conditions that prevailed in the global economy. Second, the fall of the krona did more than correct the existing imbalance. The recession, of course, reflects some unsustainable growth in the years before the crash and was in that respect inevitable, but the rate cut led to the recession becoming much greater than it would otherwise be. 6 purchasing power fluctuations and expectations of purchasing power, such as the construction industry, almost ruined its fall in these same sectors. One may ask whether such horse medicine is not both unnecessary and harmful; includes a waste of value, when capital, production equipment and a specialised workforce, which are the foundation of long-term economic growth, disappear out of the country. While modest rate cuts may facilitate economic recovery, overshoots of the kind we've been through recently not only erode the imbalances that exist, but create new imbalances and reduce the long-term production capacity of the national economy. Third, it can be pointed out that this argument turns the original argument for flexible exchange rates, i.e. that it softens economic volatility, on its head. One might ask why rapid adjustment should be a goal in itself if it involves putting a number of businesses and households out of business that financially could survive gentler adjustments, which is the "stated goal" of flexible exchange rates? The impact of a rate cut on exports is a word increased Various people have placed great emphasis on the role of increased exports in the economic recovery after the banking collapse. Sure, these effects are there, but in my opinion they are considerably overestimated. The production of Iceland's main export sectors, fisheries and aluminium industries, for obvious reasons, will not be easily increased regardless of competitiveness in the field of wages. A rate cut does not increase the rate of fish, which has biological assumptions, nor the sellable energy in the fallwaters or bowels of the earth, which cannot be used except after time-consuming research and investment. Export companies in small states are largely specialized for export and produce little for the domestic market. They cannot therefore easily increase exports by directing an increased portion of their production into the foreign market as domestic demand declines. The domestic market is simply too small for it to be the main component of the production of a domestic company that has achieved full sizeability. In order to increase exports, export companies therefore need to increase production capacity through new investment, which in many cases requires a long build-up. When the production capacity has ultimately been increased, there may no longer be an increased competitiveness. Comparisons between European countries, some of which were also badly affected by the financial crisis, reveal that Iceland's exports have not increased more than in various countries that lived at fixed rates or were within the eurozone, although contractions have been avoided in major export sectors. See figure 4 In some fixed-rate or 7 in fact, eurozone growth has been higher, but in general there does not seem to be a clear relationship between exchange adjustments and export growth. It should also be noted here that lending trends have strong co-fluctuation properties. Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates further strengthen them, especially if companies are leveraged in foreign currencies. If export companies are leveraged in foreign currencies, a sharp rate cut can even have a negative impact on exports, because although the impact on the income flow of an export company is positive, a rate cut can lead to a negative equity turn. It obstructs the refinancing and acquisition of credit for investment, which as previously mentioned is a prerequisite for exports in small states with specialised export production to increase. The rate cut and the balance of payments and foreign exchange crisis that triggered it were in some ways the result of foreign credit markets closing Icelandic companies, while at the same time contributing to the closure of some companies even further. Exchange rate fluctuations make real wages very flexible, but still deliver vague benefits for exports In view of the above, it is directed to ask how Iceland would have relied had the country been part of a currency union. This question is not easy to answer. Chapters 16 and 17 of the Central Bank's report discuss somewhat on various aspects of the issue, which 8 It's hard to explain in brief. I limit my words to a few comments. As noted in the report, countries with the most types of monetary policy have suffered serious setbacks from the global financial crisis. The stage of the events of the crisis has shifted from country to country, so it is careful to draw too strong conclusions about the end of the story before the play is over. However, research suggests that factors other than monetary and currency arrangements dictate more about the impact of the crisis, not least the state of the state of the state of the financial system, the size of financial systems and the leverage of the private sector. in fact, Iceland suffered one of the biggest deteriorations, although the state of the state budget before the crisis was (at least on the surface) one of the strongest in Europe. The financial system, however, was relatively very large and the leverage of the private sector was high. An asset price bubble and massive trade deficit, which independent monetary policy failed to restrain in the run-up to the crisis, made Iceland particularly vulnerable. Membership of a currency union precludes the rapid adjustment of relative prices and competitive positions. In contrast, it ensures better access to liquidity in the currencies that the growth spikes of the economy need. Recent developments within the eurozone show the manner in which liquidity is traded within the eurozone to areas under pressure from the others considered safer at peak times. Through the payment processor of the eurozone and its central banks, liquidity that has been put on the run in what is considered the security of German bonds or bank deposits of core countries is diverted back to those stress areas. This payment processing and liquidity remittance by central banks prevents a financial escape from leading to even more severe credit inertia, but the countries, despite this, are now grappling with the sake of the public debt crisis and weak banks. The eurozone therefore has a certain social security system. Of course, this insurance is not undisputed. It is now both criticised for going too far, i.e. that it can lead to unforeseen financial displacements between Member States, e.g. due to the interaction between a banking collapse and a debt crisis in any of them, and for going too short, i.e. regarding the system's readiness to assist countries in temporary payment problems. The Eurozone's fire safety I have come to the heart of the debate over euthanasia and the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in considerable detail in recent times. Apart from the arguments with and against Iceland's membership in a larger currency area, 9 is the eurozone solid enough to be a desirable refuge in a falling world? Is the eurozone even a "burning house," as some have put it, the safest thing to stay at a reasonable distance from? Indeed, it is right to note that the economic consequences of the eurozone problems will not necessarily be escaped by standing outside the eurozone, unless the stability of prices within it is jeopardised. The main benefit of membership of the currency union is a stable exchange rate towards other Member States, which ultimately ensures the corresponding stability of prices and prevails in the whole region. There is no evidence that the European Central Bank has lost track of its main objective, stable prices. Eurozone co-operation is also not like any other fixed-rate policy that can easily fall apart for the reclamation of market forces alone, with the infamous speculators at the helm. Even the bankruptcy of individual states does not automatically lead to a complaint, let alone a disintegration by the Alliance. States might resign unilaterally, but it is complicated and problematic in my judgment that any country has that interest. However, some people disagree with me. Assessing whether the fire protections in the house of the euro are sufficiently solid will nevertheless be one of the key considerations for voters as they weigh and assess the benefits of EU membership, because the financial crisis has exposed certain weaknesses. It is likely that when a referendum comes, further clarifying the ways in which the pillars of eurozone co-operation will be strengthened in coming years. It already seems clear that a banking union, i.e. a pan-European (at least in the eurozone) financial regulatory framework, a deposit guarantee system and probably, ultimately, an aid and settlement system for financial institutions in trouble, will be one of the two cornerstones of reform. These reforms are intended to break the "devilish relationship," which some have called so, between the banking and fiscal crisis. The European Stability Mechanism (ESM) will pave the way for conditional assistance to countries in payment problems, and it is not impossible for the fund to be used to refinance financial institutions into trouble. He also pays for the possibility that the European Central Bank can buy government bonds in the secondary market in order to facilitate monetary policy trading in the region, as the central banks of the United Kingdom, the United States and the Japan have done in abundance. The other cornerstone lies increased discipline in the field of public finances, which is necessary to prevent increased co-insurance between the two countries from leading to temptation problems. Looking further ahead, it is unlikely that a joint 10 The bond issuance of eurozone countries can see the light of day, which would be a natural channel for the aforementioned monetary policy actions. What impact do these new pillars of eurozone co-operation have on the benefits of Iceland's potential membership? Iceland's experience shows how perilous the international operations of banks can become when liquidity constraints subside. The experience of both Iceland and other European nations also shows how rapidly the treasury's position can deteriorate when a financial crisis hits. The caps protected the Treasury from the same kind of raid that has recently shaken various European countries. However, they come with long-term costs, which increase as time goes on, and they are difficult to solve without instability except over a long period of time. Membership of a banking union in conjunction with eurozone co-operation could become a considered option for Iceland, as it includes a solution to the problems of the volatile federal financial crisis, financial stability and capital movements, which have played Iceland and also several countries in the eurozone so gray. This option needs to be carefully examined against two other options that could become Iceland's lot, if the nation chooses to hold on to the krona: on the one hand, a future under the cover of capital controls with the long-term costs involved and ongoing coexistence with dynamic capital movements and flexible exchange rates, but with strict precautionary measures to reduce the instability that the interaction between flexible exchange rates and unrestricted capital movements leads to. In particular, it would have to address the risks associated with foreign currency banking. Increased security, however, will inevitably lead to higher business costs because foreign currency funding could become more expensive, particularly export sectors dependent on foreign currency credit. Iceland's economic and monetary security policy Good attendees. In the years to come, the government and the public face disastrous decisions on the arrangement of currency issues, which concern the country's economic and monetary security interests, whether inside or outside the eurozone. A balanced and sophisticated debate about the pros and cons of membership of the eurozone compared to other options is urgent. The aforementioned report on currency issues and several other publications published by the Central Bank in recent years are intended to contribute to it. Thank you. 11

Thorstein Thorgeirsson1 Interoperability of monetary and financial stability For more than three centuries, the role of central banks has evolved in various ways and in line with the circumstances and requirements of each era. Gradually, two projects, maintaining monetary and financial stability, have formed the red thread of central bank operations. This is explained by, among other things, the central role of central banks in the banking system and the macroeconomic focus in their work due to active links between monetary, financial and economic fluctuations and the ability of central banks to influence them. In recent decades, these two projects were increasingly ideologically separate. One manifestation of this is that in some countries, banking supervision was moved out of central banks and entrusted to another institution, financial supervision, which also supervised other activities in the financial system. At about the same time, central banks were granted greater independence to achieve monetary policy objectives. This trend occurred when the complexity, scope and risks in the financial system were increasing rapidly. At the same time, there was a tendency to reduce public controls and increase market freedom. There is some evidence that the ideological innovation played a role in the biggest banking crisis in the nation's history. This article discusses the lessons and ways in the organisation of financial supervision to contribute to the achievement of objectives of monetary, financial, and economic stability. It aims to better reconnect monetary and financial stability on the basis of a systematic approach. In several countries worst affected by the banking crisis, it has been considered the best to do by entrusting central banks with a well-defined and leading role in shaping and implementing monetary and macroprudential policies. The fact that macroprudential policy controls influence monetary policy interest rates and vice versa, and that each policy affects the performance of the other, there is a strong argument that they are harmonised and on the same hand. Furthermore, the formulation and implementation of macroprudential precautionary policies are based on the operation of monopoly monitoring, so it is important to also integrate these two areas of precautionary control. With the increased integration of these interdependent projects, efficiency and efficiency in the use of information and human resources in analytics and policy development are increasing. Along with clearer responsibilities, it supports the development of knowledge and timely decision-making in these areas. A number of improvements have already taken place with new regulation of banking, the development of macroprudential instruments and the introduction of the Financial Stability Council, as well as the Systemic Risk Committee. These improvements, however, rest on previous institutional structures. This work can be further strengthened by combining precautionary controls on the central bank's financial system, thereby reflecting the synergy of the policies. This is to strengthen the Financial Supervisory Authority and improve the performance of the work in achieving monetary and financial stability, with positive impact on the economy. 1. Introduction From the 1980s onwards, the ideological innovation in some countries became more prominent in increasing institutional specialization, resulting in the transfer of banking controls out of central banks and into independent financial regulation. Specialised regulators with banks, funds and insurance companies were plunged into one regulatory body to increase efficiency and transparency in the regulatory activities, but also as a response to the merger of financial institutions with different operations. In the multifaceted and complex relationships between central banks and commercial banks, the monetary and financial sectors disappear with important implications for the economy. As a result, a central bank has emerged as the authority responsible for the policies of a state in the field of monetary and credit.3 2. See, for example, Const89ncio (2015). Commercial banks, which, among other things, accept deposits from the public and provide loans, deposit widely diligent funds into a central bank account that at the same time monitors their operations. For a long time, central banks have had exclusive rights to issue cash (banknotes and coins), which lays the foundations for their other projects in the banking system. It is well known that central banks' role is to be a lender to devolved and lend funds to commercial banks against secure mortgages if the market availability of credit to them is insufficient.4 This attempts to ensure a reasonable supply of credit in the economy and in the worst cases prevent a financial crisis from digging through the associated negative consequences for economic activity and employment levels. Generally speaking, central banks no longer provide direct loans to treasuries, but this is believed to be able to promote loopholes in fiscal policy and inflation. However, there are widely agreed agreements between the State and central banks on the central bank's service role regarding borrowing for the Treasury and the management of foreign exchange reserves. As conditions deteriorated in credit markets, it added to the central bank's role of being a market maker of last resort. In doing so, monetary policy, macroprudential policy and public fiscal policy were much closer than before.5 Central banks are monitoring the flow of capital in and out of the country and trying to prevent the exchange rate from fluctuating so much that price and financial stability pose a threat. The need is also increasing for greater vigilance in the central bank's work in terms of the interaction between financial and the economy.6 Central banks also have oversight of systemically important financial infrastructure (payment and settlement systems) and are responsible for the operation of a large-scale payment and balancing system. A good organisation of precautionary supervision is necessary due to challenging conditions at home and in the international financial system. o Financial activities, which have become very complex, are likely to continue to integrate internationally. o The abolition of capital controls is accompanied by increased systemic risk. o Consultation on financial stability in the EEA is increasingly carried out in relation to the work of the EU Systemic Risk Council and the ECB's banking supervision, where central banks play a leading role. o Central Bank with precautionary supervision on board and active international cooperation is more likely to be able to limit systemic risks in domestic and international financial markets. What changes is more scope for coordination of now logistical unrelated policy committees and increased efficiency in the use of information and human resources in the Central Bank's comprehensive work with precautionary supervision on board. TTL assumes that monopoly controls will be separated from the Bank's other projects, as the focus on the work of monopoly precautionary monitoring is not macroeconomic in nature. An exception is the monitoring of systemically important banks. However, the distance between macroeconomic role and precautionary control is greatly reduced by the new structure, as these different but connected areas will be in closer communion. This includes benefits for the work of the two main committees of the Central Bank, the Monetary Policy Committee and the National Economic Protection Committee. A new report by the IMF (2017) proposes that major steps be taken to give banking supervision and regulation greater powers and independence in Iceland by combining controls on the safety and soundness of banks at the Central Bank of Iceland level. As in this report, the IMF mainly looks at the two towers of the model in this context. Many of the same arguments raised in this report are reflected in the IMF's opinion, e.g. increased risks associated with free movement of capital. The IMF also believes that the FME is not sufficiently isolated from the political process. The IMF concludes that limits in information sharing between the FME and s92 can produce conflicts, gaps and coordination problems. To fix these problems, the IMF also proposes that act No. 87/1998 on official supervision of financial activities be amended and that it be made a priority. 5. Conclusion Many reports on the lessons of the global banking crisis and the reforms carried out in the organisation of financial supervision in recent years include the opinion that the framework based on the structural separation of projects in the areas of monetary and financial stability was not good enough to counter the rise of the imbalance that led to the banking crisis. The framework may also have played a part in the fact that enough knowledge of the financial system's problems did not build up, and the government was too gliding to respond to a problem that ultimately got out of hand. Basically, the separation was based on a flawed ideology of how best to build a system of governance for the oversight and resolution of these two projects. In the aftermath of the crisis, a new paradigm has emerged based on the basic thinking that financial stability should be regarded as a systemic issue and that the structure of the control system needs to reflect that. In order to strengthen the prerequisites for financial stability, a whole set of supervision and regulatory frameworks must be prepared for the financial system. A step has been taken in this direction in Iceland with the cooperation agreement between the FME and s92 and the establishment of the Financial Stability Council. The second change is likely to partially improve decision-making, but it does not use the potential synergies in the operations of the relevant institutions. The most important step to strengthening the framework of financial stability in Iceland is to combine the financial supervisory activities as a whole at the Sea level. In addition, liquidity and equity controls on commercial banks will again be in the necessary proximity to decision-making in areas of monetary and macroprudential policy. As a result, the integration of the two areas of precautionary monitoring, monopoly and macroeconomic monitoring needs to be increased. At the same time, effective coordination of monetary policy and macroprudential policy that respects the independent role of both committees must be considered. The flow of information and the proximity of knowledge within one institution is likely to strengthen all of its work and improve the performance of policy making in these related areas. It is natural to entrust a central bank with an increased role in the field of precautionary supervision because of its importance in the monetary and credit system and the macroeconomic approach to its work. The sensible integration of these projects into one organisation is designed to increase efficiency and productivity by making better use of human resources, information, technology and knowledge in the implementation of these projects, which will lead to safer and more timely decision-making in the management system. Title: Financial literacy and economic management
text: 1 Financial literacy and economic management Conference on Financial Literacy at the House of Culture 9 September 2011 Stefan Johann Stefansson Editor at the Central Bank of Iceland (The opinions expressed are authors and do not have to reflect workplace policies Text is slightly improved from the transfer.) I have been asked to discuss the impact it could have on economic management to promote financial literacy. Would the U.S. be better? As we know, economic management is mainly of two kinds, i.e. through the state budget and then through the decisions of the Central Bank or monetary policy committees, in particular on interest rates. As a rule, the ultimate goal of economic management is improved economic well-being, but certain stability in finance and pricing is also independent objectives that also contribute to economic growth and increased welfare. I don't hope to be able to answer questions about this definitively, as it can be said that a discussion in this format is rather new, but hopefully I can come here with posts that can be useful. Since I am an employee of the Central Bank of Iceland, it is normal for the moderators of the conference to want to hear something from me about monetary policy, financial stability and financial literacy, although I note that the views I may express are mine and do not have to reflect the central bank's policies. What is financial literacy? Before proceeding further, it should be considered only what is meant by financial literacy (English financial literacy). It turns out that the concept can be understood both narrowly, i.e. with reference to individuals, and broadly, i.e. with reference to the economy as a whole. In a report by the Minister of Commerce on Financial Literacy in Iceland in February 2009, which was a member of this committee, the wide definition of financial literacy is applied to the OECD, stating that education in financial literacy is a process aimed at improving consumer living standards and promoting financial stability in the country. The narrow definition I call here so, but may have more usefulness in everyday life, is 2 the study of Breka Karlsson and Bryndis Bjarkar asgeirsdottir in the same report as follows: Financial literacy is the ability to read, analyze, manage and address financial factors that affect a person's economic well-being. Then the question arises: Can we say anything about the relationship between financial literacy, consumer living standards and financial stability in Iceland? What does the story say? If you look back, you have to admit that it seems that financial literacy has been lacking in this country. The debt bailout of parts of individuals and families and the collapse of the financial system suggest that there has been a lack of something in the ability of individuals to assess financial factors affecting their economic well-being. The ever-expanding banking system before the crash also suggests that there was a lack of knowledge and/or the government's capacity in financial literacy aimed at improving living standards and promoting financial stability. It is natural that, in this respect, the focus is on specialist institutions and governmental units that did not prevent what is afterwards seemingly obvious: that the financial system became too big and that it did not come to an end when the precipice came to an end and credit financing became more difficult. Consumers made many wrong decisions about over-sized and unfavorable loans that had serious consequences for their private finances whether they were loans for housing, car purchases, indexed loans or exchange-rate loans. Of course, much was done in good faith, and no one saw the fallout. Managers of commercial banks and savings banks also made incorrect decisions, and employees in some cases used practices towards their customers in the introduction of financial services that will hardly be considered suitable, in hindsight. Regulators and authorities failed to overcome emerging problems. One thing is fairly certain, however: Although this experience has been costly to many, she has taught a number of things about financial literacy. And I also think it's clear that if the best knowledge had been applied, it would have had a positive impact on economic management and volatility had become smaller. Now someone may say that a market economy always produces crises on a regular basis, and there is nothing to do about it. The answer to such a thing is that it is probably not possible to prevent fluctuations - but they can be tempered. We decide to some extent how painful the fluctuations will be. Before the history of the past few years is abandoned, I would like to mention two things concerning financial literacy. 3 Examples from history: Indexation The first is that, considerably after indexation had become an accepted practice of long-term loans, around or early 1980s, a number of people were still of the opinion that it paid to take enough loans because inflation would eat them up. These individuals had that time in mind, the decade ahead, when those who took unsecured loans paid them only in small part back in real terms when real interest rates were long hours negative. Depositors who placed in bank accounts that also bore negative real interest rates thus lost the purchasing power of their savings to a considerable extent. As a result, there was a large-scale transfer of assets from depositors to borrowers. As a result, credit was also scraped together in real terms and as a percentage of GDP. The savings were much smaller than they would otherwise have been. It's actually an old story, so let's not dwell on it anymore - but it's a penalty for warning. Foreign loans The other example is of loans in or tied to foreign currency exchange rates taken by individuals and companies on a large scale before the financial crash. This affected the living standards of individuals as well as on the entire financial system. When international financial markets offered credit at low interest rates, various people seized the opportunity in Iceland, both financial institutions, public bodies such as municipalities, companies, families and individuals  and took foreign loans on a large scale. Financial institutions and experts in the field argued to customers that due to low interest rates and the strong exchange rate of the krona, it would be appropriate to borrow in foreign currencies. The financial literacy rule, which can be called so, should be held largely in the same currency as income was set aside (here we are talking about economics  and not the legal profession that later emerged in exchange rate judgments). However, when viewing data on the web, it is revealed that various people warned about this, e.g. both Gylfi Magnusson, Associate Professor of Economics and Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland in 2004. And even the commercial bankers themselves warned of the consequences of this for households and business finances, as chairman Sigurdur Einarsson and economist asgeir Jonsson did in late 2004 when they presented KB Bank's forecast as it was then called. But the politely worded warnings of these and others were insignificant against the market surge that had begun. Of course, employees of financial institutions were able to sell foreign loans, and although various customers were well aware of the risks involved, there were many who did not fully realise the risks, as a survey suggests that general knowledge of the impact of exchange rate changes on loan payloads was not high. As a result, the already long-predicted rate hike of the krona after a sustained trade deficit put the finances of many households and businesses on the side. In fact, I found it strange as 4 deputy mayors in Reykjavik to monitor financial penalties on behalf of or in municipal services constantly recommend foreign borrowing and increased municipal debt by focusing on the rearview mirror instead of looking to the future and taking into account the general knowledge available. To them, the trade deficit and its possible consequences on the exchange rate did not appear to exist. Now we are actually living in currency controls for the time being, so it is not seriously testing this financial literacy rule in the near future,  as well as the legal basis for foreign loans being rather uncertain  but the general lesson we should draw from this is to have a so-called currency balance in honour and not leverage to a target in a currency other than we have income in. In doing so, we improve "consumer living standards and promote financial stability"  to refer to the definition of financial literacy. Economic Management: From financial stability to stable prices When discussing the relationship between financial literacy and economic management, it should be borne in mind that financial stability is only part of the Central Bank's economic objectives. The main objective of the Central Bank of Iceland's operations has in recent years been to promote stable prices, as stated in the Act on the Bank. Financial stability has followed. Looking at trends recently, you can see that the results in promoting stability in prices have not been as expected, although for several years after the adoption of the so-called inflation target in 2001, results have been good. Now you may ask: Does general knowledge in financial literacy  or general knowledge of finance  make any difference to the results of the fight against inflation? A 2009 survey of the aforementioned Commerce Secretary's Financial Literacy Committee shows that 65% of respondents were able to answer the correct question about the purpose of raising the policy rate  to get inflation on track. And most people know the impact of inflation on the payload of indexed loans. As is well known, it is the Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee that now makes key monetary policy decisions  which is the aspect of economic management that remains under the central bank's controls. Let us assume that the monetary policy decisions have the desired effect and that the principles laid out, e.g. in terms of the relationship between the price of money, i.e. interest rates, and supply and demand  of capital in this case  are of good value in this country. But does it matter that people know the purpose of the Central Bank's monetary policy changes? It may not change everything about the impact of prices on supply and demand that people are familiar with the law of supply and demand. However, it is a much more appropriate social environment if there is a common understanding of the need for certain decisions that affect all the majority of people and their consequences. In addition, it is likely that 5 Success would be greater. It would reduce controversy, and we could then use our power in a more constructive way. In fact, it has sometimes seemed that there were other economic laws in Iceland than anywhere else  or even no economic law  and that consumers in this country were more resistant to prices or interest rate changes than consumers in other countries and could tell various stories about it. However, research suggests that we are not so different from other nations when viewed closely. The purpose of the goal of stabilising prices is that stable prices are thought to contribute to better economic growth in the long run and thus to a better general standard of living. It is also generally accepted that inflation, especially high and volatile inflation, can be accompanied by a variety of inefficiencies and costs. It should therefore be a natural part of financial literacy education to know that the stability of prices improves living standards in general. I haven't seen any survey of people's attitudes to date, but I would think that in general more people would agree with this than the impact of central bank interest rate changes. At least a lot of people who have insurance. Controversy and doubts about the Central Bank's decisions While 65% of the public say they know the purpose of raising the policy rate, interest rate decisions by the Central Bank or its Monetary Policy Committee are sometimes controversial. Of course, it is the representatives of the 35% who do not know or believe in the purpose of interest rate changes that have somewhat to offer themselves there. So the group has often been a prominent figure who believes that the Monetary Policy Committee does not read the economic data correctly. That being said, people generally don't question the impact of interest rate changes, but when and how it's right to change interest rates. And it's a little peculiar that understanding the validity of interest rate cuts is normally very good, but when interest rates are raised, it's like the senses of some pro-life frontrunners, a few politicians and others work in a completely different way. It should be noted, however, that there is always uncertainty when an interest rate decision is made. The economic data is not perfect, it does not cover everything and it takes time to prepare it. Of course, the Monetary Policy Committee is aware of this uncertainty. In addition, it should be borne in mind that economics deals with human behavior that is sometimes a bit difficult to calculate. Is presentation and discussion understandable? What can be better done? Understanding is a key factor in financial literacy. At times, experts, and not least economists, have been accused of being less understandable to ordinary people. It is not good if the Monetary Policy Committee cannot explain its decisions. However, I think it can be said that 6 The workforce has been gradually improving in these matters. It is now time for each interest rate decision to publish not only a story, but also a detailed explanation, often in the form of an entire report, as well as the minutes of the committee's publications. In addition, journalists and various employees of financial undertakings, institutions and associations are invited to a presentation at the Central Bank on the day of the decision, managers and experts at the Bank then attend special presentations in financial institutions and give more broad talks. There are a lot of things that are being done to try to explain and explain what the Monetary Policy Committee is doing. Of course, you can always try to do better. I sometimes hear the media asking experts that they come up with human-language explanations! This is certainly a particular problem, namely explaining some area of expertise that has its own concepts and methods in ordinary language that most people understand. But this is an ongoing challenge, namely reducing the discipline of understanding that can exist between experts and the public. This kind of understanding gap will generally only be bridged in two ways  that the experts use less expert language and more what can be called ordinary language  and then by promoting knowledge  or public financial literacy. Insurance in the past and present To promote financial literacy, many things need to be considered, not only to look at the various school levels, from kindergarten, but also to the various groups that are active perpetrators of the national debate. It can be said of ordinary individuals that each is their own lucky carpenter, but it is also the case that experts, influential media outlets and politicians can be other people's fortune-makers. I think the debate about the inflation that has been raging lately is an example that can be viewed in light of this. We can start by reviewing the creation of general indexation and the situation that pertained before it was generally adopted, compared to what was previously stated. Perhaps there was some justice in it when the young people in housing and the learning bailout got gift loans, but the old people lost their life savings  as they were a few decades ago? It is desirable for people to save and set aside some of their income for future use, whether individuals, families or nations. Economic growth will normally be easier and more secure  which is to say living standards will get better. Therefore, it should be one of the financial literacy rules that people should adopt that they pay to put something aside from their income for savings or security purposes. But then the savings naturally need to keep their value  their purchasing power  whether it's done with interest or indexation. The debate over the indexation in the past is understandable given the debt problems many people have  and that even those who tried to have waded below them but could not foresee the changing circumstances for the worse. And it is understandable that borrowers want to reduce the weight of indexation in the credit industry. Some things in this discussion 7 However, it reflects, in my experience, a lack of understanding of the functionality and purpose of indexation. People often only see nominal numbers on paper, but forget to put them in a long-term context to the development of prices, assets and wages. That's why people will be kept a kind of penny-jerker  maybe you could call it financial blindness or even a money illusion. In fact, wages have in recent decades, with little exception, risen more than prices. And considering that the actual value of payments of a large proportion of indexed loans is supposed to remain the same over time, the burden normally decreases as part of wages. That being said, living standards should improve. One of the main exceptions is a short period after the financial crash. Certainly, borrowers pay higher sums if the loan is indexed for the long term in some inflation. This is because, among other things, the principal is paid down faster if loans are unsecured. But when you consider what the price development of assets and wages has been, the indexed loans don't really come out that badly. It is the payload and living standards that are of paramount importance  comparing the definition of financial literacy. Simple and understandable formulas? There are a lot of sides that can't be found here. In recent years, financial institutions could have better explained how installments and interest rates are calculated on loans. text: Jon Sigurosson's talk at a symposium of the Central Bank of Iceland and the Institute of Economics at the University of Iceland November 21, 2019 Jonas H. Haralz: Pioneer of modern economic management in Iceland I am delighted to take part in this symposium to honor the memory of Jonas Haralz, whose 6th of October was 100 years since his birth. During his long and married career, Jonas made a great contribution in many areas Icelandic society. He was one of those who made an impression on the century leading up to Icelandic national life. Jonah was a sharp and observant economist and an energetic advocate of economic and social reform throughout his life. After studying economics at Stockholm University in 1944, Jonas returned to Iceland at the end of the war. Returning home, he joined the Socialist Party and worked as an economist at the New Build Council and the Financial Council, i.e. in the control rooms of the hada and licensing system that was in place at the time. After five years of service in that arena - and as long as an active participant on the left wing of Icelandic politics - Jonah had been fully satisfied with the embarrassment of economic management and the dissent of his socialist partners. He joined forces in 1950 to work. 1 at the World Bank in Washington, where he was given a quick career and were entrusted with problematic tasks, particularly in the Bank's delegations to Mexico, Central American countries and Peru. During these years Jonas dedicated himself to the high-quality working practices of the World Bank's staff in assessing the economic situation and prospects for the national economy of these countries, with a comprehensive view of the economic reforms and measures needed to achieve an adequate balance of their economy. In these lands, Jonah was further familiar with the problems and risks of corruption that can come with centralized control and grant systems. Although he undoubtedly had a further career within the World Bank, his mind always sought home - and in 1957 Jonah agreed to take up a job as an economic adviser to Hermann Jonasson's left-wing government, although he had doubts about her willingness and ability to abandon the complex and burdensome system of multi-growth, strengthening and controlling the economy, which was then in the wild. I am sure that Gylfi . Gislason's accession to the government in 1957  when he was then Minister of Education and was also in charge of foreign trade matters within the government  contributed to Jonas' invitation to become the government's economic advisor. He became a secretary of state. 2 Ministry of Commerce from 1958 to 1961, Cabinet Secretary of the Ministry of Economic Affairs 1961-1962 and finally director of the Institute of Economic Affairs 1962-1969. He was therefore in fact the main economic advisor to governments for twelve years, 1957-1969, and had a formative effect on economic management in Iceland throughout that time and indeed much longer. But it wasn't until the end of the 1950s that there were political grounds for the overwhelming shift in policy to abandon the policies and subsidies to greater free speech in trade both within the country and between countries. The prerequisites were obtained when the government of the Independence Party and the People's Party was formed and took power in November 1959 under the presidency of olafur Thors. The government, known as the Reconciliation Government, already provided a detailed and radical action agenda to stabilise the national economy. Jonas Haralz and Johannes Nordal were the main advisors to the Reconstruction Government on economic affairs, both during and after its formation. The Reconciliation Government made the fundamental change of the economy, adopting a single exchange rate on the krona instead of 3 multiplied and decided that the aim should be made to achieve a balanced and remain in foreign trade. At the same time, the system of export benefits and import duties was eliminated, which had largely broken the link between foreign market prices and domestic prices, thereby preventing adaptation to new conditions and hindering the normal transformation and promotion of the industries. These measures also included a significant decrease in the exchange rate of the krona. At the same time, foreign exchange and import controls were abolished in stages as much as possible. However, current trade agreements with several countries, particularly in Eastern Europe, caused imports under those licenses to still be subject to permits. This was further done in order to bind this import to equally commercial countries  in fact, to ensure Icelandic export interests. These measures in the exchange rate and foreign exchange sectors were followed up by tempting them to hold back the banks' lending so that they would be hampered within the limits set by the production increase of the national economy. In recent years, the number of loans had risen from moderation. To the same end, the government's goal was not to deficit the treasury. In order to achieve this goal, new monetization was necessary. The result was that a new tax should be imposed, a sales tax. 4 In order to ensure that the restructuring measures were as fair as possible to the whole public, the government decided to significantly increase social security benefits, raise more credit to public residential buildings, bring commercial credit unions on a solid basis and review the tax system in order to reduce  and preferably abolish  income tax on ordinary wage earnings. The rhetoric is the next familiar from discussions on the economy of the past few years and decades. The government also decided to have an annual macroeconomic plan drawn up to become a guide for governments and banks on targeted economic policies. She decided to promote the promotion of the industries around the country and to prepare new projects to use the country's natural resources. The development of energy-intensive industry was started and preparations were underway for negotiations with the European market alliances. Overall, this was the most extensive economic measures ever taken in Iceland. In the end, the problem they were meant to solve was deeply rooted, for the real cause of the problem was thirty years of farming. The Reconciliation Government realised that a country that continues to live with a system of control could not become a member of the trade zones 5 two that were then formulated in Western Europe, one of the European Community, the EEC, and the European Free Trade Area, EFTA. Good relations with these business areas were  and are  vital to Icelanders. As a result, work was started on preparing agreements with the European Market Alliances. Iceland's accession to EFTA and extensive trade agreements with the European Community were both confirmed at the beginning of the next decade. The resurgence certainly brought the Icelandic economy closer to the structure in many parts of Western Europe. However, when considering, these measures remained short.... Price controls remained unchanged for many years. Interest rates were less movable and subject to government decisions, not supply and demand. Foreign exchange trade, trade in services and capital movements between Iceland and other countries were not voluntary. Exports of seafood remained subject to government permission. This in fact included patents for major exporters. There were strict restrictions on foreign investment. Agricultural policy based on domestic commodity price subsidies, export allowances and import bans on 6 farm products remained unchanged. Economic ideas from the crisis years between wars proved surprisingly life-changing. It is not until the end of the 1980s and early 1990s that a paper is broken again in free speech. Freedom to trade in capital both domestically and internationally was increased in stages. Pricing and competition issues were brought to a better level than before. The application of interest rates was given an increased role in the management of monetary policy. Iceland's membership in the European Economic Area ( EEA) then forced further changes in free speech. One of the most important milestones on this journey was undoubtedly that freedom of foreign exchange trade and long-term capital movements between Iceland and other countries were established by regulation in the summer of 1990. In 1992, amendments were made to the Foreign Exchange and Trade Act and the Act on the Central Bank of Iceland. With them, freedom of movement in foreign exchange was made a principle in Iceland and the way to abolish the last currency controls in the near term. In the spring of 1993, new rules on foreign exchange markets came into force, which meant that the Central Bank should keep the exchange rate within certain limits of the benchmark exchange rate through the purchase and sale of foreign currency on the market, but not by unilateral 7 decision. Furthermore, he should use his monetary policy instruments to influence short-term interest rates in the country, thereby increasing supply and demand for foreign exchange. However, there is still a lot of work to be done in this area, and it suffices to mention the agricultural policy, which still remains largely unchallenged. The currency controls imposed in response to the 2008 financial crisis, of course, included a huge deviation from the main policy on free trade. They week on the principle of freedom of movement of capital between Iceland and other countries aside. Fortunately, they found ways to abolish the currency in stages without delaying economic and financial stability. Governments and central governments were well-behaved from 2009 to the present day. It was part of the action plan originally proposed by the Reconstruction Government that a special central bank should be established, without ties to the nation's main commercial bank, Landsbankinn, or other commercial banks, whereas the Central Bank had since 1957 been a separate division of Landsbankinn. The government entrusted the Minister of Commerce, Gylfi . Gislason, along with Johannes 8 Nordal and Jonas Haralz to draft a bill to create an independent central bank. Previous arrangements had, among other things, been criticised for the fact that Landsbankinn's Central Bank division had not shown sufficient restraint on lending, particularly in relation to the repurchase of product loans. Another important new measure in the bill, which became law in 1961, was that the Central Bank should monitor the activities of banks, savings banks and other depositors. These changes were of great benefit to strengthening confidence in monetary policy. There was a lot of discussion about what the central bank's independence from the government should be. However, there was no dispute over the fact that the Althing elected the Board of Directors of The Board of Directors or that the Minister of Banking appointed a three-member board of directors. However, there were divided opinions as to what should be the right of the Board of Directors to make independent decisions on monetary policy control, even if they were contrary to the will of the government. The conclusion was that the Bank should cooperate closely with the Government on the management of monetary policy and make it aware of its views. As an independent and expert body, the Bank would be entitled to hold its views publicly, even if there was a dispute with the government. The ultimate power to 9 However, developing economic policies must always be with the government, and underneath it the central bank must bend. Some critics of the Central Bank Bill, which became law in 1961 - including olafur Johannesson, later prime minister - felt that these provisions in fact made the Bank more dependent on government than it had been, and a better chance of dividing powers in monetary and foreign exchange matters clearly between the parties, so that the central bank would have its own powers in a limited area. However, the legal provisions in this regard remained materially virtually unchanged for forty years from 1961, until a new central bank law was passed in 2001. But under that law, the Central Bank set one main objective  to promote stable prices  and also to be authorized to do so  with the approval of the Minister  to declare a numbered inflation target. In 2013, financial stability by law was added to the Central Bank's objectives and is now equal to the goal of stable prices. However, the newly enacted Central Bank Act No. 92, 2019, still contains remnants of the 1961 provisions stating that the Central Bank should "promote the advancement of the Government's economic policy", but this sentence is so conditioned by an important 10 supplement: "provided that it does not consider it to be contrary to the Bank's objectives"  i.e. to promote stable prices and financial stability. With these provisions, the Bank's independence from the Government is much more clearly defined than before in respect of these two main objectives. The question of how independent the central bank should be towards government is actually one of the issues in the monetary sector that will be settled late. However, the prerequisite for central bank independence will always be that its responsibility and duty of information towards national representatives is clearly marked in legislation. The aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis that hit the 2007-2008 financial crisis brought us home the truth that monetary policy that trashed many countries in the decade to the crisis and focused on the low inflation target, which should be tempted to achieve with interest rate changes alone, could not guarantee the remaining stability. By focusing on inflation targets for the formulation and implementation of monetary policy at the same time as official controls on financial activities were narrowly restricted by the fact that each individual financial undertaking follows legal precautionary rules  there is a risk that people cannot see 11 The forest for trees. The nations of the world are now seeking to fill this perverse gaps in the control system with preparedness to prevent that the financial crisis overturns again  or at least drag out of danger of it. A factor in this effort is to include central banks and financial supervisory authority with clear and unequivocal provisions of law that promote financial stability  the stability of the financial system in as a whole  and therefore to strengthen its resilience and reduce systemic risk. This includes the statutory main objectives The bank is two. In order to carry out this dual task the interest rate alone, although perhaps they could have been used with more effectively inhibiting vaccination than was done in prelude to the financial crisis. In order to bring new equipment, macroprudential instruments, which inhibit the excessive growth of lending and debt as a whole. Here are some tools for consideration, such as Requirements at hagsveiflujafnandi capital ratios 12 financial institutions, variable capital requirements to them by sector of transaction, direct restrictions on leverage ratios, mortgage rates and borrowers' payloads. In the implementation of such a policy, a solid cooperation between the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank is required. This structure has now been thoroughly implemented by new legislation integrating the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority into a single institution. It is vitally important that the Central Bank and financial supervisory authority pay sharp attention to the credit system as a whole and look for ways  and apply them  to prevent excessive growth in lending and leverage in the economy  not least the leverage of the financial institutions themselves. In order to carry out such a policy, closer co-operation between governments, central banks and regulators is needed than it has been. A monetary policy with an inflation target is inherently a more technical and expert  and at the same time, indeed a simpler  project  than the implementation of a financial stability policy. Financial stability is a multifaceted goal and often more sensitive on a political level than the inflation target alone. With the takeover of the Reconciliation Government in 1959, Jonas as an economic advisor and special confidant of olafur Thor, Bjarni Benediktsson and Gylfa . Gislason had the opportunity to use their power, experience and knowledge to develop a new economic policy of free trade and market economy. Jonas' successful work as an economic adviser to governments for many years paved the way for improvements in the field of economic management that Icelanders still live in. This great effort during the resurgence years will be remembered for a long time. Jonas' long and successful career as CEO of Landsbankinn from 1969 to 1988 and his many work under the auspices of the World Bank are no less a sign of the high confidence he enjoyed both in Iceland and abroad. He dealt with the problems of his day with boldness and traditionally sought to view them in a historical and international context. His life was an imaginative journey, and he succeeded with his great persuasion to 14 convince both themselves and others of the superiority of democratic market economy. As can be said, Jonah was entrusted with  as well as leadership in economic and banking  many other difficult positions of trust that are too many to count. The university committee's report marked a turning point in the university's history. For the first time, it drafted a comprehensive general plan for the development and future of the school over the next few decades. The committee's work was of great interest to Gylfi . Gislason, then Minister of Education. I was fortunate enough to work under the guidance of Jonas at the Economic Institute for five years and work with him thereafter for decades in various fields. Working with Jonah has a great experience for me. As head, he brought with him excellent economic skills and a deep understanding of society and its history, as well as experience and networking from his long time at the World Bank and on its behalf in many countries. Jonah was a true mentor and mentor. He was particularly good at addressing current economic problems with light and understandable words and with comprehensive knowledge. He was a powerful manager who led his colleagues with both his own hard work and words of encouragement. In addition to all this, he had experience of active participation in politics, first among socialists and later  after he left his post as director of the Economic Institute  within the Independence Party. He was chairman for a time. 16 The Economic Committee of the Independence Party and was a member of the central committee of that party from 1975 to 1987, but enjoyed respect and trust across party lines for its talents and objectivity. Jonah was productive in writing throughout his life mostly alongside his officesbut he was no less a man of the spoken word. Clarity and persuasion characterized his speech all the time. After Jonas resigned as CEO of Landsbankinn in 1988, it was my honour and pleasure to name him on behalf of Iceland to serve as the Nordic General Representative of the World Bank's Executive Committee for the next three years. From that job he disappeared in 1991 and began consulting and writing with the same enthusiasm as before, both west and east. He became world bank and international development secretary. In the early 1990s, he recorded the history of the Nordic Development Fund, which was linked to the Nordic Investment Bank in Helsingfors. That's where our paths came together yet again. Up until his last years of life, his writings were as clear and clear as the former, and the persuasion was the same as when he hired me to work in the Economic Institute in 1964. 17
