Title: Speech: Lessons from the financial crisis for economic management, financial stability and institutional structure
text: 14 January 2011 Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank: Lessons from the financial crisis for economic management, financial stability and institutional structure Moderator, good attendees I would like to start by thanking you for speaking to you today. Since becoming governor of the Central Bank, I have held a number of appointments at national level, but none of them have been outside the capital area. It has caused me considerable heartache, both because the Central Bank is the central bank of the whole country and not only the capital, and no less because I am aware that both the financial crisis and the economic crisis have come down unevenly in different regions and it is important for me to have a complete picture. But this is now improved and of course it is very fitting that it should be in Akureyri. My talk here today focuses on lessons from the financial crisis for economic management, financial stability and institutional structure. Someone might ask if this is now the most urgent thing when in some ways we are still working our way out of the economic consequences of the crash. In response, we are in many ways at a crossroads at the moment where the most urgent challenges of the crisis are either coming to an end or they are in a defined way. Last year we were able to achieve some stability. The previous year, or 2009, the massive trade deficit in previous years turned into an underlying surplus. This, along with the growing belief that Iceland would soon achieve a new equilibrium, caused the fall in the exchange rate to stop in mid-2009 and the last interventions in support of it took place in November of that year. The exchange rate then rose in the past year by a total of 17% against the euro and 12% against the so-called trade basket, and this despite the fact that the Central Bank began buying foreign exchange in the second half of the year in order to increase the share of uncommitted foreign exchange reserves. The reserves increased by 258 ma.kr during the year. at year-end 667 ma.kr, or 43% of GDP. This is one of the largest foreign exchange reserves that Iceland has ever had and it can still expand because we have access to further loans from the IMF and the Nordic countries after the recent fourth review of our economic plan with the IMF. If those loans were added together with other inflows that occurred at the beginning of the year, but subtracted from the share of the reserves that are expected to leave in the near term, such as foreign exchange deposits of return committees at the Central Bank, the reserves would amount to 593 ma.kr, or 38% of GDP, and all that may be added to the reserves is missing from the Central Bank's foreign exchange purchases on the market. If this compares with the fact that foreign installments and interest payments by the Treasury during this and next year amount to over 224 ma.kr, in which case the repurchase of its loans has been reduced in recent months, it is only hoped that all concerns about the Icelandic government's payment have been eroded and that Iceland's debt guarantee burden has fallen significantly in the last two years. Stronger exchange rates, inflation expectations, which gradually moved closer to the Fed's target, and the slack in the economy then resulted in the Fed's inflation target reached before the end of the year. These developments made it possible to cut interest rates significantly during the year and by the end of the year they were lower than at any time in just under 50 years of the Central Bank of Iceland's history. The restoration of Icelandic financial system continued despite the shocks. The big commercial banks all meet a 16% capital reprieve and by the end of the year the restructuring of the five savings banks' finances was completed. Finally, it becomes increasingly clear that when the dust of the financial crisis has fallen, Icelanders will not face a public debt crisis, nor will their net foreign debt be unusual in an international context. However, we have faced a domestic debt crisis for businesses and households, with measures to accelerate its resolution in the second half of last year. The crossroads we are at now involve the fact that stability in investment, economic growth and employment now needs to be changed. Granted, most of the evidence suggests that economic growth began in the second half of last year. However, he was not particularly vigorous and investment remains at historic lows. In addition, unemployment is still much higher than Icelanders have been accustomed to and involves significantly unused production capacity in the economy. In this context, there is much evidence that the capital controls that proved successful in promoting stability are increasingly inhibiting investment and business opportunities and could therefore increasingly start to act as a drag on economic growth. In any case, Icelanders are contracted towards EEA member countries to abolish the controls when the distress that called for them is over. It is therefore fortunate that conditions to lift the seas have improved in recent months. First of all, it comes as macroeconomic stability has increased as I have attributed above. Since then, the government's performance has improved and its credit demand is declining and if it continues on that path, there is no need to fear its unsustainable debt collection. In addition, foreign exchange reserves have increased greatly and concerns about the foreign liquidity of the national economy have fallen dramatically. What is most lacking is that the position of the banking system is considered sufficiently solid for it to be able to finance itself outside the currency. Hopes are high I hope that such a health certificate can be issued in the coming months. It should be reiterated in this regard that according to statements made in November, as well as the material made public following the fourth revision of the programme with the IMF, a new plan for the elimination of the currency is currently underway and is scheduled to be revealed by the end of February. Furthermore, it has been declared that nothing will be done regarding the abolition of controls until this plan has been published, unless it is possible that an exchange tender between offshore krona owned by foreign entities and foreign currency owned by domestic parties will be arranged and that offshore kronur can be allowed into investment in the economy under certain conditions. It is in this context that it will be so important to focus on the lessons of the financial crisis for economic management and financial stability, because if we are going to lift the caps then we are re-approaching the arrangements that were in place before the crash. This raises the question of what monetary policy can work out under those circumstances and what regulation and supervision of financial activities must be established in order for the stability of the financial system to be guaranteed under the conditions of capital freedom. Of course, it can be argued with every right that conditions will still be very different from those before the financial crisis as global conditions are different and the high systemic risks that had piled up in the financial system have already been realised and will not do so again anytime soon, not least because players in the financial market are burned and will be cautious about the long future. But future generations will think of the silent need if we let it do and don't try, like those who revolutionized the rule of law in the aftermath of the 1929 financial crisis in the United States, to formulate a system that will last longer than cautious. It is for this reason that the Central Bank has just published two reports. The second was released last month and focuses on monetary policy after the caps. The report examines what monetary policy entails, how it has been run in Iceland in a longer-term context, the problems that arose during its implementation in the run-up to the financial crisis and the advantages that are most likely to be considered after the Iceland has completed the programme with the IMF and controls have been lifted. The other was released yesterday and focuses on the role of central banks in financial supervision. It examines the nature of risks in the financial system, the tasks of financial supervision, the role of central banks, different models of financial supervision and the changes that are currently taking place around the world. It is, of course, to some extent controversial as to what are the lessons of the financial crisis for economic management and financial stability policy, and I refer in that subject to these two reports on further details, as well as to Articles I published in Shire in 2009 on the global financial crisis. It is also controversial whether monetary policy as such played a major role in the collapse of the banks that took place in this country. I've argued that monetary policy was not in the main role. But then I'm also making a distinction that I've felt is missing in the debate on these issues, where on the one hand, there is an overreaction and a fall Icelandic the economic cycle and on the other, the growth and collapse of three international banks. These two stories are certainly linked and come together in the final scene of the great tragedy of the fall of 2008, but they are also partially separate. In this light, it does not matter what the role of monetary policy was in the collapse of the banks as it of course played a major role in the economic instability that characterised the years before the collapse in Iceland. So we would have had to reassess monetary policy whether these international private banks had lived, died, or perhaps never existed. With this disclaimer, I'll draw up a list of things to keep in mind. As far as monetary policy is concerned, it is as follows: The creation of a Icelandic economy characterised by ignorance and volatility makes independent monetary policy expected to be more difficult to implement than it would otherwise be. Financial globalization reduces monetary policy activity by interest rate index in small open economies but amplifies it through the exchange rate path, which could be a problem if interest rate differential trading and unstable capital movements cause excessive fluctuations in the exchange rate not related to underlying economic conditions. Monetary policy in such countries needs better support from fiscal policy and financial stability policies. In Iceland, there were a number of peculiarities that reduced monetary policy activity, e.g. housing financing arrangements. The global conditions of liquidity excess and low interest rates made the implementation of monetary policy difficult. It is controversial whether monetary policy was too restrained or not adequately restrained. Those who argue the latter often point out in the way that monetary policy has been difficult to gain credibility, which means that the parties to the economy believed that the Fed both could and wanted to achieve its inflation target, even if it cost temporary hardship. The financial stability policy list may be much longer, but I'm going to choose from what I've thought stands out: Understanding systemic risk was lacking, but I explain in more detail what I mean by doing so below, and it got to pile up too much infrequently. There was too much emphasis on regulating and regulating individual financial institutions, but too little emphasis on risk in the financial system as a whole. In the new report, we put it this way that there was too much emphasis on monotony caution but too little on macroeconomic caution. This was based in part on the logic that the whole is the sum of the individual units, which overlooks interaction and infection. Liquidity risk was greatly underestimated, especially in foreign currency. Closely related to this was a risk in international banking that was also greatly underestimated. Financial supervisory authorities were not aggressive enough or risk-oriented, and business practice controls were conducted higher than precautionary controls. What about the institutional factor? Sure, there is a key point that the pairing between goals and devices was not sufficiently active, the responsibility of individual institutions would have had to be clearer, but also information exchange greater and cooperation better as different institutions took different roles regarding financial stability. What are the recommendations for improvement in these reports? As far as monetary policy is concerned, the first report can be understood so that the long-term choice stands between the fixed rate options considered most suitable, namely membership of the EU and its monetary union, and on the other hand what is referred to as the inflation target-plus. The report does not settle between these options, but the Bank will issue a much more detailed report in about a year or so investigating the pros and cons of the Monetary Union route and comparing it to other permanent alternatives. But what is an inflation target-plus? While the name sounds similar, it involves a close look at radical changes from the policies followed before the crash. The experience of the financial crisis, both in Iceland and abroad, suggests that more monetary policy and economic policy need to be strengthened in general. It can be concluded from the experience of recent years that it is important to apply the economic policy so as to inhibit the rapid and unsustainable increase in asset prices, which traditionally coincide with excessive lending growth, increased leverage and risk-taking, which may eventually end up with a sharp torrential downpour and, at worst, a financial shock. At the same time, it is necessary to avoid allowing the banking system to create risks that cannot be handled by domestic force. Another lesson to be learned from the financial crisis is that the traditional central bank interest rate tool does not necessarily have to be the best tool to counteract the underlying imbalance in financial markets. Nor can it be based solely on the interest rate instrument if monetary and financial stability is to be guaranteed at the same time. For that, more controls are needed. The report discusses a number of implementations of such additional tools, which have been synonymous with macro-prudential tools. Such precautions include rules on variable maximum mortgage and capital ratios and restrictions on liquidity and exchange rate risk, including a possible ban on borrowing of households in foreign currencies or very rigid capital requirements versus such risks. In addition to these rules, there would also be increased use of foreign exchange interventions to counteract fluctuations in foreign exchange inflows that amplify credit fluctuations and asset price bubbles, and in the process reduce in some measure excessive exchange rate fluctuations. In addition, the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves to be able to use when it comes to financial stability could contribute to financial stability. Finally, it is necessary to improve the framework of the policy in the public finances, e.g. through the use of financial regulations, and a more systematic interaction between monetary policy and public finance policy. There is also reason to see if the inflation target needs to be strengthened as such. It is considered to extend the horizon of monetary policy, i.e. the time when the inflation target is normally reached. This could potentially increase monetary policy's scope to counteract the underlying imbalance in asset markets. The above improvements to the inflation target itself, the systematic use of interventions in the foreign exchange market, the increased application of macroprudential instruments and improvements in the implementation of the policy in the public finances, can be referred to as "inflation target-plus", but that plus is quite large. Then I finally get to the financial stability policy and its institutional structure. Central banks have for a long time analysed and assessed financial stability because of its importance to the national economy, but also for the progress of their many projects in the financial system, but they are usually responsible for managing liquidity in the banking system, maintaining stable prices, being a lender for devolution, and keeping track of the payment and settlement systems. The risks of individuals using financial services are varied. It always comes with a risk of owning financial assets or taking on debt. Market trends can result in less value of assets or dividends, or that their debts and payments will be more expensive than expected. Financial health depends on how well you manage risk. So what is systemic risk? In professional language, systemic risk is defined as two related factors. On the one hand, it is the overall risk that arises over time and on the other, networking risks that involve the impact of individual actions on others in the financial system and that as a whole. History holds many examples of a bank's common tendency to take huge risks during the boom and then become risk-averse during the downturn. The overall risk appears in volatile lending and liquidity fluctuations linked to growing weaknesses on both the asset and debt sides of the banks. The network risk is associated with the infectious effects of infection due to the actions of others in the financial system. Thus, banks often do not take sufficient account of the impact of other people's actions on their own balance sheets. This means that the risks in the financial system are not properly identified and therefore not dealt with properly. When the systemic risk is too high, fear breaks out and then banks can fall like dominoes if risks are linked and the infectious effect is strong. It is natural to target the objectives and arrangements of the Financial Supervisory Authority with such significant risks. Monopoly controls and business conduct controls are closely linked and have the primary objective of protecting consumers of financial services and promoting financial stability by trying to maintain the strength and security of financial institutions. The monitoring of business practices focuses on transparency in information, justice and integrity and equality among market participants. However, monopoly controls focus on the liquidity and financial strength of financial institutions and collateral on deposit accounts. Before the global crisis, the work of regulators was largely based on monopoly caution, observing the positions of individual financial institutions. The financial system as a whole was then considered stable if each financial undertaking was deemed to be firmly established. Furthermore, risk was considered external in the financial system and thus independent of the actions of individual financial institutions. Macroeconomic caution is a matter of monitoring factors that threaten the stability of the financial system as a whole and the use of precautionary measures to prevent and respond to systemic risks. In recent years, macroprudential analysis has been rapidly evolving with international organizations and central banks, but The latter has often been tasked with monitoring financial stability along with price stability. Since the outbreak of the global financial crisis, various international organizations have proposed changes to strengthen macroprudential controls. Among other things, institutional frameworks need to be strengthened in order to promote a comprehensive risk assessment. There is also a need to strengthen oversight of total leverage and liquidity in the financial system. Variable capital requirements, forward-looking depreciation, leverage restrictions and liquidity rules are being viewed as potential macroeconomic instruments. Macroeconomic precautions that address cross-sectional risks aim to reduce systemic risks, such as by financial institutions setting aside increased equity that takes into account their systemic importance. The basic idea of macroprudential principles, based on risk over time, is for financial institutions to set aside capital during a boom when risk assessments are low, which can be exploited during a downturn when risk awareness is strong. It should otherwise have a volatile effect on the operations of financial institutions and promote economic stability. There is still considerable progress in implementing national precautions and controls, not least in terms of analysis and devices, as well as institutional factors, in particular the connection to monopoly precautions and controls. It should also be warned of too much optimism that the new approach will solve all problems, but new circumstances and innovations in the field of financial activities are expected to require vigilance and foresight of public regulators. [The following is material from the Central Bank of Iceland's special publication number 5; The role of the Central Bank in financial supervision, which was issued yesterday and is available on the Bank's website. There is no additional information or market-sensitive content.]

Title: Talk on the financial fluctuations in Iceland at an international research conference in Macedonia
text: 14.04.2016 orvarour Tjorva olafsson's talk on the financial fluctuations in Iceland at an international research conference in Macedonia orvarour Tjorvi olafsson, economist at the Central Bank of Iceland, gave a talk at the Annual Research Conference of the Central Bank of Macedonia, which took place in Skopje last week. The title of the conference was the 5th NBRM Research Conference - Economic and Financial Cycle Spillovers: reconsidering domestic and cross border channels and policy responses, while orvarour Tjorvi had a talk on the conference section economic and financial cycles: Synchronization and Spillover Channels. In his talk, orvarour Tjorvi discussed the results of an upcoming research paper on the financial fluctuations in Iceland over a period of more than a century, with the authors of the essay in addition to Tjorva, Bjarni G. Einarsson, Kristofer Gunnlaugsson and orarinn G. Petursson. The paper discussed the definition and measurement of the financial volatility, its main characteristics and how strongly the impact of the global financial volatility appears to be on the domestic ones, even in the very different frameworks of economic management over this long period of time. During the presentation, orvarour Tjorvi supported the material in the accompanying promotional document: Financial cycle in Iceland - 5th NBRM Research Conference.pdf Related news: Chief economist's presentation on the financial volatility in Iceland.

Title: Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of London
text: Arnor Sighvatsson Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland Euromoney Conferences The Iceland Conference 12 April 2016 Ladies and gentleman, Icelands journey from exuberance to despair  and at least half-way back again  has been difficult but informative. We can now look back at what has been achieved with some degree of satisfaction. More importantly, by looking back we can draw some lessons that should help us to address the problems we see on the horizon looking forward. After five years of recovery, the Icelandic economy has more than recovered the output it lost in the aftermath of the financial disaster of 2008 and is expected to grow this year at rate close to 4%, a pace similar to last years. More importantly, the current level of output appears sustainable, unlike the pre-crisis output, which could only be sustained as long as foreign funds to finance a double-digit current account deficit were forthcoming, in defiance of rapidly rising foreign debt. Inflation has been brought down from 18% in the aftermath of the banking crash to a rate below the 2.5% inflation target. An oversized cross-border banking sector has been replaced by a smaller, domestically oriented, simpler, better capitalised, and more tightly regulated domestic banks. Sizeable profits, albeit in large part attributable to irregular items, have improved the resilience of the banking system, and the banks liquidity position is relatively strong. Fiscal policy has been placed on a sound footing, both as a result of the measures taken to tighten policy during the Stand-by Arrangement with the IMF and as a result of the economic recovery. Public debt ratios are falling, and the outlook is for a substantial decline in public sector debt ratios in coming years. Private sector debt ratios have also declined, helped by debt relief, economic recovery, and insolvency proceedings. The banks NPL ratios have come down from some of the highest in Europe to a comparatively low level. Important progress was made last year in winding up the failed banks. They have been granted exemptions from capital controls enabling them to go into composition and pay distributions to creditors after meeting stability conditions that eliminate the huge balance of payment risk that would otherwise have resulted from their resolution. What emerges at the end of the deleveraging and winding-up process is the most favourable international investment position (IIP) Iceland has seen since the mid-1960s. If the current account remains in surplus for a few more years, as forecast, the IIP will become positive, compared to a negative position equivalent to 106% of GDP at the end of 2007, and much worse in the aftermath of the crisis. Difficult challenges lie ahead, however. The recent economic gains are not only the result of good policies, but also good fortune. Three types of positive shocks to the economy can be identified: First, the favourable effects of winding up the old banks on net external debt, on top of deleveraging since the crisis broke. Second, terms of trade have turned strongly in Icelands favour in the last two years, from a forty-year low in 2013. Third, exports have been boosted by an unprecedented boom in tourism, which last year surpassed fisheries and aluminium as Icelands largest export sector. The boom continues. In Q4/2015, tourism-generated revenues grew by 40% year-on year. While this is good news, the extraordinarily rapid increase in tourism raises questions of sustainability. The infrastructure is under strain, and it is uncertain to what extent growth in tourism is sensitive to eventual rise in fuel prices and hence airfares, the rising real exchange rate, the vicissitudes of fashion or other external factors. At some point, the current shortage of hotels rooms is likely to turn into a glut. More worryingly, the labour market has apparently become overheated. Unit labour costs rose at a rate of close to 10% in 2015 and will do so again this year, while labour productivity growth is weak. Although partly offset by the previously mentioned improvement in terms of trade, this will inevitably lead to rising inflationary pressures. This will call for tight monetary policy is spite of low current inflation, which reflects an appreciating currency and falling import prices. At the current exchange rate, the recent wage settlements are also bound to raise Icelands real effective exchange rate significantly above historical norms (albeit not as high as in 2005 and 2007), undermining competitiveness and making the economy more vulnerable to a possible terms of trade reversal and other external shocks. For European policy makers, solving problems of an economy that is becoming too strong may sound like an enviable position. However, in view of Icelands history of boom-bust cycles, we should not take much comfort from the problems policy makers in other countries are facing. On the contrary, conducting monetary policy in a very small, open economy out of sync with the rest of the developed world is a serious challenge, as we learned during the period leading up to the financial crisis of 2008. With short-term interest differentials with abroad close to 6 percentage points, a strong fiscal position, rapidly falling public and private sector debt ratios, a current account surplus, and external debt falling to historically low level, Iceland has become an attractive  albeit very small  target for a potentially huge pool of global investors desperately searching for returns. In spite of the uncertainty still surrounding the final steps towards lifting the capital controls, foreign investors have bought Treasury bonds worth 70 billion kronur (equivalent to 3.2% of GDP) over the past twelve months. This is still manageable, but it adds to a steady stream of foreign currency entering the economy via the current account, when exporters are still subject to repatriation requirements. Last year the Central Bank bought foreign currency equivalent to 13% of Icelands GDP in the interbank market, restraining the appreciation of the krona over the course of the year to 7%. In the first quarter of this year, foreign currency purchases have surged even more in comparison with the same period last year. Accumulating foreign reserves at this pace would be unsustainable were it not for the substantial amount of blocked non-residential investment waiting to be released and the potentially pent-up demand for foreign investment by residents. An auction to release blocked non-resident ISK claims is pending. Once the resulting adjustments have taken place and, subsequently, as most restrictions on the capital account have been lifted, foreign demand for domestic securities may rise further. Hence, the Central Bank has been looking at various options for dealing with potentially destabilising capital inflows by applying capital flow management tools. But capital flow management and macroprudential policies should be seen as a complement to responding to excessive capital inflows by tightening fiscal policy, not a substitute. Furthermore, whether these measures will fit with EEA rules on free movement of capital remains to be seen. Apart from dealing with volatile capital flows head-on, we also need to strengthen the resilience of the economy in general and the financial sector in particular in the event of destabilising cross-border capital flows. Much has already been achieved or is likely to be implemented in the near future: The domestic commercial banks have become more resilient. The three largest banks T1 capital ratios are over 28%. In line with CRD-IV, additional capital buffers amounting to 8.5% have recently been imposed on major banks, increasing their resilience against shocks to the economy. This includes a 1% countercyclical capital buffer effective at the beginning of 2017. Further countercyclical capital buffers will most likely be imposed as the economy picks up steam. The Icelandic banks are no longer engaged in substantial cross-border activity. Moreover, they face more restrictive NSFR limits on their foreign currency liabilities than their foreign peers. Further work on requirements for their foreign exchange balance is in progress. According to a bill to be submitted to Parliament, the Central Bank will be given powers to regulate the foreign currency exposure of parties with inadequate foreign exchange hedging. Rising foreign exchange liabilities of companies and households with inadequate foreign currency revenue or assets fed the boom and subsequently triggered enormous losses to the financial sector when the krona plunged in 2008, deepening the recession substantially. According to a draft bill before Parliament, the Icelandic financial supervisor (FME) will, following recommendation from the Financial Stability Council, be equipped with powers to impose limits on loan-to-value ratios and, hopefully, on debt service-to-income ratios as well. A new governance structure is in place to apply the macroprudential tools mentioned above: the Systemic Risk Committee and the Financial Stability Council. Confidence may take decades to build up but can be lost almost instantaneously. Ever since the crisis broke, we have worked hard to regain the confidence lost as a result of it. The fact that capital controls are still in place underlines that this work is not completed, but we have come a long way. We have broken the vicious cycle between banks and the sovereign (which affected some Eurozone countries as well as Iceland), mainly with a combination of orthodox fiscal and monetary tightening, in contrast to what some seem to believe, but also with essential help from some unorthodox financial sector ringfencing measures, including the so-called emergency legislation and temporary capital controls. The latter was a necessary evil in the absence of a proper cross-border co-insurance mechanism. These measures brought about significant short-term social and economic benefits, but at unknown long-term cost. For a very small, open economy, the benefits in terms of efficiency and cross-border risk-sharing brought about by free trade and free capital movements are essential. However, these also carry substantial risk, as we have learned. We need to find the right balance between risk and efficiency, either through participation in a proper cross-border co-insurance mechanism or by resorting to self-insurance through appropriate ring-fencing measures that preserve as many of the benefits of free capital movements as possible but without excessive risk-taking. We have learned important lessons from the recent crisis, but there is no panacea for all future problems of running independent monetary policy in a very small, open economy with free capital movements. The idea that such an economy can be isolated from the global financial cycle is a dangerous illusion, a fact made clear by a recent study showing strong spillover effects to Iceland from the global financial cycle over a period of more than a century. But if monetary policy is adequately supported by fiscal, macroprudential, and capital flow management policies, it should be possible to alleviate some of the excesses that have characterised the Icelandic financial cycle, which, after all, is only a variation on a global theme. References: Einarsson, B. G., K. Gunnlaugsson, T. T. olafsson and T. G. Petursson (2015). The long history of financial boom-bust cycles in Iceland  Part II: Financial cycles. Central Bank of Iceland Working Papers, forthcoming.

Title: Interview with Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 14.09.2007 Interview with Ingimund Fri?riksson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland Morgunbla?i? published an interview by Journalist Gr8etar J9cn92us Gu?mundsson with Governor Ingimundur Fri?riksson on 13 September 2007. In the interview, Ingimundur discusses interest rate decisions of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, the Bank's disclosure, market positions and more. Morgunbla?i? has given permission for this interview to be published in its entirety here on the Central Bank of Iceland's website. See also The Morning News: mbl.is The interview is here in its entirety: Urgent need for continued restraint The Decision of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland last week to keep the Bank's policy rate unchanged came as a surprise to few. However, some have expressed doubts that the Bank's interest rate decisions are working. The Decision of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland last week to keep the Bank's policy rate unchanged came as a surprise to few. However, some have expressed doubts that the Bank's interest rate decisions are working. Ingimundur Fri?riksson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, dismisses this entirely and says on the contrary that the results have been clearly reflected in the resolution of inflation. Gr8etar J9cn92us Gu?mundsson spoke to him about the interest rates, the turmoil in financial markets and the kr97na. The Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland has stated that as soon as prerequisites arise to lower the Bank's policy rate, they will be reduced, but not before. Governor Ingimundur Fri?riksson says that the policy rate has indeed bitten inflation. It's wrong to move forward otherwise. "If the Fed hadn't applied extra restraint, then we're probably going to have a lot more inflation today, and the hush and turmoil that came with it," he says. The Central Bank's policy rate has remained unchanged at 13.3%, since the end of last year. In total, interest rates were raised seven times last year by a total of 3.3 percentage points. Since May 2004, however, interest rates have been raised nineteen times. Vilhj87lmur Egilsson, managing director of the Confederation of Icelandic Employers, said in an interview with Morgunbla?i? at the end of last month that the Central Bank's interest rate decisions were in a pure deadlock and the Bank never saw the possibility of lowering interest rates. Other members of the business community have taken a similar stance. Ingemundur says he completely disagrees with this. "Inflation was at its peak, close to eight and a half percent, in late summer last year," he says "It has fallen slowly and bitterly since then, albeit slower than we would have preferred, but there is no doubt in our minds that it has diminished primarily because of the restraint emanating from the monetary union. We also disagree with the view that we are in some deadlock and that interest rates can never be lowered here." Changing and improving methodology According to Ingimundur, the Central Bank has gradually changed its methods of forecasting and improved them. He says that the last important milestone in this regard was reached in March, when the Bank began publishing a controlling interest rate curve alongside an inflation forecast. This was done again in July. It has also been assumed that the Central Bank could lower its policy rate in the first half of next year, which is actually a delay from the Bank's forecast in March. The changes in monetary policy implementation have been well received. In particular, the publication of the policy rate curve has been well received and has had the effect on market expectations that the Central Bank sought. When the Central Bank's interest rate decision was announced last week, it specifically stated that it saw no reason to deviate from the forecast published in July. New inflation and The macroeconomic forecast will be published in Monetary Bulletin at the beginning of November and at the same time a new policy rate curve. It's important to achieve balance Ingimundur says that the demands of various business partners, that the Central Bank should have long since begun the reduction process of controlling interest rates, can be interpreted in a way that they believe the Bank should have effectively let through inflation by not using monetary restraint. Such developments cannot be controlled and the inflation and for it cannot be restrained and for it according to suitability let alone inflation expectations. The progress of recent losses shows how difficult it can be to get a grip on inflation that has gotten out of hand. "The most urgent task in economic management in this country is to balance the economy and that it needs to be calmed down every year. It's everyone's interest. Inflation is bad. It badly affects the economy of households that owe a lot in indexed loans and is causing a stir in business. Of course, we're navigating a difficult cruise with a massive trade deficit and underlying inflation that's still 5-6%, but that drives the balance to be reached as soon as possible." He says that in order to succeed in fighting inflation, there is a need for continued restraint on the part of the Central Bank. Of course, there is a need for continued restraint from those involved in public finances, both state and local, and it also requires care in the labour market. The Central Bank has stated that it will respond to the inflation outlook, whether it deteriorates or improves from what it has been, and that will be sustained. "What is needed now is strict restraint in all areas of the economy. We have applied it in monetary terms and indeed raised the possibility, most recently last week, that there are certain downsides in the trading process that make monetary policy not return at full weight, especially not at the long end of the bond market. Those flaws are primarily in the arrangement of real estate mortgages. It is important to take steps to enable the Central Bank to have the impact it needs to have. While interest rate hikes don't strike out at that end of the market, the property price is rising, as it has done in recent months." The Central Bank has also pointed out that it would strengthen the domestic bond market if the Treasury gave more of its own bonds even if it did not need credit. As a result, there would be some direct costs for the Treasury, but from a long-term point of view, there would be a more active domestic capital market. The Government would also have more easy access to that market if it needed credit again. The Housing Financing Fund revised Ingimundur says the Central Bank does not have a public opinion on how it is right to change the public housing loan system. "What matters to the Central Bank, however, is that the changes will be made that will allow monetary policy to have the desired effect. But it is also important that in the future residential loan system that will be formulated here, there will also be a solid foundation under the bond market. We have pointed out these issues for several years, including in the Bank's publications, in reviews to the Althingi and in reports to the Minister. Very little has happened, however. International organizations have also pointed out that it is time to rethink the role of the Housing Financing Fund. In this regard, particular attention can be drawn to the international monetary fund's reviews, most recently this summer. The fund's reports show that those they have worked have worked hard to study very thoroughly the arrangements for housing loans in Iceland. We agree with the International Monetary Fund's recommendations in this regard." He says the Fed is waiting for signs of a slowdown in the real estate market. The bank would have preferred that such signs had already emerged. It would be unequivocally compensated for the current situation if interest rates on housing loans were raised, as has happened with the banks. The fund, on the other hand, finances itself in a market with a government guarantee for a very long time, where the yields have been the lowest, and therefore it has been able to go more modest in interest rate increases in the past than otherwise. "It would help us, however, if interest rates on mortgage lending increased more than they have done, so returns at the shorter end of the indexed bond market were better reflected in the fund's lending rate. The purpose of monetary restraint is to make credit more expensive so that investments and consumption are postponed until conditions have changed." The FED has expressed concern about the consequences of the Central Bank's monetary policy and believes that it plays a part in the instability of the economy. In this regard, the Association has pointed to possible changes in price development targets relating to the Central Bank's inflation target, which they believe may have a fundamental impact on the development of collective bargaining agreement negotiations between the social partners. Among the proposals of the Association is that the Central Bank's inflation target is based on the consumer price index without the housing stock, but in the past that point has accounted for about half of the inflation rate in Iceland. In another place, the Confederation of Icelandic Employers has proposed that it should be abandoned from determining one specific numerical value for the Central Bank's inflation target. Third, they have pointed to the possibility of setting limits on controlling interest rates between Iceland and other countries. Aristotle doesn't like these ideas. "We think it's an advantage to have the housing stock inside the inflation measure. It reflects a large part of household living costs, and the consumer price index with housing costs is a more consistent measure of inflation than the index without it. In addition, house prices are a leading indicator. If it rises rapidly, it suggests a rise in private consumption later. So we don't want the house price to be taken out. In some places where it is not inside the index on which an inflation target is based, people miss it," says Ingimundur, who believes similarly applies to other Fed ideas about changes to the inflation target. "We don't think they're good. I think it's very dangerous to relax something about the goals we have about inflation. We should be able to achieve the inflation target with sensible policies and good market arrangements, and there is no reason to relax anything about the demands made there. It is unequivocal in our minds that monetary restraint has been successful. However, we have a problem stemming from the expansion of the past years, which is to some extent rooted in heavy industry construction, and not least in the changes that occurred in the mortgage market in 2004 and happened very quickly, leading to rapid growth in private consumption. It should be noted that these changes occurred at a time when global interest rates were at historic lows. If the monetary policy trading process were more favourable, if more restraint stemmed from the public finances, both state and local governments, if wage progress had been more consistent with the inflation target then inflation would be lower. However, we are still struggling with this great tension in society, although we sometimes hear that it is very slowing down. The state of the labour market does not indicate this. Unemployment is below one percent. While the labour market is as excited as it actually is, it is not possible to conclude that it is slowing down significantly." Ingimundur said the Bank last week decided not to change the policy rate and then declared that there was no reason to deviate from the inflation forecast published in July. "We also made it clear that if the inflation outlook deteriorated, the Banking Authority would act and the same applies if the outlook improves from what was forecast. Of course, we will be monitoring progress very closely over the next few months. The outlook, however, is unusually uncertain at the moment due to conditions outside the world, but as in the end, they are most vulnerable to uncertainty about the exchange rate of the kr97na. It will be very dependent on what happens in international markets." The turmoil is not surprising Ingimundur says there is no way to tell if there is a recession ahead for the global economy. The case was not clear enough for that. However, we would have expected that there would be changes in the markets. It would have been predicted many times internationally that there would be changes in the global environment, and the Central Bank would also have done so in its publications. They could be very sudden. "There has been an extraordinary supply of liquidity in international markets in recent times. Interest rates have been at historic lows and in some places even have to go back a hundred years in time to find another one. And the risk appetite has been immense. It has also been pointed out that the risk has not been properly priced. There would be too little difference between risky and risky investments. This situation had to change, and that's exactly what's happening now. It was hard to see exactly how that would happen, however, but during the day it came to pass that there were difficulties in the U.S. real estate loan market that triggered the changes. We don't see the end of this scenario, but it's clear that financial institutions around the world are very cautious at the moment," says Ingimundur, pointing out that interbank markets have not been as agile as usual, and there has been liquidity shortages. Central banks in the West and east have met this with an additional remit. "That's not the case here, and it doesn't look like it's going to be necessary. Attention, however, is increasingly focused on what the impact of this progress may be, whether it will lead to a decline in the national economy of the large industrialized countries. Loan conditions have deteriorated because of this turmoil, and it will be guarded here. However, there is nothing that specifically indicates that a crisis is imminent. There are no prerequisites for having any such prophecies up there now." The euro is not wise The debate over the kr97na and the possible adoption of the euro as a currency in this country has been more intense in the past than in the past. Ingimundur says that it is not the central bank's job to decide which currency is used in Iceland, it is a political decision. The Central Bank operates in accordance with the 2001 Act. The Bank is entrusted with the main objective of promoting stable prices as well as other objectives such as promoting the stability of the financial system. "Nevertheless, the Central Bank has expressed the view that it would not be prudent to adopt the euro in Iceland instead of the krona, except by joining the European Union. And I think there's reason to warn that something is going to be whistled in this respect. It should be noted that if there is the slightest chance of Iceland joining the European Union over time, I think it would be particularly inadvisable to adopt the euro unilaterally. This is because, among other things, we would then have to spend some of the foreign exchange reserves to buy euros, which would be in circulation here, which would not have to be done with membership of the Union. There are now banknotes and coins in circulation in the amount of well over ISK 61 billion. By membership, by itself we would get here euros. With the unilateral adoption of the euro, we would lose so-called mint profits, which is not great, and it would flow undivided to the European Central Bank. And we would not enjoy any of the positions involved in being in a monetary union, to be involved in decisions, nor to enjoy the co-insurance and cooperation that would be involved there, if we unilaterally adopted the euro." The unilateral adoption of the euro would presumably disappear the central bank's role as a lender to devolution for the financial system. He would then no longer be a potential backer of the financial institutions, and they would not even have a refuge in any central bank. Lastly, and then, regardless of the manner in which the new currency would be adopted, the Treasury guarantees large sums of money in indexed bonds in kr97nur that have been issued on the domestic market for a very long time and are inexpressible. It is not guaranteed that the corresponding revenue will be guaranteed if the currency is changed. Ingimundur says that public debate about the possible adoption of the euro sometimes sounds as if it automatically stabilizes the economy. "Of course it goes far away. Sometimes it seems that it seeks to divert attention from the current problem that does not go away even if it stops thinking about it. With the adoption of another currency, an independent monetary policy would be out of the question. The responsibility that would be placed on the shoulders of those in charge of public finances and those in charge of the labour market would be much greater than so far if stability was to be ensured. Failure to do so would lead to a deterioration in Iceland's competitive position, which could ultimately lead to recession and unemployment." The crown was enough so far Finally, he mentioned that ideas that had also been heard about linking the kr97na to another currency were unrealistic. Such a connection would require great sacrifice if it were to be credible, and the issue is whether there would be support for such a move. "So I think it's advisable to be careful and not make any decisions that might come to our heads later. Interests and perspectives need to be considered for the long term when discussing which currency to use in Iceland. Whatever the outcome in this regard, the demand is that there will be a policy that ensures balance in the economy," ingimundur says, adding that the kr97na has been good enough for us so far and can continue to do so. "Certainly the exchange rate has fluctuated somewhat recently, but so has the exchange rate of other currencies, including the world's major currencies. They have moved a lot towards each other in the past, which has also had an indirect impact on the krona. Indeed, exchange rate fluctuations are not of convenience, but it should be noted that the market offers opportunities to protect against the effects of exchange rate changes." Title: The Governor's address at the opening of an exhibition of memory money and artifacts owned by Kristjn Eldjrn
text: 14. september 2012 Address Governor Mar Guomundsson at the opening of an exhibition of memory money and items that were owned by Dr. Kristjan Eldjarn, former President of Iceland. The President of Iceland, Mr. olafur Ragnar Grimsson, former President of Iceland, Mrs. Vigdis Finnbogadottir, Ministers, former Governors of the Central Bank and other good guests, I welcome you all to this exhibition of memory money and artifacts that Dr. Kristjan Eldjarn, the former president, acquired during his career. These and other memory chips and items owned by Kristjan have been held by the Central Bank of Iceland's Coin Collection and the National Museum of Iceland, but hereafter Kristjan's children will hand them over to the museum for ownership. We are honored to receive this generous gift on the 30th anniversary of Christian's death. The Central Bank and The National Museum of Iceland's coin collection was created by the merger of material from the National Museum of Iceland and the Central Bank. Each party is the owner of the material it proposed, but the Central Bank is responsible for the day-to-day operation of the museum. The prelude was that in the early 1960s, Landsbanki islands  The Central Bank began to consider its archives and history. This work was carried out by Haraldur Hannesson, an economist, who also raised interest in Iceland's coin history. When the Central Bank moved its museum operations to a grand building at Einholt 4, it was started to register and sort collectibles owned by the Bank. Subsequently, the national museum's coin ownership was placed in the new museum. A formal agreement on the establishment and operation of the Central Bank of Iceland and the National Museum of Iceland was concluded in January 1985 and ratified by the Minister of Education. Under the agreement, the collection has a multifaceted role. First, it is intended to bring together the most advanced set of public currency in Iceland, i.e. to collect a national currency that can shed light on Icelandic business practices. Furthermore, record sources on the history of Icelandic price gauges and business practices, as well as compiling a good overview of the official currency of the Nordic countries and samples of the currency of other nations, ancient and new. The museum also organizes cooperation with the central banks of Iceland's major trading nations on the exchange of samples of the official currency. The goal is also to collect and conduct material related to mint, such as memory chips and medals, and to organise and participate in exhibitions relating to the above 1 materials and publish high-quality coverage of them, as well as tampering with and maintaining a source collection of coinological materials. Dr. Kristjan Eldjarn, national monument keeper, and Haraldur Hannesson, curator of the Central Bank of Iceland, were pioneers of the establishment of the coin collection, but Dr. Johannes Nordal, governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, loyally supported the establishment of the museum and its progress, and the three godfathers of the museum can be counted. text: 14.10.2005 Governor Eric Gudnason's speech at a meeting of the National Federation of Small Boat Owners October 14, 2005 14 October 2005: 14 October 2005: 14 October 2005 I am grateful to you for discussing the situation and prospects of monetary policy. Shortly thereafter, the Central Bank of Iceland published its quarterly publication Monetary Bulletin, the third this year. Anyone who has read it will be familiar with many of the things I have to say here. By law, the Central Bank of Iceland sets very clear objectives. The main goal is to promote stable prices. A joint statement by the Government and the Central Bank of March 2001 describes in more detail how this should be handled. Another objective, also important, is to promote an active and secure financial system, i.e. to have an overview of the strength of financial institutions operating here and the risks they might face. I will discuss the aforementioned objective here, i.e. the rule that we control monetary policy are aimed at low inflation. To do so, the Bank has only one instrument, the control rate, which is the interest rate applicable in the Bank's transactions with credit institutions. Monetary policy The objective of monetary policy is that inflation, as measured by the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX, is normally close to 21/2% in each 12-month period. It should be noted that the goal is not only to keep inflation within the so-called tolerance range (1-4%) but as close as possible to 21/2% as a rule. The Bank shall publicly outline its assessment of the state and outlook for the economy and, among other things, publish an inflation forecast two years ahead. The Act of 2001 granted the Bank full independence to apply its controls, i.e. to determine its own interest rates without consulting the authorities. The impact of central bank interest rate changes sweeps the economy with considerable delay, so it is necessary to look ahead to decisions on interest rates. Central bank interest rate decisions often have a rapid impact on short-term interest rates, but it may be much longer before the effects on long-term markets begin to be felt, and indeed they can be of various kinds. All of this depends on expectations that play an important role in the capital market. Six months have passed since the introduction of the inflation target and the fallout from the exchange rate target. First after the change, the exchange rate fell and we got an inflation shot. It lasted only a short time and in 2002 inflation slumped rapidly and remained low until 2004, but since the first half of that year it has increased. When trying to assess how well this policy suits our economy, it needs to be borne in mind that the second half of the time since the inflation target was set, conditions have been extremely unusual. The largest investment in Iceland's history was undertaken, foreign interest rates have been lower than a century and in the domestic financial market there have been major changes. While inflation is now higher than the target, I don't think it shows in any way that inflation targets are not suitable in this country. It's been too long since its recording to make that judgment. When it was decided to build a smelter and a power plant in East Iceland, the Icelandic population was fairly well balanced. The Central Bank believed at the time that although the scope of the construction was very high on the scale of Icelandic economic policy, appropriate measures could avoid a major imbalance caused by them. Two other things have caused the current imbalance in the national economy and are best represented by a massive trade deficit with foreign countries and inflation beyond targets. First, the construction of heavy industry and power plants became higher than originally anticipated, as in addition to the construction in East Iceland, it was decided to undertake the expansion of a smelter in Hvalfjorour with the associated energy generation. In addition, the The timetables for the project were designed to be much heavier in 2005 than originally planned. In the beginning, they were expected to spread over a longer period of time and their weight would come later. This made it more difficult than it would otherwise be to respond appropriately. The other factor that has caused an imbalance in the national economy is the massive change in the mortgage market in late 2004, when commercial banks and savings banks began providing such loans on completely different terms than previously available. In a report prepared at the request of the Minister of Social Affairs and published on the Central Bank's website in the second half of last year, the Central Bank pointed out the problems that could come with the increase in loan rates and loan amounts of the Housing Financing Fund. Already there were plans for such increases, along with a reduction in the interest rate on housing loans, commercial banks and savings banks entered this area with great force and have now provided new housing loans that are rapidly approaching ISK 300 billion. This development was not foreseen by no one, its impact emerged very quickly and until then there had been some way to respond to it with timely monetary action. A significant portion of the new loans have been spent on the repayment of other and less favourable loans from both the Housing Financing Fund and pension funds. However, it is also clear that households have spent part of the new loans to finance private consumption, reflecting, among other things, a very high import and trade deficit. The Central Bank considers banks and savings banks to have gone overboard in this regard. In the long run, it is of course pleasing that competition in the capital market benefits households in the country, as well as property-indexed loans that the financial foundations of the banks rely on the financial foundations of the banks as pointed out by international rating agencies and the International Monetary Fund. The change, however, came at a very unfortunate time. There is reason to urge credit institutions to be careful in their lending decisions and to consider the security of loans. Furthermore, the Central Bank has pointed out many times the need to consider the future role of the Housing Financing Fund in the financing of housing purchases and how it can be handled on the one hand and banks and savings banks on the other hand, to, among other things, rely on the foundations of the domestic financial system and remittances to those who for some reason do not have the same access to housing loans as in general. Last but not least, there is reason to urge the country's households to pay close attention to their finances and be careful not to undertake commitments that can prove heavy-handed as time goes by. According to an analysis by the Central Bank of Iceland, the imbalance in the economy is much greater now than it thought it was at the beginning of June when it published this year's Issue II of Monetary Bulletin. The Central Bank reported its estimate a fortnight ago, raising its interest rate by 0.75 percentage points. Interest rates have risen by almost 5 percent since May last year. This has given rise to media coverage, at the banks' analysts and elsewhere. I would like to mention a few things that have been discussed in the past few days. We at the Central Bank welcome the discussion of monetary policy, our policies and our methods criticised. In fact, I believe that there may be a significant improvement in this debate over the last few years, not least by the analysts of the banks. Sometimes we feel like there might be a misunderstanding. The issuance of bonds in ISK Icelandic in the international market Interest rate hikes by the Central Bank of Iceland have inevitably resulted in an increase in interest rates between Iceland and other countries and has become greater than has been known since restrictions were eased from the transfer of capital between Iceland and other countries. In many other parts of the industrialized world, interest rates are at or near historic lows. As a result, investors seek investment options that yield higher returns than are offered in many other places. In recent times, those familiar have paused Icelandic the crown. This progress in itself needs not come as a surprise, and it is a folly of the freedom to transfer capital unhindered across countries. Icelandic investors have had easy access to foreign financial markets and now foreign investors are giving themselves to Icelandic the krona. There is nothing to say about this, but we must negotiate ourselves to these changing circumstances. The short-term effect has been mainly reflected in declining returns on certain categories of Treasury bonds in the domestic market and in the increase in the exchange rate of the krona. It's hard to know how much of an impact it is on the exchange rate. However, it may be considered That's a little higher now than it would have been if it hadn't come to this bond issue. What the effects will be in the long term is impossible to say. The bonds issued on the international market have a variety of loan periods so they do not all due at the same time. Furthermore, it is possible that this progress will create bonds that will be maintained so that bonds in ISK Icelandic will be created in the bond portfolios of foreign investors for the time being. This cannot be explained at this stage. The foreign investors have a very short experience of trading in Icelandic kronas. We know that foreign investors have sought to gather information on Iceland, the state of the krona and the economy in general and the outlook ahead. They have therefore sought to make informed decisions about investments in bonds in Icelandic isk. The experience determines how lucrative these investments will be and what their interest will be as they progress and the difference between domestic and foreign interest rates decreases again. Unlike the assessments of the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance, it has been noted that it is unfortunate that different assessments of the outlook are presented by the Central Bank on the one hand and the Ministry of Finance on the other. The Central Bank's new forecast includes somewhat higher growth in private consumption in the near future and stronger economic growth than in ministry figures. You may ask whether these two parties should agree on a single prediction. I think it would be very misguided and I think the ministry's experts actually feel the same way. It would greatly diminish the central bank's independence if it did not assess its position and prospects with the assumptions it considers to be the right thing to target at any given time. The methods of forecasting may be different and assumptions as well. For example, assumptions about changes in interest rates and exchange rates are not the same in the forecasts of the Bank and the Ministry. No one is surprised if the outcome is different. The other is so different that everyone who deals with prediction wants to reform methods by prisoners and learn from each other. Therefore, it is natural, when the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance have set out their forecasts, that their experts compare them and break them down so that their understanding is increased. Such communications are carried out and are intended to contribute to the advancement of prediction. Did the money go on holiday? The Fed has been criticized for its high interest rates these days. It has also been heard that he should have raised interest rates sooner and more than he has done in the past. It was mentioned, among other things, that he had given too long between the last two interest rate changes, which were introduced on 3 June and 29 September. In this regard, it came from one of the analysts that monetary policy was not allowed to go on holiday. I want to assure you that monetary policy did not go on holiday. In the summer months, as in other months, the Central Bank was asked whether interest rates needed to be changed. The result, not doing so, may seem strange given that the increase at the end of September was quite large. But this explains that the outlook had changed considerably after new macroeconomic figures from Statistics Iceland were published and a new inflation forecast had been drawn up. In the morning, Statistics Iceland published the Consumer Price Index at the beginning of October, which was found to have increased by 4.6% from October last year. The latest measurements of the index strongly bear the mark of high domestic demand. They are reflected, among other things, in the increase in the price of goods and services that are not subject to competition from abroad, as well as an increase in the exchange rate in recent months, only to a limited extent in the price of imported goods. This is especially true in the price of cars. The power of demand, which has come as a surprise, is reliably a major factor in this unfortunate development. In the past, there have been calls for the Central Bank of Iceland to adopt the practices frequented by central banks abroad whose inflation targets are to announce in advance when it holds meetings to decide on interest rates. At the time, the Central Bank published its rules on monetary policy decisions and announced that they would be reviewed as appropriate. For example, it would be considered to be considered in advance what the decision dates of the year will be. This has been debated and scrutinised at the Bank for some time now and it is possible that special interest rate decision days will be announced in due course. They could be more than release dates Monetary policy means that on days other than the monetary bulletin issuance dates, the Central Bank would issue an announcement on the Interest Rate Decision of the Board of Directors whether it will be in the process of changing interest rates or leaving them unmolested. Should the Central Bank strengthen its foreign exchange reserves through further foreign exchange purchases? It has been mentioned that the Central Bank could increase its foreign exchange purchases for two purposes. On the one hand, to strengthen the foreign exchange reserves and on the other to contribute to the decrease in the exchange rate of the krona or to discourage further increases in the exchange rate. The bank now buys twelve and a half million dollars a week, including ten to meet the government's repayment of foreign loans next year. For the time being, there is some construction of the resource. A decision on further acquisitions is not yet available, but it is clear that it would be based on the Bank's view on how large the foreign exchange reserves need to be. It would not be aimed at achieving any change in the exchange rate, as the Bank does not have an exchange rate target. In addition, central bank interventions in the foreign exchange market have limited effect on exchange rates except perhaps for a very short period of time. Furthermore, the Bank's foreign exchange purchases increase liquidity in circulation, which can be a problem. Do you want to reduce the insurance of financial obligations? It has also been mentioned that the widespread spread of indexation of capital in Iceland delays the dissemination of monetary policy and therefore it should be checked whether the use of indexation can be reduced. In fact, there have been a number of arguments that insurance should be reduced. At some point, it was argued that inflation could not be achieved unless the indexation is eliminated. It has now been thoroughly disproved. It has been argued that indexed loans would be expensive for borrowers. In this regard, I would like to point out that unsecured loans are generally more expensive. Borrowers, however, need to realize that when they take a indexed loan, they are actually negotiating many loans ahead of time, because they get indexation on each maturity largely borrowed. Therefore, the payload of indexed loans is light in front of the loan period but heavy towards the end. It is natural and self-evident that the indexation is examined attentively, considering that its abolition or less use than it currently is could make monetary policy quicker so that interest rate changes at the Central Bank are spreading earlier to the economy. However, it is not certain that it is. It can be pointed out that interest rates on indexed securities here on the market have been rising a little over the last few days and there are no other explanations more immediate than that this is due to the Central Bank's last interest rate change. Would it be appropriate to adopt the euro? It is sometimes mentioned that Icelanders should adopt the euro as their currency even without membership of the European Union. The Central Bank has discussed this issue in speech and publication, and more have done so*. The Central Bank has warned that people will simplify our options in this regard. If the euro were adopted as a currency here by a unilateral decision Icelandic the government, it would certainly deliver lower interest rates, but this route has many drawbacks for an independent state and might not be in harmony with the European Central Bank. The exchange rate would no longer exist as a benefit instrument and a security valve, under the current circumstances there would reliably be higher inflation than there is now, and if there was a recession here than a boom in the countries of the Monetary Union, unemployment would likely rise here. It is highly unlikely that we will be able to join the Monetary Union without membership of the European Union. Even if such secondary membership was available to us, which does not seem likely to happen, the next certainty is that we would have to meet the conditions of the Maastricht Treaty on membership of the Monetary Union. These include low inflation, low interest rates and the fact that the relevant country has been in the EU's exchange rate partnership, ERM2, for at least two years without the exchange rate going beyond tolerance. Clearly, we will not meet these conditions in the near future. It can be noted that several central and eastern European countries have recently gained membership of the European Union and are later seeking participation in the Monetary Union. On the part of the European Central Bank and others in the leadership of the European Union, there has been a strong emphasis on the importance of these nations meeting all the conditions for participation in the Monetary Union. It is therefore highly unlikely that they would agree to set any precedent that they might be able to use to shorten their way into the Monetary Union. Icelanders have chosen to stand outside the European Union and have not expressed an interest in membership. Heading the nation's mind to adopt the euro as a currency would be the closest thing to joining the European Union with all obligations and advantages associated with it, including membership of the Monetary Union. However, the decision to do so depends on more factors than merely concerning the nation's currency, and the process would take several years. Of course, this is first and foremost a major political issue. We therefore need to continue to peddle as a nation with its own currency, which under the conditions of free capital movements requires very disciplined economic management. Monetary policy restraint over the next few years, conditions in the economy will be unusually difficult from the point of view of monetary policy. In fact, they will be a test of how well the current policy suits a small, open economy. The Central Bank believes it is imperative that monetary policy passes this test and that inflation does not deviate from its inflation target for a short time. It is the central bank's duty to aim for this, and for that it has only one tool, interest rates. The Central Bank is serious about keeping inflation closest to the inflation target over the next two years and in the long term although it may for a time come down various industries. The current special circumstances make monetary policy management particularly problematic and in many ways have an undesirable effect on its functioning. This is reflected in, among other things, the fact that increased restraint is currently coming down very differently in individual sectors of the economy. It comes down export sectors but bites little on individuals so far. In these circumstances, there is reason to warn against the notion that there are simple solutions to ease the problem of export sectors for example. It has been suggested, among other things, that it would be appropriate to let inflation through in order to help the export industries. It is right to be warned about these ideas. If inflation were to be allowed through, as it is put to be, which would happen with a more relaxed monetary restraint, the real exchange rate of the krona would rise due to higher inflation in Iceland than abroad, workers would apply for an increase in the purchase fee beyond what would otherwise be, and the remaining national economy would not only have a high real exchange rate but also high inflation with the associated distortion of the working conditions of the business sector and the financial difficulties of indebted households. In addition, it would take even more drastic measures to quash those inflation than those necessary to hold back inflation now. Inflation has on average been considerably above the inflation target since it was adopted. The Central Bank therefore has some work to do to create credibility on monetary policy and is determined to do so. It won't be done without a fight. Governments and business partners can ease the Bank's efforts and contribute to lower costs than otherwise in curbing inflation. Regardless of whether the Bank enjoys such reinforcements, it will unhesitatingly continue to work towards the progression of the inflation target. In the long run, it is for the best interests of both business and individuals.
