Title: Meetings of the Governor of the Central Bank of Brussels on 27 and 28 September
text: 14.10.2016 Meetings of the Governor of the Central Bank of Brussels on 27 and 28 September On 27 and 28 September, Governor Mar Guomundsson gave two talks in Brussels, as well as meetings with the board of the EFTA Surveillance Authority (ESA) and senior Officials of the European Commission in the economic and financial markets sectors. In particular, we talked about capital controls and macroeconomics. The Governor gave a keynote speech at a seminar of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) on 27 September. The seminar addressed the problems for banking systems and financial stability inherent in membership of the internal market without membership of a banking union. The agenda and account of the conference can be found on the EFTA website (see Policy Seminar: Half in  half out of the Banking Union ). The governor's speech was entitled "Half in  half out: What are the risks for small open and financially integrated economies?" On 28 September, the Governor of the Central Bank was the frontrunner at a closed seminar at esa where he discussed the release of capital controls and systemic risks in Iceland (see Lifting capital controls in Iceland). In connection with the seminar, he had a special meeting with the Board of Directors of esa. The day before, he had held two meetings with senior European Commission officials, those of Financial Markets Commissioner Olivier Guersent (DG-FISMA; Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union) and Servaas Deroose Deputy Director of Economic Affairs (DG-ECFIN; Economic and Financial Affairs). The meetings discussed in particular the implementation and disposal of capital controls and the precautions that have been implemented or planned and aimed at promoting financial stability under the conditions of unrestricted capital movements. Title: Deputy Governor's introductory remarks at the Nordic Central Bank Conference on Cybersecurity
text: 29 November 2018 Deputy Governor Rannveig Siguroardottir. Introductory remarks at the 2nd Annual Nordic Cyber in Finance Conference, Helsinki, 29 November 2018 Let me begin by saying that this conference is both timely and interesting for me, as I have only been in office for five months. Given that I come from the monetary policy department at the Central Bank of Iceland, cybersecurity has not been much on my agenda until now. It is, nonetheless, a very important topic. The Central Bank of Iceland, and other central banks are facing several new challenges in this area, both in the financial sector generally and central banking more specifically. Last week I attended an interesting macroprudential policy conference at Danmarks Nationalbank. The discussion paper prepared for that conference was called While the sun is shining, prepare for a rainy day. Sitting there, I pondered what the discussion paper for this conference today might be called. Perhaps something like The snowstorm is here  what do we wear? Cybercrime is now the worlds fastest-growing type of crime. It has shot up to second place on the list of the top ten business risks worldwide, after not even making the list five years ago. The financial sector is particularly important because it greases the wheels of our economies, and cyber risks pose mounting threats to the financial system. Developments since the emergence of the internet show that new technologies have brought with them new challenges. We only need to think of robotics, artificial intelligence, blockchains, and smart phones with 5G Wi-Fi to realize the extent of the changes that lie ahead for financial services. New technologies also bring opportunities. The Austrian economist, Finance Minister, and banker Joseph Schumpeter demonstrated in the 1920s that successive waves of technological change raise productivity, income, and living standards. However, we know from long experience that technological change often results in costs involving new risks that must be addressed in order to optimise the net benefit. So while FinTech will broaden consumers range of choices in financial intermediation, it also brings new risks, both to the security of transactions and to privacy. To maintain financial stability and real economic activity, we need payment and settlement systems that are secure. As a result, cybersecurity has moved from being a technical issue to a central bank issue. That is why the Nordic central banks have set up this forum for discussion and cooperation so as to foster closer cooperation on cyber resilience and cybersecurity. Today the focus is on financial market infrastructure. One of the questions being asked in this section of the conference is, What challenges are likely to emerge with new operating models and new actors in the financial sector? As I said before, the FinTech snowstorm is already here. The newest challenge with respect to cybersecurity is the emergence of new players offering financial services, some of whom have not provided financial services before. The question therefore becomes: What technology are they using? Is it established, or is it new and unknown technology? We also know that attitudes towards security and operational risk are important. But with tech firms rushing to offer new products to the market, there is the risk of insufficient emphasis on security. This is a risk that must be monitored  not only for new products or for new players, but also for incumbent businesses. Tech giants like Google, Apple, and Alibaba look set to become dominant players. Their advantage comes from providing cross-border services and having already gathered significant information about users. They are already present in the Nordic marketplace. This development may lean towards monopolies, as it can create entry barriers for new and smaller players in the market. If that proves to be the case, it could have a negative impact on competition and go against the aims of the PSD2 (the recent EU Directive on payment services in the internal market (2015/2366). This risk is greater when the payment mechanisms are outside the jurisdiction of the relevant state. Then there is the question of supervision. Will the new solutions be supervised, and if so, how? The challenge here is that many new solutions are global, and thus outside the European Economic Area or the European Single Market. Such supervision thus requires crossborder cooperation among supervisors. The challenge for the supervisor is also to maintain a comprehensive overview of the market. For the legislator, it is a challenge to stay on top of rapid technological developments, as rules tend to lag behind technological changes. Financial market participants must commit fully to guarding the system. Cybersecurity needs to be promoted at all levels. With respect to this fast-changing technology, keeping one step ahead of antisocial elements is a constant challenge. As I see it, cooperation is the only way forward. It is vital that all financial system entities work together on all fronts  within and between countries  to identify and address vulnerabilities. We need to share both our successes and our mishaps. We must do as mountain-climbers do  tie ourselves together  because we are all in this together: central banks, financial service providers, FinTech firms, consumers, regulators, and politicians. And our success in combining forces will determine whether we reach the mountain peak or have to go back to base camp again. All systems can break. This is why some of us still use paper banknotes, even though they are not the most sophisticated technology. But their security has been improved upon over recent centuries. Try imagining what would have been the main topic at a conference in Florence at the time of the first Medicis. As with paper money, the technologies we are discussing here today will become more secure, although we will encounter blizzards. Our role is to prevent or reduce the likelihood that those blizzards will create systemic risk.

Title: Talk at the breakfast meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce
text: 16. March 2005 Arnor Sighvatsson, Chief Economist: Is the iceland plane overheating? Talks delivered at the breakfast meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce The development of Icelandic economic policy may be envious to many. Economic growth is excellent, investment in bullish growth, exports devalued, stock prices have multiplied in a few years, the purchasing power of wages has greatly increased, unemployment is low and is declining and inflation  it is, after all, modest when it is considered an increase in housing costs, which either is not really a target, because the cost of capital has fallen so much that individuals can now finance a fifth of the more expensive housing than before without taking on a greater payload, In addition to their earnings, their income has increased. As a symbol of this nation's prosperity, the crown boasts a strength that hardly has historical precedents. The economy is full of vigour and self-confidence, the companies organise Viking trips on foreign soil, not by raiding foreign lands as in the past, but by picking up the checkbook and buying some well-chosen businesses  and the checking accounts are full of foreign credit  that are given, or next. The banks are fully involved in the legions and raking up profits like never before, although they are now offering loans to the country's households at lower interest rates than previously known. These are good times. Yet it is now so with us the practitioners of the sad science that few things cause us more anguish and anxiety than the prolonged and unbroken stream of good news. That we sneak up on the suspicion that the sum of a large number of good news is bad news  that anything too good to be true is actually false and at the end of the day bad. Icelandic the national yacht has been sailing both skates for some time and the Iceland engine has rotated at full speed, further increasing the momentum. The world is floating in cash that is available in search of returns. Financiers have accepted ever greater risks in order to improve returns. This funding is pouring into the Icelandic national economy. Under these circumstances, one of the greatest construction phases in the nation's history has begun. The government has improved and reduced restrictions on public access to credit at the same time as the national financial system has been revolutionised and the economy restructured. It's all for good, individually, but maybe not all at once. The problem is to consume it all at once without overpowering the Iceland machine. What happens if the foreign fuel that drives growth rises in price  if the foreign fuel that drives the growth increases in price  if the foreign 2 Are the interest rates going up? We have some examples of what can happen - and the tracks scare. The Iceland machine has become hot, at least some parts of it. If it wasn't, the Fed would have almost raised interest rates by 31/2 percent in less than a year. Signs of overheating can be seen in many parts of the Icelandic national economy o First, the overheating is that inflation has been rising for some time. True, it is still confined to goods and services that do not live in foreign competition, but this is customary. Experience shows that such inflation is a leading indicator of general inflation. Secondly, it appears in the increase in property prices. Never before has the price of a house risen so rapidly in a short period of time, and never before has it been so high. It is true that the cost of financing residential purchases has fallen and it is true that individuals' income has increased so much that they now can now afford to buy more expensive apartments than before. There is also, of course, something to do with the city's population now estimating the proximity to the city centre at a higher price than before, for example because it costs less than before to finance the pressure and because of the changing family structure. It is also true that many other countries in the world are going through a similar phase. None of this, however, changes the growing difference between the market price of housing and construction costs. These differences involve a lot of incentives to build. And there is a lot built, not enough to satisfy the demand yet, but that it will come and one good rainy day will be too much housing coming on the market and the price will fall, at least in real terms. 100% loans will no longer be talked about  but rather 90% of assets, 80% of assets, depending on their value in proportion to the loan on them. The price of a residential property has reached heights that do not last long. That's not to say it can't go up yet more, before it falls. o Third, the overheating appears in a trade deficit that has already become as large as it has been before. However, it is clear that it is going to increase significantly due to investment this year, as well as the factor income deficit being actually abnormally low due to the low foreign interest rates in the past year. A large trade deficit is a rather pleasant phenomenon while lasting, but uncomfortable when it shrinks, because it traditionally happens either through a decrease in the currency exchange rate or a decline in domestic demand, unless exports grow the more. When the trade deficit has become this great before in the nation's history, a recession or significant rate cut has always followed. This makes the situation even more vulnerable that at the same time money has flowed out of the country due to domestic purchases of foreign securities and companies. The sum of these three, SI-21639 - Arnor Sighvatsson's talk at the breakfast meeting of the Chamber of Commerce 3 The trade deficit, foreign securities investment by domestic parties and direct foreign investment, has been called basic balance. In 2000, a major overheating year, the base balance accounted for a fifth of GDP, or roughly double the trade deficit, which at the time was considered unique and not likely to repeat itself. The economy was therefore subject to massive credit inflows that required significant adjustments in the national economy as it began to dwindle. Last year, the base balance amounted to about a third of GDP, and will occur if the likelihood is even bigger this year. Of course, this won't last long. o Fourth, there is an overheating in the rapid growth in lending and money supply. Prolonged lending expansion and monetary growth simultaneously with rising asset prices are always considered risk signals. It doesn't take a hardened "monetarista" to consider the prolonged double-digit growth of money supply a significant risk marker. o Fifth, the overheating appears in a huge credit inflow. This credit inflow is not only necessary to finance large trade deficits and direct as passive investment, but it also represents the foreign lending growth of the banking system. Net inflows of credit amounted to approximately 70% of GDP in the previous year. Of course, there is also a lot of asset formation, but not as much. The national debt point has deteriorated greatly, as well as rapid growth and rapid changes in its balance sheet always involve risks, although the changes may be desirable in themselves. o Finally, the overheating appears in the rise in real exchange rates, which is actually partly due to the Central Bank's response to it. The real exchange rate is now approaching previous historical limits and it is safe to say that it will not be allowed to last long. The question is when, how quickly and under what conditions its inevitable adaptation will occur. How can the bank deal with this? In law and in a joint statement by the Central Bank and the Government in March 2001, the Bank has set one main objective, to keep inflation close to 21/2%. In order to achieve this goal, the Bank essentially has one tool, the Bank's control rate. This tool has been used by the Central Bank in recent months and this has encouraged an increase in the exchange rate although other forces are also involved. The high exchange rate is undeniably down to individual sectors of the national economy, and the impact on some sectors may be extremely harsh and indeed undesirable. It's natural to ask if this is necessary. SI-21639 - Arnor Sighvatsson's talk at the breakfast meeting of the Chamber of Commerce 4 It is therefore in response that historically, real steering rates are not particularly high, and therefore less if you take into account the high levels of activity that lie ahead and other factors that have pushed demand. However, in the current situation in foreign markets, it cannot be avoided that monetary policy dissemination takes place largely through the exchange rate. This is undesirable, but unfortunately inevitable. Less adherential monetary policy may lead to a lower nominal rate for a short period of time, but not necessarily to a lower real exchange rate in the long run. Lower interest rates would eventually result in higher inflation and an increase in wages, which would probably eventually bring real exchange rates to a similar level to what would be up to the cube if adjourned monetary policy was followed. The main difference is that inflation would be much higher when it came to the inevitable adjustment of exchange rates at the end of construction. In order to quash inflation under those circumstances, it would take an even higher rate of control than is needed to keep it under control now. If the economy were to be in such a position next year, when eventually major construction is drawing to a close and it is probable that reducing capital inflows could put the Fed in an extremely difficult position. There is a risk that a very high level of monetary restraint could intensify a recession after construction, perhaps causing a collapse in asset prices and financial instability. For these reasons, the Central Bank has considered it far more desirable to grapple with the inevitable  and certainly undesirable  side effects of austerity monetary policy now rather than later. The real exchange rate of the krona is certainly higher than it has in a long time. It is not impossible that it will rise further. However, fluctuations in the real exchange rate of the krona are no greater than what is happening in other currency regions, but Icelandic the economy is inevitably more susceptible to them than most other countries. The impact of changes in control rates may take up to two years to emerge. The Central Bank cannot therefore expect to have much impact next year unless it takes timely action. Late restraints involve greater risks to the financial system. In this light, the implementation of the Central Bank's monetary policy should be examined at the moment. The engine needs to be slowed down before it gets even warmer. SI-21639 - Arnor Sighvatsson's talk at the breakfast meeting of the Chamber of Commerce

Title: Discussion on the Monetary Policy of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Arnor Sighvatsson1 Discussion in chaos There have been many criticisms of the Central Bank of Iceland's monetary policy in the past, mixed with discussions on future monetary and exchange rate arrangements in Iceland. It is normal for criticism to be made in light of the fact that inflation has for a long time exceeded the Bank's target of 2.5%, cf. a statement by the Central Bank and the Government of Iceland since 2001. The Fed has no reason to wail from such criticism. An analysis of what has gone wrong is a prerequisite for better results to be achieved in the future. Confusing debate Given that inflation has for a long time been above the Central Bank's target, but not below that, it is difficult to understand some of these criticisms. The debate, mildly speaking, has been confusing and extreme. It brings together criticism of the implementation of monetary policy within the current monetary framework and discussion of possible future monetary arrangements. In many cases, the conclusions drawn seem to be the opposite given the motive. For example, some seem to conclude that inflation was above the Central Bank's target that monetary policy was too inclusive, although it is almost impossible to conclude the opposite. It is argued that policy rate changes are a doughy weapon in the fight against inflation, and therefore concluded that that this is why the Central Bank should use it with greater leniency. Logically, it seems to conclude the opposite; A small weapon needs to be used more aggressively. However, the same parties who argue that there are only bitter machetes in the Central Bank's arsenal have put forward the view that the Central Bank should set more targets than just keeping rates steady. Why bitter control rates that are not enough to achieve one goal should be enough to achieve more goals is a mystery. A lively exchange of views on monetary policy is welcome, but it would be desirable that consistency in reasoning be greater. In order to try to resolve the complexity of arguments that have emerged in recent times, it is appropriate to divide it into three separate chapters. First, the reasons for the deviations that have occurred need to be analysed and the effectiveness of monetary policy to date assessed. Second, the question must be answered as to what the Central Bank could have done better in terms of the objective it has been set. It is also natural to assess in that regard what other parties, particularly the government, could have done to mitigate the negative side effect of adherent monetary policy. Third, we need to assess whether the monetary policy framework itself needs improvement. There are changes to the inflation target itself, e.g. whether it is too high, too low, wrongly 1 The writer is chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland. The opinions expressed in the article are the authors and do not have to reflect the views of the Central Bank. defined or whether more radical fundamental changes to the monetary policy framework are needed, e.g. some form of fixed-rate policy or participation in a currency union. A newspaper article is not a forum to answer all these questions, but I want to try to bring the debate to a more logical level than it seems to me to have been in so far. Economics experiment  how big a slap can the monetary policy of a small country with floating exchange rates cope? Economic policy in recent years has included a major experiment in economics. The central bank of the smallest country in the world with floating exchange rates is tasked with regulating monetary policy according to the inflation target at the same time as "the greatest implementation in Iceland's history". At the same time, changes have been made to the financial system that greatly push up demand. At the same time, taxes were reduced. To make it even more difficult for the Central Bank, all this was done at a time when global interest rates are at a century low. While these are well-known facts, there is reason to hold them to account because they seem to have been forgotten in the battle of criticism that the Central Bank's monetary policy has suffered in recent months. Since the Central Bank set an inflation target in 2001, inflation has averaged 4.7%, i.e. compared to a twelve-month increase in the consumer price index, as provided for in the March 2001 statement by the Government and the Central Bank of Iceland. Inflation has also varied greatly over the period, ranging from 1.6% to 9.4%. A central bank whose main goal is to maintain stable prices has, when all kurl come to the grave, only one tool to achieve this goal. Granted, there are other controls, such as a change in reserve requirements or interventions in the foreign exchange market, but they are more incoherent than controlling interest rate changes, as well as their activity eventually passing through the interest rate path and is therefore ultimately largely the same nature as the impact of controlling interest rate changes. If the Central Bank has failed to keep inflation normally close to its inflation target, it is therefore difficult to come to a conclusion other than that the policy rate has on average been too low. Comparison of the controlling interest rate curve and the interest rate cycle calculated using the so-called Taylor rule suggests the same. Reasons for mistakes and leads to improvements Notes that control rates have sometimes been lower but seem reasonable afterwards there are more than one. Both forecasts (the Central Bank as others) and the first estimates of macroeconomic accounts underestimated the growth of domestic demand, particularly in 2004. Sometimes underestimation in early estimates has actually been more than an underestimate in forecasts, as happened in 2006. To what extent deviations are explained by incomplete data, incorrect models or incorrect assessments by experts and the Board of Directors of the state of the economy and the dissemination of monetary policy is the subject of an investigation that is not complete. However, it is possible to assume that all of the above failures were involved in some degree. In some ways, it is to blame for uncertainty that will always be there. However, it is important to continue to improve what is possible. In this way, central bank experts continue to develop models to improve their forecasts. Significant progress has been made in this area over the past two years. Ways to improve the first estimates of national accounts are also under review. In March, the Central Bank began publishing the most efficient policy rate curve with the aim of improving transparency and monetary policy dissemination. Despite the above, criticism of the Central Bank domestically has not focused on what appears to be directly relevant, that policy rates were at times full low. On the contrary, many critics have argued, unlike experts from international organizations and the Central Bank, that the Central Bank's policy rate has for a long time been too high. Even some of those who in 2005 criticized the Federal Reserve, probably rightly, for raising interest rates too late, now seem to have turned the page. This is even more strange given that the underlying inflation rate is far above the inflation target, or just under 7%, and the labour market is swelled to the extreme. Critics are therefore either saying that there is no relationship between controlling interest rates and inflation, or that the metric that the Central Bank follows is wrong.2 The former would be a major issue and concerns a fundamental choice between running an independent monetary policy or not. The latter, if true, could be fixed within the current framework of monetary policy. So let's get to it first. Is the monetary policy inflation measure wrong? Like other central banks with inflation targets, the Central Bank of Iceland's objective was defined by the reference to a broad price index, the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX. It would be considered to target an index that excludes volatile items, as some central banks have done. The argument would be that these volatile items, such as fuel prices, do not have a long-lasting impact on inflation and are outside the monetary policy sphere of influence. The result in 2001 was that the benefits of choosing a broad scale were heavier on the methane bowls. However, the criticism in the past, as in 2005, is primarily focused on the housing stock.3 How best to take house prices into account is not beyond doubt. Title: Speech at a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce
text: 16 November 2012 The economy, monetary policy, capital controls, the choice of currency policy and the next steps Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland. Breakfast of the Chamber of Commerce, 16 November 2012. Moderator, good attendees. It is a years-long tradition for the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce to hold meetings like this on the state and outlook of the economy and monetary policy as a result of the Central Bank publishing its autumn forecast. But now there's more to it, as the title of my speech is unusually long. This is partly due to the fact that last September the Central Bank published an extensive report on Iceland's options for currency and exchange rates, and as a result, there has been a lot of discussion in society. The second reason is that in recent weeks there has been considerable debate about how the resolution of the fallen banks' out-of-pocket costs relates to plans to loosen capital controls. It does not provide careful discussion on all of these related topics, so as before, I would like to thank the Chamber of Commerce for the initiative to organize this meeting. But like last year, I'd like to start by looking one year back and looking at how I assessed that situation and outlook for the national economy. I felt the big picture was that the economic recovery that had been expected had gone ahead, but the stability had not proved as solid. It accounted for 3% growth in 2011 and 21/2% for the next three years. It is now estimated that growth will be around 21/2% this year and next year. This is a fairly good economic growth in the international context, as can be seen on Slide 1, but it also shows that the economic recovery has had broad foundations in the growth of exports, private consumption and business investment. 1 Last year's problem, however, was thought to be inflation, which had grown progressively as 2011 progressed and was increasingly rooted in domestic factors, not least due to subsequent wage increases. Inflation had reached a temporary high in September 2011 at 5.7%. It was thought that she would remain on that swing until the first few months of 2012, but then it would rebound and indeed be quite close to the inflation target by the end of the year but fully achieved in 2013. However, this did not go away. Inflation peaked at 61/2% in the first few months of this year and did not start to rebound until the spring and was still at 4.2%. This time it was a rather weak exchange rate than wage trends that explain the deviation, as wage momentum has been less than some thought could occur, reflecting some degree of a weaker recovery in the labour market than had been hoped. This is one example of many that the Central Bank has generally been better at forecasting economic growth than inflation, as detailed in the recently published Monetary Bulletin. One important reason for this is the large fluctuations in the exchange rate, which are sometimes in a weak relationship with underlying economic conditions. The exchange rate of the krona beats our small economy strongly into inflation, but the impact on economic growth is much more dampened, including where the impact of exchange rate changes on national spending on the one hand and trade balances on the other are in the opposite direction. 2 This slide shows this clearly. It shows on the left a comparison of the Central Bank's forecast for GDP made in November 2008, i.e. just after the financial crash, and the current statistics. The correlation is almost unbelievable, both regarding the depth of the recession, the timing of the turnaround and the strength of the boom. And remember, it's always hard to predict, but quite especially after a very big hit has hit the national economy. I know that this film has attracted attention among various economists outside the country and I can safely give the compliment as I came nowhere near. On the right, however, you can see how forecast errors of inflation are closely related to the deviations of actual exchange rate trends to those calculated in each time's forecasts. This is really just one side of how surplus fluctuations in exchange rates make the implementation of monetary policy more difficult, but this is considerably discussed in the currency report which I come to more detail below. So let's turn to the Central Bank's current assessment of the state and outlook on the economy. This slide shows the main draws in the forecast published by the Fed on Wednesday. The growth rate will be around 21/2% this year, followed by a 2013-2015 growth rate, rising to almost 3% next year and heading for over 31/2% in 2015. This is behind increased business investment in 2014, including energy-intensive heavy industry, and increased exports in 2015. Along with this trend, unemployment decreases, which will be just over 4% in 2014 and falls below that in 2015. At the same time, production slack is decreasing and will be gone in 2014. Inflation, according to the forecast, will peak this quarter at 4.4% but will then fall next year, as the right part of the slide shows, and will reach its target by mid-2014. This is despite a considerable weakening of the krona in the autumn, but this is offset by the fact that the slack in the economy is currently considered higher than previously expected, and then inflation in the third quarter was lower than expected in the Bank's forecast from August. The forecast is based on the assumption that the exchange rate will remain unchanged at the level it was at when it was completed, which was about 162 kronor in the euro. Furthermore, it is assumed that the increase in labour costs beyond productivity increases is in line with the deflation rate at the 3 in 2013 and 2014, or about 21/2% each year. Both of these assumptions are, of course, uncertain. I have in speeches here at this forum in recent years expressed concern over the relatively low growth in exports despite historically very low real exchange rates. There is therefore reason to pause that the Central Bank's newly published forecast only accounts for about 11/2% interest rates on exports each in 2013 and 2014. Granted, Iceland seems to hold roughly increased market share against the major trading partners it earned during the global economic recession, which is due to weak growth in these countries. Iceland's export growth, if this goes ahead, will therefore be much lower than that of world trade. It has been noted many times that the low growth in exports despite the low real exchange rate is partly because a large part of Iceland's exports are subject to production restrictions that are either subject to natural conditions or require considerable investment to overcome. That's where the knife is in the customer. Investment has been relatively low since the financial crisis, and although it is now growing, it is historically low in proportion to GDP, but indeed this and next year similar to that of the US and UK. In fact, this low level of investment is not inconsistent with the experience of other countries that have been in deep financial crisis and also have partially reasonable explanations for high leverage and high investments before the crisis, cf. Slide 3. That doesn't change the fact that what would help Iceland both to create solid assumptions about economic growth and to release capital controls would be precisely foreign investment in export operations. So I'm going to turn to monetary policy at the moment. The Monetary Policy Committee decided this week to raise the Central Bank's interest rate by 0.25 percentage points, citing persistent inflation above target, high inflation expectations and the fact that the economic recovery appears to be offset by the headwind of global development and would not be threatened by the interest rate hike. Furthermore, the Committee stated that based on the Central Bank's base forecast, it could be assumed that the Bank's nominal interest rate after the change- 4 una would be sufficient for the inflation target to be reached during the forecast period. In other words, the Bank's interest rate hike process, which began in August 2011, was over for now. However, that disclaimer was made in the committee's statement that the review of collective agreements in the new year is compatible with the resolution of inflation to the objective. And of course, this is, as always, subject to reservations that other assumptions do not change significantly, including regarding the exchange rate of the krona, and that external shocks or buoyancies do not change the state of the national economy to a large extent. But such changes can trigger changes in monetary policy adherence, whether for an increase or a decrease depending on their nature. But anyway, the interest rate hike process lasted over a year and included an increase in nominal interest rates of 1.75 percent in six steps. It is worth noting given that in the autumn of 2011, some believed the interest rate hike in August was based on some sort of misunderstanding and that it would likely be the shortest interest rate hike process in history. But the story was different. At the time of the interest rate increase, the Bank's mortgage interest rate was 6%, which was previously the Bank's effective policy rate, but now in our opinion they are closer to the average trading account interest rate and deposit bond interest rate, or 5.4%. This includes nearly 1% real interest rates, so they have risen by almost 2% since the early part of the year. It's also worth noting that they are also accurately in line with taylor's calculated growth for the fourth quarter compared to 1% balanced growth. But that tells a limited story because, as I discussed here last year, good monetary policy is based on more than simple formulas like the Taylor Rule. I now turn to the debate about national debt, the resolution of the out-of-pocket costs of the fallen banks and the release of capital controls. I'll have time for the inevitable to be brief, but more opportunities will presumably be given in the near future to explain these issues. The discussion in the past has in some ways been helpful as it has contributed to a much greater understanding of Iceland's balance of payments problem and the tasks the Central Bank faces regarding the implementation of the controls with regard to the out-of-pocket costs of the fallen banks. But at the same time she has been in sections of confusing and probably implied a much greater woe than actually looms over In short, the situation is that the Icelandic state can handle its debts well and does not have a debt crisis. The net foreign debt position of the national economy will be manageable after the out-of-pocket settlement and, if you overlook Actavis, which skews the picture regarding the underlying national debt situation. It is a planning task to figure out what this situation is and the Central Bank will continue in the future to improve its assessment of it. In May, it was estimated at around half the GDP. There have been suggestions that this is an underestimation, but on closer inspection only one of them seems to pass, namely that presumably the share of domestic parties in out-of-pocket payments is somewhat less than expected. But even if it's adjusted for it, it doesn't change the debt situation to a large extent. The Central Bank has already begun a very extensive work to refine the assessment of the debt situation. The result could be anything higher than half of GDP, but there is no indication now that the picture is fundamentally changing. In the unlikely event that net debt levels were assessed nearly one GDP, it would not be at all 5 Uncontrollable and, indeed, far from it. The Central Bank's forecasts indicate that the underlying trade surplus in the coming years is in the range of 2-3% of GDP, and keep in mind that, in the balance of trade, all interest payments and dividend payments have been counted to foreign parties for Icelanders' debts abroad and foreigners' assets in Iceland. A trade surplus of this magnitude and economic growth of around 3% manages to reduce net debt in proportion to GDP fairly quickly and safely. Iceland's problem is different. This means that domestic parties, other than the Treasury and a handful of others such as e.g. Landsvirkjun does not have access to foreign credit for construction and refinancing. This means that some parties therefore have to pay down their foreign debt much faster than is desirable, which puts pressure on the Icelandic the krona. This means that foreign parties have large vacant krona assets, which would put a lot of pressure on the Icelandic the krona if it all flowed out at once. Iceland of the problem of payment. That's exactly the problem that capital controls are meant to address. I'm now going to show you some slides describing how payments from out-of-pocket payments from the fallen banks could affect this problem, which are actually two problems and could be called the offshore krona problem and on the other, the refinancing problem. 6 What is now available is to find ways that the resolution of the estates will not have a negative impact and preferably a positive impact on the balance of payments and financial stability in Iceland. They exist and I've hinted to some extent what they might be, but it's waiting for a better time to outline them more accurately. I had the currency issues in the title and I have to say a few words about them, even though it's starting to get frustrated with time. In the shortest case, it seems to me that the conclusion of that debate at this point is that we have two options that are not yet clear because they are in the formulation, namely on the one hand a better framework for the krona and on the other a better framework for the euro. There is little we can do to create a better framework for the euro, so there we can do little more than keep an eye on it. However, we can try to create a better framework for the krona and should be tempted because it will also be of use to us if the country chooses to follow later on the eurozone path. So what's the next step? Yes, I think in the near future we should give priority to the work that relates to solving Iceland's balance of payments crisis. This includes measures to increase investment and exports, ensure a surplus on the Treasury in the coming years, renegotiate foreign debts that are too short, work to open up access to foreign credit financing, set precautions for the financial system that are sufficient under the conditions of unrestricted capital movements, and work on loosening capital controls. The latter, in my opinion, will involve some revision of the existing plan in coming months. 7

Title: Speech at a conference of the International Monetary Fund, the Central Bank of Estonia and the Central Bank of Sweden
text: 13 December 2013 Managing capital flows in a financially integrated area: Lessons from the Icelandic financial crisis Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland Remarks at a conference on Nordic-Baltic financial linkages and challenges Tallinn, 13 December 2013 I would like to thank Eesti Bank, Sveriges riksbank, and the IMF for inviting me to speak at this most interesting event. In my remarks, I will focus on those aspects of the Icelandic financial crisis that are most closely associated with the topic of this session, which is financial integration. I will draw out some salient features of that story and then link them to several lessons that might be of more general relevance. In the autumn of 2008, two separate but interrelated sub-stories of the recent Icelandic financial and economic saga converged in a tragic grand finale. These are: 1. Icelands boom-bust cycle and problems with macroeconomic management in small, open, and financially integrated economies. This is a story that has played out many times around the globe, and many of its elements have been seen before in Iceland. 2. The rise and fall of three cross-border banks operating on the basis of EU legislation (the European passport). This story was much more unique, as it involved the first banking crisis in Europe since the EU single market was formed in the early 1990s. Let me briefly discuss each of these in turn, in order to set the stage for the policy discussions. First, the macroeconomic boom-bust story. All the usual suspects were present: very strong capital inflows fuelling a credit and asset price boom that subsequently turned into a bubble at the same time as the economy overheated and an unsustainable external position developed, as could be seen in a doubledigit current account deficit. And macroeconomic and prudential policies were not up to the task. 1 At the deepest level, this part of the story was related to three factors: 1. The complications that tend to arise with macroeconomic management as very small, open economies become more and more financially integrated; 2. The specific conditions of ample and cheap credit at the global level; 3. And major policy mistakes in Iceland, both of the type that would be deemed to be such in any book (such as giving an already overheated economy a demand stimulus), and those more closely related to the orthodoxy prevailing at the time: freely floating exchange rates, interest rate policy focusing mainly on low inflation in terms of goods and services, and good micro-supervision; and let the markets do the rest. The first factor is perhaps of interest here. The process runs as follows: Domestic interest rates at the longer end of the maturity spectrum tend to become more closely correlated with the global rate, or the rate of the largest trading partner, and less correlated with the domestic policy rate. This means that monetary transmission tends to go increasingly through the exchange rate channel, which is only a problem, however, if the exchange rate behaves badly. Unfortunately, there is a lot of evidence to suggest that it does. Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP) does not hold except over long horizons. Interest rate differentials give rise to widespread carry trading, which is by nature a bet against UIP. Exchange rates thus diverge from fundamentals for protracted periods, followed by sharp corrections. So the exchange rate often seems to be as much a source of shocks and instability as a tool for adjustment and stabilisation. Ultimately, these cycles can take the boom-bust form and, in extreme cases, can result in serious financial instability or crisis. The research on this phenomenon is still ongoing, but there is a lot of evidence to suggest that the problem would not disappear even if macroeconomic policies in the traditional sense were perfect. 2 This process was important in the Icelandic episode. The capital inflows were driven by the traditional push and pull factors. But when a benign upturn originally driven by FDI in the energy-intensive sector turned into overheating, and fiscal and other demand levers pulled by the Government were either insufficiently used or pulling in the other direction, monetary policy was overburdened and the increased interest rate differential that resulted pulled in further capital and carry trade positions. Let me now turn to the banking part of the story. Before the collapse, the banking system had expanded very rapidly, growing in just five years from a combined balance sheet of less than 2 times GDP at the end of 2003 to 10 times GDP. Most of this expansion was cross-border, and a significant part of it was really off-border, having little to do with Iceland, as both financing and investment took place abroad. Around two-thirds of the balance sheet of the three cross-border banks was denominated in foreign currency. As is typical for banks, the FX part of the balance sheet had a significant maturity mismatch. However, there was no safety net of the type that we have in a national setting to back it up. This turned out to be the fatal flaw in the whole setup, although we now know that these banks were also undercapitalised, which might have done them in at a later stage. But so were several European banks that were considered solid at the time  and some of them are still around! In the panic that gripped global financial markets after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, Icelands big banks were faced with a wholesale run on their foreign currency liabilities and were therefore heading towards a default on those liabilities in the absence of LOLR assistance in foreign currency. However, given their size, it was impossible for the Icelandic authorities to provide such assistance on their own. Given the lack of international cooperation, the Icelandic authorities were forced to consider radical solutions. Although they were probably not articulated fully at the time, these solutions entailed several goals: preserving a 3 functioning domestic payment system, ring-fencing the sovereign in the case of bank failures, limiting the socialisation of private sector losses, and creating the conditions for the reconstruction of a domestic banking system. In essence, the adopted solution saved the domestic operations of the banking system and let the international part to go into a resolution process. The new banks were created by carving the domestic assets and liabilities out of the old, failing banks. The new banking system amounted to 1.7 times GDP. To a significant degree, these measures were successful in keeping the domestic payment system and basic banking services up and running, which was a key factor in dampening the effect of the banks failure on the economy. There were two key elements to the policy response during the autumn of 2008. The first was crisis management vis-a-vis the failing banks, which I have just mentioned. The second was the economic programme developed by the Icelandic authorities in co-operation with the IMF. The programme had three key goals: stabilisation of the exchange rate, fiscal sustainability, and reconstruction of the financial sector. Comprehensive capital controls were an important element in the programme, but their rationale was to help to stabilise the exchange rate in a situation where the currency had fallen more than 50% in 2008, where foreign krona positions that were a legacy of carry trade and capital inflows amounted to around 40% of GDP, and where a large fiscal deficit that had to be financed in the domestic market had developed. The capital controls therefore gave monetary policy more scope to help stabilise and turn around the real economy once inflation came down. Subsequently, they shielded the eocnomy from the financial spillover effects of the crisis in the eurozone. But the problem is that they are still in place, over five years after the climax of Icelands financial crisis. . The reason is that Iceland is still facing a balance of payments crisis that is a legacy of former capital inflows and the unwinding of these big cross-border banks. There are three elements to this, as is described in this slide:. contractual foreign debt payments in the next few years, well in excess of reasonable expectations of the size of the current account surplus; offshore kronur, a legacy of the carry trade, which still amount to 20% of GDP; and potential krona payments, from the old banks to foreign residents, amounting to another 25% of GDP. 4 We can see from the Icelandic case, and indeed many others, that although financial integration can offer many benefits to small, open economies, it also potentially entails significant risks that can turn into a nightmare if left unchecked. In Icelands case, it was a pretty dramatic. What are the lessons, then? In the interest of time, I will briefly mention a select few. The first issue that I would like to mention is the need to monitor closely both net capital flows that immediately affect the economy  especially credit growth, asset prices, and domestic demand  and the developments of gross external assets and liabilities that might not affect the economy until risks materialise and banks are undergoing the transformation from being international in life to being national in death. During the financial crisis, there have been numerous cases of vulnerabilities in gross positions coming home to roost, such as the dollar-denominated parts of European banks balance sheets. In Iceland and similar cases there is also a statistical issue here that needs to be acknowledged: the distinction between flows that actually entered or left the country at the time and those that were simply flowing offshore in both directions but were booked through the Icelandic headquarters and thus recorded in the countrys BP and IIP. The second lesson relates to the EU framework for cross-border banking, which clearly facilitated the cross- and off-border expansion of the Icelandic banks through the so-called European passport. It was and is deeply flawed. 5 The basic problem is that the freedoms are not matched by public action and frameworks at the EU and EEA level. Bank size relative to country size was assumed to be a matter of no concern, and FX risk was largely ignored. Based on the Icelandic experience, a banking union makes perfect sense, but only fully for the eurozone, and even then it has to include all three elements  common supervision, resolution, and deposit insurance  in order to break the deadly embrace of banks and sovereigns. In the interim, I think small countries, especially those with their own currencies, will have to impose their own prudential measures in order to defend themselves against the risks they face. The third lesson relates to the structure of the financial sector in small, open economies in the absence of robust and credible international or regional safety nets. To my mind, international financial centres cannot be located in such countries without some ex ante mechanism that at least partly insulates the domestic economy from the risks involved. In some sense, this is what Iceland did in the nick of time in early October 2008. Furthermore, in very small, open economies with their own currency, like Iceland, the international activities of domestic banks and FX risks on their balance sheets must be limited and regulated. In this context, we have been thinking about the prudential regime that must be in place in Iceland when we have lifted capital controls and Icelandic banks are again free to use their European passporting rights. We will have more stringent restrictions on permissible currency mismatches than in the past, also taking into account positions of unhedged households and companies, but more importantly, we will, through some combination of LCRand NSFR-type ratios in foreign exchange, put strict limits on FX maturity mismatches. The combination of these and other measures will make it impossible for the banking system to attain the size and cross-border reach it had before the crisis. The big question is whether it will be deemed compatible with the EEA Agreement. More generally, I think the distinction between macroprudential measures and capital controls can be more complex than many make it out to be. The fourth lesson is on capital flows: Deal with the inflows if you want to avoid the risk of having to introduce comprehensive capital controls on outflows, which can work as in Iceland but have increasingly negative side effects on the economy. The measures that can be taken to deal with the inflows include adopting correctly aligned macroeconomic and macroprudential policies, leaning into the wind by buying part of the inflows into foreign exchange reserves, and even in extreme cases, deploying selective capital inflow management tools. The final lesson from all of this is that if we are going to reap the benefits of financial globalisation, we must make it safer. 6

Title: Address at the Bank's annual meeting
text: 17. March 2016 Address ?97runnar Gu?mundsd97ttir, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the 55th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 17 March 2016. Honorary President of Iceland, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, Governors, Ambassadors of Foreign Countries and other good guests. I would like to welcome you here with the 50th and fifth annual meetings of the Central Bank of Iceland. The role of the Board of Directors is in particular to monitor the Bank's operations as well as to confirm the rules and recommendations of the Governor. The Council consists of seven members elected after each parliamentary election. However, I was elected to the Board of Directors a year ago and was then assigned to give it leadership. Last year, the council held 15 meetings. As stated in the annual report presented here, the Central Bank carries out regular tasks as well as various initiatives at any given time. The biggest initiative last year was undoubtedly the steps taken in partnership with the government to release capital controls. This can be read more in the Bank's annual report, which is currently underway. As stated in the annual report, the Central Bank of Iceland's main objective is to promote stable prices. At the same time, the Central Bank shall promote financial stability. At the beginning of 2015, inflation was below the Central Bank's inflation target, which was rising during the year. By the end of the year, it was just below the inflation target. In the field of financial stability, assessments were carried out on the settlements of the winding-up estates of the old commercial banks and the impact on the liquidity of the operating banks. Stress tests showed that overall, the banks were fairly well equipped to deal with shocks. At the same time, households' benefits have improved, their debts have fallen and the purchasing power index has risen. The company's position was also strengthened. This year was the first full year of operation of the Financial Stability Council and the Systemic Risk Committee working for the Council, while the Central Bank does a variety of work for the Council and the Committee. The Central Bank preserves foreign exchange reserves in order to reduce the impact of fluctuations in capital flows to and from the country and ensure the treasury's liquidity in foreign currency. The reserves increased by ISK 123 billion during the year and amounted to ISK 653 billion at year-end. The Central Bank carries out the task for the Treasury to handle foreign borrowing by the Treasury, as well as the execution of domestic tenders, and handles state guarantees and communications with international credit rating agencies on behalf of the State. The rating agencies raised all government credit ratings during the year following the introduction of the government's plan to abolish capital controls in June. The Central Bank conducts foreign exchange controls and worked during the year on important exemptions for forced contracts between fallen commercial banks and savings banks, as well as numerous other exemptions, received notifications of new investment, confirmations for foreign exchange transactions and carried out research on the basis of rules and the Foreign Exchange Act. The last foreign exchange auctions according to the investment plan and the Treasury securities route were held during the year. Furthermore, the collection and processing of statistics and various publications of publications in the field of economic affairs and research are an important part of the Bank's operations. Information on all of this can be found on the Bank's website. It should not be forgotten that the two companies that are owned by the Central Bank of Iceland and carry out specific projects, i.e. The payment provider and the Central Bank of Iceland's Portfolio. I'm going to focus a little bit on the financial performance and economy of the Central Bank. According to the income statement, profit from the Central Bank of Iceland's operations in 2015 amounted to ISK 5,651 m.kr. profit in 2014 was 11,220 m.kr. The Bank's performance thus decreased by 5,568 m.kr. from the year before. Net interest income decreased by 3,151 m.kr. between years. Interest income from domestic assets decreased by 1,431 m.kr. attributable to the capital reduction in bonds and the sale of domestic assets. Interest expenses on domestic deposits increased by 4,385 m.kr. due to the bank's large foreign exchange purchases during the year. Interest expenses for foreign debt decreased by m.kr 2,330. and that's where the heaviest repayment of loans from the IMF and Poland weighed heaviest. The Bank's other operating income increased by 5,394 m.kr. between years. This is the most important income transfer due to the revaluation of the value of domestic bonds from the ESea portfolio. Foreign exchange losses in 2015 amounted to 119 m.kr, attributable to increased interventions by the Bank, which were found to be at historic highs during the year. The Bank's operating expenses decreased by 301 m.kr. between years, mainly due to a decrease in service charges related to the operations of companies owned by the Bank. Wages and related expenses increased by 12.6% between years, mainly due to contractual increases due to collective wage agreements. The Bank's assets totalled 916,977 m.kr. at the end of 2015, but there were 953,598 m.kr. at the end of 2014. Foreign assets increased by 123,587 m.kr during the year. The Bank's equity was ISK 78,760 m.kr. at year-end 2015 and the Bank's capital ratio was 8.6% compared to 7.9% at year-end 2014. It has been decided to allocate the Bank's profits and deposits in reserves, a total of ISK 14.9 ma.kr, to strengthen the Bank's equity. At the end of 2015, there were a total of 178 employees here at the Central Bank. However, the gender ratio is fairly equal to 53% of male employees versus 47% of women. The executive group consists of five men and five women. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Bank's employees for their exceptionally good work and cooperation during the year. In particular, I would like to thank the Board members, the Governor, the Deputy Governor, the Secretary of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their exceptionally good cooperation. We are now listening to the address of Bjarni Benediktsson, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, and after that, the case of Governor M87r Gu?mundsson.

Title: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland at the annual meeting
text: Speech at the 48th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland by Svein Harald oygard, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland (Spoken word applies) Honorary Prime Minister of Iceland, Honourable Ministers, Mrs. Chairman of the Board of Directors, good guests: I welcome you all to the 48th Annual Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. As the Chairman of the Board of Directors has mentioned, here are the bank's annual accounts, which the Prime Minister has confirmed, together with the annual report for 2008. 2008 was an unusual year, not only for the Central Bank, but for iceland's economy as a whole and for the global economy. I'm not going to talk about the progress of the financial crisis and the actions that were taken in its wake. Reports have been published tracking those events and more will follow. One of them will be the Central Bank's financial stability report, which is due in October this year. The Bank's staff also assists the NTSB on the banking collapse and a special prosecutor for prisoners. I would like to point out, however, that our payment systems and domestic payment services withstanded the pressures of the crisis. In recent years, the Central Bank has taken precautionary measures, such as introducing bailouts and authorization locks into the main domestic systems. These improvements reduced the risks of the Parties and agreements in the systems and enabled them to maintain full operations despite the immense pressures of october's crisis. Payment processing between countries was very difficult, but the Central Bank was able to intervene in payments for the banks and their customers by utilizing their own accounts and credibility. This was needed again in March this year when three more banks came out of business due to the crisis in October. Payment systems are often considered technical and even everyday challenges. People expect to always have access to their accounts and make payments within the country and between countries whenever necessary. That's how it should be in a modern and efficient economy. But as the financial crisis hits and the uncertainty and risks of the Parties intensify, there is no small achievement that payments continue to be received. In this area as well as others, central bank employees and our partners did an incredibly good job. In my speech today, I want to focus on the future, not the past, and especially on what needs to be done to create stability in the Icelandic the economy and prepare the ground for economic recovery. In particular, I will focus on several areas where I consider it urgent to take action and resolve problems. Despite increasingly widespread and severe global economic crises, international Iceland are still seen as a symbol of how badly a country can be affected by a financial crisis. This creates yet another difficult challenge on top of all others and adds to the need for clear vision and tangible results. When the vision is clear and we have demonstrated the ability to action, Iceland should have assumptions to become a model for other countries on how to achieve a rapid economic recovery. In my opinion, we should not set our sights lower. It may be difficult to change attitudes that way, but it is of paramount importance to stimulate investment in Iceland and to re-create export-driven economic growth. The Act on the Central Bank of Iceland was amended in February 2009. The new law stipulates that monetary policy should be decided by the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee, which consists of three representatives from the Bank and two members outside the Bank who are both professors of economics. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the members outside the Bank, Anne Sibert and Gylfi Zoega, for their very helpful and sensible suggestions at the committee's meetings. Businesses and households in the country have been badly affected by the economic downturn and the weakening of the krona since early 2008. In view of the egregious debt situation of households and businesses, which have taken both indexed loans and loans in foreign currencies, the Monetary Policy Committee is committed to reducing inflation and stabilising the exchange rate. Inflationary pressures appear to have decreased and inflation is rapidly declining. The Central Bank expects inflation to approach the 2.5% inflation target in early 2010. Capital flows are very testing for all economies, but especially small and open economies. The influx of capital and the associated strengthening of the krona increased the imbalance that led to the financial crisis. We are now faced with a large group of investors who want to sell financial products in Icelandic kronas. The capital controls have therefore been in force since 28 November and were tightened at the end of March. The Central Bank is now further tightening its controls on compliance with the rules and establishing a new control unit. Rules are being amended in such a way that banks will be obliged to report alleged unauthorised transactions, in much the same way as EU anti-money laundering rules stipulate. Since currency controls hinder unrestricted outflows of capital, they are an unfortunate but indispensable part of measures aimed at protecting balance sheets and promoting sustainable economic recovery. They also create greater scope to lower the rate of control. It is important for the economy to have the policy rate cut substantially and the Monetary Policy Committee has already taken the first steps in that direction with its policy rate decisions on 19 March and 8 April. Nevertheless, high control rates are still considered necessary  until measures have been taken to ensure a more solid economic base. Those who make monetary policy decisions now face a difficult choice: on the one hand, to rapidly lower the policy rate, with the associated risk of instability; however, having to decide on interest rates that are high in international comparisons for a national economy that needs lower interest rates. Some argue that high interest rates, among other things, lead to high interest payments on foreign bonds in Icelandic kronas, and that the average only adds to the sickness. Similarly, they insist that lower interest rates would reduce interest payments, thereby strengthening the dollar and easing the burden of high interest rates for households and businesses. It should be pointed out, however, that only a small proportion of foreign bonds in Icelandic kronas collect interest rates linked to the Central Bank's policy rate. Therefore, interest payments abroad decrease less than would be expected. Furthermore, these foreign investments in isk Icelandic are only a fraction of foreign loans Icelandic companies and households, although there are quite a few. If this were the case, it would pose a real risk to many. Fortunately, there is a capable other way that is not as risky. Based on the current plan, five of the main prerequisites for a significant reduction in control rates should be achieved in the coming months: 1. The plan to adjust the state budget in the near term will be implemented and must create confidence that Icelanders are well equipped to deal with the government's debt levels. The plan will be in line with Iceland's success in recent years, with the second lowest public debt in Europe before the financial crisis. Everyone should be aware, regardless of political interests, that Iceland needs  now as never before  a solid foundation for public finances. This is compulsory for those in charge of the economy as well as the Central Bank. Requests for expenses that would otherwise have been approved must be rejected or recommended against them. All available means should be used to avoid the state having to take over private sector debt beyond what has become, with the aim of maintaining the financial strength of the Republic. 2. The restructuring and refinancing of the banking system must be completed. In all developed countries, it is considered crucial to running an efficient banking system. Research suggest that a functioning financial system is a key prerequisite for long-term economic growth. Therefore, negotiation processes in the financial sector should be continued and the restructuring and refinancing of the banks as scheduled. This is part of addressing risks relating to indexed loans and foreign currency loans in the new banks. The good news is that important preparatory operations are now about to end. 3. With declining domestic demand, funds will be available to pay down the nation's accumulated debt and draft increased employment in the future. It is already clear that exports of goods and services have become greater than imports. The country benefits from the world's leading fish industry, the fine premises of the tourism industry, renewable energy and its-based businesses, and a privately diverse economy. Iceland has earned a worldwide reputation for flexibility in the national economy and the competence and efficiency of the population. 4. Although the current situation within the country and abroad does not yet give the opportunity to lift capital controls without jeopardizing stability, the Central Bank of Iceland regularly assesses their effectiveness and seeks ways to lift them in stages as soon as circumstances permit. The Central Bank also assesses special measures that could enable the most impatient investors who have been bound by currency controls to divide their bonds into Icelandic kronur in a manner that does not degrade the Bank's foreign exchange reserves. 5. Negotiations on bilateral loans, other negotiating processes and the International Monetary Fund review should soon be concluded. In March 2008, the Central Bank of Iceland tried to enter into currency swap agreements with other central banks. Talks with the central banks of the three Nordic countries led to currency swap agreements announced in mid-May 2008. These agreements are currently in force and I would like to thank the Nordic central banks for their co-operation. While efforts are underway to complete these projects, a restrained monetary policy backed by effective currency manipulation will continue. In current monetary policy, the preliminary objective of establishing a stable exchange rate is taken into account, but the inflation target remains the long-term limit. However, the exchange rate of the krona has been very unstable in March and April. As noted in the monetary policy committee's latest announcement, this is partly due to temporary factors, such as relatively high seasonal interest payments on foreign bonds in Icelandic kronas. In general, I consider that all the main priority measures in monetary and fiscal policy in the coming year are to a greater or lesser extent the same  regardless of whether Icelanders choose to take advantage of a system of flexible exchange rates on the basis of the krona or adopt alternative currency arrangements such as among members of the European Monetary Union. But in an effort to contribute to public debate, the Central Bank is now working to update the 1997 report on the lead-up to and impact of the creation of the European Economic and Monetary Union - EMU. Similarly, a research report will be prepared on the pros and cons of different exchange rate arrangements, including entry into EMU. A key part of this analysis will be the question of the role of the krona in reducing economic volatility or as an independent source of volatility. In a recent report, Finnish banking expert Kaarlo Jannari has pointed out that it is imperative that the various governments have closer economic consultations and in setting rules. I wholeheartedly support this viewpoint. The Central Bank will do its utmost, on the basis of the Act on the Central Bank, to force, support and point out the resources that may be useful in order to complete the necessary measures in coming months. I also believe, like Kaarlo Jannari, that the current situation calls for greater coordination in the work of ministries and other governments dealing with matters related to economic policy and financial life. Although this does not fall within the Central Bank's scope of operation, I strongly recommend that the responsibility for such matters be entrusted to one, and only one, ministry. This is of particular importance when attempting to ensure coordinated action and the safe implementation of government policy over the next three to six months. Informed, targeted, efficient and co-ordinated procedures are crucial in solving the problems associated with the "old"/"new" commercial banks. It should take precedence over all authorities, the Central Bank, creditors and banks and their representatives. This case does not tolerate any delay. Jannari also proposes that we merge the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority, or at least bring these institutions under the same oversight  and that the Financial Supervisory Authority be entrusted with increased powers. The Bank supports this view, which appears to be consistent with sentiments that are to be welcomed across Europe. The importance of the Central Bank's role as a "devolution lender" has become increasingly apparent  as well as how much it costs, and thus the importance of close cooperation between central banks and regulators. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the International Monetary Fund, chairman of the delegation Mark Flanagan, his representatives in this country Franek Rozwadowski and all members of the International Monetary Fund delegation for their contributions and support. It seems to me that they have the interests of Iceland and the international financial system at the forefront of all their work. Good guests: These are important and urgent tasks for the future. We need to improve the road map for the road ahead. The first task is to rebuild the banking system and then work on stability, including stable inflation and financial stability with appropriate policies, thereby creating a solid foundation for economic growth and increased employment. Each month that Without the fundamentals being clear, the benefits are prevented from re-emerging and the cost of it for the national economy reaches billions of dollars per month, and the cost to society would be incurred in suffering for Icelandic nation. The Central Bank is responsible for policy development in some of the areas mentioned above, in particular monetary policy. Although the Bank is based on its role and independence, as provided for by the Act on the Central Bank, it will also work as far as possible with institutions, companies and other authorities in Iceland to lay the foundations for new economic growth and stability. It is my hope and belief that together we will make Iceland a model for rapid economic recovery for other nations. I thank the audience.
