Title: Open meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee with the Parliamentary Economic and Business Committee
text: 19. september 2019 The Governor's introductory remarks at an open meeting of the Parliamentary Economic and Business Committee on the work of the Monetary Policy Committee I will be here for the first time as Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland for a meeting on the MPC report, which is accompanied by Gylfi Zoega, a member of the Monetary Policy Committee. You have received a report from the Monetary Policy Committee on its work in the first half of the year as well as other material. These include the last Monetary Bulletin with the latest update to the Bank's macroeconomic and inflation forecast, a recent statement by the Monetary Policy Committee and the committee's minutes published on 11 September. It has been seven months since members of the Monetary Policy Committee last attended a meeting of the Economic and Trade Committee. The exchange rate of the krona is now quite similar to what it was then, but inflation has fallen slightly from 3.4% to 3.2%. At the same time, the outlook for economic growth has deteriorated somewhat this and next year and the Bank's main interest rate has been reduced from 4.5% to 3.5%. Icelandic economy is on its way to a downturn after eight years of continuous economic growth. Since GDP reached a low following the financial crisis in 2010, it has grown by over a third. In recent years, there has been some stability in the economy. The expected contraction for the year is relatively mild, with the Fed forecasting a 0.2% contraction this year and for the economy to rebound next. In line with these developments, the Central Bank has begun an interest rate cut process and cut interest rates for the third time this year in August. The exchange rate of the krona has been fairly stable in recent times, although the economy has slowed and the country's main export sector  tourism  has been shocked. When you look at history, the progress has usually yielded as a result of the downturn. Furthermore, the balance of payments has been very unbalanced, the trade deficit has been unsustainable and otherwise imbalanced in the national economy. Today the situation is different, we have a trade surplus, a positive external position of the national economy and the relatively strong pillars of foreign trade. In addition, the Central Bank has a strong foreign exchange reserves in order to ensure stability in the event of this. In the long run, interest rates in Iceland have been sidelined in recent decades. And then not only if you look at short-term interest rates, as is often done, but also if you look at long-term interest rates, which are of paramount importance to the real economy. Long-term interest rates in the bond market have fallen considerably in the past two years, especially so far this year and are at historic lows. In a longer context, real interest rates have been trending downwards since the early 1990s, so we have seen Iceland move closer to what is known abroad in terms of interest rates. Among Western countries, however, it is a privilege to have positive nominal growth in order to stimulate the economy  as we have now done this year. Many nations around us live with negative nominal interest rates that have actually put a floor under further interest rate cuts. Looking ahead, the current interest rate cut process could continue as indicated in the monetary policy committee's last statement; lower inflation expectations going forward and continue to slow in inflation. Then, or, that the growth outlook deteriorates from what the Bank's latest forecast assumes. There is some uncertainty as to how the tourism industry can cope with both cost increases and the setbacks in foreign flights that the industry has suffered. Overall, money management has been successful in recent years. It would be very good news if the recession is not greater than predicted,given the huge economic boom that has been in recent years. It is also important that good price stability has remained for the last six years. This stability shows the success of monetary policy and gives good hope that the inflation target in Iceland can be followed up for the future.

In order to achieve this goal, it may be necessary to run an adhering monetary policy for longer than many now seem to imagine or hope for. It is unrealistic to expect the Central Bank to be able to act on its monetary policy so that the so-called "soft landing" will be secured. The emphasis on such a move is likely to lead only to a far-reaching and ultimately even more painful adjustment  and above all higher inflation. I am convinced that in the long run it will prove to be more successful for the esta of the population that the Central Bank will focus on the objective entrusted to it by the Althingi, to keep rates stable. Title: Speech at a conference at the World Bank
text: A presentation by Jon Sigurgeirsson at a World Bank Global Forum on Law, Justice and Development, Washington D.C., 10 December 2012. Let me begin by thanking the organisers for inviting me to speak here today. I have been asked to speak on the case of Iceland and share some of our experiences from the resolution process. Given the title of todays seminar  sovereign debt resolution  I would like to begin by setting the record straight. The Republic of Iceland did not default and has never defaulted on its sovereign obligations. Its ratings may have fallen from triple-A to triple-B, but the sovereign has maintained an investment-grade rating. At bottom, Icelands crisis was a private banking problem with fiscal consequences, combined with a severe currency crisis. The banking crisis in Iceland had been brewing for quite some time, but the symptoms were blurred by an abundance of global liquidity and mispricing of risk. It turned out to be a spectacular crisis: one that did away with 90% of Icelands financial system virtually overnight, taking with it the credit that had taken years to build up. The impact on the economy was devastating and bought the country to the altar of the IMF in November 2008. In my presentation I will focus on three areas: a brief history and a summary of the run-up to the crisis, crisis resolution, and the role of the IMF. The free-state As this is a conference of lawyers, I feel compelled to say a few words about early Icelandic history. The country was settled in the 9th century, and one of the settlers first tasks was to establish a parliament. By the end of that first millennium, it was said that the Icelanders had no king, only law. Icelanders went on to do great things during this period. I regret to tell you that it didnt really work out so well, but in any case, the Golden Age lasted a good 300 years before the country fell under the Norwegian Crown in the 13th century. The reason for the demise of the so-called free-state has been a topic of popular debate for several centuries in Iceland, and theories are numerous. Legal historian James Bryce wrote that medieval Iceland should be of interest to the student of politics and law because it produced a constitution unlike any other in recorded history, as well as engendering a body of law so elaborate and complex that it is hard to believe it existed among men whose chief occupation was to kill one another. Recent history By the time Iceland regained control of its own affairs at the turn of the 20th century, it was among the poorest and least developed countries in Europe, without any infrastructure. But before the 20th century was out, Iceland ranked among the most affluent nations in the world. This remarkable transformation was based on abundant resources, globalisation, good neighbours, and good governance. The latter part of the 20th century brought on liberalisation, deregulation, and privatisation, and in 1994 Iceland joined the European Economic Area, thereby gaining access to single market of the European Union. This included the adoption of EU laws and regulations on financial market activities. Free movement of capital enabled the Icelandic banks to dive headfirst into the globalisation of finance. Finance was seen as the new frontier. The Icelandic banks became truly international, acquiring subsidiaries and opening branches abroad. The emperors new banks The newly privatised banks attracted the best and the brightest  lawyers, MBAs, and engineers  but they were young and inexperienced, and the explosive growth of the system meant that supervision and regulation had no chance to keep pace with them. At the same time, the world was swimming in liquidity, so that money poured into the Icelandic banks. And the banks had the Good Housekeeping seal of approval from the big four international audit firms and up to triple-A ratings from the rating agencies, under the tacit assumption that the sovereign would step in  even when their size mushroomed to 10 times GDP. And they took maximum advantage of this opportunity. The banks appeared extremely successful, providing well-paid jobs for educated young people, providing tax receipts, and bringing affluence to the public. They were seen as national champions, and it became government policy to nurture them. Unfortunately, in this millennium, the Golden Age lasted only three years. When the rush of global liquidity came to a halt, the Icelandic banks were left high and dry, with no real lender of last resort in foreign currency. In the face of this, the Icelandic government was faced with an awful choice: should they attempt to save the banks or be forced to let them go under? An emperors safety net Much like the rest of the world, Iceland was in crisis mode more or less throughout 2008. The currency began to depreciate significantly. The banks CDS levels began to show signs of distress early in the year, and the authorities sought to obtain liquidity support, both through swap agreements with central banks in the countries where the Icelandic banks had operations and through debt offerings. Their efforts yielded limited success. Going to the IMF was not considered a feasible option because the problem wasnt seen as a sovereign debt issue. At the time, the authorities were operating under the assumption that the banks were solid and were merely facing liquidity problems. The authorities invited the IMF for a secret mission in the spring, followed by an FSAP mission during the summer of 2008. While valid concerns were expressed, liquidity was seen as the main concern. Following the collapse of Lehman in mid-September 2008, the distress in the market became so acute that the Icelandic banks came to the authorities for help. After exhausting all other possibilities, the authorities finally came to the conclusion that they could never do a credible job of rescuing the banks. It was an unusual decision, given the pressures involved and the fact that some of our neighbouring countries were providing blanket guarantees during those very days. Resolution Given the scale and complexities of the problem, it was impossible to rely on any manual for resolution. The authorities sought to protect the signature of the sovereign and maintain a banking and payment system. They enacted emergency legislation, giving the Financial Supervisory Authority the powers of a shareholder meeting, taking over the banks, splitting the commercial banks into domestic and foreign operations, and prioritising and providing a blanket guarantee for domestic deposits. None of these actions were considered traditional medicine, but they worked to a large extent. The domestic payment system stood the test, and the population retained access to their bank accounts. As was to be expected, expanding the rule book did not come without consequences. First came a drove of very angry bankers, followed by concern and suspicion from neighbouring countries. There was a very scary period when the UK authorities served Iceland with a terrorist order, naming the Ministry of Finance, the Financial Supervisory Authority, and the Central Bank, and all international flows to the economy were blocked. The phones that had been ringing off the hook suddenly went silent. At that stage, the Central Bank resorted to rationing foreign currency. The authorities were unsure how to pay for food and medicine. Lessons In terms of lessons, Iceland is a rather unique case. The banks became so much larger than the economy itself that it was almost comical. The assets of the Icelandic banks were estimated at well over 100 bn euros in 2008. In the context of the firepower used in the global financial crisis, this figure does not stand out. However, in a sovereign context it is larger than Argentina and goes some way towards the size of the current Greek problem. Lets not forget that Icelands population totals 320,000. Cross-border banking resolution proved unnecessarily messy. On the one hand, it may have been a function of the severe strain on the system at that time, where it was every country for itself, but clearly Iceland and the creditors would have benefitted from greater international cooperation and clarity. Obviously, this is an area where work is underway for a banking mechanism, but unfortunately that work has proven difficult. In the resolution process, Iceland benefitted from efforts to engage the creditors and provide an open dialogue. A tradition of guidance by the rule of law, which I have highlighted earlier, also played an important part. While it was important to engage the creditors, it was also important to remind them on a regular basis that the balance sheet of the Republic was not part of the discussion. As an overall guiding principle, a great deal can be said of the power of transparency and predictability. These are at the core of the Principles of the IIF. The role of the IMF The IMF arrived in Reykjavik in the wake of the crisis. They did an excellent job in designing a well-balanced and successful programme for Iceland, and our neighbouring countries provided valuable support. The design of the programme made it acceptable to the public. Iceland also benefitted greatly from the IMF legal department in taking on incredibly complex financial sector issues. Again, to put things in context, the Central Bank of Icelands legal department had a staff of two at the time. Should Iceland have gone to the IMF earlier? Iceland is not unique in its hesitation to call in the IMF. Recent examples are all around us. This is a problem that probably wont go away. Elected authorities do not want give up the reins to the IMF until every other possibility has been exhausted. In retrospect, one wonders what would have happened in Iceland had the IMF been called in before the banks collapsed. What would have been the advice of the IMF staff? Would Fund staff have received a mandate from the Executive Board to let the banks go? When the collapse took place, Iceland found itself in a dispute with some European countries over deposit insurance. I will not enter into that topic here; it is before the courts in Europe and awaits a ruling. This dispute resulted in individual countries holding up reviews of Icelands programme in the IMF Executive Board. I shouldnt have to stress that the IMF is a multilateral institution and should not fall prey to bilateral disputes. If the IMF is to be entrusted with an enhanced role in resolution mechanisms, such issues must be considered. Epilogue In a sense James Bryces rather caustic comment on the Icelanders  still applies today, and much like the demise of the free-state, the collapse of the Icelandic banks will remain a topic of debate for years to come. My time is limited, and I have only touched on a few items in my presentation, that I found relevant to this forum, but let me close with a brief epilogue. Following the collapse of Icelands banks, it quickly became clear that their capital position was nowhere near what had been reported. This brings me to highlight the role of international accounting standards, which at the time seemed bereft of all common sense when it came to evaluating assets. On a related subject, allegations of mismanagement began to emerge soon after the collapse. Some now await judicial attention. The resulting bankruptcies rank among the largest in corporate history. According to Moodys, the collapse of the Icelandic banks combined ranks second, only after Lehman. The question in my mind is this: How much did the practises of the Icelandic banks differ from the practises of their counterparts in neighbouring countries?

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 17 April 2009
text: 18.04.2009 Statement by L87ra V. J9cl92usd97ttir, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 17 April 2009 Honourable Prime Minister, Ministers, Governor and other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 40th and eighth annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. At the conclusion of my introductory remarks, Governor Svein Harald 85ygard will give his annual meeting speech. Finally, Prime Minister Johanna Sigurdardottir addresses the meeting. At the end of the meeting, I invite the attendees to accept refreshments. The Prime Minister has confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2008 with his signature on 31 March. The Bank's annual report for 2008 is published today and is due at the end of the meeting. Good attendees. In 2008, the Central Bank of Iceland was heavily involved, as were other institutions, companies and individuals. According to the income statement, the loss for the year amounted to ISK 8.6 billion, compared to ISK 1.2 billion in the previous year. Losses will be increased despite an increase in the Bank's net interest income, amounting to ISK 20 billion in 2008, compared with ISK 6 billion in the previous year. The explanation lies primarily in the fact that the position sizes calculated by interest rates have increased considerably on average between years. Thus, total assets at the end of 2007 amounted to almost ISK 500 billion, but a year later amounted to ISK 1,200 billion. Furthermore, the development of the exchange rate had a major impact on the Bank's operations. In 2007, the kr97na strengthened and the Bank suffered an exchange rate loss of almost ISK 6 billion. There was a big change in 2008. In addition, a rate cut resulted in a rate gain of ISK 44 billion, as the Bank's exchange rate-based assets were somewhat higher than the exchange rate-based liabilities as is traditionally the case. The year-on-year change therefore amounted to approximately ISK 50 billion. Most of these exchange rate gains had been observed during the collapse of commercial banks in early October. However, there was little difference between the Bank's exchange rate-based assets and liabilities in the last three months of the year. The severe hardships that hit global financial markets last year led to a general liquidity shortage and high demand for central bank liquidity remittances. The Central Bank of Iceland was no exception. In some cases, loans were made against mortgages that proved unsafe when Icelandic financial institutions fell into choice one after the other. It was necessary to write off loans and the charge amounted to ISK 75 billion, but such charges have been rare in the Bank's books. There was an agreement that the Treasury bought certain mortgages and day loans against smaller financial institutions where the underlying mortgages were in bonds issued by the three commercial banks. In addition, the Treasury bought several mortgages with solid mortgages. In total, the book value of these assets purchased by the Treasury amounted to ISK 345 billion, while the purchase price was ISK 270 billion and was paid with a indexed bond. The difference, 75 billion, was charged on the bank's books. It is probable that the Treasury will have to bring these acquired assets down rather than the transaction was decided in this way with the aim of ensuring that the Bank's capital position remained largely unchanged from the beginning of the year until the end of 2008. Finally, it should be clarified that the Bank's other operating expenses increased from ISK 1.5 billion to ISK 3 billion. This is mostly due to an increase in specialist advice purchased by the Bank, which was largely related to the collapse of commercial banks in early October, with an increase in consultancy costs of ISK 1.1 billion between 2007 and 2008. Since fees were higher than revenues of almost ISK 53 billion after the release of exchange rate differences, no contribution from the Bank to the Treasury for the year's results will be made. In 2007, it amounted to a contribution of just over ISK 2 billion, representing one third of ISK 7 billion in profits in that year without exchange rate differences. The Bank's balance sheet shows that foreign assets in resources have increased by ISK 266 billion, amounting to ISK 429 billion at the end of 2008. Based on the exchange rate of the euro, the reserves have risen from 1.8 billion euros to 2.5 billion euros. A large part of the increase in isk is therefore due to exchange rate differences, but explanations are also seeking a real increase in the value of the reserves in foreign currencies. Loans to deposit institutions and other financial institutions totalled ISK 483 billion at year-end 2008, compared to ISK 308 billion at the end of the previous year. It should be noted here that loans purchased by the Treasury from the Bank are not included in these figures. For the Bank's loans at the end of 2008, the Bank's view is a solid mortgage, but taking into account the current situation in the financial market, it must be raised that there may be some uncertainty that these claims may be fully collected. The Bank's foreign debt has increased by ISK 240 billion in 2008, amounting to ISK 2 billion at the end of 2007. The first part of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) remit was 560 million SDRs, equivalent to ISK 104 billion at the end of 2008. Furthermore, liabilities have increased as a result of the loan repayments of the Nordic central banks, which concluded swaps with the Bank, with a balance of ISK 76 billion at the end of 2008. In addition, short-term loans were taken from the World Bank for International Payments (BIS), totalling approximately ISK 58 billion at the end of 2008. Deposits of deposit institutions and other financial institutions increased considerably in 2008, with the largest difference between deposits in domestic foreign exchange accounts and deposits. Deposits totalled ISK 396 billion at year-end 2008, compared with ISK 153 billion at the end of the previous year. Finally, treasury deposits with the Bank increased from ISK 211 billion at year-end 2007 to ISK 403 billion at year-end 2008. This is mainly due to the exchange rate difference between a loan that was taken for an increase in the Bank's resources at the end of 2008, a new loan for an increase in the reserves and an increase in the Treasury's trading account with the Bank. The Bank's equity amounted to ISK 82 billion at year-end 2008, compared to ISK 91 billion at the end of the previous year, and the difference is explained by the loss for the year. The Bank's financial statements in other respects report cash flows, which include reports that funds from operations amounted to ISK 14 billion, as well as information on real currents on the financial and capital side of the Bank's balance sheet. Finally, the Bank's accounts follow detailed explanations of important points. 2008 will be remembered for a long time due to the huge revamp that occurred in the financial markets. In Iceland, the first half of the year was characterised by growing difficulties in the financial system and the economy as a whole, both due to internal and external circumstances. In the second half of the year, the big Icelandic the three commercial banks went bust a few days apart. Emergency legislation was enacted, the operations of the banks were taken over and divided into old and new banks, and for a time the Central Bank took care of their payment services abroad. The government entered into talks with the International Monetary Fund on cooperation to stabilise economic stability. The bank was involved in many of the factors mentioned above. It is clear that in this scenario, the central bank's staff tested a lot. On behalf of the Board of Directors, I would like to express my gratitude for the well-done work during the year. It is clear that the Central Bank is now awaiting many important tasks. To me, the most urgent task is to ensure exchange rate and price stability, which will be a prerequisite for protecting the balance sheets of businesses and households.

Seinni tilvitnunin er ur nidurlagi |?essarar skyrslu, en |?ar segir: <e3>En f?a nidurstodu ma draga af |?essum vidreedum og ummadum manna, sem svo vel til )?ekkja, en voru audvitad settar fram med misskyrum haetti, ad islenska bankakerfid vzeri i mikilli hsettu, ekki sist vegna |)ess hvemig pad hefur panist lit, skipulagslitid og dgjetilega a undanfbmum arum, i f?vi trausti ad lansfjarutvegum yrdiaetid leikur einn. Markadir verdi almennt lokadir islensku bonkunum a.m.k. neestu tolf manudi og telja po sumir ad 24 manudir se liklegri timi hvad pad vardar. Audvitad parf ad undirstrika rzekilega pa ovissu sem i slikum fullyrdingum feist. En nidurstadan er rokstudd svo, ad pegarmarkadur loks opnist muni storir, oflugir og j^ekktir bankar fa adganginn fyrst, en sidast kemur ad minni bonkum og islenskir bankar verda mjog aftarlega i rodinni. Og pau <d2>model<d3> ad fella islensku skuldabrefin i <d2>vafningspakka<d3>, sem gerdi pau eftirsoknarverda voru, eru horfin ur myndinni og munu ekki koma aftur. bad mundi vissulega ekki hjalpa Kauppingi a nokkum hatt ad flytja hofudstodvar sinar ur landi, eins og sumir vidmailendur toldu alitlegan kost, en pad mundi hins vegar letta stodu annarra banka mikid og vera jakvaett fyrir tjarmalalif Islands eins og stadan er, |?vi f?a mundi verda talid ad islenski Sedlabankinn og rikid myndu geta bjargad peim bonkum sem eftir vzeru fra falli, ef su neydarstada yrdi uppi. bad var talin ein meginskyring a haum CDS kjdrum pessara banka, ad pessi stada sem sedlabankamenn veeru ad kynnast til fulls mina og kyngja, vzeri tiltolulega vel pekkt a markadi og |?vi hefdi skortsstada verid tekin a islensku bankana i trausti pess ad markadir yrdu peim algerlega lokadirlengi og til vidbotar kasmi ad islenski Sedlabankinn og rikid vgeru ekki af J^eirri steerd og styrk til ad hafa bolmagn til ad bjarga peim fra falli, pott vilji staedi til pess. Sumir toldu ad pad eina sem gaeti slegid a J?essi haueftira kjor vzeri ef islenski Sedlabankinn gseti nad samningi vid erlenda sedlabanka um ad veita bankanum fyrirgreidslu i naud, sem dygdi til pess ad hann geeti stadid ad sinu leyti til vid bjorgunaradgerdir a islensku bankakerfi. Nidurstadan er f?essi: bad er ljost, ad islensku bankamir [] hafa stefnt ser og pad sem verra er, islensku fjarmalalifi, i mikla hsettu, og jafnvel i hreinar bgongur, med abyrgdarlausri framgdngu a undanfbmum arum. Heettulegt er ad hafast ekkert ad i peirri von ad markadir opnist oveent og allur vandi verdi f?a ur sogunni. Naudsynlegt er ad hefjast J?egar handa vid ad vinda ofan af stodunni svo him verdi ekki oleysanleg. Ekki er hzegt ad utiloka ad miklu fyrr raetist ur markadsadsteedum og adgengi ad fjarmagni en nu er talid. Ekkert bendir |?6 enn til |iess og ef menn lata ser nasgja ad lifa i voninni verdur of seint ad bregdast vid f)egar ljost verdur ad vonin raetist ekki.<d2> begar menn heyra allar |?essar tilvitnanir, sem beedi hafa verid settar fram opinberlega og oopinberlega, fyrir alia J?a menn er malid vardar er undarlegt ad heyra hrop gerd ad Sedlabankanum vegna |?ess ad hann hafi setid hja og ekki gert ser grein fyrir astandinu og f?vi ekki getad varad adra vid. bessi deemi og svo mdrg, morg onnur sem heegt veeri ad rekja ef timi gzefist til syna gloggt, ad Sedlabankanum var vel ljost, jafnvel betur en odrum, hve alvarleg stadan var, og radlagdi eindregid ad brugdist yrdi vid. <e3>Rekum sedlabankastjorana<d2> er hropad a torgum og undir taka J^eir sem telja ad bankastjoramir liggi vel vid hoggi og arodursmaskinan fylgir vel a eftir. Arodursmaskinan, sem - hefur verid misnotud grimulaust undanfarin ar -eins og Egill Helgason, verdlaunasjonvarpsmadur ordadi |?ad sidastlidinn sunnudag. Nu ma vel vera, ad gott veeri ad sedlabankastjoramir feru ad geraeitthvad annad en |?eir gera nuna, en pad er onnur saga. En pad er slaandi ad peir sem gera nu hrop ad Sedlabankamonnum pogdu punnu hljodi, pegar bankinn reyndi ad vara alia vid sem mest hann matti. bad parf ad rannsaka allt, er sagt nuna og pad parf ad velta vid hverjum steini. En pad er ekki verid ad rannsaka neitt og pad sem verra er, pad er ekki verid ad upplysa almenning um eitt eda neitt. Sedlabankinn oskar eindregid eftir |)vi ad hlutur hans i addraganda bankahrunsins verdi rannsakadur til fulls og pad verdi gert sem allra fyrst og fengnir til pess ferustu erlendir serfrasdingar. Sedlabankinn kvidir ekki J^eirri rannsokn. Verdi nidurstadan hins vegar su, ad hann hafi brugdist, parf engan bankastjora ad reka, a.m.k. ekki pann sem her stendur, hann mun fara an nokkurrar tafar og an nokkurra eftirmala. Eg itreka ad Sedlabankanum finnst ekki adeins asskilegt ad pattur hans verdi rannsakadur, hann beinlinis krefst pess vegna peirra asakana sem uppi hafa verid hafdar, jafnvel af abyrgum adilum. ba verdur frodlegt ad sja hvort margir adrir adilar hafi hreinni skjold en Sedlabankinn i peim efnum. En vid pau timamot sem nu hafa ordid, pegar talad er um rannsoknir og ad velta eigi vid hverjum steini, af hverju er pa ekkert upplyst um hvers vegna bankamir hrundu? Af hverju fer almenningur, sem a ad borga brusann, og sa brusi er engin smasmidi, engar gagnlegar upplysingar j}6tt allt aetti nu ad vera a bordinu hja peim sem hafa mal hinna follnu banka i hondunum og allt ad blasa vid eins og opin bok. Nidurfelling forradamanna Kauppings a abyrgdum sinum og annarra hafdi legid fyrir vikum saman an pess ad nokkud vzeri um pad upplyst. bad var ekki fyrr en hneyksladir starfsmenn laku pessum upplysingum ut sem j^ser urdu almannaeign. Og sidan hefur ekkert verid upplyst, hvemig |ovi mali verdur fylgt eftir. Abendingar sem barust um ad kalla til logreglu strax 1 upphafi hafa ekki fengid brautargengi. Eru menn ad bera fyrir sig bankaleynd i f)essu sambandi? Bankaleynd a ekki lengur vid hvad |?essi atridi vardar. Su reidi sem kraumar i jijddfelaginu og hzegt er ad beina i ymsar attir af arddursmaskinum er ekki sist kraumandi vegna |?ess ad pad er ekki verid ad upplysa almenning um eitt eda neitt. Af hverju hefur pad ekki verid upplyst ad einn adili skuldadi eitt pusund milljarda i islenska bankakerfinu og pa er eingongu verid ad tala um vidskiptabankana <a3>>rja, ekki sparisjodina, lifeyrissjodina eda ymsa adra adila, sem vidkomandi skuldadi ne erlendar skuldir sama adila. Eftir ad bankaeftirlitid var fzert fra Sedlabankanum gat hann ekki atlad ser upplysinga um slikt. Hann gat ekki vitad pad. En pad vissu adrir, a pvi getur ekki verid neinn vafi. Eitt pusund milljarda skuld eins adila i islenska bankakerfinu er erfitt ad skilja, jafnvel svo erfitt ad menn leida hana hja ser. En pad ma ekki vikja ser undan ad horfa a pessa mynd. Einn adili skuldadi med odrum ordum bonkunum premur um eda yfireitt pusund milljarda krona, bad er hzerri fjarhzed en allt eigid fe gomlu bankanna saman lagt. Bankastjoramir sem lanudu hver fyrir sig hlutu ad vita ad samanlagt vzeri dzemid pannig. Vegna pess ad peir horfdu ekki adeins a lansfe eigin banka, heldur fengu peir oil gogn vegna vedtoku adur en stzerstu einstoku lan bankans voru veitt, eda pad skyldu menn aetla. Og eftirlitsadilar hljota ad hafa vitad pad lika og hafa pvi teygt sig med olikindum langt til ad finna ut ad sami adili vzeri oskyldur sjalfum ser vid pessar adstzedur. Hvemig i oskbpunum gat petta gerst? Hvada heljartok hafdi vidkomandi a bonkunum og ollu kerfinu? bad er algerlega vist ad ef erlendum vidskiptaadilum bankanna hefdi verid pessi stada ljos, hefdu oil vidskipti vid bankakerfid pegar verid stodvud erlendis fra, og bankamir hefdu i kjolfarid hrunid. Er hugsanlegt ad umrzeda hefdi vaknad i pjodfelaginu um pessi atridi og onnur, ef allir frjalsir fjolmidlar, sem er reyndar skondid ord i pessu samhengi, hefdu ekki verid i hondunum a eigendum bankanna? Og pad hefur verid upplyst ad nyju bankamir haldi afram hattum gomlu bankanna og lati menn sem skulda yfir pusund milljarda i bankakerfinu ekki i gjaldprot, en gangi fljott og vel ad Joni og Gunnu, sem eru po nu ordin eigendur bankanna a ny. Menn virdast ekkert hafa laert eda eru jafn hrzeddir og fyrr. Eg itreka ad Sedlabanki Islands hvetur eindregid til pess ad hlutur hans i bankahruninu, sem ymsir vilja gera sem mestan verdi rannsakadur. Su rannsokn verdur einfold. Starfsmenn Sedlabankans hafa ekkert ad ottast. En pad er hlalegt ad pratt fyrir pau hrop sem skipulogd eru og gerd eru ad pessari stofnun, feirri stofnun sem ein varadi vid prouninni a annad ar, f?a er pad svo ad sennilega zetti Sedlabanki Islands ad vera lang lang aftastur i rannsdknarparfarrodinni. bad er meginkrafa ad pad se upplyst hver hin raunverulega stada bankanna var. bad rannsoknarferli, sem pegar hefur verid kynnt, er med ollu oframbzerilegt og ofullnzegjandi. bad er allt ad |?vi skondid ad sja tilburdina i ollum peim skipulega arodri og herferd sem fram hefur farid, m.a. af halfu j^eirra sem mesta abyrgd bera a bankahneykslinu. Reynt hefur verid ad ljeda |?vi ad almenningi ad ord sem fellu 1 vidtali vid mig i Kastljosi, )?egar eg reyndi ad skyra a mannamali 1 fyrsta sinn fyrir almenningi, hvad veeri ad gerast, ad J^au hefdu ordid til |?ess ad bresk yfirvold hefdu sett hefndarverkalog a Island og fryst eignir Landsbankans. betta er endurtekid 1 sibylju, sidast i Stod 2 i gzer med mjog oskammfeilnum hzetti, en pad merkilega er ad Bresku yfirvoldin hafa aldrei haldid pessu fram, aldrei minnst a petta einu einu ordi, pott vitad se ad beedi peir Gordon Brown og Alistair Darling seu miklir ahugamenn um Kastljosid og horfi a pad nanast a hverju kvoldi! heir hafa hins vegar skyrt hvers vegna j^eir gripu til pessa oyndisurreedis. bad hafa ekki oil samtdl verid birt hvad pessi mal vardar og pess vegna er audveldara ad bera fram tilbunar sakir og koma peim inn hja trugjbmu folki 1 gegnum pafjolmidla sem - grimulaust hafa verid misnotadir 1 mdrg ar - eins og pad var ordad af sjonvarpsmanninum. Eg hef engar ahyggjur af pessu vegna pess ad pegar malin verda rannsokud, pa hljota fleiri samtol ad verda birt. Mer er kunnugt um efni peirra og mer er kunnugt um hvad i raun redi afstodu breskra yfirvalda. Ageetu fundarmenn bad var dhjakveemilegt ad fara nokkrum ordum um pad sem eg hef rakid her ad framan vegna hinna omaklegu arasa sem a Sedlabankanum hafa dunid eftir bankahrunid. Eg hefdi purft ennpa meiri tima til pess, en eg mun fara nanar yfir petta mal a odrum vettvangi sidar. En vid eetlum okkur einnig ad horfa til framtidar, serstaklega 1 ljosi peirrar spar sem serfreedingar Sedlabankans birtu nu fyrir faeinum dogum 1 Peningamalum bankans. bad hefur verid ordad svo ad su spa se dokk. bad parf engan ad undra. bad vard myrkur um midjan dag i Islenskum bankamalum si. oktober og myrkrid er dokkt, eins og karlinn sagdi. Hitt er annad mal ad efnahagsspar hafa stadist heldur ilia a sidustu arum og po ekki verr hja serfrzedingum Sedlabankans en hja odrum peim sem buid hafa vid hvad hviklyndast astand. En hafi verid erfitt ad spa ad undanfomu ma segja ad nu keyri um pverbak, pvi dvissupEettimir eru nu 1 adalhlutverki, en peir <a3>>settir sem segja ma fyrir med nokkud oruggri vissu eru 1 aukahlutverkunum. bo ma segja ad ef gloggt er i skyrslumar rynt, ad midad vid stasrd afallsins j?a eru vonimar tiltolulega bjartar. Hvemig get eg sagt petta, pegar augljost er ad atvinnuleysi muni aukast mikid og vitad se ad innlendar skuldir muni vaxa mjog mikid. Netto erlendar skuldir attu ekki ad aukast mikid, en nu hefur verid akvedid ad basta vid verulegum skuldabagga a pjodina, an pess ad log standi til pess og er pa gengid lit fra fvi ad Alpingi sampykki pa geminga sem kynntir hafa verid. bad la ekki fyrir pegar spain var gerd og mundi |)vi veentanlega gera myndina enn dekkri en ella vseri og pyngja peerfatasktarbyrdar sem a pjodina eru settar. bad er ljost ad skyrslan ber med ser ad samdrattur i hagvexti verdur verulegur, reyndar stodnun og afturkippur um skeid og atvinnuleysi mun fara vaxandi, jafnvel svo ad fad nalgast fad sem menn eiga ad venjast a evrusvzedinu, fangad sem draumar margra leggja nu leid i f^eirri miigsefjun sem gengur yfir. Hvemig get eg f?a sagt ad fratt fyrir allt kynni J^essi dokka skyrsla einnig vonarglzetur? Ju eg segi fad vegna fess ad j^ratt fyrir hid mikla afall ma segja ad i spa serfrzedinga bankans felist einnig ad fjodin geti tiltolulegafljott komist lit ur versta hluta vandans. I Peningamalum er til frodleiks synd mynd um hagvoxt i kjolfar kreppu og syndur samanburdur margra landa sem gengid hafa i gegnum slikar kreppur. Island er a marga lund betur sett og betur til fess fallid ad rifa sig ut lir kreppu af fvi tagi,heldur en fau samanburdarlond sem fama eru synd, sem tlest hver, ef ekki oil, eru mun skemmra a frounarbrautinni komin efnahagslega en Island. Og Island hefur synt adur ad vidbragdshradi fjodarinnar er verulegur og geta hennar til ad laga sig ad adstzedum mikil. A moti kemur hitt og ur fvi skal ekki dregid, ad fad sem er lakara en a samanburdarmyndinni mi, er ad um fessar mundir er heimurinn allur i efnahagslegum motvindi og fad gaeti haft ahrif til ad hzegja a endurreisninni her. Til ad mynda er hagvoxtur mi ad verda neikvzedur i fyrsta sinn a evrusvzedinu og ljost ad astand far fer versnandi. bad farf ekki ad draga lir okkur kjarkinn fvi spamar syna gloggt og okkar eigin tilfinning stydur fzer spar ad fjodin hefur fulla getu til fess ad na vopnum sinum hratt, fegar hiin nzer ad helga sig verkefninu. Audvitad erum vid ekki ad rzeda um vikur eda manudi, fremur eitt til tvo ar. begar stzersti hluti bankakerfisins hrundi a orfaum dogum i oktober og Bretar settu brzedrafjod sina I Nato a lista med verstu hrydjuverkambnnum heimsins, fvi far stod ekki adeins nafn Landsbankans heldur einnig rikisstjomar Islands var ekki furda fott gjaldmidlasambond milli Islands og annarra rikja lomudust fullkomlega. Margur var pirradur yfir fvi ad fad tok faeina daga ad koma lagmarksgjaldeyrisfjonustu i horf af halfu Sedlabankans, sem i raun var fo kraftaverk vid fessar adstzedur. Og sidan hefur tekist ad tryggja voruflutninga til og fra landinu nokkud snurdulitid midad vid umfang vandans. Sedlabankinn hefur annast fa milligdngu sem bankamir onnudust adur og hefur fvi fylgt gridarlegt alag a bankann og starfsmenn hans. Sii skipan hvorki getur ne ma standa lengi, en fetta gat Sedlabankinn vegna fess ad menn hofdu haft nzegilegt frek og nzegjanlegan styrk til ad standa gegn fvi ad gjaldeyrisforda hans vzeri hent a bankabalid. Ef hann hefdi brugdist i feim frystingi, fa vzeri ekki hzegt ad frnna ad fvi fo ad gerd vzeru mi hrop ad bankanum og matvzelum vzeri hent i hiisnzedi hans. En af fessum astzedum fa hefur Sedlabankinn getad tryggt og getur afram tryggt afallalausan innflutning a medan litflutningstekjumar eru ad koma hikandi heim, en fyrir fvi hiki eru i rauninni ekki lengur neinar astzedur. Innan farra daga munu allir feir sem vilja geta fengid gjaldeyri til hvers konar voruvidskipta ogferdalaga, fott hdmlur a fjarmalavidskiptum verdi afnumdar i odrum afongum. Utflytjendur eru ad skada sjalfa sig og adra i fullkominni skammsyni med fvi ad draga fad ad koma med gjaldeyrinn sinn heim til fjodarinnar. beir furfa ekki ad ottast ad geta ekki fengid allan fann gjaldeyri sem J?eir furfa og fegar feir furfa. Gjaldeyrisfkedi verdur jakvstt a nzestu arum hvad voruvidskipti vardar og ofarfi ad astla ad erlendir fjarfestar rjuki burtu 1 einni kos, fegar gengid tekur ad fljota frjalst a nyjan leik, jafnohagstastt og fad verdur feim i byrjun.Verdbolgan mun lzekka hratt a nzesta ari og vextir einnig. Godir fundarmenn Eg legg ad lokum aherslu a ad fad verdur ad fare ad upplysa fa sem borga brusann hreinskilnislega hvemig bankamir stodu adur en feir fellu og hvemig menn hogudu ser adur en fad gerdist. ba fyrst mun hefjast upplyst umrseda. Ef til vill i upphafi med f unga reidinnar, sem ekkert er vid ad segja og skiljanleg er, en havadamenn munu fa fljotlega missa tokin a atburdarasinni og fad er fad mikilvzegasta sem nu getur gerst vid uppbyggingu a efnahagslifi fjodarinnar. Fullyrt hefur verid ad Nordurlandafjodimar hafi ovzent sett fram fau skilyrdi ad vid tzekjum a okkur umfram lagaskyldu aheettu af yfir 600 milljarda krona skuld vegna icesave reikninga, ella myndu fzer ekki vilja lana okkur miklu lsegri upphasd hver fjod. Eg vil ekki rengja fessar upplysingar, fott eg hafi ekki sed neitt skriflegt um fair. Vinir okkar Feereyingar settu a.m.k. enga slika afarkosti fyrir sinni adstod. bad hefur verid sagt, ad sannir vinir seu feir hoglatu englar sem lyfta undir mann fegar madur sjalfur hefur misst flugid. Feereyingar eru fess hattar englar, hafi feir heila fokk og blessun.

Title: Contribution from the Central Bank of Iceland's chief economist at the World Bank's working meeting in Basel
text: Central Bank of Iceland Economics Department 11 January 2010 Iceland  current policy issues The Icelandic economy experienced a currency and banking crisis in 2008, with the banking collapse turning out to be the largest in history relative to GDP. A sharp contraction in the real economy followed with inflation shooting up to more than 18% following the collapse of the currency. As a result, Iceland applied for financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund. The scope for monetary policy to soften the contraction in the real economy has been limited due to the overriding goals of stabilising the currency while hard-hit domestic balance sheets are restructured and rebuild, and getting inflation under control again. Although automatic stabilisers were allowed to work fully in 2009, the scope for fiscal policy to offset the contraction in private demand has also been limited due to the sharply deteriorating public debt position. Macroeconomic developments have broadly played out as initially forecast, although the contraction in 2009 has proven to be smaller than initially feared. Although the recession has yet to bottom out, the recovery is expected to start early this year, but growth will be moderate over the medium term. Background The Icelandic economy has, on average, grown by roughly 2% since the beginning of the 1990s, down from 4% in the period 1970-1990 (Chart 1). Output, however, remains volatile, with the standard deviation of output growth remaining in the region of 3-4% for the whole period.1 After the high inflation period of the 1980s, came a period of relative exchange rate stability and rapid disinflation (Chart 2), supported by liberalisation of capital movements, opening of the economy and improvements in competitiveness (Chart 3). Iceland adopted a formal inflation targeting framework in March 2001, after the previous exchange rate peg came under growing pressures in the late 1990s. The target was formulised 1 The sample moments are somewhat affected by the large contraction in 2009: excluding 2009 gives a sample average of 3.3%, which is much closer to the estimated trend growth rate, and a standard deviation of 2.9%. 1 as a 2.5% point target for the twelve month change in consumer prices, with a 1.5% threshold band. Monetary policy succeeded in bringing inflation down to target in late 2002 after a short period of overshooting as a result of the depreciation of the krona following the exit from the exchange rate peg. However, inflation started to drift above target in late 2004 with evergrowing domestic imbalances creating new inflationary pressures. Inflation eventually moved outside the threshold band and has for the most part remained outside it since September 2005 (Chart 2). The growing imbalances can mostly be traced directly or indirectly to government decisions: privatisation of the state-owned banks completed in 2003; large investment projects in the aluminium sector in 2003-6; large tax cuts at the same time; and structural changes in the domestic mortgage market in 2004 with new legislation allowing a big government-owned mortgage lender to offer higher loan-to-value ratios and to engage in more aggressive lending policies. This led to strong responses by the newly privatised commercial banks, resulting in increased competition through ever-lower mortgage rates and significantly easier access to credit. These domestic imbalances where further amplified by unusually low international interest rates and the rapid expansion of the Icelandic banks balance sheets (Chart 4). A large consumption boom (Chart 5) and growing external imbalances (Chart 6) followed. In June 2008 the Icelandic banks assets were roughly 200 billion US, or roughly ten times GDP, of which 41% were in foreign subsidiaries. The responses of monetary policy to the growing domestic imbalances proved to be too timid and too late (Chart 7). The currency and banking crisis The dynamics in the build-up and aftermath of the Icelandic crisis are similar to many previous crises but the Icelandic crisis stands out in terms of its scale. The Icelandic banking system is the largest banking system, measured as percentage of GDP, ever to have collapsed (Chart 8), the level of indebtedness of the private sector is without precedence (Chart 8) and foreign currency debt is excessively high compared to other crises countries (Chart 9). A key element of the overheating of the domestic economy and the boom-bust cycle was a large asset price bubble, fed by ample global liquidity and lax lending policies leading to a large appreciation of the krona and enormous increases in other asset prices (Charts 10 and 11). Ever-increasing doubts concerning the viability of the domestic banking system and the deteriorating access to global liquidity led to a sudden stop of capital inflows in early 2008 as the FX-swap market, the main channel of inflows and an important wholesale funding market for the Icelandic banks, broke down. The sudden stop weakened the krona and pricked the domestic asset price bubble (Charts 10 and 11) and led to a sharp adjustment of domestic demand (Chart 5), on top of an unavoidable cyclical adjustment of the economy. The announcement of emergency swap agreements with other Nordic central banks in May 2008, 2 policy rate hikes and increased issuance of non-bank debt provided temporary support to the krona. The Icelandic cross-border banks nevertheless collapsed shortly after the failure of Lehman Brothers in the panic of autumn of 2008 as their sources of foreign currency funding completely dried up and the capacity of the Icelandic authorities to substitute private FX funding with public funding was limited. Domestic financial markets seized up and entered a new and deeper state of crisis. The FX market dried up completely with the collapse of the banking system and the domestic market became disconnected from the offshore market where the krona continued to depreciate. Refinancing of the Central Bank was necessary due to financial losses in relation to its lending activity as the Bank had made active use of its balance sheet in its unsuccessful efforts to prevent the crisis. The domestic economy entered a sharp recession following the banks collapse. The most recent Central Bank of Iceland baseline forecast assumes an 8% contraction in output in 2009, followed by a 2% contraction this year before returning to modest growth rates in 2011-2012 (Chart 12). This, however, does not fully reflect the large adjustments in domestic expenditure, with private consumption collapsing by more than 16% in 2009 and close to 30% in 2008-2010. With investment also falling, partly due to the completion of large investment projects, domestic demand is projected to fall by close to 20% in 2009 and about 31% in 2008-2010. This large adjustment of the real economy is also reflected in a sharp fall in employment levels and an enormous and unprecedented rise in the unemployment rate, with unemployment rising from roughly 1% in Q3/2008 to 8% in Q1/2009 (Chart 13). The unemployment rate is expected to continue to rise and peak in the middle of this year at roughly 10%. Employment is not, however, expected to increase again year-on-year until late 2011. An important factor explaining why unemployment is not expected to rise even further, given the large contraction in domestic demand, is the composition of the adjustment in domestic expenditure. With a significant share of the reduction in private consumption directed towards imported durable goods (Chart 5), import penetration falls from a previously high level and leads to a large positive contribution to growth from net exports (Chart 12), resulting in a much smaller loss in output and jobs. Also affecting this large trade contribution is the fact that Icelandic export volumes have not been hit by the global demand contraction to the same extent as in many other countries (Chart 14), with the global crisis mainly affecting Icelandic trade through deteriorating terms of trade (Chart 15). This expenditure switching towards the domestic economy and relatively robust exports are further facilitated by the large depreciation of the real exchange rate (Chart 3). The outlook for a continued low real exchange rate and favourable terms of trade developments will support an export led recovery of the economy and generate a significant trade, and eventually, current account surpluses to finance the large external debt of the economy (Chart 6). 3 Policy responses to the crisis Iceland requested a two-year Stand-By-Arrangement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in the amount of US 2.1 billion (1190% of quota) on 24 October 2008, which was accepted by the Funds Board on 19 November 2008. This was soon followed by bilateral loan commitments from European neighbours amounting to US 2.75 billion. This, together with other loan commitments and standing facilities, provides funding for the IMF program amounting to roughly US 5 billion, or approximately 42% of Icelandic 2009 GDP at current exchange rates. In addition to this, the UK and the Netherlands have provided loans amounting to roughly another US 5 billion to the Icelandic deposit insurance scheme, to cover payments of the minimum deposit guarantees to depositors in the online Icesave accounts of the UK and Netherlands branches of the failed Landsbanki. With the krona depreciating by roughly 50% in trade-weighted terms and against the euro (Chart 16), domestic balance sheets took a huge blow, as households and businesses were not only heavily indebted but also had a large share of their debt denominated in foreign currency (Chart 17). The large depreciation thus came on top of a drastic reduction in the availability of credit, enormous losses of private wealth and large reduction in disposable income. This was further aggravated by a sharp rise in inflation, which peaked at 18% in January 2009 (Chart 2), also hitting households balance sheets through widespread use of financial indexation to inflation. The centrepiece of the economic programme agreed upon by the Government, Central Bank and the IMF has therefore been to stabilise and support the currency in an attempt to protect vulnerable private sector balance sheets while the restructuring phase and the recovery of the economy takes place. To support the currency in the wake of the currency crisis, the key policy rate of the Bank was initially hiked to 18%. Furthermore, temporary capital controls were introduced to stem the threat of massive capital flight from non-residents and residents alike. These measures to provide support for the currency have broadly proven successful, with the krona stabilising as the year progressed, albeit at a low level (Chart 3 and 16), supported by a gradually declining risk premia (Chart 18). Thus, the Central Bank has been able to start easing the monetary policy stance and gradual removal of the capital controls. The main refinancing rate at the Bank is currently down to 10%, whereas the deposit rate at the Bank is down to 8.5% (Chart 19).2 The first step to easing the controls was taken in late October with abolition of restrictions on inflows and further plans to remove restrictions on outflows in sequenced steps have been made public. In response to the liquidity crisis in 2008, the Central Banks balance sheet expanded significantly as the Bank accepted ever-increasing types of collateral (Chart 20). This started earlier than experienced in other countries. The expansion of the balance sheet has also been greater than in most other countries as the balance sheet continued to expand up to the collapse of the commercial banks in October 2008. Since then the size of the balance sheet 2 With ample liquidity in the financial system, the most important Bank rates have now become rates on deposits rather than lending rates. 4 has been broadly stable, with almost non-existing collateral lending being offset by systematic increases in the Banks foreign reserves through the IMF programme, and seizure of assets that the failed banks had used as collateral. Government finances have come under enormous constrain following the financial crisis. The general government balance has turned from a surplus of 5% of GDP in 2007 to a deficit of 13% a year later and more than 15% in 2009, as the Government had to refinance the banking system and the Central Bank and strengthen the foreign reserves of the Bank (Chart 21). The Government also experienced a large revenue fall with the collapse of domestic demand, asset prices and the real exchange rate and rising costs due to higher unemployment. With Government debt low prior to the crisis, automatic stabilisers were allowed to work fully in 2009 in response to the crisis. However, the sharply deteriorating debt position of the Government allows very limited scope for further fiscal stimulus, with broad-based fiscal consolidation measures (including tax hikes and expenditure cuts) taking effect from this year to ensure a sustainable debt path (Chart 21). This limited scope for a fiscal stimulus has partly been replaced by allowing households to withdraw some of their third-pillar private pension savings, which many liquidity constrained households have benefitted from. The size of the scheme, in terms of GDP, is broadly similar to fiscal stimulus packages that many countries evoked in response to the crisis (Chart 22). The economic outlook Macroeconomic developments have broadly played out as expected, although the contraction in 2009 is turning out to be smaller than initially feared. The output contraction is assumed to have bottomed out in Q4/2009 and output is forecast to start recovering in Q1/2010, about two quarters later than among Icelands main trading partners (Chart 23). Icelands output contraction is therefore both more severe and more prolonged than among its trading partners. The recovery is initially driven by net trade but later on by a gradual recovery of private consumption (Charts 5 and 12). The outlook is obviously shrouded in uncertainty and the latest events in the Icesave-dispute could contribute to delaying the recovery. Inflation is forecast to continue to decline, especially from the latter half of this year (Chart 24). Inflation excluding indirect tax effects is projected to fall below target and remain quite low for some time if the krona remains stable or appreciates, as assumed in the baseline forecast. Headline inflation will, however, remain above target until the middle of 2011 due to increases in indirect taxes.
