Title: The Speech at the Banque de France Symposium
text: 8 July 2013 Preserving the credit of the sovereign through a financial sector meltdown  the case of Iceland Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Speech at Banque de France, International Monetary Seminar 2013: Sovereign Risk, Bank Risk and Central Banking, Paris, 8 July 2013. I would like to thank Banque de France for inviting me to speak at this interesting seminar. This session is on resolving sovereign debt crises and the relative roles of the public and private sectors in that process. My comments will obviously be based on my own countrys experience during the financial crisis, which is a case of a sovereign debt crisis being avoided in spite of the meltdown of a large part of the financial sector and the countrys deepest recession since the interwar period. That result was achieved by relatively good fiscal position prior to the crisis, by a refusal  based on need rather than stubbornness  to rescue private cross-border banks with public money, and by on-going medium-term fiscal consolidation that was an important part of the economic programme developed in cooperation with the IMF. The bottom line is that all sovereign obligations have been honoured; the sovereign has maintained investment-grade credit ratings and market access. In order to distinguish between the parts of this story that provide lessons that are applicable to the rest of the world and those that do not, we need to get some of the facts straight, because to this day there are still several misconceptions floating around about what was done in Iceland during the crisis. The collapse of Icelands three cross-border banks in early October 2008 was the most noticeable event in the unfolding of the financial crisis. The combined balance sheet of these banks was 10 times Icelands GDP (see Figure 1), and their combined bankruptcy, measured in terms of balance sheets, ranks second in size in the international history of corporate failures, only after Lehman Brothers. And this happened in a country that ranks among the smallest in the world! We are still dealing with the complications that this entails, as can be seen in our overblown and unbalanced IIP and the controls on capital outflows. 1 Figure 1 Before the collapse, the banking system had expanded very rapidly, growing in just five years from a combined balance sheet of less than 2 times GDP at the end of 2003 (see Figure 1). Most of this expansion was cross-border, and a significant part of it was actually off-border, having very little to do with Iceland, as both financing and investment took place abroad. Around twothirds of the balance sheet of the three cross-border banks was denominated in foreign currency. As is typical for banks, the FX part of the balance sheet had a significant maturity mismatch. However, there was no safety-net of the type that we have at the national level to back it up. This turned out to be the fatal flaw in the whole setup. Why were these big risks allowed to build up? I do not think we yet have the research and the consensus to provide a reasonably undisputed list of the main causal factors in this process; however, I think four factors will rank highly on that list. The first of them is Icelands membership in the European Economic Area (EEA) beginning in 1994, which made it possible for the banks to operate more or less freely throughout the area on the basis of home licencing but with 2 national supervision, safety net, and crisis management and resolution. The other three causes are the privatisation of the Icelandic banking system in the early 2000s in a manner that placed the major banks in the hands of risk-loving investment bankers, the global conditions of ample and cheap credit that prevailed in the years prior to the international financial crisis, and the tendency in Iceland both to adopt international and EU regulations without critical analysis of Iceland-specific risks and to base supervision to a significant degree on mechanical checks of adherence to those regulations. In the panic that gripped global financial markets after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, these banks were faced with a wholesale run on their foreign currency liabilities and were therefore heading towards a default on those liabilities in the absence of LOLR assistance in foreign currency. However, given the size of the banks, it was impossible for the Icelandic authorities to provide such assistance on their own. There was actually a plan to nationalise one of the banks in late September 2008. Fortunately it failed, as nationalising the bank would have turned a private banks foreign currency refinancing problem into a sovereign problem, with the serious risk that the sovereign might have defaulted on such foreign currency payments, thus initiating a full-scale sovereign debt crisis. Figure 2 gives a sense of the potential scale involved in the case of the three banks, by comparing the foreign currency liabilities of the banks and the Central Banks FX liquidity at the time. Figure 2 3 Based on published financial accounts and the analysis of the supervisor, the Icelandic authorities assumed that the banks were solvent. On that premise, the authorities tried to build defences against potential foreign currency liquidity problems at the banks by negotiating swap lines and tapping foreign capital markets, in both cases with limited success. Now, however, we know that there were hidden vulnerabilities in the banks capital positions. However, given the lack of international cooperation, the Icelandic authorities were forced to consider radical solutions. Although they were not necessarily articulated fully at the time, these solutions entailed several goals: preserving a functioning domestic payment system, ring-fencing the sovereign in the case of bank failures, limiting the socialisation of private sector losses, and creating the conditions for rebuilding a domestic banking system. In essence, the adopted solution saved the domestic operations of the banking system and let the international part to go into a resolution process. The new banks were created by carving the domestic assets and liabilities out of the old failing banks. The idea was then that the Government would recapitalise the banks and place compensation bonds in the estates of the failed banks. However, valuing the assets and liabilities proved a complicated process in the middle of an economic and financial crisis, and a solution emerged where the estates of the failed banks became majority owners of two of the banks and kept a small equity stake in the third, which was otherwise recapitalised by the Government. The new banking system amounted to 1.7 times GDP. In order to stop an incipient run on domestic deposits, all deposits in Iceland were declared safe and all deposits in Icelandic-headquartered banks were given priority over other unsecured claims, including the deposits of the Icelandic banks in branches abroad. As a result of these measures, the domestic payment system functioned more or less seamlessly throughout, and there was uninterrupted access to deposits in Iceland. The run on the domestic banks stopped, but at its peak, demand for cash tripled and the Central Bank almost ran out of banknotes. International payment flows were seriously affected, however, not least because of the freezing order imposed by the British authorities on Icelandic banks, but also because of a general distrust among foreign counterparties. Why did the Government give a verbal blanket guarantee for domestic deposits only and not for deposits in the banks foreign branches? After all, this distinction probably added fuel to the fire of the so-called Icesave dispute about the settlement of deposit guarantees in Landsbankis Dutch and British branches. The short answer is that such a guarantee would never have been credible. As a result, it would not have stopped the run on these deposits and, if attempted, might have bankrupted the Government. At the time, the Central Bank of Icelands FX reserves amounted to 2 billion euros, while the foreign currency deposits in Landsbankis Dutch and British branches totalled 11 billion euros and payment of the EU minimum deposit insurance would have required 4 billion euros. The sovereign was completely closed off from 4 foreign capital markets at that point. Furthermore, in economic terms, given that these deposits were used to a significant degree to finance illiquid assets in these same countries, such a payment, if possible, would have amounted to a net transfer of resources from Iceland to these countries at a time when Iceland was going through its deepest financial and economic crisis in the post-war period! That made no sense. The only possibility of a speedy pay-out of deposit insurance in order to contain contagion was for the authorities in the host countries to pay it and leave the issue of settlement with Iceland for a later date. And this was what they did. From the beginning, there were legal arguments about the merits of such claims. In spite of that legal uncertainty, the Icelandic Government took part in several good-faith attempts to reach a negotiated solution. However, it proved impossible to get ratification through the Icelandic political process, in two cases involving referenda. In retrospect, it is clear that the main reason for this was the Icelandic peoples unwillingness to shoulder financial liabilities that had not been clearly signed by those mandated to do so on behalf of the nation or proven in a court of law to be sovereign obligations. Instead, these were seen as the debts of reckless private bankers. Now the EFTA court has ruled that it was indeed not a sovereign liability. In any case, the recovery from the estate of Landsbanki will cover 100% of all deposits in foreign branches. Without the priority given to deposits in the Emergency Act of October 2008, the recovery to be paid to these depositors would be much lower. This case provides important lessons about the design of deposit insurance within the EU and the clarity of wording, or lack thereof, in EU directives. This case also highlights the link that must exist between deposit insurance and the LOLR function. Part of the rationale is to prevent and stop runs. But at the end of the day, that only works if bank liabilities are flowing to a central bank that has the mandate, willingness, and capacity to recycle them against collateral and expand its balance sheet as needed. This means that, in the absence of arrangements for currency swaps, it must take place mostly in the same currency in order to work. So the bottom line is that a sovereign default was avoided in spite of an almost unprecedented financial collapse and the worst economic recession since the interwar years. A key to that result was the attempt to ring-fence the sovereign from the collapse of these three cross-border private banks. However, the avoidance of default during such a severe crisis does require the willingness to use the means available to avoid that outcome and the ability to endure the temporary hardship that might come with it. Even if the Icelandic authorities tried to avoid the socialisation of private sector losses in the case of the collapse of the three-cross border banks, the direct 5 fiscal costs of the financial crisis were enormous. In this case, it is difficult to distinguish between the cost of the banking crisis and the recession that would nevertheless have occurred in Iceland in 2009, as a result of the unavoidable macroeconomic adjustment following the serious overheating of the economy in 2005-2007. Be that as it may, the direct fiscal costs of capital injections into domestic banks, losses on government guarantees, the blanket guarantee of domestic deposits, and the refinancing of the Central Bank are estimated to have amounted to one-third of year-2010 GDP. The net might turn out to be somewhat lower, however; for instance, there will be some recovery on the collateral of CB lending to failed banks. Gross government debt went from under a third of GDP before the crisis to a peak of one GDP, and net debt rose from around a tenth to two-thirds. As a result, there was no fiscal space to save banks 10 times GDP, and attempting to do so would have bankrupted the country. Indeed, Iceland had to embark on a medium-term fiscal consolidation programme even as output was still contracting, in order to stop government debt from reaching an unsustainable level and to rebuild the external confidence needed for the sovereign to regain market access. The overall fiscal effort (measured by changes in the cyclically adjusted primary balance as a percentage of potential GDP) amounted to 10 percentage points 2010-13, more than that of Ireland during the same period (although Ireland will overtake Iceland if the expected effort for 2014 and 15 is added). This effort has been sufficient to create a primary surplus and, along with growth in the economy from H2/2010 onwards, to put debt on a downward trajectory as a share of GDP, which is predicted to be 85% gross and below 60% net in 2015. But this has not come without significant pain, and again, would not have been possible if private bank liabilities had been guaranteed more than was needed to keep the domestic payment system and basic banking services up and running. Let me conclude by summarising some of the potential lessons from this tale: 1. Iceland did not allow its entire banking system to collapse, it did not nationalise its banking system, and it did not default on sovereign debt. So, in spite of what one sometimes hears, the Icelandic case does not teach any lesson on the pros and cons of such measures. 2. Iceland avoided sovereign default through a good initial fiscal position, the ring-fencing of the sovereign as much as possible from collapsing cross-border banks, and a medium-term fiscal consolidation programme. The lesson is to practise fiscal prudence and avoid the socialisation of private sector losses. 3. Iceland protected its domestic payment system and deposits. The lesson might be bail-in, separability in resolution between the public utility element of banking from the rest, and deposit preference. 4. The EU system for cross-border banking is deeply flawed. Existing official reform proposals are a step in the right direction but do not fully address the problems revealed by the Icelandic experience. 6

Title: Speech on the pension system in Iceland in an international context
text: 14. October 2011 Icelandic the pension system: strengths and weaknesses in a global context Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland. A symposium in honour of Hrafn Magnusson, former managing director of the National Union of Pension Funds, held in Harpa on 14 October 2011. Moderator, dear Raven, the guests of the forum, I am delighted to speak at this meeting in honor of Hrafn Magnusson. I met Raven to some extent when I was economic adviser to the Minister of Finance from 1988 to 1991. Then, as was often later, the pension funds were being negotiated on government funding and other issues, but I was also for a while chairman of one of the many major committees that for many years prepared framework legislation on pension funds. I got to know Raven best when we sat together on the board of the Pension Rights Collection Fund. However, it wasn't until after I became chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland in the mid-1990s that I became genuinely convinced that the pension system that had developed in Iceland was an important part of the strength of the Icelandic economy. I was still convinced of this when, around the turn of the century, I wrote a detailed report on the Icelandic pension system, compared it to the theoretical stereotypes and pension systems of other countries, and analysed its potential impact on the country's economy and financial system.1 I received a lot of support from Hrafn and orgeir Eyjolfsson, then managing director of the Pension Fund of The Verzlunarmanna Pension Fund, in this work which, through his knowledge of the pension system and experience, saved me at the same time from a variety of errors. What was this view based on? To answer that question, it is necessary to remind us what qualities we are going to have a good pension system. There must, of course, be a channel for savings to old age. But if it is to be well structured, it also needs to take into account the risk factors faced by individuals and society and relate to people's life spans. These are risk factors, for example, marked by life expectancy, work capacity, demographics, labor productivity and asset returns. Furthermore, we can claim a good pension scheme that some income equalisation is embedded in the system, at least we can make the minimum requirement that it does not contribute to the increased income difference. They want to 1 See: Mar Guomundsson, "Icelandic the pension fund system", reproduction, published. National Union of Pension Funds, 1995 and Mar Guomundsson, "Icelandic the pension system: Structure and learning", Monetary Bulletin 2004/1, published by the Central Bank of Iceland, 2004. 1 that the pension system has certain flexibility and that there is scope for the individuals to have a choice. Finally, we want the pension system to have a positive impact on the economy, i.e. boost savings, increase economic growth and contribute to the development of the financial system. These are huge demands and to some extent these goals will conflict. There seems to be considerable consensus that in order to meet these requirements, at least in part, a good pension system needs to be based on three pillars. First, a tax-financed social security system that pays a flat or income-related pension. Second, compulsory membership of pension funds based on full fund-raising and subject to official supervision. Third, optional pension savings, often with tax advantages. Why three pillars? Sure, we need them to be able to mitigate target collisions, to make the system as a whole more resistant to individual traumas and to have flexibility for individual choices. This is well known and is the best-known representation in the World Bank's 1994 book Averting the Old Age Crisis.2. By the turn of the century, the Icelandic pension system had acquired many of these qualities. The social security system pays a low basic pension but a much higher supplementary pension, which is, however, income-related, also towards a pension of other origins. This means that, along with the fact that employment-related pension funds reach maturity, the share of social security in pension payments falls. At the turn of the century, however, social security payments were still somewhat higher than the pension payments of the funds. It was not much, however, and the pension payments of the funds then became greater than social security soon after the turn of the century. It is interesting in this regard that among the member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Iceland recently had the highest share of pension payments outside the social security system. Among other things, the social security system's pension payments in terms of GDP amount to well less than a third of what happens and goes among the member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The general pension funds have grown rapidly in recent decades. It was crucial that the obligation membership was that all employment income was paid, that operating expenses overall have been relatively low and returns have over long periods been good. At the turn of the century, the Icelandic pension funds were the third largest among EU and EFTA countries measured by a percentage of GDP assets, which was then around 80%, followed by Switzerland and the Netherlands. Shortly before the global financial crisis, Iceland had surpassed those countries. The prospect was that the funds would grow much more as they had a considerable amount of time to reach full maturity in the sense that most of the pensioners of the funds had not uploaded rights in an entire working life. This showed that the pension burden, or the proportion of pension payments on premiums, was still less than 50%. At the time, it was estimated that the future size of the pension funds would be highest at around one and a half GDP. They had to 2 World Bank, Averting the Old Age Crisis, World Bank Policy Research Report, Oxford University Press, 1994. 2 It's almost so big before the financial crisis, but it wasn't "real" as I'll come to later. It is worth noting that it is not easy to categorise the Icelandic pension funds according to traditional international criteria for funds that are on the one hand based on defined rights where the employer carries the investment risk and on the other hand on defined premiums where the individual fund member carries the investment risk. Of course, some of the funds have employers' responsibilities and would be defined as funds based on defined rights, but by law, only the state, municipalities and banks can guarantee pension funds. But the others are not all clean premium funds. The investment risk is borne jointly by the fund members and there is the possibility of a certain risk distribution across generations. This has advantages and disadvantages, but the positive aspects occur, among other things, when that property collapse, which may happen once in a lifetime, rages on. The third pillar of the pension system developed later in Iceland but in many other places. It wasn't until 1998 that legislation was passed on tax incentives for optional pension savings, but they were then increased in the years that followed. These savings then increased by big steps, reaching its base of 10% of GDP in 2002 and 15% in 2007. That practice can be disputed, of course, but these savings have been an important factor in the financial and economic crisis. So far, the prepayment of these savings has amounted to nearly 4% of GDP. In terms of demand impacts, these payments equate to stimulating fiscal measures without appearing as increased deficits or leverage. But, of course, in an economic sense, it is being borrowed from the future. Of course, joining future funds may be justified when temporary tribulations pass, but there is always a debate at any given time on how far to go. I now turn to the impact of the pension system we have built on the economy and financial system. The first thing we need to keep in mind in that regard is that there are always those who are employed at any given time who sustain retirees, regardless of how the system is structured. The consumption of the pensioners is part of the national output of each time produced by those who are then employed. In this regard, there is therefore no fundamental difference between pass-through systems and fund-raising systems that the Icelandic does in large part. In a small and open economy, however, the design of the pension system can affect this burden in at least four ways. First, with its impact on the employment of those who are older. Second, by influencing the capital base that the working have at their disposal and thus on the productivity of the workforce. Third, by building foreign assets that constitute a requirement for the production of those active in the business sector of other countries. Fourth, by promoting the development of financial markets which in turn could lead to better utilization of capital and thus higher labour productivity. There may be significant differences in the impact a pass-through system or fund-raising system has on these four factors. In some cases, we see this 3 positive effects clearly in the Icelandic the pension system, but in other cases the picture is more blurred or it is too early to tell the outcome. It is clear that the negative impact of pension funds on the employment of the older ones is much lower here than in many other countries, including where the pension scheme is broadly neutral regarding early retirement, as the employment rate of the older ones is relatively high and the same can be said of the active retirement age. Thus, the official retirement age is 67 years, which is higher than in many neighbouring countries, however, who have had to move towards us in this regard due to the ageing population and the difficult state of the state budget. As for the employment rate of older people, 35% of 6,574-year-olds did payroll work for at least one hour a week last year, which is high in international comparison. It will be interesting to see to what extent the current economic crisis will change this. However, the impact on productivity and economic growth through higher savings trends and investment levels remains difficult to confirm, as macroeconomic savings have long been low in terms of GDP, and especially in the run-up to the financial crisis. Indeed, the development of a pension system through fund-raising can, under certain conditions, contribute to increased macroeconomic savings, thereby increasing production capital and economic growth. Of course, it is difficult to know what would have happened without the accumulation of pension funds, and so far this effect has been difficult to confirm. It is also concerning that Icelandic households have been among the most indebted in the world. In Denmark and the Netherlands, household debt in proportion to disposable income has actually been even higher. In both of these countries, pension assets in the second and third pillars of the pension system are very high. It is possible that people trust such systems better than public pass-through systems and are therefore more willing to accumulate debt in the belief that their pension is secure. Once again, it will be interesting to see if the financial crisis will have a significant impact on this pattern. Thus, it is possible that the positive impact of the Icelandic pension system on macroeconomic savings has yet to emerge. In terms of foreign assets, however, the picture is clear. The funds shortly built up large foreign assets and amounted to 26% of total assets before the crash, i.e. at the end of 2007. These assets accounted for 7% of the nation's gross foreign assets and 29% of its foreign securities assets, which is of course significant. In addition to moving some of the national pension burden in the future to abroad, these assets have become an important reserve for the nation when there was a drastic turnaround in capital flows to the country in 2008. But this investment is, of course, risky, as the trends of recent losses have shown. The impact on the development of financial markets in Iceland is also felt and it is obvious that the pension funds contributed significantly to their growth. In fact, for a while, there were concerns that they had become too overwhelming, and it was a sign that their share of outstanding market-listed bonds amounted to 40% at the end of 2002. The overthrow of the banking system suppressed these concerns 4 from a period of time but now they watch again, although in a different form. The other is clear that since the capital controls have halted the funds' foreign investments for a while, they have played a key role in funding the government's deficit in affordable terms now in the first years after the crash. The treasuries of various small European nations are envious of the Icelandic at the moment in this regard. Nevertheless, it is of course concerning, and hopefully a temporary situation, that the market share of the pension funds in market securities was over 50% and nearly 70% in residential bonds. But this belief in the strengths of the Icelandic pension system; is it still there after we have gone through one of the greatest stress tests of all time as almost the entire banking system of the country collapsed and the pension funds lost out on that huge amount of money and are now more losing a lot on their foreign investments? I'm going to keep you in suspense about it for half a minute because it's necessary to first say a few words about the financial crisis as such. The financial crisis that raged here is part of a global financial crisis, and as is often the case in such cases, both the international and domestic roots of the events that occur at any given time. I have written about the global part of the financial crisis in an article published in Shire in the spring of 20093, showing that the causality is complex, i.e. from gaps in the global monetary system and the interaction of exchange rate and monetary policy in China and other emerging markets on the one hand and in the United States on the other, and to shortcomings in the regulatory and regulatory framework of the financial system and its individual parts. As for the domestic aspect, it is important to note that it brought together two stories, one of which consisted of amazing domestic economic volatility and economic failures, and on the other, the expansion and collapse of international banks based on EU regulations headquartered in Iceland. The financial crisis first appeared as a liquidity crisis, but there were underlying concerns about the capital position of banks that have not disappeared. Then the crisis develops into a confluence of a balanced payment crisis, a banking crisis and a national debt crisis in some countries. And on both sides of the Atlantic, the story is still ongoing. It is therefore too early to settle what the consequences it will have in the long run on pension funds and human thinking about the design of pension schemes. So I'll come back to Icelandic pension system. Pension funds have of course suffered a significant blow with negative returns of 22% in 2008 and a decrease in assets from 134% of GDP in 2007 to 119% at the end of 2009. But then we have to remember that part of this trend is correction. The asset price bubble and corresponding returns on pension funds were partly foaming. In that sense, that yield was never real. Roots and reactions", Baptisms, 183rd year spring 2009. 4 5 We always knew that a crisis of this kind was one of the biggest risks a pension system based on fund-raising. The system certainly got hit, but it didn't break, and there's nothing to say at this point that looking ahead, real returns in the financial market will be lower than economic growth, but that's a condition that a pass-through system pays off better than a cash-raising system. My belief in the strengths of the Icelandic pension system is therefore basically the same as before. But it depends, of course, on us learning our lessons from the financial crisis so that it will actually be an event that doesn't happen more than once in a lifetime. We must draw the right lessons regarding incentives and risk management, regarding accounting rules and asset assessments, on regulatory and regulatory issues, on economic management and on the interplay of the economy and financial system. In this regard, I have happily observed that the pension funds, for their part, have set up a process to draw their lessons. One of the things that has been mentioned in this regard is that the funds need to be critical in the future. But it's also about all of us. Finally, I'd like to look back a little bit back to the early days of the pension funds, i.e. to say the collective agreements of 1969 and what happened in the following years. But now we are at a crossroads, and others are taking over. Raven, you can be proud of your great contribution. 6

Title: Why has the crown risen?
text: Why has the crown risen? Thorarinn G. P8etursson Since the beginning of the year, the exchange rate has risen by a fifth against the average of other currencies, and since the current rate of increase began in the middle of last year, the increase amounts to just over a quarter. This is a huge increase in a relatively short period of time that has naturally attracted attention. But why has the exchange rate risen so much and what is the monetary policy aspect of the increase? Is there any reason to be concerned about the rate hike, and could it even be the forerunner of a new coal mine, comparable to the one that happened here in the autumn of 2008? The rate hike primarily reflects an external buoy in simple terms, it can be said that the main cause of the rate hike is to seek the success of companies in export operations in selling their products in international markets. It has the highest remarkable growth in tourism in recent years, but in volume exported tourism has grown by 20-30% every year since 2011 and since the second half of last year the annual growth rate has been more than 40%. In the third quarter of this year, the extent of tourism at fixed prices was therefore almost three times that of the same quarter five years ago. This far exceeds the growth of other exports and the average growth in demand of our major trading countries. What happens when a new export industry grows from little to one of the main industries of the national economy in no time? For one thing, the national export revenues increase significantly, and this raises national income levels and the financial wealth of the public grows. On top of this, the second buoyancy is a significant increase in export prices in proportion to the prices of the goods and services we buy from abroad, which can largely be attributed to favourable developments in the price of seafood and a decrease in global oil prices. Both of these buoys make the domestic wealth increase, which raises the exchange rate of the kr97na. The two buoys also come with strong growth in domestic demand, which tries considerably on limited domestic production factors. Demand for the workforce is growing rapidly and a growing number of companies operate at or beyond full capacity. Under such circumstances, it is normal d0 and in fact desirable d0 for the exchange rate to rise. This helps to restrain domestic inflationary pressures that inevitably arise when domestic production factors are tested, including by steering domestic demand to some extent out of the national economy, i.e. imported goods and services. Thus, there will be less pressure on domestic production factors, as well as higher exchange rates making it easier for domestic companies to apply, for example, labour to other countries to meet high domestic demand. But more happens as the new export industry grows as fast as it actually is. As it competes to some extent for the same domestic resources as other export industries, its growth pushes up the exchange rate to dismantle other export activities while creating space in the national economy. This is an old-fashioned theme in Icelandic economic history where great success in tourism plays the same role as gifted catches in the fishing industry in the past. The rate hike in recent times therefore reflects a significant extent the inevitable adaptation of the national economy to external boomers. The increase is therefore part of an adaptation process that helps create tourism space in the national economy but also contributes to slowing its growth so that it will be better aligned with the growth of limited domestic production quality. The rate hike also eases the aggression of domestic production factors by directing some of the demand generated by the buoyancy out of the national economy. In addition, the increase brings the portion of the buoyancy from the export companies to the public through the increased purchasing power of homes in the same way as The rate cut during the financial crisis eased domestic companies by partially shifting the burden to households. But what about monetary policy? Until now, there has been no mention of a possible monetary policy share of this trend. Due to strong economic growth and the growing aura of domestic production factors, domestic interest rates have had to be higher than interest rates in neighbouring countries. There is still a considerable slack in place, allowing them to have some economic growth without inflationary pressures. The positive interest rate differential supports otherwise the higher exchange rate of the kr97na, so monetary policy can strengthen and accelerate the exchange rate adjustment previously described. However, this is not weighing heavily on the trend lately. The rate hike is not explained by a speculative influx of capital in search of higher returns, but such an influx has been abject after the Fed introduced a separate cash flow tool earlier this year. For some time now, the Central Bank has opposed pressure to increase the exchange rate by buying a considerable portion of foreign exchange income that has flowed into the country. For a long time, the Bank did so in order to build strong foreign exchange reserves for the disposal of capital controls. In the past, the Bank's acquisition has also reflected its efforts to reduce the risk of the kr97na overstating during the current period of prosperity and then falling swiftly as fortunes turn around. Monetary policy, on the whole, has rather held back an increase in the exchange rate of the kr97na. Is there any reason to worry? While the rate hike has natural causes, it is understandable that export companies are concerned about their position. There have also been concerns that the rate hike will follow a rate collapse as it happened here in 2008. It should be remembered, however, that the exchange rate collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 reflected a national economy that lived far on the subject and financed high spending levels through borrowing from abroad. The massive trade deficit peaked at almost a quarter of GDP in 2006. The deficit can be attributed to strong growth in domestic demand at a time when macroeconomic savings were at historic lows. The foreign debt of the national economy far exceeded its assets, which also shows how dependent the national economy was on foreign funding. Now everything is different. Macroeconomic savings are at historic highs, a handsome surplus has been on trade with foreign countries for eight consecutive years, and recently the remarkable success of the foreign assets of the national economy exceeded its foreign debt for the first time since measurements began. It is therefore difficult to see that a similar exchange rate collapse should occur in the near future. However, tourism growth will inevitably slow down. Nor is it impossible to backlash the industry or a reversal of the national trade terms. Under such circumstances, the developments described above could rebound to some extent and the exchange rate of the kr97na may yield. It would soften the national economy's adjustment to its lackluster position. The point is that businesses and the public do not commit based on expectations that current success will continue for the time being. It is also crucial that strict restraint will continue to be taken into account in economic management. In this context, it would be desirable for other arms of economic policy to be more closely aligned with monetary policy. Increased adherence to the management of public finances would reduce the need for restraint in the implementation of monetary policy and relieve pressure to increase the exchange rate. A wide range of direct tariffs on tourists would also be designed to slow down their demand and reduce pressure on the exchange rate, thereby reducing the negative impact on other export industries. The writer is chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland and a member of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee. The views expressed herein do not have to reflect the views of the Bank or others on the Committee.

Title: Speech at a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce
text: How do we promote a more stable financial system? Statement by Governor Mar Guomundsson at a breakfast meeting of the Chamber of Commerce on the future of the Icelandic financial system, 13 September 2013. After the financial crisis, we face the task of reforming the structure of the financial system and the regulatory framework on which it operates. At the same time, we need to improve what went wrong regarding the system's risk monitoring and monitoring of individual parts of it. The goal is to promote a more stable financial system. Professor Mark and good friend Charles Goodhart sometimes says something in the way that any fool can make banks pretty much safe by raising capital and liquidity requirements out of control and banning all that seems most dangerous. There are at least three truths in this: First, we need rather better thoughtful rules that focus on the essence of risk than more and more heavier regulation. Second, more security could be at the expense of the functioning and driving force of the system once a certain level of security is achieved, with negative consequences for economic growth. Third, it cannot be a goal to fully prevent financial institutions from going bankrupt. On the contrary, it is part of a healthy financial system that it can take place but then without threatening the system as a whole or sending a large bill to the taxpayers. In this light, it is important that in designing a new regulatory framework for the financial system, we take into account the best possible analysis of the risks embedded in a financial system of the kind we have built up in the West in recent centuries and on what went wrong during the financial crisis. In Iceland, we need an additional good analysis of icelandic risks and to beware of adopting international or European regulations thoughtlessly. The financial system has a variety of roles, but the most important ones are to communicate financial savings in investment, to manage and distribute risks to those who can best carry it, and to be the channel of payment processing and settlement forums. While banks are one of the most important units of the financial system, this does not mean that they need to play all these roles. Thus, one might think of a system where there were guaranteed deposits in special banking institutions that could not be invested in except relatively readily available and trusted assets, and they would then be 1 at the same time, the main channel of payment processing. Another part of trading savings in investment would then be carried out through other forms of financial institutions or directly through bond and stock markets. But this is not the system that we and most, if not all, developed nations have had. On the contrary, we built up banks that played all these roles and various exists, such as investment for our own account and all kinds of leveraged bets. This involved both strength and weakness. I have often benefited from drawing up a stylized extreme example of what banks do to explain what the risks in that activity lie. They accept money from countless savers and tell them they can get the money tomorrow if they want and then turn around and hand it over to few investors for, for example, five years. This can be based on the experience that under normal circumstances it is only a fraction of the depositors who withdraw their money on a given date and those who do so hand it over to someone else who then deposits it into some bank. This system has produced huge benefits in investment, progress and economic growth. But it involves a high level of risk of two types: on the one hand, the loan could be scrapped in the borrower's co-ops, as future benefits are always uncertain, as well as sometimes over-indebted investors. Then the Bank's assets and equity are scrapped, and when it is exhausted, the Bank goes bust. I sometimes liken this to the bank dying of cancer, and the build-up is often quite long. However, depositors could suddenly take up losing confidence in the bank and withdraw their deposits on a large scale. Then the bank cannot, without assistance, pay out and then runs out of money for that reason or puts long-term assets on fire sale and equity burns up. This can be likened to death from a heart attack, as the war of death can take off very quickly. Those of you who have seen Mary Poppins saw an old-fashioned bank raid of this kind that was unfounded if I recall correctly. But an exposed bank with a huge time discrepancy between asset maturity and liabilities can easily go bust in a bank raid even if the assets are in order. Granted, other banks could help up the prosecution if they otherwise consider the bank to have enough equity, and that often happened in such raids on banks in the UK before the days of the Bank of England as a lender to devolution. Another important historical example is the 1907 U.S. financial crisis, which was followed by the fact that it was deemed necessary to establish the US Federal Reserve in its current Form1. But if there is a raid on the entire banking system, for example because it is reasoned and even properly suspected that some banks are 1 Sja serstaklega: Robert F. Bruner, Sean D. Carr, The Panic of 1907: Lessons Learned from the Markets Perfect Storm, 2009 2 from cancer but no one knows what are the damaged apples in the basket, yes then the problem becomes miserable. The solution found was to use central banks as lenders for devolution2. If cross-border capital movements are overlooked, the money withdrawn from banks usually flows to the central bank, and it can give it back against solid mortgages while they are present. Later on, deposit insurance was added. But such a safety net creates a temptation problem and leads to excessive risk-taking. Therefore, it takes regulation to restrain it and surveillance to ensure that it is followed. But banking controls also evolved within central banks where they wanted to know if individual banks had enough equity to be loan guards. This system worked fairly well for a long time, not least in developed countries during the period during which cross-border capital movements were smaller than later occurred, partly due to capital controls, and financial activity was simpler. But it failed in this last financial crisis. This is because part of the financial sector with risks of the exception of kind escaped regulation and controls, and another part escaped beyond the safety net. On the one hand, there were activities in the so-called shadow banking system where the foodity transformation took place without the associated capital requirements and controls, and although the parent companies usually had access to a central bank's liquidity remit, these activities involved liquidity risk largely hidden from central banks and regulators. However, there was a great increase in cross-border banking activity with associated balance sheets and liquidity risk in foreign currencies that were not protected by central bank liquidity remittances. Icelandic banks were a good example of this. Of course, there were a number of other things I don't have time to explain here, instead referring to the articles and speeches I have given on the subject, such as my article in Baptism in 20093. But a few things 2 Sja: Thornton, H., An Enquiry into the Nature and Effects of the Paper Credit of Great Britain, 1802 og , Bagehot, W., Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market, Wiley Investment Classics, 1999. 3 Mar Guomundsson, Hin aljoolega fjarmalakreppa. Raetur og viobrogo, Skirnir, 183. ar, vor 2009; M Gudmundsson & T Thorgeirsson, The fault lines in cross-border banking: Lessons from the Icelandic case , SUERF publication 2010/5, pp. 141-165; Mar Guomundsson, The financial crisis in Iceland and the fault lines in crossborder banking FIBE, Bergen, 7. januar 2010 ; Mar Guomundsson, To what extent do international and EU reform proposals address the fault lines in cross-border banking? High-Level Meeting for the Middle East & North Africa Region, Abu Dhabi, 27. november 2012 2.pdf. 3 I must mention, however, that are important about the task of promoting a more stable financial system without stifling the driving force of the system, especially those that are important to us in this small open economy that we have here in Iceland. They are as follows: Global trade balance imbalances, volatile capital movements and a large supply of cheap global capital in the run-up to the financial crisis. Macroeconomic imbalance in Iceland: trade deficits, capital inflows, lending expansion, asset price bubbles and the subsequent explosion. EEA regulation on cross-border banking and capital movements involving unprotected risks in banks' balance sheets, especially among smaller countries with their own currency. Private sector over-leverage related to super-optimism on the future and the high availability of cheap capital. Leveraged bets and hidden equity problems. Compression and connection of risks and therefore associated with an unhealthy relationship owners of a bank. Weaknesses in the overall view of risks in the system as a whole, including lack of information on the part of those who could have provided it. Lack of what is now known as macroeconomic caution, i.e. the use of precautionary measures such as capital and mortgage rates with the aim of promoting the stability of the financial system as a whole, and the total is more than the sum of the individual shares. Here it is about reducing volatility in the financial system, controlling common risks through transmission and connections, and reducing negative interactions between the financial system and the real economy. I have now partly described the problem as important so that we respond to it rather than create new problems. But what do we need to do to get rid of it? What does a more stable financial system look like and what regulatory frameworks will be around it? Looking at the above analysis, it's clear where to go. We need a financial system where unprotected risks cannot threaten the public quality of the system, namely guaranteed deposits and payment processing. In this respect, there are three possibilities: First, certain activities are simply banned or priced out of the system. Second, there is some kind of separation or fence so that the public quality can be protected from the bookmaker without taxpayers receiving a high bill. Third, more is taken into account under the safety net, and capital and liquidity requirements are also raised and improved. These 4 leads have all their advantages and disadvantages and I find there a lot of evidence that the result will be some kind of mix, which may make sense given the uncertainty about how individual actions will work. Make sure this journey has begun a long time ago. At the international level, an action plan drafted by the FSB and confirmed by the leaders of the G20 countries has been carried out and is now finding its way through Basel and Brussels and is flushing our shores.4 This is where we are most important at this moment the implementation of Basel-III on higher and better capital and liquidity requirements, and this work is currently being carried out by the government. There we must be careful of the old translation and marking compulsion. We need to do our own analysis of our risks and adapt implementation and additions on the basis of that. The Central Bank, for its part, has tried to propose, including the publication Precautionary Post-Capital Controls, in which it reviews the restrictions on foreign exchange risk in the balance sheets of financial institutions and unprotected domestic entities that it believes must be in place after capital controls have been eased. The move remains, but it seems to me that if the proposed regulatory framework had been in place in the run-up to the financial crisis, Icelandic banks would not have been possible to become as large as it actually became, except perhaps through subsidiaries abroad that would have been less risky for Iceland, and the huge unprotected liquidity risk in foreign currencies would have been much lower. A lot has also been done in this country regardless of international regulation. Thus, some of the most obvious things about the regulation and supervision of individual financial institutions have been improved. But there is much left, not least to complete the institutional structure of macroeconomic caution and make decisions about what extent and how we want to put fences around the public quality of the system. Regarding the latter, we can actually allow ourselves to take more time into the discussion and see something longer to where global developments lead to the fact that our banking system is currently simple, with good capital and liquidity and devoted behind capital controls. I'm not going to trace this thread any further than instead ask what a more recreated stable financial system might look like, and then I have Iceland in mind: 4 Sja t.d. Improving Financial Regulation, Report of the Financial Stability Board to G20 Leaders, 25 September 2009, Financial Stability Board; og Progress since the Washington Summit in the Implementation of the G20 Recommendations for Strengthening Financial Stability, Report of the Financial Stability Board to G20 Leaders, 8 November 2010, Financial Stability Board /. 5 It will be smaller and simpler than before the crash. It will focus more on the core business of banks - to communicate Well between savings and investments. In doing so lies precisely the intensity of banks: to follow up on long loan agreements and apply to asymmetrical information. It will have higher and better capital and liquidity hedging. It will mainly focus on the domestic economy. It will be limited in international activities, at least as long as we are not part of a larger safety net. There will be a more secure framework for both monopoly and macroeconomic caution. Finally this: This development will not only be due to official regulation and restrictions. The marketing processes and decisions of the financial institutions themselves will play a key role. After all, it's the owners and managers of banks who are responsible for that responsibility, and they have to choose business models that work out in a given environment. However, that sentence must not be an excuse for public bodies not delivering their own. They are the ones who shape the environment. History shows that no other party can handle preventing systemic risk and grappling with its consequences. 6

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 21.03.2003 Statement by olafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors, at the Annual General Meeting on 21 March 2003 Honorary ministers, the President of the Althing, other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 40th and second annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. At the conclusion of my introductory remarks, the Chairman of the Board of Directors Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson will give an overview of the development of economic and monetary policy, the Bank's monetary policy and its implementation and the prospects ahead. After his speech, Prime Minister David Oddsson will address the meeting. At the end of the meeting, attendees are invited to accept refreshments. At a meeting of the Board of Directors today, the Prime Minister confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2002 with his endorsement. At the Central Bank's annual meeting two years ago, the Prime Minister presented a new framework for monetary policy and a new bill on the Central Bank of Iceland, which was passed as a law from the Althingi less than two months later. The change in the framework and the new law meant that the Central Bank was set one of the main objectives, namely to promote stable prices, and it was granted independence in order to use its instruments in order to achieve its objective. I believe that the experience has shown that these changes have proved to be intriguing. The new framework and the new law make very strong demands on the Central Bank for professional practices, transparency and information sharing. These requirements have been sought by the Bank to meet with ambition and I insist that it has been successful. The changes in 2001 were of utmost importance and included at the same time a new monetary policy framework and a legal framework and confirmation of changes in the Bank's work that had taken place in recent years. As a consequence, the Bank's main objective is now to promote stable prices, but it also has other important objectives such as promoting an active and secure financial system, including payment systems in iceland and abroad. The Bank's operations have changed greatly as soon as its challenges have been tailored to what can be called central bank fundamental challenges anywhere. This development is reflected, among other things, that the bank's employment values at present are approximately 40 fewer than they were 10 to 15 years ago and that now more than half of the Bank's employees are university-educated professionals, but were less than a third at the beginning of the last decade. In the new Act on the Bank, the supervisory role of the Board of Directors was sharpened from the previous law and increased in it from five representatives to seven. A report on the bill said that the increase in the Board of Directors was consistent with its supervisory role and that it ensured its wider composition and that more views were found during consideration by the Board of Directors. Article 28 of the Act states that the Board of Directors monitors that the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with the laws applicable to the operation and that the Board of Directors shall always inform the Board of Directors of the main aspects of the Bank's policy and of the rules it establishes. In other respects, the Board of Directors specifically performs tasks considered and specified in Article 28 of the Act. The supervisory role of the Board of Directors includes that the Board of Directors appoints the General Auditor of the Central Bank of Iceland and sets him a letter of appointment. The Auditor General therefore acts on behalf of the Board of Directors and his role is of utmost importance. The Auditor General shall cooperate closely with the Auditor General and both review the Bank's annual accounts and whatever in his work which their minds may be on at any given time. I thank the Auditor General and the Auditor General for their good work over the past year and good cooperation with the Board of Directors. As mentioned earlier, the Prime Minister today confirmed the Central Bank of Iceland's financial statements for 2002. During that year, profit from the Bank's operations amounted to ISK 2.1 billion. The contribution to the Treasury amounted to just over ISK 700 million and excluding the Bank's profit amounted to ISK 1.4 billion. A change was made to the rules on the Central Bank of Iceland's financial statements and financial statements last year, which included the termination of the calculation of a price change transaction. The Central Bank's equity continued to grow in the past year when the Treasury contributed to it with initial capital amounting to ISK 4.5 billion. At the end of 2001, the Bank's equity amounted to just over ISK 40 billion, compared with ISK 34 billion at the end of the previous year. The Central Bank's operating expenses in 2002 amounted to just under ISK 1.1 billion, including THE ISK 103 million cost of printing banknotes and mints and nearly ISK 40 million of real estate expenses. At the end of 2002, the Bank had 110.4 full-time equivalent positions and had increased by 21/2 during the year. The Bank's results and operations are detailed in its annual report, which is published today. Finnur Ingolfsson, CEO of the Bank, resigned at the end of September after nearly three years of service at the Bank. I take this opportunity to thank Finn Ingolfsson for a pleasant cooperation with the Board of Directors during his time as CEO. The Prime Minister installed Ingimundur Frioriksson as Deputy Governor of the Bank from 1 October to an indefinite period, but no longer than one year. The Prime Minister also re-appointed Birgi isleif Gunnarsson chairman of the Board of Directors from 1 February to the end of July 2006. The current Act on the Central Bank of Iceland states that the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland should be elected after elections to the Althingi. The term of office of a sitting Bank of England is therefore nearly over. The Board of Directors held 19 meetings in the year leading up to the meeting. I thank the members of the Board of Directors for their very enjoyable cooperation and well-done work. I also thank the Board of Directors and the Bank's employees for all the good work over the past year and a pleasant cooperation with the Board of Directors.

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 21. March 2013 Address Lara V. Juliusdottir, Chairman of the Board of Directors. Delivered at the 52nd Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 21 March 2013. Honorary Prime Ministers, Ministers, Governors, Ambassadors of Foreign Countries and other good guests. It has now been almost four years since the current Board of Directors took office and ahead of the parliamentary elections, a new Board of Directors will be elected. On this occasion, there is no way to look over the road and review the main challenges of the Board of Directors and the institution we operate for the past four years. When the Board of Directors began operations in the spring of 2009, the consequences of the banking collapse in October 2008 were to emerge with full force. Unemployment, economic recession, government deficits, currency shortages and debt crisis had to be tackled. The Central Bank had to undertake projects that do not belong to the normal operations of the Central Bank, and the newly elected Board of Directors had to work hard to resolve projects that were not precedented in the activities of boards of directors in the past. Here I mention the establishment of the Bank's Holding Company, which took over the operation of assets that collapsed after the bank collapsed. You can also mention the creation of the payment service. It has also had to enforce the currency controls that were deemed necessary to be imposed in relation to the economic plan of the government and the International Monetary Fund. The purpose of the measures is and must ensure the greatest stability in exchange rates and to prevent premature outflows of foreign exchange, which could undermine financial institutions and the country's economy. The Board of Directors closely monitored the progress of the IMF and government's economic plan, which ended in August 2011. It must be assumed that the results have been excellent, although all difficulties caused by the bank collapse are far from over. Among the unresolved tasks are emissions controls, the formulation of monetary policy for the future and, most importantly, meeting the Central Bank's primary objective, which is stable prices in line with its inflation target. Last year, the Central Bank of Iceland published a number of interesting publications and economic descriptions, the highest of which is the special publication Options in Currency and Exchange Rates. This extensive work provides a very good overview and analysis of Iceland's advantages in currency and exchange rates. I think that's where experts have laid a good foundation for an informed discussion on this important issue. I encourage as many people as possible to read this report and draw their own conclusions on which way Iceland is best suited in the future. 1 The annual report presented here briefly describes the varied activities within the walls of the Central Bank. There have been no changes in the Bank's management team over the past year. The number of employees was 178 at the end of last year. I will now briefly describe the financial performance and economy of the Central Bank of Iceland and its members. According to the operating accounts, profit for the year 2012 was more than ISK 14.3 billion, which is similar to the previous year's results. Interest income decreased by almost ISK 20 billion, mainly due to a decrease in interest income from domestic assets as well as a decrease in interest income from foreign deposits. Interest expenses decreased slightly, or by nearly a billion, and amounted to approximately ISK 27 billion. Net interest income therefore amounted to ISK 14.7 billion. The exchange rate difference was positive by ISK 4.7 billion, compared to ISK 7.4 billion in 2011. Other operating income increased by over ISK 700 million between years and amounted to ISK 5.4 billion at year-end. Operating expenses decreased by 70% between years from ISK 26.7 billion to nearly ISK 8 billion mainly due to reduced impairment of claims held by the Bank. The Central Bank's assets amounted to ISK 1,068 billion at year-end 2012 and ISK 1,581 billion in the previous year. The reason for the decrease is mainly prepayment of foreign loans by the Treasury and the Central Bank. About 53% of the initial loan amount was repaid from the IMF and 59% of initial borrowing with the Nordic countries. Assets in excess of liabilities, the Bank's equity, amounted to ISK 98.1 billion at year-end, an increase of ISK 14.3 billion. Income tax for companies owned by the Bank for the year 2012 amounts to just over ISK 2.2 billion. Dividend payments according to the rules on contributions to the Treasury amount to nearly ISK 2.2 billion. That's about 4.4 billion. Good attendees During the 2008 economic crash, public confidence in many community institutions, including the Central Bank, declined significantly. Trust and credibility are key to solving many of the problems the Central Bank deals with. I would like to mention the release of capital controls, the decrease in inflation expectations and the acquisition of credit domestically and abroad. It is an ambition for the current Board of Directors and all employees of the Bank that the Institution enjoys the trust of the people of Iceland and we believe that something has been achieved in this regard. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Board of Directors and the Bank's employees for their excellent cooperation during the year. I would also like to mention that in these four years I have worked with two bankers, Mar Guomundsson and Svein Harald oygard, and deputy CEO Arnor Sighvatsson. I would like to thank them for their excellent cooperation over the years. We are now listening to the address of the Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, after which Governor Mar Guomundsson will speak. 2
