Title: Speech on the objectives and role of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Jon Sigurdsson, Governor of the Central Bank: Objectives and roles of the Central Bank of Iceland 19 September 2005: 19 September 2005 Good belongings The Central Bank of Iceland operates in the environment of free money markets. This environment has changed and evolved in Iceland in recent years. The Central Bank operates in close contact with the so-called money markets and interbank markets, the krona market and the foreign exchange market. The Central Bank is the bank of the banks and the bank of the Treasury and it is a business center and security centre in the nation's financial system. The money markets are then in a multifaceted mutual relationship with other markets, the manufacturing markets and the services markets. We work in a free market economy where self-irresponsible parties meet in business. The Central Bank of Iceland aims all its activities to strengthen and strengthen the markets and ensure their stability and security. In the market, limited action, such as a slight increase or decrease in interest rates, - which is the cost of using capital -- works all over the market and affects the last or next decision, a decision that is on the periphery of paying off, making it easier or more difficult. Therefore, it is referred to as a marginal operation and a marginal effect. A minor change allows an increase in overall activity or, on the contrary, contraction and restraint in market activity. This needs to be kept in mind. Operating in a free market, with marginal and marginal effects. These measures are traded across the markets through a so-called trading process that takes a certain trading period, but in Iceland it is valued up to two years. First, the Central Bank's actions in these interbank markets work, causing banks' activities to become more expensive or cheaper and increase or decrease in the same way, and then this affects their activities in other markets. And that's how it continues to work throughout the economy, business and business. The main objectives of the Central Bank of Iceland are legislated by law. It should contribute to the stability of the development of prices, and on the basis of this inflation target, a special agreement has been reached with 2 the government that the inflation target should be based on 2.5 % in the past 12 months at any given time according to the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX. In addition, the Bank has set the objectives of promoting security in the nation's financial system and to take care of the nation's foreign exchange reserves and foreign exchange systems. It is the bank of the banks and the bank of the Treasury, as mentioned earlier, and it has patents for banknote printing and mint mint in the country. In addition, the Central Bank handles a wide range of communications with domestic and foreign entities and institutions. The description above the marginal measure of interest rate change in the money market applies to the Central Bank's interest rate changes. Here is full interest rate liberalisation and a free floating market rate on Icelandic the krona. The Central Bank's interest rate changes work across the financial system and affect other interest rates and, together with other forces of influence - at the exchange rate of the krona, but here no authority of the Central Bank applies. The effect of the Central Bank's interest rates works out across the system through a trading process during trading hours, which is why they are called controlling interest rates. Interest rate changes by the Central Bank of Iceland result in similar interest rate changes from commercial banks and other parties and work to increase or contract in business activities. The Central Bank of Iceland's policy rate is short-term interest rates, week-long lending rates, in so-called reversible transactions. These transactions are so named because in them the Central Bank lends the commercial banks liquidity for one week and then this transaction goes backwards and people renew them weekly according to the needs of the banking system. That's how they actually form a continuous chain. For example, the question is whether the activity is increasing, stagnating or decreasing, and interest rate changes are affecting all of this. In contrast to reversible transactions, the commercial banks, the Treasury and other financial institutions have business accounts for deposits in the Central Bank. Central banks use various methods for their economic management. For a long time people focused on direct interference in the development of money supply, with the so-called reserve requirement. This has been put off in many parts of our part of the world, as interest rate changes actually have the same kind of impact on activity in the economy but do so in a more balanced way as a general broad action and acts the same on all parties at once. People say that inflation has become so and so high, which is why the Central Bank must intervene with interest rate changes. It's not exactly right here. The Central Bank does not change its policy rate because inflation in the past 12 months has evolved this way or the other way around. The Central Bank makes decisions on the policy rate on the basis of forecasts for the time being. Inflation is measured by the consumer price index compared to the previous 12 months. But we 3 Decisions on control rates are people thinking about the future, about trading processes and trading hours. Of course, interest rates now and in the near future will not affect what has passed, but on the coming future. In order to be able to make these forward decisions, these decisions for the time being ahead, the Central Bank needs careful expert work, and the Bank has a select team of experts in economics, statistics, foreign exchange, financial studies and monetary policy to deal with the tasks. Monetary policy decisions are traditionally made based on forecasts and models that provide information about the outlook ahead. The Central Bank must be forward-looking in its actions and decisions, because all these actions or omissions primarily have an impact into the future. Other parties in the markets are also forward-looking in their actions. All contracts, loans and other transactions are based on plans for the time being and on expectations of what goes hand in hand during the contract or trading period. Expectations and foresight are the main factors and assumptions in the business and financial life. The expectations, so-called economic expectations, are the most important factor in progress when you look at everything. The bank must act in accordance with this. The impact of his actions is based on his having credibility and credibility is assessed, among other things, on these indicators in the free market. But in this, conditions dictate uncertainty and risk. People try to scrape ahead, trying to weigh and assess the status, outlook, efforts and trends in the economy. Central Bank analysts are constantly working to formulate forecasts for the future on a solid basis of academic and professional research. And decisions on control rates and other actions are based on these assumptions. The Central Bank has a goal to enforce and it has the tools and functions to use. No central bank controls the progress of the economy or trade in society. But a central bank can have a certain effect through a trading process during trading hours, as previously described. And by applying to the inflation target with changes in control rates, the Central Bank can have a significant impact on the value of the currency, in our case Icelandic the krona, and thus on the price trends on the whole. But then other governments will have to operate in the same direction and go ahead with the central bank. Other forces also have a huge impact on the progress. Activities in the state budget, surplus or deficit in the budget, the activities of the largest municipalities and the activities of major public institutions -; All of this matters. It is argued that there is no consistency between actions 4 Central Bank of Iceland and plans for fiscal affairs. The International Monetary Fund has expressed concern that the Central Bank must use its devices too harshly in these circumstances. It has also been pointed out that the municipalities are not pulling together. And the commercial banks and the Housing Financing Fund are responsible for overheating in lending, which is the main root cause of inflation at the moment. In discussions on exchange rate issues, attitudes are often heard from the time when the exchange rate was controlled by government measures. But now the exchange rate Icelandic the krona is a free floating market rate. The Central Bank of Iceland may affect the short-term development of the exchange rate, but other forces of influence act no less on the exchange rate. The exchange rate has played a role in the monetary policy trading process because the raised exchange rate beats inflation. But other currencies are also in motion, and changes in the economy are also having an impact. It is necessary to make a difference between nominal rates and real exchange rates and nominal interest rates. Real interest rates are the remaining interest rates when inflation has been taken into account. Clearly, real interest rates are much lower than nominal interest rates when inflation is in place. The real exchange rate measures changes in competitive positions between the Icelandic of the economy and other economies, with regard to labour costs and for general prices. Of course, the business community is interested in the nominal rate, but it's only for a short time. The main concerns of the economy, of course, are focused on the real exchange rate. The central bank does not have a formative effect on real exchange rates. That's where deeper economic forces work. The focus is now on working not with invitations and bans but through responsible participation in free market activities. Emphasis is placed on ensuring that all activities are transparent, that market participants and the public can understand the Central Bank's decisions and actions and can foresee the expected response to progress in the financial system and economy. In order to ensure this is the best possible, emphasis is placed on high-quality academic and professional practices in today's central banks, and they are entrusted with independence in the face of other governments. The Act on the Central Bank of Iceland contains provisions on the inflation target, whereas the Bank has full independence on actions, time of action and on its instruments and methods. The act contains provisions on a seven-member Board of Directors, which is responsible for supervision and consultation on various matters. The Board of Directors consists of three CEOs appointed for seven years each, one of whom is specifically appointed chairman of the Board of Directors, a special office. In various countries, in addition to the Board of Directors, there is a special monetary policy committee appointed by the Minister. It has become a means of entrusting the role of the Board of Directors to the Board of Directors of this Committee, as it is believed that this is how the Bank will be more independent in the face of a government than it would otherwise be. 5 People are asking if the Bank of Iceland's monetary policy has ceased to have an impact. In response, of course, it only works in the economy of the Icelandic krona. Iceland's business world has become global and our monetary policy only touches Icelandic part. But in this economy, monetary policy works as planned. If it doesn't work properly, then it may be because other governments and influential forces in business are straddling in other directions. As a result, the waves are higher than they would be if there was a fair consistency in the policies and actions of all involved. The Central Bank of Iceland has established rules on working methods for preparation and decisions on monetary policy, control rates and other matters in this context. These issues are constantly under review and processing among experts at the Bank. Every month, meetings are held to observe and draw conclusions. These meetings include the three GOVERNORS, deputy governor, five managing directors of special divisions and departments in the Bank, as well as several other experts. There are professional discussions and people try to weigh and assess the situation, prospects and forecasts. At the end of the day, the three governors make a decision based on the proposal of the Chairman of the Board of Directors. The decision is then made public by press release and media conference. In an agreement with the Government on the inflation target mentioned earlier, it was decided that if inflation rises above 4.0 % or below 1.0 % the Board of Directors shall send the Government a special report on the reasons and circumstances of inflation development and on the actions that the Bank will take in order to bring inflation to the inflation target of 2.5%, and furthermore with a forecast of how long this will presumably take. The Central Bank of Iceland is a business centre and security centre in the nation's financial system. But the Bank is also a service institution to the whole public, because it aims to ensure security and stability in the value of the krona, and that is of course one picture of the purchasing power of the public. I thank the audience.

Title: Speech by Governor at a breakfast meeting in Harpa
text: 28 November 2013 The financial crisis in Iceland and Ireland: what are the lessons five years later? Opening address at half-day Central Bank of Iceland conference in Harpa, Reykjavik, entitled The financial crisis in Iceland and Ireland: What are the lessons seen to be five years later? President of Iceland, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, On behalf of the Central Bank of Iceland, I would like to welcome you all to this morning meeting, held five years after the collapse of Icelands three cross-border banks, the enactment of the emergency legislation, and the beginning of the Icelandic authorities economic programme with the IMF. And incidentally, it is exactly five years ago today that Icelands Parliament, Alingi, passed legislation on comprehensive capital controls. At this short conference, which we call The financial crisis in Iceland and Ireland: what are the lessons five years later? the focus is on the situation that faced these and other small countries with big banks in the autumn of 2008, how we managed the first phase of the crisis, and the policies that were put in place to mitigate the effects of the shocks that were hitting us. Joining us today are three highly distinguished speakers who will take the floor after my opening remarks. First is Patrick Honohan, Governor of the Central Bank of Ireland, who took office in September 2009 and has played a key role in dealing with the crisis in Ireland. Then we will hear from Geir Haarde, Prime Minister of Iceland in the autumn of 2008, who oversaw both crisis management during the banking collapse and the design of the economic programme with the IMF. Our final speaker is Franek Rozwadowski, who until recently was the resident representative of the IMF in Iceland. It is well known, both in this country and among scholars of the international financial crisis around the world, that almost 90% of Icelands banking sector failed in the first week of October 2008. What is probably less well known is that at that point, Iceland was already on its way into a recession after an unsustainable boom and serious overheating during 20052007 and a currency crisis in the first half of 2008. The banking collapse and the associated wealth loss and further currency depreciation made the recession significantly worse, of course, as did the recession that hit the global economy in the fourth quarter of 2008. That autumn, two separate but interrelated sub-stories of the recent Icelandic saga converged in a tragic grand finale. These are: 1. Icelands boom-bust cycle and problems with macroeconomic management in small, open, and financially integrated economies. This is a story that has played out many times around the globe, and many of its elements have been seen before in Iceland. It might have been somewhat more extreme this time around, but it wasnt fundamentally different. 2. The rise and fall of three cross-border banks operating on the basis of EU legislation (the European passport). This story was much more unique, as it involved the first banking crisis in Europe since the EU single market was formed in the early 1990s. The combined balance sheet of these banks was 10 times Icelands GDP, and their combined bankruptcy, measured by the size of balance sheets, ranks third in size in the international history of corporate failures. And this happened in a country that ranks among the smallest in the world! We are still dealing with the repercussions of it, as can be seen in our overblown and unbalanced IIP and the controls on capital outflows. Before the collapse, the banking system had expanded very rapidly, growing in just five years from a combined balance sheet of less than 2 times GDP at the end of 2003 to the aforementioned 10 times GDP. Most of this expansion was cross-border, and a significant part of it was really offborder, having little to do with Iceland, as both financing and investment took place abroad. Around two-thirds of the balance sheet of the three cross-border banks was denominated in foreign currency. As is typical for banks, the FX part of the balance sheet had a significant maturity mismatch. However, there was no safety net of the type that we have in a national setting to back it up. This turned out to be the fatal flaw in the whole setup, although we now know that these banks were also undercapitalised, which might have done them in at a later stage. But so were also several European banks that were considered solid at the time! In the panic that gripped global financial markets after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, Icelands big banks were faced with a wholesale run on their foreign currency liabilities and were therefore heading towards a default on those liabilities in the absence of LOLR assistance in foreign currency. However, given their size, it was impossible for the Icelandic authorities to provide such assistance on their own. Liquidity risk was generally underestimated in the build-up to the crisis, both by the financial industry and by supervisors. This applied even more to FX liquidity risk, which can be more lethal due the lack of backstops and safety nets. For example, before the crisis, European banks had built up huge USD-denominated balance sheets that were balanced to a large extent  except, of course, in terms of maturity. This became a major problem when there was a run on such dollar-denominated bank liabilities postLehman, and many big European banking names might not be with us today had it not been for the USD swap lines granted to the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, and the Swiss National Bank. When I was still at the Bank for International Settlements, I gave a speech here in Iceland on financial globalisation to an audience of high-level European bankers. In that speech I discussed the risks associated with the internationalisation of banking and said:   emergency liquidity assistance will be complicated or even impossible for central banks to deliver when internationally active banks face liquidity problems in currencies other than that of their home country. Iceland is a case in point.1 That is essentially what happened in the autumn of 2008. But this was in May 2007, before the international financial crisis emerged in August that same year. Then it became gradually more obvious and the Icelandic authorities tried to build defences and seek international support, but with limited success. Given the lack of international cooperation, the Icelandic authorities were forced to consider radical solutions. Although they were probably not articulated fully at the time, these solutions entailed several goals: preserving a functioning domestic payment system, ring-fencing the sovereign in the case of bank failures, limiting the socialisation of private sector losses, and creating the conditions for the reconstruction of a domestic banking system. In essence, the adopted solution saved the domestic operations of the banking system and let the international part to go into a resolution process. The new banks were created by carving the domestic assets and liabilities out of the old, failing banks. The new banking system amounted to 1.7 times GDP. On the whole, these measures were successful, which was a key factor in mitigating the effect of the banks failure on the economy. The domestic payment system functioned more or less seamlessly throughout, and there was continuous access to deposits and basic banking services in Iceland. International payment flows were seriously affected, however, not least because of the freezing order imposed by the British authorities on Icelandic banks, but also because of a general distrust among foreign counterparties. Normal payment flows were restored through a concerted effort by the Central Bank in the ensuing months. 1 See : Financial globalisation and challenges for prudential policies and macroeconomic management, 18 May 2007, I have painted the banking crisis and the immediate policy responses with a broad brush, but I expect that Geir will give you a fuller story. It will also be interesting to hear from Patrick what the essential features of the Irish banking crisis unfolding around the same time are seen to be now, five years later. Let me turn now to the macroeconomic part of the saga. I do not have time to discuss the macroeconomic build-up to the crisis, as the focus of this short meeting lies elsewhere. But to set the stage, let me say very briefly that all the usual suspects were present: very strong capital inflows fuelling a credit and asset price boom that subsequently turned into a bubble at the same time as the economy overheated and an unsustainable external position developed, as could be seen in a double-digit current account deficit. And macroeconomic and prudential policies were not up to the task. Quite the contrary: there was a policy conflict between monetary policy and the demand levers pulled by the Government, and the risks inherent in capital flows, FX balance sheets, and credit and asset price booms were left under-regulated and insufficiently supervised. But as so often before in this country, we dealt more effectively with the crisis than the build-up. There were two key elements to this. The first was crisis management vis-a-vis the failing banks, as embodied in the Emergency Act submitted by Prime Minister Geir Haarde to Parliament shortly before the banks failed. The second was the economic programme developed by the Icelandic authorities in co-operation with the IMF. The programme had three key goals: stabilisation of the exchange rate, fiscal sustainability, and reconstruction of the financial sector. Comprehensive capital controls were an important element in the programme, but their rationale was to help to stabilise the exchange rate in a situation where the currency had fallen more than 50% in 2008, where foreign krona positions that were a legacy of carry trade and capital inflows amounted to around 40% of GDP, and where a large fiscal deficit that had to be financed in the domestic market had developed. The capital controls therefore gave monetary policy more scope to help stabilise and turn around the real economy once inflation came down. Franek will discuss the IMF programme in more detail, but I would like to make one more remark regarding fiscal consolidation, as it is such an important part of the story. The crisis hit Government finances hard, as can be seen from this slide. It was therefore of vital importance that Government debt was relatively low immediately before the crisis. However, fiscal consolidation was needed earlier than some considered optimal at the time from a demand management perspective, in order to regain internal and external confidence and open market access. The effort was huge, as can be seen from this slide, but back-loaded, as automatic stabilisers were mostly allowed to work in 2009. And it did not derail the recovery that began around the middle of 2010. The policy responses mitigated the recession but could not stop it from becoming the deepest in Icelands post-war history and a severe one in international comparison, as can be seen from this slide. But Iceland was not the hardest hit, as can also be seen from the slide, and this would be still clearer if we were to look at the labour market. Iceland lost 12% of GDP from peak to trough, slightly more than Ireland. However, as was probably also the case in Ireland, that peak was unsustainable and was associated with a significant positive output gap. Iceland has regained 7% since, which is significantly more than Ireland but less than Latvia, which suffered a much deeper recession. Finally, I would like to mention selected lessons that I think can be drawn from this experience. First, dealing with failing big banks in small countries: Guaranteeing the entire banking system in Icelands case would probably have resulted in sovereign default and the bankruptcy of the country. In general, taking such a step with big banks in small countries is risky, especially if a significant part of their balance sheets are in foreign currencies. The alternative is to save only key infrastructure elements, such as the domestic payment system. Second, dealing with volatile capital flows: Deal with the inflows if you want to avoid having to take drastic measures to deal with the outflows. That includes adopting correctly aligned macroeconomic and macroprudential policies, leaning into the wind by buying part of the inflows into foreign exchange reserves and, in the limit, deploying selective capital inflow management tools. The FX risks of banks and private sector entities need close monitoring and prudential limitations. Third, the design of the financial sector in small, open economies: The financial sector has to be smaller than it has been in countries like Iceland, and international activities must be restricted as long as such countries are not part of a credible multilateral safety net. The idea of building international financial centres in countries like Iceland and Ireland is dead  for the time being, at least  as it is not safe under the current framework. Fourth, the EU framework for cross-border banking: It was very much this framework that facilitated the cross- and off-border expansion of the Icelandic banks through the so-called European passport. It was and is deeply flawed, and it contributed in a significant way to both the Icelandic banking crisis and the crisis in the eurozone. The basic problem is that the freedoms are not matched by public action and frameworks at the EU and EEA level. Bank size relative to country size was tacitly assumed to be a matter of no concern, and FX risk was largely ignored. Based on the Icelandic experience, a banking union makes perfect sense, but only fully for the eurozone, and even then it has to include all three elements in order to break the deadly embrace of banks and sovereigns. In the interim, I think small countries will have to impose their own prudential measures in order to defend themselves against the risks they face. Let me conclude here and give the floor to Patrick Honohan.

Title: Statement at the Breakfast Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce
text: 22.05.2002 Statement by Birgiur isl. Gunnarsson at the Breakfast Meeting of the Chamber of Commerce Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland gave a speech at a breakfast meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday 22 May 2002. The speech is published here on the Central Bank of Iceland website. At the end of the speech you can see a link to the pictures that Bird used for clarification with his speech: Good attendees Three questions are posed in the conference, which are: What are the outlooks for prices' Lower interest rates further' How does the status of exchange rates come to the economy' I will endeavour to answer these questions at the time I have at my disposal and start with the pricing issues, as it is the central bank's main role under the law to promote stable prices. So far this year, the 12-month rise in the consumer price index has declined rapidly. Inflation thus measured peaked in January, when it was 9.4%, the highest inflation measured since October 1990. In May, the 12-month inflation rate was 5.9%. As inflation increased in Iceland over the past year, it declined in the major trading countries. So far this year, it has averaged 11/2%-2% in trading countries, but somewhat higher in Europe, or roughly 21/2% in the Eurozone. In the past year, there is no need to multiply this time. Her reasons have been discussed in detail before, including at breakfast meetings here at the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce. I'm going to focus first and foremost on the transition in pricing issues that have occurred this year, their reasons and how permanent they are. Services in the general market weigh nearly a quarter of the consumer price index. In May, it had risen by 8.9% in 12 months, so it has played a significant role in inflation. General services are susceptible to wage increases, but it is interesting that it has stagnated for the last three months. The price of public services has over the past three months fallen slightly, and there is a strong government action. In May there are first clear signs of a fall in house prices, but the housing stock index has been rising steadily for quite some time. The Central Bank's monetary policy has created grounds for declining inflation. So far this year, three factors have contributed to the deterioration of inflation: the increase in the exchange rate since the end of November, the deterioration of demand tensions and the actions of the People's Liberation Army aimed at providing trade and public bodies with restraint in price decisions. Asi's pressure on providers of public services has resulted in at least 1/2% lower consumer price index than otherwise. It is more difficult to assess the extent of the impact on trade because it is difficult to distinguish them from other factors that have contributed to lower price increases or lower prices at the same time. Reduced demand for durable and semi-durable products limits the store's scope for a price increase. A figure shows that there is still some lack of the rate cut that occurred last year in the price of a durable and semi-durable imported goods. This, together with another, encourages some caution in determining interest rates, but this effect may never occur, that this gap seen there will not close, among other things, due to increased competition in the store. The Central Bank publishes a quarterly inflation forecast and the last forecast was published at the beginning of May. Let's first look at its main premises. Wages are expected to change in line with collective wage agreements, but less wage momentum is now expected than in previous forecasts. In the past, there has been clearer evidence than before that tensions in the labour market and in the economy as a whole are turning into slack. This is reflected in less pay momentum over the last few months than in recent years. It is now expected that wage momentum over this year will be only 1/2% and that there will be nothing over 2003. In The last forecast, however, was expected to be 1% payroll momentum over each year. Over 2004, 1% of wage momentum is expected to happen with a decent balance in the national economy. The prerequisites for productivity growth in 2002-2003 remain unchanged from the last forecast. Assumptions about the development of import prices in foreign currencies take into account the calculations and forecasts of the International Monetary Fund and the OECD on the development and prospects of prices in international trade and the futures price of oil in the global market. As usual, the exchange rate is expected to remain unchanged from the forecast date, but at the time of the forecast the exchange rate index was 133 points. In fact, it has risen since this value and was on record yesterday 129.4 points. All of these assumptions are given, inflation is forecast to be 2.8% from the start to the end of this year, which is slightly lower than forecast in February. However, the forecast is more significant over 2003. Inflation is now forecast at 2.3%, but 3% in the last forecast. Inflation is expected to fall below the 41/2% tolerance level in the autumn, and remain below the 4% tolerance limit in 2003 and be down to the 21/2% inflation target by the end of 2003 and fall below the target in early 2004 with unchanged monetary policy. Forecasts are always accompanied by some uncertainty and the greater the predicted ahead, which is why this figure shows uncertainties. I will not elaborate on them here but refer to a detailed discussion in Monetary Bulletin published on the Bank's website at the beginning of May and will be published in print tomorrow. I'm going to give you the indications that the tensions in the economy have been significantly relaxed all the way until the second half of 2001. There have been clear signs in recent months that tensions in the labour market are being significantly relaxed. Rising unemployment at the end of last year and so far this year suggests a reduction in excess demand for labour. From April last year to the same month this year, unemployment rose from 2.1% to 3.2%. Employment declined and the number of hours worked per week fell from 43.7 to 42.8 during the 12 months. This development raises the question of whether there has already been a slack in the labour market. That the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate should still be at the lower limit of the projected equilibrium unemployment rate, which could be 21/2-31/2%, does not suggest that this is conclusive. Decreasing tensions in the labour market have led to a sharp decline in wage momentum, as I have already mentioned, and indeed so that no wage momentum was measured between the fourth quarter of 2001 and the first quarter of 2002, and there is evidence of negative wage momentum for individual groups. There is a number of other indications that tensions in the economy have been significantly relaxed. Private consumption has decreased significantly and the annual decline in national expenditure in the third quarter of 2001 was 7.3%. Economic growth, however, was fairly high in the last quarter of 2001, or 4.6% from the same quarter the previous year. There must be reservations on quarterly measurements, but according to the latest figures from the National Institute for National Statistics, economic growth in the whole of 2001 was 3%, which is far more than might have been expected given the public debate almost all of last year. Recent evidence of turnover seems to support the view that there has been a slowdown in private consumption. Credit card sales, for example, have declined at an increasing pace since the end of 2001. The lending expansion of depositors is now fully deflated. It must be taken into account that exchange rate and indexed loans increase nominal value in line with the price increase of currencies or the price indices they are tied to. Without this update, the 12-month growth in lending by depositors was steadily declining last year and by the end of the year had reached just under 71/2%. This trend has continued this year. Similarly, lending by depositors increased by almost 21/2% in the first three months of the year converted to an annual change. If you look at the credit system as a whole, you still can't say the same thing. Other credit institutions somewhat picked up the slack in lending rates for depositors last year. For example, pension funds' treasury loans increased by nearly 28% in the twelve months to the end of February, which corresponds to about 17% in real interest rates. However, it seems to have slowed down their increase in recent months. The increase in housing loans has also been huge. They increased by 19% last year, or by just over 91/2% in real terms. As a whole, lending increased by 181/2% last year or without exchange rate and price updates by nearly 8%. In recent years there has been a lot of production voltage in the national economy, i.e. production has been much higher than the production capacity. This production voltage peaked in 2000. It was also very high in 2001, but it is now expected that this year the production voltage will disappear, with slight slack forming and peaking next year, when it will be just over 1%. Such slack is necessary for the time being to ensure normal balance and price stability. The question is often heard as to whether the momentum of price hikes will now rage over when it is clear that the red canvases held. Of course, there may be some increases that have been postponed until the beginning of May. It is, however, the Central Bank's view that this will not be the case to any extent that distorts the inflation resolution the Bank has forecast this year. So I'll give you the prospects for further interest rate cuts. In order to counteract the tensions raised here in 1999, the Central Bank raised its policy rate in stages steadily until the end of 2000 that the Bank's policy rate had reached 11.4%. Given the improving inflation outlook and sluggish tensions, the Fed has cut its policy rate three times this year, or by 1.3 percentage points. Since November, the Bank has cut its interest rate by 2.1 percent. Its policy rate is now 8.8%, 2.6 percentage points lower than when it was at its highest level. Despite these declines, monetary policy remains restrained if you look at inflation expectations and inflation forecasts. It is therefore strongly the Central Bank's view that it is desirable for its real interest rates to continue to fall in coming months. In the debate on interest rates, however, one must not forget the Central Bank's main objective of keeping inflation around 21/2%. The existing inflation forecast, which, among other things, is based on the indicators I have mentioned, suggests that there will be assumptions to lower interest rates further in the coming months. However, the Bank considers it preferable to do so in more and smaller steps than few and large ones. This would also be in line with the Bank's interest rate hikes at the time, as well as the fact that central banks in general consider it more desirable to stand up to interest rate changes, because too big steps can have a devastating impact. It's not about the money market. The next price measurements will, of course, dictate a lot of interest rate cuts in the coming months. I'm just going to go back to this year's exchange rate. The Central Bank persistently argued over the past year that the decrease in the exchange rate of the Icelandic krona after it floated towards the end of March 2001 and until the end of November was beyond economic assumptions in the long term. Indeed, the decline could be explained by an imbalance in the foreign exchange market due to trade deficits and other foreign exchange outflows, as well as expectations and mistrust. However, the rate cut was considerably higher than was needed to achieve external and internal equilibrium in the national economy as well. The real exchange rate of the krona in the fourth quarter of the past year was almost 15% below the ten-year historical average and there were various other arguments that it would rise in the coming months. The question was first and foremost whether it would happen with a nominal rate increase or rising inflation. Last year's trade deficit was significantly reduced and that trend will continue this year. It is also possible that he will disappear with everything. This reversal is only partly explained by the exchange rate cut in the krona. There is also a decline in national expenditure resulting from the Central Bank's monetary policy and that household and business spending had become so high that they had to rebound regardless of changes in the exchange rate of the krona. The real exchange rate in the second quarter of this year is estimated to be approximately 81/2% higher than in the previous quarter of 2001 compared to relative prices and just under 15% based on relative labor costs per unit. This would mean that the real exchange rate would start to slog up in the exchange rate in the first quarter of last year, before the biggest rate cut occurred. The estimated real exchange rate in the second quarter of that year will be about 7% or 2% below the ten-year average depending on whether it is based on consumer prices or labor costs per unit. There is a lot of uncertainty about what the balanced exchange rate of the krona is at any given time and it is of course one of the advantages of the inflation target that the monetary authorities do not have to form a detailed examination of it. However, it is very difficult to conclude now that the exchange rate has exceeded the equilibrium rate. The position of the Icelandic of the krona at the moment should by no means be an inhibitor of Icelandic business. The outlook for foreign exchange flows to and from the country gives rise to the assumption that a good balance should be able to prevail in the foreign exchange market this year. Good finders, the progress that now seems to be being achieved in rebuilding stability and bringing inflation down to normal levels is primarily the result of the austerity of monetary policy that has been followed in recent times. High interest rates have reduced investment and private consumption, which in turn has contributed simultaneously to a smaller trade deficit and a better balanced labour market. As a result, wage momentum has stopped and companies must increase productivity and reduce costs instead of raising prices. It turns out once again that inflation is a monetary phenomenon. The initiative of the social partners was created in this soil and came at the right time. This was extremely important and undoubtedly contributed to the acceleration of inflation resolution and that it is likely to eventually come with lower costs in the form of lost economic growth and unemployment than it would otherwise be. As a whole, there is no choice but to Icelandic economy has come out of good shape in recent times, and there is no reason other than to look brightly at the future in terms of prices, economic growth and living standards. Title: Chief Economist's article on whether public debt can be reduced without anyone bearing the cost in Frttablai on February 23, 2012
text: 23.02.2012 Thorarinn G. Petursson's article on whether public debt can be reduced without anyone bearing the cost in Frettablaoio on February 23, 2012 orarinn G. Petursson, chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland, wrote an article in Frettablaoio on 23 February 2012 (also published on visir.is) titled: Is it possible to bring down public debt without anyone bearing the cost? The article is accessible here: Is it possible to reduce public debt without anyone bearing the cost? The demands for a general debt cancellation are noisy and there are regular reports of various people who believe they have found a way to do so without anyone bearing that cost. It's not: in the end, someone has to bear the cost of such write-offs, and that's probably largely Icelandic taxpayers. Route 0 The most obvious way to bring down the public debt is for the owners of the loans, i.e. national credit institutions, to bring these debts down by writing them off. For example, if this is 200 ma.kr. (a common figure in the general debate on the issue), diminishes the equity of these credit institutions as a result. Since taxpayers are mostly owners of these loans (through their assets at the Housing Financing Fund and Landsbankinn), they bear most of the costs. The remainder hits domestic pension funds and foreign owners of other credit institutions. It is not impossible that part of the rest (or even all) will eventually hit taxpayers as these entities try to claim government cash benefits in court. Route 1 Someone thought they had found a way past letting taxpayers pay the bill by having the Fed print money for the amount, allowing the public debt to be brought down without any costs incurred. On closer inspection, it turns out that it doesn't add up at all. To understand that, it is extremely important to realize that money generated by the Central Bank (either through their "actual" printing or through the electronic increase in deposits of credit institutions in the Central Bank) is the Central Bank's commitment and is therefore on the bank's debt side. The Fed is printing 200 ma.kr. to bring down public debt, a debt is generated on the Central Bank's balance sheet of 200 ma.kr. but no asset to offset (he acquires 200 ma.kr. public debt to credit institutions but brings it down to nothing by writing it off). That means that something else on the central bank's debt side needs to be reduced in return for this to work out accountingly. This is the central bank's equity, which scraps them by 200 ma.kr. And what about it, someone can say. Sure, the Central Bank is owned by the taxpayer and the deterioration of its capital is therefore nothing more than an account of the taxpayer in the same way as in Route 0, except that in this case, the taxpayer definitely bears the entire cost undivided. Route 2 In an attempt to avoid diminishing the Central Bank's equity in this way, someone else thought it would be a good idea to create a separate holding company owned by the Central Bank and that the losses could be transferred so that it could not be seen on the Bank's balance sheet. A closer look reveals that it doesn't matter, of course. At first glance, the Fed's balance sheet would certainly look better: it would have 200 ma.kr. property (claim to this holding company) versus the increase in obligations due to the money printing. But the holding company's balance sheet now has 200 ma.kr. liabilities to the Central Bank but no asset (the Company acquires a 200 ma.kr. public debt to credit institutions but brings it down to nothing by writing it off). The equity of the holding company is therefore negative by 200 ma.kr. and the Central Bank owns the holding company that is worthless and therefore ultimately has to write off what gives exactly the same result as in Route 1. Route 3 Once again, someone thought they had found a way past this. What if the Central Bank prints money, gives it to debtors but on the condition that they pay down their loans and on the condition that credit institutions put that money right back into the Central Bank that put them back into the holding company? In that case, the Fed should certainly have 200 ma.kr. property (claim to the holding company) versus 200 ma.kr. increase in obligations due to the money printing and the holding company should also have 200 ma.kr. property (the money deposited by the Central Bank from credit institutions) versus 200 ma.kr. his debt to the credit institutions. The claim of home credit institutions has therefore effectively been changed to their claim to the holding company. The claim is therefore not gone, and the cost of writing it off lands either on credit institutions or the Central Bank. That 200 ma.kr. the payment of credit institutions into the Central Bank's holding company is tied up for ever (and therefore effectively taken ownership), this is essentially a lost asset for the credit institutions as they can never redeem it to themselves and use it (the same result as Route 0). However, if the credit institutions can access this asset, the loss will ultimately be the Central Bank (the same result as Routes 1 and 2). Final words Although the debts of domestic households and businesses have fallen considerably over the past two years, they are still heavily indebted and many are living in difficult debt positions. So the resolution of their debt issues is urgent. However, a general debt reduction to all is an extremely incoherent action as a large part of it would ideally benefit those who need it little. It would also be very costly, and that cost would have to be Icelandic taxpayers to bear one way or another. Pretending it's not is both misleading and irresponsible. The writer is chief economist at the Central Bank of Iceland.

Title: Statement by the Chairman of the Board of Directors at an international conference in Reykjavk in June 2004
text: Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors Price stability and financial stability in Iceland1 On behalf of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this conference on the interaction between price stability and financial stability in small open economies. It is an honor for the Central Bank of Iceland to hold the conference in cooperation with SUERF2. We are grateful to David Llewellyn, Eduard Hochreiter, Beatrix Krones and Michael Bailey of SUERF for their particularly pleasing cooperation in preparing the conference. In particular, I welcome the conference's keynote speaker Andrew Crockett, governor of JP Morgan Chase International and former governor of the World Bank of Basel. The topic of the conference is timely and enjoys increasing attention both inside and outside central banks. I am confident that presentations and discussions at the conference will increase our understanding of the interplay between price stability and financial stability and on factors that we will choose to focus our attention on in the coming days. In this regard, we will enjoy the guidance of accredited contributors and participants. I thank those who kindly agreed to have a presentation at the conference and submit essays, and I look forward to hearing their contributions. In what follows, I will briefly describe our own experiences in the field of price stability and financial stability. The current Act on the Central Bank of Iceland was passed in 2001. With them, the Central Bank was entrusted with the primary objective of promoting stable prices. The Bank was granted so-called instrumental independence, i.e. independence in order to work unhindered towards its main objective, the Bank's financial independence was strengthened, and the act included clear provisions on transparency and financial statements towards the government and the public. The act also stipulates that the Central Bank should promote an active and secure financial system, including payment systems in Iceland and abroad. In other words, the Bank was entrusted with tasks in the field of financial stability as well as working towards the main objective of stable prices. 1 Address at the opening of a conference between SUERF and the Central Bank of Iceland in Reykjavik on 3 June 2004; translated from English. 2 Societe Universitaire Europeenne de Recherches Financieres. English name The European Money and Finance Forum. This is a consortium of economists at universities, commercial banks and central banks. At the same time as the law came into force, a joint statement by the government and the Central Bank adopted an inflation target. It became the ballast of monetary policy. The inflation target was defined as a 21/2% increase in the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX over a twelve-month period. This framework requires very high-quality practices on the part of the Central Bank. The Bank regularly publishes macroeconomic and inflation forecasts. The inflation forecast is the ballast of the inflation target policy. In its quarterly publication, Monetary Bulletin, the Bank publishes a detailed analysis of the progress and outlook for economic and monetary policy. It also publishes the Board of Directors' arguments for decisions in interest rates, as well as providing clear evidence of what to expect in the implementation of monetary policy as we look ahead. In this respect, the Bank seeks to speak as clearly as possible. When the inflation target was set to be the ballast of monetary policy, there was a strong imbalance in the economy. A lot of tension began in the second half of the last decade. In the beginning, it was characterized by direct foreign investment and exports, and then the economy was relatively well balanced. Later, the expansion turned into overheating and strong growth in private consumption, which was driven by, among other things, the rapid growth of lending in the financial market, where freedom of action had been greatly increased. An imbalance developed in the national economy. Over time, the growing imbalance led to a change in expectations for the worse, at least in part due to the rapidly growing trade deficit with foreign countries. The exchange rate began to fall, falling by a third in a year and a half until late 2001. This progress was affected by inflation as rising import prices were reflected in domestic prices. When the inflation target was adopted, the increase in the consumer price index over the last twelve months was 4%. The exchange rate of the krona continued to fall for the time being, and inflation climbed considerably above the upper tolerance of the inflation target. The Central Bank followed an adhering to monetary policy and steadily raised its policy rate to a historic high. In the end, this led to a rapid decline in inflation, having peaked in January 2002. By the end of that year, it was below the inflation target, and thus has remained the longest since the latest measurement. The Central Bank has now had an inflation target for over three years. We believe this policy has been effective. Inflation was relatively rapidly accelerated after the new policy was adopted at a time of great imbalance in the national economy. There are also clear signs that the inflation target has gained credibility in the markets and in society as a whole. Rather, this policy will be tested in the near future, which will include exceptionally high direct foreign investment in the aluminium industry and the construction of connected power plants that will be financed by borrowing. SI-17470 2 Our experience strongly suggests that the policy of inflation targets can be followed in small open economies just as in large economies with robust financial markets. The policy requires a lot of discipline and expertise from central banks. The emphasis placed on financial stability in the Central Bank Act of 2001 is normal and in line with the accepted objectives of the Central Bank. The Central Bank of Iceland was responsible for banking supervision until the end of 1998, when it was combined with supervision of the activities of insurance companies in a new institution, the Financial Supervisory Authority, with which the Central Bank cooperates closely. While the Central Bank was responsible for banking supervision, its attention was of course focused on individual institutions and supervision that their activities were compatible with applicable laws and regulations. Prior to the transfer of banking supervision from the Central Bank, the Bank had already turned its attention to financial stability in a broader sense in a parallel way as other central banks at the time. This was part of the fact that in 2000 the Bank began publishing twice a year reports on financial stability in its quarterly publication, Monetary Bulletin. One reason the Bank was increasingly focusing on financial stability in a broader sense over the last decade was that, along with increased freedom in financial markets, an understanding that a weak financial system could undermine economic and monetary stability in the same way that economy imbalances and sluggish economic policies could undermine a stagnant financial system. A sound financial system, including secure payment and settlement systems, is also an important prerequisite for effective monetary policy. The last restrictions on capital transfers between Iceland and other countries were lifted in the middle of the last decade. Free speech increased in the financial market, and there were significant structural changes. Thus, over time, the Treasury reduced direct ownership of domestic banking institutions and completely disappeared from it. This progress led to fierce competition by financial institutions in the domestic market and linked the domestic capital market to a much closer bond with global capital markets. As a result, in its analysis of financial stability, the Central Bank traditionally focuses its attention on the sensitivity of the financial system to changes in the external environment, including the availability of foreign credit for refinancing, and the sensitivity of the financial system to sudden changes in the exchange rate of the krona. The progress in the Icelandic of the economy in the second half of the last decade and so far was in many ways comparable to what happened elsewhere in the Nordic region over a decade ago. It is not necessary to say that the experience there gave rise to some concern about the underlying strength of Icelandic financial system. The Central Bank frankly expressed concern in its financial stability reports, perhaps clarified in May 2001. At the same time, the International Monetary Fund published its assessment of the Icelandic financial system and expressed concern about the strength of the financial system in the face of massive imbalances in the national economy and a relatively weak banking system, according to fund experts. The Experts SI-17470 3 pointed to the rapid decline in the exchange rate of the krona and would weaken the position of the banks and pose a risk to them. In the first half of the expansion period, when lending and foreign borrowing grew at their fastest pace, not least foreign short-term loans, the Central Bank imposed liquidity reprieve on depositors. The purpose of this was to restrain the growth of foreign loans and force their longer loan periods. Another precautionary principle established by the Central Bank concerns the foreign exchange balance of the banks. It greatly limits their ability to take direct currency risk. In addition to these rules, the Central Bank may endeavour to influence the banks with public pressure, e.g. in its financial stability reports and through other official or unofficial statements and messages. The Bank has used all these means with varying degrees of success. In accordance with the traditional role of such a bank, the Central Bank of Iceland may grant so-called loans to devolved administrations if a domestic bank runs into liquidity difficulties. The Central Bank has also systematically built up foreign exchange reserves in order to strengthen the economy's liquidity outwards. The adjustment of the Icelandic economy after the overheating period from 1998 to 2001 was particularly confrontational. I mentioned earlier that inflation had fallen below the Central Bank's inflation target in late 2002. A trade deficit of 10% of GDP in 2000 was completely gone in 2002, lending growth stopped, and unlike in some parts of the Nordic region at the beginning of the last decade, Icelandic banks remained relatively solid at the end of the adjustment and have strengthened their position significantly since. No doubt there are a number of explanations for this rather favorable progress. For example, good external conditions during the transition period, sequestration of fiscal policy, the rapid disappearance of the trade deficit with foreign countries, the rapid reversal of the exchange rate after it was minimal and the rapid decline in inflation in 2002. In 2003, the International Monetary Fund followed up on its 2001 assessment, pointing out how well the Icelandic economy's adaptation had been successful, greatly increasing the strength of the financial system and important changes in laws and regulations on financial institutions and supervision of them. As I have already mentioned, the stability of prices is the main objective of the Central Bank of Iceland's monetary policy. The second main objective is to promote the stability of the financial system. The Bank's analysis of financial stability focuses on macroeconomic factors and the strength and position of the financial system as a whole. The Bank is working towards these main objectives with great professional ambition. These two challenges actually support each other in the Bank's work and enjoy the close cooperation of the Bank's employees. Both challenges have led the Central Bank to look further ahead than it would otherwise in its assessment of the outlook for economic and monetary policy and the formulation of its policies. This should lead to improved economic and monetary policy controls. SI-17470 4 There is still much blurred about the interaction between price stability and financial stability, but I mentioned previously that a solid financial system is a prerequisite for economic stability and monetary stability and effective monetary policy, and that sluggish economic policies could undermine stagnant financial institutions. Since freedom was implemented in the domestic financial market, we have never been in a position where concerns about progress relating to the position of financial institutions have been directly affected or contrary to monetary policy decisions. Our goal is to prevent this from happening. The risk that may have been posed to the financial system at the end of the last expansion period disappeared due to the rapidly establishing stable prices and achieving internal and external balance in the national economy. I repeat that I welcome you to this conference and expect your stay here to be enjoyable. SI-17470 5

Title: Talk on changes in the real estate loan market and more
text: Good attendees Icelandic households have benefited from the development of an economy in recent years. Purchasing power has grown, the employment situation has been excellent and new possibilities have opened up in the credit market. Asset prices have risen sharply, pension savings have increased and profited well when looking over a long period of time. Household debt in Iceland is on the higher side compared to various other countries, but household equity is also on the higher side, so the net position is well acceptable. Things are good and hopefully it will get even better. But there may be dangers along the way. Easy access to credit invites home the risk of too far being reached. Asset prices are high and may not remain high in the long term. I'm going to address only the changes that have taken place in the real estate loan market, the risks of households from high leverage, encourage moderation and common sense, and ultimately briefly discuss the Central Bank and its role. There was a lot of reform in the credit market last year. The Housing Financing Fund rode the wad in the middle of the summer with the restructuring of its securities issue and a more targeted market connection of interest rates. In the autumn, there was considerable competition in the real estate loan market after KB Bank and later other credit institutions began offering real estate loans to the public. This resulted in interest rates on real estate loans falling considerably, and the refinancing of older and less favourable loans opened up new dimensions in this market. It should be welcomed that interest rates on housing loans have fallen recently and the possibilities for refinancing older loans have been used by many to ease the payload or to shorten loans. But often the opportunity has also been used to further increase the debt, and we have strong evidence that loans taken to refinancing mortgages have been used for leverage beyond the loans that were being repaid. It is estimated that the average increase in leverage can be around 10-12%. New loans from banks and savings banks with mortgages in residential housing amounted to about 120 ma.kr. at the end of last year, which could mean increasing the public budget by 12 - 14 ma.kr. A lot of real estate transactions have as a result of these changes, property prices have spurred up and is now the main root cause of consumer price increases in recent months. If we now deviate from household risk of leverage, there are four factors they should consider before the arc is upstaged: payment burdens, mortgage assets, exchange rate risk and inflation. While the proportion of household expenditures has soared in recent decades, it can be difficult to deny yourself various consumption items in everyday life, so the part of household money to be used for debt installments is needed. It's hard to get involved in this stuff. A slight disruption to the running of the home can have a sad effect on family life and existence. Sometimes people assume that assets can be freed up without notice to pit debt, but it doesn't necessarily go ahead, sometimes money is lost on instant sale of assets. More often than not, it is also too late and the damage will be greater as a result. A modest payload is the best advice. Nowadays, you can buy insurance that can be taken in the event of an unexpected incident and makes sense for a household to consider it. The key to the home's payment capacity is to plan off. Another issue of liquidity is the loan term. When investing in assets that last for a long time, it is normal to distribute payments over a long period of time. There's nothing wrong with borrowing money for a few decades. The other should be kept in mind, however, that income during the lifetime of an ordinary family can decrease when taking a pension. In itself, everyone has the option to set aside a larger share of income than is required for pension savings, but most people do not choose to do so. Therefore, it is natural not to commit for too long, it can lead to hardship when it was least necessary. The temptation to reduce the payload in the present at the expense of longer bindings is high, but it can be precarious. For example, it is highly illogical to borrow for a car purchase that lasts longer than the intended use of the vehicle. It can lead to a snowball effect of debt accumulation that is difficult to get away from. Overpricing is another risk factor that households need to consider. A report commissioned by the Central Bank for The Minister of Social Affairs last year (published on the Central Bank's website in November) published the conclusion of a study on the impact of property price changes on mortgage eligibility. It applied, among other things, a statistical model that simulated price changes and looked at how many cases there would be overpricing of the assets. One conclusion was that if property prices exceeded 30% above the average price of the past 20 years, it would be almost certain that a 90% mortgage would exceed the market value of the property. That is, it is almost certain that the property would be overpriced sometime during the loan period, probably preferably in the first few years after the loan was taken. The price of the real estate market in Iceland is about 50% from the calculated average for the past 20 years. It can therefore be assumed that it will not be very long before the situation arises that some households will look forward to losing funds if the apartment needs to be freed up by selling at an unfavourable time. In the last six years, property prices in the capital area have increased by 100%. It doesn't take much expertise to predict that prices can fall significantly in a relatively short period of time. Such a decline could prove disastrous for households. For example, you can take a property purchased at ISK 20 million and mortgaged 90% for a loan. If property prices suddenly fall by 20%, the value of the property on the market is ISK 16.7 million, while the loan stands at ISK 18 million. This is not to blame if the household's liquidity has been properly assessed, then the loan will continue to be paid off and it is possible of course that the price will rise again and everything will be honoured. However, if the home has to sell the property after a price cut, another equity or there will be a need for increased borrowing. This can put you at risk of home bankruptcy. The demand for real estate here in the capital area has for some time been greater than the supply, but there is no law that there is a persistent situation. Fluctuations in supply and demand are well-known, and the option of building yourself has reliably become more prosperous now than in the past as market prices are higher than construction costs. However, the risk of overpriced mortgages is not just a risk to households, it can also hit banks, savings banks and the Housing Financing Fund badly for. It is therefore important that this risk factor is considered before a home owes itself for residential purchases. From conversations with various people, I have come to understand that there is a lot of car loans being partially or completely exchange-oriented. This has been able to finance automotive purchases at low interest rates, and lately the exchange rate trend has been extremely favourable to those who owe rate-based loans, not to put it stronger. It is understandable that this is tempting many. It should be kept in mind, however, that interest rates abroad have been unusually low for some time and interest rate hikes have already begun in several countries that will burden the payload. Interest rates in This country are also rising and the interest rate differential is in such a way that it encourages foreign borrowing. The second factor, however, is probably more important than there is an exchange rate effect. We don't have to look far back in time to find a more than 30% drop, followed by a similar rise Icelandic the krona. From mid-2000 to late 2001, the Icelandic isk decreased by 35%. It is probable that a foreign loan can be very favourable if you look over a period of several years, but fluctuations in installments due to exchange rate developments can be high and they can prove heavy-handed if there is a narrow estate. For a household that only has income in Icelandic ISK, it may be a warning to take exchange rate risk beyond the impact on commodity prices due to exchange rate changes. Inflation is one of the main enemies of households because the biggest household debt, the real estate loans, is by far part indexed. We Icelanders have fought many hilarity with the inflation ghost, and although it has had to be hatched, we need to be constantly on the lookout. Favourable exchange rate developments and competition in domestic markets have been favourable to households in Iceland. The price of imported goods, apart from gasoline and oil, for example, has almost stagnated in the last 12 months. However, inflation measured by the consumer price index is 4% at the moment, causing a great development of house prices there. But more factors are affected, products produced in Iceland have risen in price and likewise services, both private and public. Inflation diminishes the purchasing power of households, and it can also feed itself if it is not reined in. It is therefore in the household's interests that inflation is kept under control, but it can also affect inflation. Great consumption is usually fueled by inflation. Icelandic households showed in 2001 and 2002 that they respond swiftly to changing circumstances. As the dollar got tougher, consumption snapped up and the trade deficit that had been generated by overcapacity disappeared quickly. The experience, however, is that consumption usually does not decrease until after the damage is done, so it would be good for households to become more forward-looking and respond sooner to warnings. Households, however, can also prove important in other ways, for example, if the economy has slowed down too much, it is a benefit that households increase their consumption, thereby pushing the economy back into action. Now I've traced the main risk factors for household leverage, and then you may ask yourself what's the point? Is there a patent that solves all the problems? Of course not. However, common sense goes a long way towards solving most of our problems. Moderation, custody and counselling are the key words. Every time we make a choice, we have a choice. Is there a real need for a particular item or service? Do I have to buy such big, small, expensive, cheap, huge or small? How should I pay for? Some of the decisions are obvious, while others need to be considered. Let's study the options, consider the need for moderation, and we're going to get out of the way. Let's assume the unexpected and take steps to meet uncertainty if needed. We are our home and our actions can have a huge impact. There is a good prospect of homes making good progress, but there is still every reason for households to be aware that there may be dangers to the road that needs to be tackled. Inflation, as mentioned earlier, is one of the main risk factors for households. The country's households have a strong ally in the fight against it, which is the Central Bank of Iceland. The Central Bank has the primary role of promoting stable prices and promoting an active and secure financial system. With a joint statement by the Government and the Bank in March 2001, the Bank set the goal of keeping inflation closest to 21/2%, defined as an increase in the consumer price index. It's a difficult role, but the bank is using every effort to handle it well. The Bank has an elite team of experts, but an economy is a complex phenomenon, and human knowledge and prophesying are constrained. Therefore, there is no chance of The bank is always right. The Central Bank predicts inflation two years ahead and is resorting to interest rate changes in an attempt to steer clear of inflation as close as possible to a target. Research in Iceland, as well as abroad, suggests that it takes interest rate changes of 1 - 2 years to fully emerge. Exchange rate changes also have a very big impact on prices, however, they occur very quickly. There is no certainty there, however, and more often than not, assumptions change without much notice. This is what we experienced last fall when a new landscape in home credit access opened up with the introduction of banks into the real estate loan market. At the same time, it emerged that construction related to the construction of smelters would be earlier and greater in scope than previously anticipated. In addition, the government decided in what way the proposed tax cuts would be implemented. Thus, in just a few weeks, the assumptions of the forecasts that the Central Bank had made earlier this year had been reformed. This was followed by a new projection that attempted to take the changes into account. The Board of Directors subsequently decided to increase the Bank's policy rate by one percentage point. In fact, that change shattered the forecast that was published at the same time, because in the preparation of an inflation forecast, interest rates have always been expected to remain unchanged throughout the forecast period. The same applies to the exchange rate of the krona, i.e. it is assumed that this will not change from the forecast date. Uncertainty is one of the main folly of the economy, and the Central Bank as well as the rest of society need to constantly adapt to changing circumstances. Inflation may soon rise temporarily above the 4% tolerance set in 2001 when new monetary policy arrangements were adopted. It will call for the Bank's explanation and test its responsibilities. The outlook is also that later this winter inflation will reduce and banks' analysts have predicted that it will be below the Central Bank's 21/2% target by the end of the year. The Central Bank's next inflation forecast will be published on March 22. Through active information sharing and transparency in operations, the Bank has developed its role, but the current structure of matters is relatively recent and experience will gradually build up both within the Bank and abroad. Economies are complex manifestations, and around the world experiments were carried out for a number of years aimed at finding suitable ways to steer them. For a long time it was thought that central banks could through their actions controlled interest rates, employment, economic growth and household performance by using their tools rationally. This view has not stood the test of time. There are many participants in the economy and their goals vary. Therefore, the management of the economy, whether that thought works or not, must be a collaborative effort between different parties with different objectives. It has been helpful to set central banks the main goal of keeping inflation under control, but the experience of it is relatively short, about 10 to 15 years, during which time inflation has fallen from 30% to 4% globally, as measured by the International Monetary Fund. It is not a definitive judgment on the ability of central banks to control inflation because everything in the world is fleeting. The Central Bank of Iceland has a certain role and therefore performs professionally, ambition and passion. One of his most important tools is to communicate information about the state and prospects of the economy to all participants of society. The Bank has sought to inform the whole public of its role and actions and submits them to the Court of National Life at any given time, e.g. this appointment will be posted on the Bank's website before the opening of markets on Monday. The Bank publishes Monetary Bulletin four times a year, describing its economic developments and its views on the future and reassessing its decisions. Open discussion of the Central Bank, its work and role is important and necessary for restraint for the Bank and society. Since this appointment has largely been about household risks of increased leverage, I want to summarize my findings in just a few words, so I resort to austerity folklore: "It's better to go slow and get it than to go fast and get it anyway."
