Title: Talk about high rates and economic problems
text: Moore Gudmundsson:1 24 June 2003 - Here Teens Movies H87gengi? and hagstj97rnarvandinn Good attendees. I would like to thank the Industry Association for organizing this meeting. The debate about the problems we face in favour of heavy industry is of utmost importance. It is a prerequisite for us to successfully navigate the national economy catastrophically through the turbulent waters ahead that we are correctly analyzing the problem. If the navigational map and the direction are mad, however, we are prone to overthrow the cutters. On a ship, it may be enough for the captain and captain to know the route, but for the crew not to rebel, it is better that it is also aware of it. At least that's true in today's society. That's why conversation is so important. This discussion is not about to begin at this meeting nor will it end here. It began at the beginning of this year when it became clear that a significant increase in rates in the final weeks of last year could persist. In the beginning, it was somewhat misleading, and various argued that the increase was the Fed's fault and that it could easily fix the exchange rate, and that even without the long-term consequences for the inflation target set by the Bank in a joint statement by the Government and his in March 2001. Now I think most people have realized that this is much more complicated. The debate, but also the opinion of the OECD and the International Monetary Fund, has therefore helped create a deeper understanding. I'm going to talk about this issue today, in particular, the issue of monetary policy. However, this will only be done to some extent about the overall context and the role of other economic management. First, I will review what the exchange rate trend has been in recent months and where we are at in terms of real exchange rates. As a result, I'm going to try to clarify what's causing this trend in terms of what was happening at the time. It will focus on the proposed heavy industry projects and I will then discuss their economic impact and in particular on the real exchange rate of the kr97na. Then I will ask the question how serious this trend has already become for the economy and what flashes may be in the air in that regard. Then I turn to monetary policy and its potential to influence the exchange rate. Finally, I'll talk about what's best for us to deal with the problems we face. 1 Chief Economist of the Central Bank of Iceland. I would like to thank Arn97ri Sighvatsson, e7sgeir Dan92elsson, Gu?mundur Gu?mundsson, Gylfa Zoega, Ingimundur Fri?riksson, J97n Steinsson and eelafur Erni Klemenssson useful tips and El92n Gu?j97nsd97ttir and Gu?mundur Sigfinnsson for their assistance with data and drawings. I am solely responsible for the content of this issue. 2 The exchange rate trend ahead of last year the exchange rate rose after the huge dip it took in 2000 and 2001. This trend was welcomed by all, as the rate had fallen significantly beyond what the external and internal balance of the national economy required in the medium term, as would often be the case when the exchange rate falls due to high imbalances and lack of trust. Had the exchange rate remained as low as it was in late 2001 for a longer period of time, it would have threatened both the inflation target and financial stability. By the spring of 2002, the exchange rate had become close to what many considered to be a balanced exchange rate, or around 130 m.v. exchange rate index. It is worth underlining, however, that the numerical estimate of the equilibrium rate is at any given time subject to enormous uncertainty, and it may as well have been at least 5% higher or lower. In fact, many would say that the uncertainty gap is much wider. At least it stayed on this gap throughout the year. Towards the end of October, the hike was similar to that of the spring and had fluctuated in a rather narrow range apart from some reinforcement in the high summer. But then the exchange rate is steadily strengthening and is currently over 6% stronger than then, and was actually last month about 10% stronger than at the end of October. It is true to point out that this trend coincides with a sharp decline in the exchange rate of the US dollar against the euro, or just over 15%. Of course, this development is entirely independent of domestic economic development and outside the influence of domestic economic management. However, it has meant that the kr97na has strengthened by over 16% against the US dollar. It has, of course, had considerable consequences for the performance of those who export in US dollars and have not used exchange rate hedging to mitigate risks. It is worth noting, however, that the exchange rate against the euro has been relatively stable during this period, as shown in the accompanying figure, and was actually slightly lower yesterday than at the end of October. 3 Figure 2: Exchange rate against exchange rate index, dollar and euro 1 October 2002 - 23 June 2003 October 31, 2002 100 105 100 95 90 Gag n v art g en g isv 92sit9a lu 8 5 Gag n v art d or home Gag n in art ev ru 80 Or N DJ Source: Fry lab an k in easlan d s. F M AM J Where has this trend brought the real exchange rate, which is more important than the nominal rate when we are considering the impact on the performance of the export and competitive sectors? As shown in the accompanying figure, the real exchange rate has risen considerably since the dip it took during the overshoot of the exchange rate index in 2001. In the current quarter, it can be estimated that the real exchange rate is somewhat above both the 10-year and 20-year historical average. It is now similar to the high peak of the last boom but fortunately far below what it was towards the end of the 1980s. 4 Figure 3: Quarterly real exchange rate 1986:1 - 2003:2 1980 100 130 120 110 Based on prices 100 90 80 70 60 1986 1988 1990 Source: Fry lab an k in easlan d s. 1992 1994 Aimed at the sat n n 1996 1998 2000 2002 What explains the rate hike? The increase in the exchange rate must have clarifications in the changes or new information presented during this period. When you look closely, it seems to me that the rate hike is rooted in three factors, all of which are closely related. First, increase confidence in the growth and stability of the national economy. Second, expectations for heavy industry. Third, the positioning of foreign investors in the domestic foreign exchange market. By the end of last year, the inflation target had been reached and it was clear that the trade deficit had disappeared. At the same time, the likelihood of fjarda87l's heavy industry construction was increasing and was subsequently confirmed early this year. The outlook for economic growth was therefore sparked and the chances of the exchange rate falling again anytime soon became low. Foreign parties had shown growing interest in the domestic bond market due to high interest rates, but generally defended themselves against exchange rate risk, and their bond purchases thus did not affect the exchange rate of the kr97na. There is evidence, however, that after decisions on heavy industry projects were made, foreign entities were increasingly taking unprotected positions in bonds or even entering direct short-term speculation in support of the kr97na. However, how much of a factor this point plays in the development is difficult to say at this stage. But how and why do major industrial projects in the coming years affect the exchange rate of the kr97na in the here and now? This is because foreign exchange market participants know that these projects will be accompanied by significant net foreign exchange inflows, i.e. beyond what is needed to finance imports and wages to foreign workers as a result. This contributes to higher exchange rates when the time comes, which affects the exchange rate immediately as foreign exchange market pricing when capital transfers are unrestricted is largely based on forward-looking expectations. The second reason is that it is known that central bank interest rates will rise 5 as the construction progresses and this is immediately reflected in long-term interest rates where there is a strong relationship between them at any given time and expected short-term interest rates. The interest rate differential against foreign countries therefore rises to the long end of the market and it sucks in more capital and raises the exchange rate. It is therefore a misconception that heavy industry projects cannot have a significant impact on the exchange rate now because of the far reach of their high peak, i.e. in 2005 and 2006. The point of this relationship is that it is known exactly that this high top will come and when it will be. In addition, there will be significant foreign exchange inflows as a result of these projects already during this and next year, especially if nor?ur87l's expansion is expected, as market participants seem to do, as these projects are part of the forecasts of public bodies. Estimated net foreign exchange inflows due to Fjar?a87l and Nor?ur87l and related power plants are thus over 18 ma.kr. This year and next year, compared to nearly 30 ma.kr. In 2005 and 2006. However, nor?ur87l's expansion in this phase is not in decline and the exchange rate could therefore be reduced if it is not achieved. Figure 4: Estimated net foreign exchange inflows due to heavy industry projects 2003-2010 Ma.kr. (fixed price in Jan 2003) 40 30 Nor?ur87l (left axis) 20 Fjarda87l (left axis) Total (right axis) % af VLF 2003 4,0 3,0 2,0 10 1,0 0 0,0 2003 2004 2005 Source: Fry lab an k in easlan d s. 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 But isn't monetary policy the main explanation for rising rates, as has been claimed? When you look closely, that explanation does not add up. During the period under consideration here, monetary policy has all gone to easing, as shown in the accompanying picture. Central Bank interest rates have fallen considerably in recent months and the same applies to interest rates against foreign countries. Granted, interest rates have risen again in recent weeks due to interest rate cuts abroad, in which case the exchange rate of the kr97na has also fallen, indeed for completely different reasons. The reserve requirement has also been reduced and the Central Bank has purchased substantial amounts of foreign exchange in order to improve its foreign exchange position. Granted, both experience and theory teach that the effects of such foreign exchange purchases 6 the exchange rate is rather short-lived, if any, but in any case it is not possible to say that the Bank's actions were aimed at raising the exchange rate. Figure 5: Short-term interest rates and interest margin against Abroad 2002-2003 (weekly figures) % 11 10 9 St? riv ex tir 8 7 6 5 Sk ammt92marau n v ex shooting 4 (including SI's policy rate and inflation load 3 Treasury notes, now for about 4 years) 2 1 Sk ammt92mav ax tamu n u r v 9c tl9a n d J F MA M J J e7 S ON D J FMA M J Source: Fry lab an k in easlan d s. 2002 2003 In this regard, it is worth reminding how interest rates affect the exchange rate when capital transfers are unrestricted. Under these circumstances, returns on domestic and foreign bonds tend to seek balance, taking into account expected exchange rate changes and special risk loads. In other words, domestic interest rates will be equal to foreign interest rates plus the expected rate cut in the domestic currency (and risk loads). All the otherwise, the increase in domestic interest rates is causing the higher the exchange rate now and expectations of a corresponding decrease in the exchange rate in the future. This means that the interest rate differential needs to be increasing if it has one to explain a higher rate, but on the contrary it has been going the other way for most of this season. Risk load complicates this picture, and with the recovery of stability, it is likely to have decreased and the interest rate differential thus becoming more active than before, which otherwise contributes to a higher exchange rate. In addition, interest rates at the long end of the market have not fallen to the same extent as at the short end, e.g. due to expectations related to heavy industry projects. In addition, long-term indexed interest rates in Iceland are very high compared to interest rates in the trading countries where such shares exist. Of course, it can be rightly argued that monetary policy here played an indirect role involved by promoting stability and increased confidence, which in turn results in a higher nominal rate. If it hadn't worked, it's likely that the nominal rate would be lower than it is now. But inflation would then also be higher, and the real exchange rate may not be lower at all, which is, after all, what matters to the export and competitive sectors. 7 It is important to keep in mind that heavy industry projects will raise the real exchange rate. As a result of the construction, demand in Iceland will be higher than it would otherwise have been over some years and this will pull up prices and wages compared to those in trading countries. Monetary policy cannot change this except for a short period of time, however, it can affect how the real rate increase is divided between nominal rate hikes and inflation beyond what happens in trading countries. The impact of monetary policy on real sizes such as economic growth, real exchange rates, trade balances, etc. rarely lasts longer than 1-2 years. After that, the effect is only on inflation. This is true if monetary policy is within normal limits. Far too sluggish monetary policy that leads to excessive inflation over a longer period of time can of course reduce economic growth and the same applies to far too hard monetary policy, leading to severe deflation. The same is true if the defense of a fixed-rate strategy leads to excessively high real interest rates over a longer period of time, cf. Argentina. Raising real exchange rates is one of the ways the economy is to create scope for construction. This increase therefore does not imply that the exchange rate is developing abnormally and deviating from the equilibrium rate, at least not the equilibrium rate in the medium term, but rather the equilibrium rate that rises during construction. But is there a problem? Isn't this just a natural mechanism of the market law that will eventually deliver the desired result? Of course, there is a certain argument for such a position, but my opinion is nevertheless that this is a problem. In my opinion, Icelanders are now, for the first time in any significant way, experiencing what has been called the "Dutch illness". It is based on the fact that capital inflows and the use of limited workforce and resources for the development of a new export sector narrowly avoid existing ones. The problem is twofold. First, this is a temporary increase in the real exchange rate, which, however, is long-lasting enough to significantly damage the current export and competitive sectors. The danger is that when the real exchange rate falls again, their foundations have weakened so that it takes them a considerable amount of time to take over again. Second, there is always a risk that exchange rate fluctuations will exceed themselves, both on the rise and downward trends, including unstable expectations. This could lead to a currency devaluation when construction is completed, which would be difficult for economic management to tackle. So the question is this: are there ways to reduce the rise in the real exchange rate during the construction period, without sacrificing the inflation target and economic stability? The answer is yes, they exist. In the past, various central bank spokespeople, but also the International Monetary Fund and others, have pointed out what these routes are. They do not involve driving the exchange rate down for a short period of time with monetary policy measures, because it contradicts inflation targets and does not deliver lower real exchange rates as we move forward. They also do not involve primarily monetary policy restraint, as it contributes to higher exchange rates for a while and is mainly affected by exports and competition sectors. No, these routes involve measures that offset the temporary increase in the equilibrium rate that the heavy industry works entail. It directly faces restraint in the public finances and construction cuts during heavy industry projects, but also increased supply of foreign labour and other manufacturing factors. 8 We've heard from the debate lately that there's a growing understanding of this. We are discussing ways to make it easier to import labour during the construction process. And earlier, we heard that the Treasury Department is now working on a plan for the government to offset the state budget in the coming years. It is clear, however, that the scale of these projects is so great that the increase in real exchange rates will not be completely prevented because of them, nor that central bank interest rates will rise. It is therefore important that the export companies prepare for the fact that the real exchange rate of the kr97na does not fall and can even rise further. It raises the question that I turn to next, how serious the situation in these sectors has already become due to the increase in the exchange rate. The most debate has been about the state of the fishing industry, so I look at it first and foremost. The margin of listed fisheries companies in the 1st quarter of this year was much lower than at the same time last year, or 24% now compared to 34% then. Part of this trend can of course be attributed to the higher exchange rate of the kr97na, but more factors also arise, such as specific problems in the shrimp industry and haddock, reduced capelin fishing than at the same time last year and some decreases in the price of seafood in foreign currencies. In addition, fish processing has problems due to income exchange problems within the fishing industry as raw material prices to fish processing plants have not followed up on the export price of products. The real exchange rate of the kr97na is likely to increase in the range of 1-2% between the first and second quarters and this will further diminish the performance of fisheries and other export sectors. In contrast, fishing rights in cod and other species will increase in the new fishing year, so the performance may not be diminished as the year progresses, as it often happens. It should be noted that 2001 and 2002 were one of the best in terms of performance in the history of fisheries. The performance of listed companies in the fishing industry could therefore easily be better this year than in 2000, for example. It should be noted that the equity position of listed fisheries companies was just over 34% at the end of the 1st quarter and better than the previous year and probably one of the best for a very long time. The fishing industry is therefore better equipped to take on volatility than it has been, fortunately. So it's a big exaggeration to pretend he's in some cold coal. Monetary policy and the exchange rate The Central Bank's inflation target can withstand the fact that the exchange rate of the kr97na will in the near future be somewhat lower than it is now. Inflation is currently somewhat below the Bank's inflation target, although so-called core indices are closer to that. According to the Bank's latest inflation forecast, inflation is expected to remain below the Bank's inflation target until the fourth quarter of next year. Then it's heading higher, not because of the exchange rate, but because it's then expected that pressure for heavy industry construction will begin to tell. The exchange rate of the kr97na was yesterday nearly 2% lower than expected in the Bank's last forecast, but this does not fundamentally change this picture. Isn't that something the bank can do to lower the rate? That's far less than various people think. Experience shows that interventions in the foreign exchange market that do not coincide with changes in central bank interest rates usually have limited and transient effects. Our experiences in this field in recent years are detailed in an article by Ger?ur easberg and ?97rarin G. P8etursson in the first issue of Monetary Bulletin this year. The same applies and for the same reasons for actions such as those of the Treasury taking domestic loans to pay 9 Foreign. It must be borne in mind that the Central Bank has in recent months bought prohibitively from the currency on the market. Between last autumn and May 16, the Bank had purchased currency for 18 ma.kr. On that day, it was announced that the bank would increase its acquisition from 11/2 million every trading day to 21/2 million. This means that the bank's foreign exchange purchases this year will be around 42 ma.kr. Assuming that the exchange rate of the kr97na remains as it was on 19 June. This is equivalent to all estimated net foreign exchange inflows due to Fjar?a87l and Nor?ur87l and related power plants this year, the next and most of the inflows in 2005. Despite this, the exchange rate of the kr97na decreased only for two days after this change was announced, by a total of 1.7%, but then returned. It may of course be that this acquisition plays a part in the decrease in the exchange rate in recent days, but as with other interventions that do not coincide with changes in control rates, the long-term effects will be nonexistent. It is difficult to reassess an interest rate cut given the latest inflation forecasts and the latest figures for economic growth in the first quarter. You may be asked what effect it would have on the process. Under the current circumstances, it can be argued that those effects would be little to none as long as there continues to be a belief that the Fed will do what is necessary to meet its inflation target. This is because the exchange rate is not high because the Central Bank's policy rate is now high, but because of expectations that they will be high in the future. As long as those expectations remain unchanged, interest rate cuts now do little more than raise expectations of how much interest rates will rise later. We need to change those expectations. In this case, there are three possibilities. The first is that the market is overestimating the impact of heavy industry and/or other factors in the state of the economy. The task is to try to correct it. Sometimes it can be clearly seen that markets have surpassed themselves, such as when U.S. stock pricing included either much higher long-term economic growth than could realistically be considered, or that profits were heading over time to 100% of national income. However, there is often no certainty that "experts" food is better than the market. In this case, it is not in any conclusive way to claim that the market's expectations are wrong. The second possibility is that the Fed simply goes against its credibility and convinces the market that it will not meet its inflation target. In the long run, the Central Bank can determine the level of inflation and thus the nominal exchange rate of the kr97na. This path is extremely dangerous, however, as progress made in building confidence in stability would soar in weather and wind, interest rates would rise sharply due to increased risk loads, but in the long run no progress would be made in lowering real exchange rates. The result would be first and foremost increased inflation. A third possibility is then to convince the market that it will not try monetary policy as hard as has been thought as other economic policies will carry a larger share of the burden. To do so, a credible public plan for countermeasures in the public finances and plans to use foreign labour are the best ways.

Title: Central Bank governor's words following the introduction of the MONETARY POLICY Committee's statement
text: August 29, 2016 Governor's introductory remarks at an open meeting of the Economic and Trade Committee on the work of the Monetary Policy Committee Members of the Monetary Policy Committee last attended a meeting of the Economic and Trade Committee on 25 April. Since then, there has been considerable news as far as monetary policy is concerned. First, in June, a special reserve requirement was placed on the influx of capital from abroad into the bond market and into deposits. As a result, this influx has almost stopped. The deterioration in the monetary policy trading process that followed has almost disappeared. Second, inflation has continued to decline and remained lower than the Central Bank's last forecast since May, which was based, as in recent forecasts, on a technical assumption of the unchanged exchange rate from the forecast date. However, the exchange rate had risen by 61/2% since May, when an interest rate decision was taken last week. According to the newly published CONSUMER PRICE INDEX this month, inflation is now 0.9% and therefore fall below the lower tolerance of the inflation target. On this occasion, the Central Bank will in the near future send a report to the Government as required by the Bank's laws. In addition, the growth in money supply and lending overall has been very modest in the past. Third, inflation expectations have continued to approach inflation targets, and they were before last week's interest rate decision on most scales at or very close to the target, both in the short and long term. Fourth, the Central Bank's interest rate was cut by 0.5 percentage points last week. This decision was taken in reference to the developments I have traced here, the increase in real interest rates that have resulted from it and the assessment of the state and outlook of the economic situation presented to the MPC meeting and published in Monetary Bulletin published last week. A key factor in this regard is the Committee's view that it looks like inflation can be kept at targets in the medium term with lower interest rates than previously thought. How much lower, of course, is uncertain and will be revealed in the coming months. This also calls for the likelihood of rising tensions in the national economy and plans for major steps in the release of capital controls in the coming months on a cautious basis for determining interest rates in the near future. The next interest rate decisions will therefore depend on the economic progress and how to deal with the release of capital controls. Of course, this trend involves very satisfying news. It is understood that we are making more lasting progress on the inflation target than ever before in its history. The credibility of monetary policy has become greater than it has been, as inflation expectations at targets are evidenced. In this regard, it was pleasing to see that long-term inflation expectations declined further as a result of last week's interest rate decision. Thus, the difference between interest rates on non-indexed and indexed bonds decreased to five and nine years in both cases by 0.3 percentage points on Wednesday and Thursday, with the first case 2.4% and 2.6% in the second. Since these differences in interest rates involve both inflation expectations and risk loads, long-term market expectations after the interest rate cut are likely to be in good harmony with the inflation target. That's not to say that the bear is gone. According to the inflation forecast published by the Central Bank last week, inflation looks set to remain below target until next year if the exchange rate remains unchanged but will then increase and for a while exceed the target when import prices stop falling and the impact of a rate hike will fade away. It is, however, our task to work towards the fact that this forecast does not come true and that the ballast of inflation expectations at targets will remain, even if there will be fluctuations in exchange rates and inflation in the future. Favourable external conditions that appear, among other things, in a significant improvement in business rates, high tourist flows and low global inflation certainly play a very big part in the positive developments I have made here a topic of discussion. Inflation, however, has been below target for a high third year. It has become too long for it to be explained without reference to the impact of monetary policy. In more than two years, a less conservative monetary policy would have skeptically delivered higher inflation. An analysis of the impact of inflation in the past supports this conclusion. In addition, the increase in the exchange rate of the krona in the past is not independent of monetary policy. Monetary policy has a stake in this success, and probably far greater than many believe. Higher interest rates have, among other things, contributed to lower domestic demand than otherwise, contributing in part to a sharp increase in disposable income allocated to savings. As a result, trade surpluses and foreign exchange inflows will be more than otherwise pushing for the strengthening of the krona. In addition, relatively high interest rates and credible statements by the Monetary Policy Committee that everything needed to keep inflation at targets may have led companies to be more arrogant about rolling out expenses for wage increases to prices. I'm going to stop here and look forward to having an interesting discussion with you hereafter about a variety of issues relating to monetary policy.

Title: Speech on the occasion of the issuance of a new ten thousand kronor banknote
text: 24. October 2013 New 10,000 kronor banknote Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland. Speech on the occasion of the issuance of a new 10,000 ISK banknote, Central Bank of Iceland, 24 October 2013. Ministers, board members, governors and other good guests. We're here to celebrate the fact that today the new 10,000 bill went into circulation. It is not an everyday occurrence that new banknotes are put into circulation in Iceland, as it is eighteen years since it last happened with the 2,000 bill. Even further, a more pricey bill than the existing ones was issued, or twenty-seven years, when the 5,000 bill was put into circulation. But why is a new banknote needed with a higher nominal value? Isn't banknote use of banknotes overwhelmingly in This Country anyway? Indeed, it is true that we use credit cards more than many other nations, but it is expected that about 90% of retail sales have cards, as the use of banknotes and coins, or what can be called cash, was down to about 1% of the value of GDP over the last decade, or up until the banking crash in the autumn of 2008, when usage more than doubled. At present, about ISK 38 billion is in cash in circulation in Iceland, which is about 2% of GDP. Despite the doubling, it is still among the lowest known in comparative countries, but Norway and Sweden are on a similar level. But even before the above increase, there had been a need to issue a more pricey bill, as the Central Bank began preparing for its issuance already in 2006. An example of the need is that in banknote studies it is often assumed that if the share of the most valuable banknote in banknotes in circulation exceeds 70%, it is time to issue a new banknote. The current 5,000 note has been above this mark for about 6 years and had an 87.3% share at the end of last year. In comparison, when the 5,000 ISK note was issued in June 1986, the share of the most valuable note, which was then ISK 1,000, was 74.5%. In the rest of the Nordic region with an independent currency, this ratio ranges from 24-54%. In light of this, the issuance of a 10,000 note must now be considered a modest action, which is marked by, among other things, the fact that Icelandic payment processor is in large part electronic and highly efficient. The purpose of the issue is first and foremost to make banknote use more efficient as demand is different with fewer banknotes than before. It should not be disguised here that the need for the issuance of a new banknote is, after all, bad news as it is rooted in excessive inflation in this country in recent decades. When two zeros were taken from the Icelandic krona in early 1981, the most priced banknote was ISK 500. That's about 20,000 at the moment. The value of banknotes has therefore soared by nearly 98% during this period. The majority of that deterioration took place in the first decade, however, as inflation averaged just under 31% in the 1980s, rising to 102.7% in August 1983. The value of banknotes decreased by 93% in the 1980s. In the 1990s, however, inflation averaged about 3%, but just under 6% so far this century. Historically, some progress has been made in reducing inflation in Iceland. This can be done even better, however, as inflation is currently around 4% which means that the value of money is scrapped by over 32% over a full decade. With 21/2% inflation, which is our target, the corresponding figure is less than 22%. So there's nothing to work for. Icelandic banknote history, of course, goes back further than to 1981, and foreign banknote history is much longer. Paper notes issued by central banks are one form of money and are in a long historical context relatively new. Money in one form or another has followed the man since at least sumerian times about 10,000 years ago, but money is things that are generally accepted in a particular region or country as payment for goods and services, and for settling debts. Many societies at first developed commodity money where certain products became generally recognized price gauges and intermediaries in trade, such as metals, waders, fish or livestock. The gold eventually won in that competition. Later, debt approvals or checks on such valuables developed, thus becoming eligible for settlement of transactions and liabilities. Paper notes were initially such checks that were redeemable in a particular product, often gold. They could be issued by individuals and their associates, and later it was mainly private banks that issued such checks or banknotes. Even later, central bank notes evolved without redemption in gold or other commodities like the one we are currently issuing. In each step I have traced above, the efficiency of payment processing increased, but since such bills are no longer redeemable for other valuables, they, after all, build on the value produced in the country in question and can be bought for them and the trust that exists in the state that issues them. The first recorded records of the use of paper notes date back to the 8th century in China. There are still collections of banknotes used in China in the 11th century, but the best known are the 14th-century Chinese banknotes that italian explorer Marco Polo reports on his return. In Europe, it was the Italian financial powers and the Dutch who started using such papers first. Sweden, however, rode the wad of bank notes, because their central bank predecessor - formally established in 1668 - issued banknotes in 1661 that were the first banknotes not linked to bank deposits but were based on confidence that the bank's owner could obtain from the bank for him the value of its amount. It was therefore tempting for the Bank to issue banknotes in increased quantities, which at first resulted in a great deal of precipitation in the Sweden but ultimately to inflation and that depositors in those days could not get their deposits in hard cash, i.e. in copper, except at lower prices. Some then said that people would never try this novelty in payment processing again  issuing paper money  but such pessimism did not last long. The banknote issue gradually established itself at the end of the 17th century at the same time that the Bank of England is established and began issuing banknotes, or in 1694. However, the story of the banknotes in the Sweden is a reminder of the temptations that come with issuing paper money and how too much supply can contribute to inflation. Icelandic history of banknotes begins officially in 1778 with the legalization of Danish curry notes printed Icelandic text (the note is visible here in the coin collection). These banknotes were not very popular, as in the time of the monopoly, most people adhered to the traditional merchandise trade elsewhere, and Icelanders trusted precious metals rather than curry banknotes Danish. When Landsbanki islands was founded in 1886, the National Trust of Iceland issued a series of banknotes with a crown value instead of state dollars, which had long been commonplace. With the advent of the Nordic Monetary Union in 1872, the Nordic countries all changed their currencies and merged with a standard krona, although issued individually for each country and with its national characteristics. Each country's treasury guaranteed the banknote versions, which were gold-insured until the Great Depression of the 1930s. The issue of banknotes in Iceland is uninterrupted from 1778 to this day and various parties have been responsible for this work, the Danish Kurantbanki, the National Treasury of Iceland, the National Treasury of Iceland, islandsbanki, Landsbanki islands, Landsbanki islands-Central Bank and now the Central Bank of Iceland. Over the past 235 years, a total of 63 different versions have seen the light of day, including the one we are currently promoting. Because it was mentioned that banknotes have been redeemable in various metals, also in Iceland, it can be pointed out that islandsbanki's 1904 series of banknotes said that islandsbanki paid the holder against the relevant banknote value, from 5 to 100 ISK, in gold  but these notes are visible here in the collection. The coin collection you see here is actually part of the Central Bank and The National Museum of Iceland's Coin Collection, which is part of the national museum option, but the Central Bank maintains it in collaboration with the National Museum of Iceland. Here, copies of the new banknote will be preserved for the time being, as I'll come in more detail afterwards. We are now putting into use a new 10,000 cash note, but what will the future hold in this regard? There are no plans for a bigger bill at this point and whether it will be needed later on depends on inflation and demand for banknotes in general, including this new banknote. It is now more immediate to consider possible changes in the future regarding the least priced coins and even look at whether a 500 kronor banknote should be replaced with coins. However, no decisions have been made regarding this issue. In general, the future depends on the demand for cash, which in turn is determined by inflation and technological developments. It is the Central Bank's policy to meet demand in a cost-effective manner while otherwise being impartial regarding the use of cash, i.e. neither attempting to encourage or discourage in this regard. In many parts of the world, plastic banknotes are being scrapped instead of paper notes, and it cannot be ruled out that it will ever come under scrutiny in this country. By law, the Central Bank of Iceland has the exclusive right to issue cash. The Bank drafts the issuance of banknotes or coins with a new value, as applicable to the isk 10,000 note, and has new coins entered or printed new notes upon confirmation by the Minister. Preparations for the issue of this banknote began as previously stated in 2006, but the project set aside for other projects at the end of 2008 and the production of the banknote was postponed. In 2011, however, it was decided to re-launch the project on the basis of the hard work that had already been put into it, both on the part of the designers, the Central Bank's employees and the manufacturer with whom we have been cooperating. Artist Kristin orkelsdottir designed the banknote, which has managed the design of Icelandic banknotes since 1981. Her co-designer and co-designer is Stephen Fairbairn. It is as ever the British company De La Rue that printed the 10,000 note, which company and its predecessors have been printing banknotes for Iceland for 83 years. The banknote has already piqued the curiosity of central banks in charge of putting other and more cumbersome currencies into circulation. The banknote includes a new multidimensional security feature called Optiks, which show and other security features are designed to create greater confidence in the banknote. The banknote is dedicated to Jonas Hallgrimsson, but the banknote contains references to Jonas' work as a poet, Icelandic man, folklorist and naturalist. On this occasion, two songs will be sung by Jonas' poems later, and it is singer Hanna Dora Sturludottir who performs them with the accompaniment of Anna Guony Guomundsdottir. Having said that, I would like to thank all those who have put their efforts into circulation, staff at the Central Bank, the Board of Directors and in banks and savings banks  and most importantly, I would like to thank Kristin orkelsdottir and Stephen Fairbairn for their part in the successful design of Icelandic banknotes over the last decade. I would then like to hand over a 10,000 ISK note to Bjarni Benediktsson, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, for the preservation of national museum options. I would like to finally give the word to the Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, but he handles the central bank's affairs within the government, and thus the issue of banknotes.

Title: Statement by Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 25. March 2010 Address Lara V. Juliusdottir, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 25 March 2010 Honorary Prime Ministers, Ministers, Governors, Ambassadors of Foreign Countries and other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 40th and ninth annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. At a meeting of the Board of Directors earlier today, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Trade confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2009 with his signature. The Bank's annual report for 2009 is published today and is due at the end of the meeting. 2009 was a year of great deprivation at the Central Bank of Iceland, no less than in 2008. The Act on Amendments to act No. 36/2001 on the Central Bank of Iceland was passed on 26 February 2009 and entailed that instead of a board of directors composed of three governors, there will be one Governor and one Deputy Governor. At the beginning of the year, the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland consisted of Chairman David Oddsson, Eirikur Guonason and Ingimundur Frioriksson. Ingimundur retired on 9 February 2009, but Davio Oddsson and Eirikur Guonason resigned as Governors of the Central Bank of Iceland upon the adoption of the act on 26 February. The prime minister subsequently decided to temporarily install Norwegian Svein Harald oygard as Governor of the Central Bank and Arnor Sighvatsson, the Central Bank's chief economist, in the post of Deputy Governor until those positions had been advertised. Mar Guomundsson was appointed Governor of the Central Bank for a term of five years as of 20 August 2009 and Arnor Sighvatsson as Deputy Governor for four years as of 1 July 2009. Amendments to the Act on the Central Bank also resulted in a change in practice regarding the Bank's interest rate decisions. The Monetary Policy Committee took office and it is its role under the Act to make decisions on the application of the Bank's monetary policy instruments. Originally, the Monetary Policy Committee consisted of Svein Harald oygard, Governor of the Central Bank, Arnor Sighvatsson, Deputy Governor, orarinn G. Petursson, Chief Economist, Anne Sibert, Professor at Birkbeck University in London and Gylfi Zoega, Professor at the University of Iceland. Moore Gudmundsson then took a member of the Committee when he took over as Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland from Sveinn Harald in August. Many activities are now accommodated within the walls of the Central Bank, which has not been operating there for a long time and is a direct result of the collapse of the Icelandic banks in the autumn of 2008. In the autumn of 2009 it was decided to strengthen the operations of foreign exchange controls within the Bank and foreign exchange controls are now an independent unit directly under the supervision of the CEO. The main tasks of the Foreign Exchange Supervisory Authority during the year have been general supervision of currency controls, inspection of special violations of foreign exchange laws and regulations and the processing of exemption requests. Foreign exchange controls were a part of the Central Bank's operations for many years, but the department was laid off when its last employee retired at the end of 1999. During the banking collapse, it also happened that significant demands on domestic financial institutions secured by mortgages of various kinds fell to the Central Bank. Some of these claims were transferred to the Treasury, but the Central Bank provided advice to the Treasury on their treatment. In 2009, most of the claims were prepared for out-of-pocket financial institutions, but the actual asset management has now taken over. At the end of the year, the decision was taken to transfer these assets to a separate subsidiary of the Central Bank of Iceland entitled The Central Bank of Iceland's Asset Portfolio ehf. or ESI. At the same time, another subsidiary, Solvholl ehf., was established, which is an operating company and is the only function of maximising the value of the assets in the holding company and putting them in price. This will be done when market conditions allow and with the approval of the board of directors of the holding company. At the end of last year, ESi's book valued assets amounted to ISK 491 billion. As is well known, the restoration of the financial system has been going on for the whole of last year and is soon seen as the end of that project. The Central Bank of Iceland has been actively involved in this work. It should also be noted that the Central Bank still has a certain part of the payment processor with foreign countries, but aims systematically to complete that role. The Central Bank has cooperated extensively with the International Monetary Fund during the year in relation to the Fund's economic plan and government Icelandic. Last year, a total of 12 delegations arrived in Iceland. The Bank's cooperation with the Fund's experts has been a success and a great anchor for the Central Bank to be able to approach the Fund in various fields. In 2009 was a year of major changes in the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland and a new Board of Directors was elected twice during the year. Jon Sigurosson, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors requested a solution from the Council on 26 January and 19 February, Valgerour Bjarnadottir requested a solution from the Board of Directors. The New Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland was elected to the Althingi on 16 March and the members of the Council elected Lara V. Juliusdottir, agust Einarsson, Friorik Mar Baldursson, Katrin Olga Johannesdottir, Jonas Hallgrimsson, Ragnar arnason and Ragnar Arnalds. The Board of Directors was re-elected after the general election on 11 August and the members of Lara V. Juliusdottir, agust Einarsson, Hildur Traustadottir, Katrin Olga Johannesdottir, Magnus arni Skulason, Ragnar arnason and Ragnar Arnalds were elected. Magnus arni Skulason requested a release from the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland on 12 September and Daniel Gros was elected in his place on 15 October. On December 15, Bjorn Herbert Guobjornsson was elected to the Board of Directors instead of agust Einarsson, who asked for release from the Council. Let us then consider the Bank's financial statements for 2009, which this time constitutes a consolidated financial statement for the subsidiaries added during the year, i.e. The Central Bank of Iceland ehf. and Solvholl ehf. According to the income statement, the profit for the year amounted to ISK 500 million. In 2008, however, there was a loss of almost ISK 184 billion in the Bank's operations before recovery from the Treasury, which rebuilt the Bank's equity. These recoverys amounted to ISK 175 billion and, taking into account, the Bank's final loss amounted to ISK 8.6 billion. The development of the krona affects the Bank's operations due to foreign assets that are traditionally greater than exchange-related liabilities. This effect was unusually strong in 2008, when exchange rate gains reached ALMOST ISK 44 billion as a result of the krona devaluation. In 2009, the krona weakened only slightly, or by 7% from the beginning of the year to the end of the year, with a exchange rate gain of ISK 3 billion for the year. The release of the exchange rate difference resulted in a loss of ISK 2.5 billion from the Central Bank's operations during the year. Net interest income decreased by just over ISK 4 billion, which is partly attributable to a decrease in net interest income from foreign exchange reserves where foreign interest rates on bank deposits and securities have fallen between years. The Bank's other operating income increases by over ISK 1 billion due to the valuation of gold. Operating expenses decreased between years, mainly due to the unusually high cost of expert advice due to the banking collapse of 2008. Wage costs increased by 9.7% during the year, which is explained by, among other things, an increase in the number of employees. The Bank's total asset position decreased slightly during the year but still stands at just under ISK 1,200 billion, as at the end of 2008. At the end of 2009, the Bank's foreign assets accounted for 41% of total assets. At the end of the previous year, the Bank's foreign assets accounted for 47% of total assets. Foreign assets in foreign exchange reserves increased by ISK 56 billion during the year. The real increase in the reserves was financed by borrowing, on the one hand, with a loan from the International Monetary Fund amounting to ISK 20.8 billion and a loan from the Nordic countries totalling ISK 54.8 billion. Foreign debt decreased by ISK 38 billion, mainly due to the repayment of swap agreements with the central banks of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which amounted to EUR 100 million from each bank. The Bank's foreign debt amounted to ISK 241 billion at year-end 2008, but now amounts to ISK 204 billion. At the time of the bank collapse, the bank's loans against mortgages secured by bank notes were upsetting. The bank had borrowed against mortgages that proved unsafe despite being assessed as trustworthy when the loans were granted. There was an agreement that the Treasury bought a large part of the bank's mortgage position when the banking collapsed. Nominal mortgage loans of ISK 345 billion were purchased by the Bank at the end of 2008 and the purchase price amounted to ISK 270 billion paid on an indexed interest-bearing bond. In 2009, interest and indexation for the bond was approximately ISK 36 billion. At the end of 2009, it was decided that the Central Bank should buy back the assets in question, as well as outstanding claims that had been established for the securities loans of Endurlani state and then sell a special subsidiary owned by the Bank, The Central Bank of Iceland's Portfolio ehf. The Central Bank paid ISK 134 billion for these assets and the bond stands at ISK 161 billion at year-end. Finally, government deposits with the Bank increased from ISK 403 billion at year-end 2008 to ISK 446 billion at year-end 2009. This is the largest difference between the Treasury's foreign exchange accounts at the Bank, which increased by 46.8 ma.kr. This increase is explained by new borrowings from Nordic central banks at the end of 2009. The Bank's equity amounted to ISK 82.8 billion at year-end 2008, compared with ISK 82.3 billion at the end of the previous year. The difference is explained by the profits for the year. Good attendees. 2009 has been an eventful and challenging year for the Bank. The Bank's operations have been marked by resolving the problems posed by the collapse of the banks. Even though the road was rocky, it's been pretty good. A number of tasks await a solution, although it appears to be in sight that the Bank's operations will return to normal. Finally, on behalf of the Board of Directors, I would like to take this opportunity to express gratitude to all Central Bank employees for their well-done work during the year, but they have put in a lot of work throughout this period and often worked darkly in between in the unusual circumstances that have been. I would also like to thank the Board of Directors for their good cooperation over the past year. I would then like to invite the Governor of the Central Bank, Mar Guomundsson, to take up the case.

Title: Address at the annual meeting
text: Address 25. March 2020 Gylfa Magnusson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland. Delivered at the 59th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 25 March 2020. The Prime Minister, the Governor and other members of the Central Bank. I'm here with the 50th and ninth annual meetings of the Central Bank of Iceland. The meeting now has a different format than normally as you can see. Participants in the Bank's premises are a handful, but the content of the meeting is instead available in a webcast. This is one of many actions taken within the Central Bank due to the current global virus. The role of the Board of Directors is, as before, to monitor that the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with the laws applicable to its operations and to confirm various decisions and rules established by the Bank. In the past year, the Board of Directors was appointed so that the chairman was Gylfi Magnusson. Other members were orunn Guomundsdottir, Sigurour Kari Kristjansson, Frosti Sigurjonsson, Bolli Heoinsson, Una Maria oskarsdottir and Jacqueline Clare Mallett. The Board of Directors held 19 meetings during the year. The main focus of the Central Bank's work was, as before, related to the management of monetary policy and financial stability. In addition, there was a lot of work due to changes to the Act on the Bank during the year and the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority. The merger went into effect at the beginning of the year. On this occasion, I would like to welcome the employees of the Financial Supervisory Authority to work in a merged institution. The decisions on the board of directors in law also changed somewhat. It will affect its work and structure even if the fundamental role of the Council does not change. Then came a few breakthroughs in late summer when Mar Guomundsson resigned as Governor after 10 years in the job and asgeir Jonsson took office, with the Governor attending all meetings of the Board of Directors. According to a law in force last year, the Central Bank's main objective was Iceland to promote stable prices. At the same time, the Central Bank should financial stability. Inflation was somewhat above 21/2 percent 1 the inflation target, at the beginning of the year, or about or just above three percent, but declined considerably towards the end of the year and was two percent in December. The Monetary Policy Committee kept the Bank's main interest rate unchanged at the beginning of the year, but in May the interest rate cut process began, when interest rates were reduced by 0.5 percentage points. The Committee decided to cut interest rates over the next four meetings and the Bank's main interest rate was reduced by a total of 1.5 percentage points during the year. In 2019, there was increased uncertainty about economic development, although it was not clear how much of an impact a viral epidemic would have on the economy and human life this year. Risks in tourism were realised in the first half of the year with the collapse of wow air. As the year progressed, uncertainty about the progress of the economy increased, both in Iceland and abroad. During the year, corporate debt growth slowed and household debt growth was modest. The position of the big commercial banks at the end of the year was solid; capital ratios were high, both historically and internationally, and liquidity was well above the minimum. One of the central bank's main functions is to preserve the nation's foreign exchange reserves. The stock market has been quite large in recent years. Last year it increased by almost ISK 86 billion and amounted to ISK 822 billion at year-end. Exchange rate changes largely explained the expansion of the resource in Icelandic ISK calculated. The Central Bank handles professional and financial relations with international institutions in its field of work, such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, foreign central banks and financial supervision. According to a special agreement with the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, the Central Bank handles foreign borrowing by the Treasury, as well as the execution of domestic tenders, the purchase and redemption of Treasury securities securities, the conclusion of main broker contracts and the management of securities loans to the main brokers. The Bank is responsible for risk and credit management of the Treasury's loan portfolio, performs tasks regarding government guarantees and more related to it. A number of changes were made to the Bank's projects during the year. The Central Bank carried out foreign exchange controls, i.e. supervision of the implementation of Act No. 87/1992 on Foreign Exchange and the implementation of the Act on the Treatment of Krona-Denominated Assets Subject to Special Restrictions or the So-Called Offshore Krona Act. Projects in the field had declined significantly in recent years, as capital controls had almost fully been released, although guidance, supervision and research still needed to be carried out. The Central Bank of Iceland's foreign exchange controls were formally established in September 2009 and were abolished as a separate division within the Bank at the beginning of May last year and the remaining projects were transferred, among other things, to the Financial Stability Department. At that time, the Central Bank of Iceland's portfolio was ehf. terminated in the first half of the year, together with its two subsidiaries. The portfolio was established at the end of 2009. Its balance sheet was approximately ISK 491 billion. The Central Bank fully funded the company 2 and was its equity at the beginning of 1 m.kr. At the time of the company's dissolution, it had paid the Central Bank and the Treasury more than ISK 652 billion. According to the income statement, profit from the Bank's operations amounted to just over ISK 22 billion in 2019, while the previous year the profit was just over ISK 35 billion. The Bank's profits can largely be attributed to a positive exchange rate difference in the bank's large foreign exchange reserves due to some decrease in the exchange rate of the krona. The Bank's operating expenses amounted to just over ISK 4.2 billion, of which wages and related expenses amounted to just over ISK 2.9 billion, an increase of 2.3% from the previous year and other operating expenses increased by 11%, mainly due to the merger of the Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority. In addition, net interest expenses were just over ISK 9 billion, or just over ISK 4 billion lower than the previous year. The Bank's assets amounted to ISK 840 billion at the end of the year and approximately 95% of the Bank's assets were foreign. Equity increased from ISK 58 billion to ISK 82 billion. The Bank's equity ratio was 9.8% at year-end, compared with 7.7% at year-end 2018. At the end of 2019, there were a total of 177 employees at the Central Bank, four fewer than the previous year. The gender ratio remained fairly even, with the Bank employing 89 men and 84 women at the end of the year. At the beginning of the year, the Central Bank of Iceland received formal equal pay certification, which is a certification that the Central Bank operates a wage system that meets the requirements for an equal pay standard. An equal pay analysis also revealed that there was no significant, unexplained pay gap between the sexes. Although the Central Bank of Iceland's core tasks have not undergone drastic changes since the Bank's establishment in 1961, i.e. to promote stability in prices and to rely on the foundations and functions of the financial system, the implementation and organisation has changed at certain intervals, e.g. with legislative amendments in 1986, 2001, 2009 and 2013 related to interest rate liberalisation, inflation targets, the establishment of the Monetary Policy Committee and increased emphasis on financial stability. There was some change in the central bank's projects and structure with the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority at the beginning of the year. The Board of Directors and employees of the Bank have been in attendance at the time of the merger. The Bank's role has been expanded and it is the role of the Board of Directors to monitor that everything is going smoothly in accordance with laws and regulations. In the current state of financial infrastructure in Iceland, it is even more urgent than usual that the Bank has adequate capital, tools, tools and human resources to handle the transactions and communications that can be required by the Central Bank. With the amendment that led to the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority at the beginning of this year, changes were made to the arrangements of the Bank's supervisory board. The main changes to the governance structure are that three committees are now making decisions on the application of the Central Bank's powers and controls regarding monetary policy, financial stability, i.e. macroeconomic caution, and financial supervision. It is unchanged that the Governor manages and is responsible for the central bank's operations and exercises decision-making powers in all matters of the Bank which are not entrusted to others by law. Three deputy governors are now leading issues 3 the Bank in the areas in which they are appointed to lead and at the same time be responsible for preparing work for the Bank's statutory committees, sitting on committees and making joint decisions with the Governor as further provided for in the Act. One deputy governor leads on monetary policy issues, another issues of financial stability and a third issues relating to financial regulation. The Bank's new organisational chart, which came into force at the beginning of the year, reflects the Bank's tasks under amended law. The Bank's core divisions are now seven and the four support divisions. At the same time, the organisational chart is central to the governor's office. After the merger, the Bank's employees spring a total of about 290. I would like to finally take this opportunity to thank the Bank's employees for their good cooperation in 2019. I would like to thank the members of the Board of Directors, the Deputy Governor who held that position in 2019, the Secretary of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their good cooperation. I would also like to extend my special thanks to the governors of the Central Bank of Iceland, Mar Guomundsson and asgeir Jonsson, for their cooperation.
