Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Federation of Icelandic Savings Banks
text: 25.11.2010 Statement by Governor M87r Gudmundsson at the Annual General Meeting of the Federation of Icelandic Savings Banks 25 November 2010 M87r Gu?mundsson: Speech at the Annual General Meeting of the Federation of Icelandic Savings Banks Moderator, good attendees I would like to start by thanking you for the kind invitation to address you here today. I have long believed that savings banks are an important part of our financial system and can become so that also in the future the right to play is held. But I'll come closer to that later. First, I want to say a few words about the state and outlook for the economy and then discuss the state of the financial system, but the Central Bank today released its second report this year on financial stability. Our current economic situation is characterised by the fact that great progress has been made regarding stability, but a strong improvement has so far been made. First, let's look at the stabilization signs. First of all, the external imbalance of the national economy has disappeared. The enormous trade deficit of the overheating years has turned into a handsome underlying trade surplus, which overlooks the calculated interest rates in the out-of-pocket banks, but those interest rates will only be partially paid. The trade surplus supports the exchange rate, but so does the currency controls. In fact, the rate hike stopped in the middle of last year, and the exchange rate subsequently required no support through the Central Bank's interventions, which have not taken place since early November last year. So far this year, the trade road has strengthened by just over 13%. Since then, the Central Bank has lagged on the other volatility since late August, buying foreign exchange on the market for just over 4 ma.kr. It's not much, of course, but narrow is a major indicator and you can increase your purchases as the influx of foreign exchange increases from now. Inflation has now fallen from about 18% in early 2009 to 2.6% according to the latest measure published this morning. The Central Bank's inflation target, which is 21/2%, has therefore been achieved, and if tax implications are overlooked, 12 months of inflation is actually below target, or at just under 2%. Exchange rate stability and subsequent increases have, of course, played a central role in this deflationary deflation. But the slack in the economy has actually also played a considerable part, as well as relatively cautious monetary policy given the circumstances. It is by no means self-evident that this success would be achieved, and the slack alone does not create price stability as countless historical examples show. In addition, the exchange rate stability and inflation expectations were needed to decline towards target. This success would not have been achieved by now if the utmost demands for swift and premature reductions in interest rates had been met. Interest rates, of course, have fallen dramatically. Thus, the Central Bank's effective policy rate has fallen from 18% at the beginning of 2009 (then seven-day mortgage interest rates) but are now just over 41/2% (average deposit interest and interest rate on deposits) and have never been lower in the Bank's nearly fifty-year history. The Monetary Policy Committee concluded in its last statement that there is still scope for further reductions in central bank interest rates provided that the exchange rate remains stable and inflation rebounds as predicted. The latest inflation measure underscores this scope. Given the slack in the economy, active real control rates of between 2-21/2% are simply too high after the targets for exchange rate stability and inflation have been reached. But what about the economy, has it begun? According to the forecast published by the Central Bank earlier this month, so be it. Seasonally adjusted GDP should have increased between the second and third quarters. The evidence that has emerged since reinforces that prediction. But quarterly GDP measurements have been unstable and subject to major revisions. We get the Office for National Statistics' first estimate of third-quarter GDP in early December. According to the Central Bank's forecast, economic growth will then continue in the near term. Thus, GDP will increase by just 2% between 2010 and 2011, followed by 2.7% in 2012 and 3% in 2013. This will be enough to make unemployment fall as of the second quarter of next year, but unemployment usually falls some time after economic growth has recovered. It is then predicted that it will fall steadily during the forecast period, rising by 3% by the end of 2013. But these are as they say "just forecasts" and the uncertainty is greater than in the average year. External factors can change the picture, but governments can also have a considerable impact on development, both for good and for evil. Thus, economic growth could be lower if there is a backlash to the global economic recovery, if there are further delays in large investment projects that have been in the backbone, and if households choose to fix their net asset position faster than expected here and save more and consume less. The negative effects of the latter, however, will in the long run die out, and in a small open economy as Icelandic the long-term effects should be positive. However, economic growth could also be much higher, especially if Iceland's risk load in international markets falls sharply in the near future, the trajectory is paved into foreign credit markets, direct foreign investment increases and general business investment becomes stronger. The 3% growth rate as currently forecast in 2012 and 2013 is of course a good one in the average year. But summarized, economic growth in 2011 and 2012 is weak given the huge slack currently in Icelandic economy. What's more, the foundations are not well solid as the contribution of foreign trade to economic growth is negative and investment will be significantly below the historical average even though it will increase considerably from the present. One of the factors holding back economic growth is the low level of investment at the moment and indeed in the coming years, according to the Bank's forecast. This development of the investment level is not inconsistent with the experience of various other nations that have lived with high investment rates in the run-up to the financial crisis. Yet, of course, there is a certain concern and an important task to work towards the fact that this will be "just predictions" because nothing is inevitable in this respect. I have recently emphasized in my speeches that although interest rates of course have some impact on the level of investment, it is probably at the moment far from being the most influential factor, especially after interest rates have become as low as they actually are. I think here other factors play a much more role like risk aversion as a result of the financial crisis, uncertainty about demand and the operating environment, reduced access to foreign credit and poor corporate balance sheets. This needs to be done, and that's why it's so important that more powers get into financial restructuring of businesses and indeed households as well. But then we come to the position of financial institutions because these works will seek the better the more solid they are. There is still uncertainty about the capital position of financial institutions and the debt position of households and businesses. It is important to reduce this uncertainty in order to create confidence in the financial institutions and investment and the national economy to recover. The Supreme Court's second judgment on rate-based loans handed down in the Month of September struck a floor under the negative impact of an illegal exchange rate guarantee on the financial institutions' equity, although there remained some uncertainty about how broad the problem is. The Minister of Economy and Commerce's foreign exchange rate bill is therefore an important step in order to accelerate the outcome of that regard, thereby contributing to more momentum in the financial restructuring of households and businesses. In the coming months, it will become clear whether the illegality of exchange rate guarantees will result in the owners of financial undertakings having to contribute to them with increased equity. However, that will not be enough to give the financial institutions the health certificates needed to significantly loosen the currency controls. Funding for financial institutions is now protected by the caps and the government's statement that deposits are fully secured. It is important that trust in the financial system is sufficient to make the funding of the system pass without these safeguards. In this regard, it is also an important challenge to rebuild the functioning of financial markets that previously played a major role in financing and risk distribution, and to reopen access by financial institutions and other entities to foreign credit markets. These will be projects in the near term, along with work to develop regulatory and regulatory measures that are more effective in reducing the likelihood of financial shocks than the pre-crash arrangements. The regulation of financial activities in Iceland will of course take a lot of account of what happens in that respect at an international level. There has been a lot of work done in the past to formulate a regulatory framework for financial activities that takes into account the lessons of the financial crisis. An important milestone was reached in Basel on 12 September when a meeting of central bankers and the CEOs of the financial regulators of the countries that are members of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision confirmed new criteria regarding capital ratios, leverage ratios and bank liquidity. The package now goes by the name Basel-III and in terms of equity will take effect in stages between 2013 and 2019. The new benchmarks mean that the minimum requirements for bank equity will be increased considerably and its composition is improved by increasing the weight of book value capital. Including the so-called precautionary fund, the requirement for book valued equity increases from 2% to 7%. The goal is for financial institutions to be able to cope more fully in the future. In addition to the above minimum requirements, a flexible capital requirement in the range of 0-2.5% is expected to be determined for the banking system as a whole in each individual country, taking into account the of general credit development and other factors that may affect the risk of the system. Such flexible capital requirements are classified as macroprudential controls rather than monopoly controls, because it has the effect of reducing credit and asset price fluctuations, thereby easing the economic volatility. The use of control instruments in the field of macroeconomic caution must be based both on macroeconomic analysis and on the analysis of risks in the financial system as a whole. This involves more than the addition of the risks of individual financial institutions. The use of such financial stability policies must then be synchronized with monetary policy. This needs to be borne in mind when deciding how and by whom these controls are applied, but it is up to each nation to be self-imposed. Icelanders need to familiarise themselves with the new guidelines in Basel-III, which will find their way into EU regulations and thus enter the Icelandic through the EU Convention. Furthermore, Icelanders must not forget what they became so slippery in the run-up to the financial crisis that international norms regarding rules on banks' own and liquidity include minimum standards that may not be enough for the supervision and management of the domestic financial system. A number of work has also been carried out in Iceland to improve regulation and supervision of financial activities. Amendments have already been introduced to the law that will remedy a number of vulnerabilities that were in the regulatory framework of domestic financial institutions, such as loans against mortgages in their own shares, loans to owners and large exposures. Work is ahead to remedy recriminations that were on the structure and equipment aimed at preserving financial stability. In this regard, it has been called for the Act on the Central Bank of Iceland and the Act on Public Supervision of Financial Undertakings to be reviewed. In this respect, international experience and the review currently taking place around the world in terms of macroeconomic caution, financial supervision arrangements and the involvement of central banks in both must also be considered. In recent months, the Central Bank of Iceland has been working on a review of this and will publish a report on the subject in the coming weeks. In recent months, the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank of Iceland have worked jointly to formulate proposals for cooperation between the institutions on assessing systemic risks in the financial system, mutual exchange of information and joint databases. The results will appear in the near future in an improved cooperation agreement between these institutions. In doing so, the two main regulators of the financial system are joining forces to remedy the recriminations that were on the division of labour and information exchange before the crash, as far as possible within the current legal framework. We are also continuing to work to improve the functionality and security of payment processing systems. Thus, the owners of the Icelandic Banks' Data Centre and Fj9algrei?slumi?lun hf. signed a framework agreement on 15 November aimed at separating infrastructure and competitive operations in payment processing. The Central Bank of Iceland will then withdraw from the Icelandic Banks' Data Centre but will fully take over the operations of The Icelandic Multimedia Service. In the future, he will own and operate the infrastructure of the system. It is my hope that these changes will result in the system of payment processing in Iceland becoming both safer and more active. But shaping infrastructure, regulation and supervision is not enough. We also need to try to figure out what kind of financial system we want and need to have in this country. There, factors such as the size of the system, composition and its relationship with the global financial system are important. This issue will not be dissected here, but it now needs to get better on the agenda of the debate than it has been. In my opinion, the banking system is still too large in relation to national needs and it is inevitable that there will be restructuring in the coming months, both through the actions of public bodies and market bodies. From the point of view of promoting the security of the system, it is then important that the financial undertakings are as diverse as possible regarding business, ownership and financing. When all financial institutions are the same, the nature of the risk is also the same for all of them, and certain shocks are therefore more likely to incorporate the system as a whole than they would otherwise be. This was one of the main problems with the banking system in this country before the crash. Finally, we need to formulate a strategy for how the banking system's Icelandic ties to the global financial system will be handled after currency controls are lifted. In my opinion, some precautions will need to be put in place that limit the international activities and foreign exchange-related risks of the banking system after the lifting of currency controls, at least as long as the Iceland is not a member of the European Monetary Union. It's in this context that I see the role of savings banks. They add to the diversity as well as having a certain advantage in evaluating local opportunities and risks and enjoying local trust and goodwill. However, it is important that the savings banks limit their operations to the factors in which they are competitive and do not go into risky investment banking. Indeed, the savings bank system has suffered major setbacks and their share of loans and leases of the financial system was only 4% at the end of June. But they have about a third of the turnarounds in the country, and with the financial restructuring of the savings banks that have taken place in the past, it should be possible to shoot feet under important savings banks. Many remain in operation and in the local area, and their founding shareholders in the future will have the opportunity to buy back from the state its holdings. Although the write-down of initial capital now is a painful operation, it is going on even shorter than what the banks' shareholders had to endure. As before, I challenge savings people to seize this opportunity and start building for the future.

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 26.03.2002 Statement by eelafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland at the Bank's annual meeting on 26 March 2002 Address to the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland on 26 March 2002, Honourable Ministers, President of the Althingi, other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 40th and first annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. At the conclusion of my introductory remarks, the Chairman of the Board of Directors Birgir easleifur Gunnarsson will give an overview of the development of economic and monetary policy, the Bank's monetary policy and its implementation and the prospects ahead. After the speech of the Chairman of the Board of Directors, Prime Minister David Oddsson will address the meeting. At the end of the meeting, attendees are invited to accept refreshments. At a meeting of the Board of Directors earlier today, the Prime Minister confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2001 with his signature. 2001 marked a turning point in the history of the Central Bank of Iceland and the implementation of monetary policy. I recall that at the Bank's annual meeting a year ago, the Prime Minister presented a statement by the Government and the Central Bank on inflation targets and a change in exchange rate policy. At the same meeting, the Prime Minister announced that the government had been introduced a bill to the New Act on the Central Bank of Iceland and that it would be presented to the Althingi. The Althing passed the bill in May with the votes of all members present at its final dispensation. It can therefore be said that there was an unusually broad consensus on the framework in which the new law created the Central Bank of Iceland and the monetary policy administration in general. The law gave the bank a very high level of responsibility. The act included sharpening the provisions on the role of the Central Bank's Board of Directors from the previous law and providing for an increase in the number of members of the Board of Directors from five members to seven. A report on the bill said, among other things, that the increase was in line with the enhanced regulatory role of the Board of Directors. It ensured its wider composition and that more views would be found during consideration by the Board of Directors. According to the Act, the Board of Directors shall, among other things, confirm the main draws of the Central Bank's structure, determine the remuneration and terms of employment of the CEO, oversee internal auditing and hire the Chief Auditor, confirm the plan for the Bank's operating expenses and annual accounts, supervise the Bank's assets and operations, and confirm rules established by the Board of Directors on the preparation, justification and presentation of monetary decisions, on the mandate of employees to oblige the Bank, on the authorisation of employees to sit on the boards of institutions and companies outside the Bank and rules of procedure for the preservation of the foreign exchange reserves. A new board of directors was elected to pass the act. The term of office lasts until a new Board of Directors is elected after the election to the Althingi. The new Board of Directors elected four members who were members of the previous Board of Directors, namely eelafur G. Einarsson, Dav92? A?alsteinsson, Ragnar Arnalds and ?r9astur eelafsson. In addition, Hannes H97lmsteinn Gissurarson, J97n Sigur?sson and Sigr92?ur Stef87nsd97ttir were elected to the Board of Directors. Ingunn El92n Sveinsd97ttir disappeared from the Board of Directors and is hereby thanked for her good cooperation. According to previous law, the Minister appointed the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Board of Directors. The new law stipulates that the Board of Directors shall elect a chairman and vice-chairman from its own ranks. At the first meeting of the new Board of Directors, the person speaking here was elected chairman and David A?alsteinsson vice-chairman. In the absence of two members, Erna G92slad97ttir and Krist92n Sigur?ard97ttir attended a meeting of the Board of Directors earlier today. The new law stipulates that the Board of Directors appoint three bankers. The Board of Directors is responsible for the Bank's operations and exercises decision-making powers in all its matters which are not entrusted to others in the Act. Under previous law, the Minister appointed the CEO for a term of five years and they elected the Chairman of the Board of Directors from their own group for a term of three years. The new law stipulates that the minister appoint the governors, including the chairman of the Board of Directors. The term of office is seven years and possible I'm going to reinstate a banker once. Sitting bankers at the time of the entry into force of the Act should sit out the time they were last appointed. After the adoption of the act, the Prime Minister appointed Birgi easleif Gunnarsson chairman of the Board of Directors. A number of changes that occurred from previous legislation affect the Bank's financial statements. The provision on hard-funding was repealed, thereby repealing the provision that the Central Bank of Iceland contribute funds to the Science Fund. Second, the provisions of the Act on the National Economic Institute, which entailed that the Central Bank paid part of its operating expenses against the Treasury. Third, the provision for the Minister to appoint a special inspector was repealed. The Central Bank's audit is now in the hands of the Internal Auditor and the National Audit Office. Fourth, the provisions on the Central Bank's contribution to the Treasury changed in such a way that instead of paying half the average profit of the past three years to the Treasury, it now pays two-thirds of its profits in the fiscal year to the Treasury. However, as long as the Bank's equity is below a certain defined minimum, the Bank pays only a third of its profits to the Treasury. On the basis of the new act, the Prime Minister issued new rules on financial statements and the preparation of the Central Bank of Iceland's annual accounts in December 2001. In 2001, profits from the Central Bank's operations amounted to nearly ISK 800 million. The Bank's payment to the Treasury amounted to ISK 262 million, with the exception of the Bank's profit amounting to ISK 523 million. Payment to the Treasury and other public charges and the Bank's statutory contributions to public entities amounted to just over ISK 360 million. The Central Bank's equity increased considerably in the past year when the Treasury contributed additional initial capital in the amount of ISK 9 billion. At the end of 2001, the Bank's equity amounted to just over ISK 34 billion. A report on the bill passed on the Central Bank a year ago argued that it was necessary to substantially strengthen the Bank's equity. The same meaning cannot be added to profits from the Central Bank's operations as from the operations of competing companies. The main purpose of the Central Bank is not necessarily to turn a profit, but first and foremost to enforce monetary policy in accordance with the objectives set by law. Since the Bank's role implies an imbalance between exchange rate-based assets and liabilities, its performance is traditionally susceptible to changes in the exchange rate of the kr97na. The Bank's book valued exchange rate gains amounted to ISK 970 million in the past year. The Central Bank's operating expenses in 2000 amounted to 884 m.kr. including the 18 million cost of banknotes and coins and 40 million of real estate expenses. It can therefore be said that the Bank's actual operations cost ISK 826 million. At the end of 2001, the bank had 108 full-time equivalent positions. The Bank's performance and operations are detailed in its annual report, which is published today. As it happens, there have been significant changes in the Bank's workforce over the past year. A total of fourteen employees retired from the bank in the past year and are regrettable in all of them. Seventeen new employees were hired by the Bank and all are welcome to work. The Board of Directors held 23 meetings in the year leading up to the meeting. I thank the members of the Board of Directors for their very enjoyable cooperation and well-done work. Good attendees! I would like to finally thank the Board of Directors, auditors and employees of the Bank for a good and enjoyable cooperation with the Board of Directors over the past year.

Title: Statement by Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Chairman of the Board of Directors, at the Annual General Meeting on 26 March 2002
text: 26.03.2002 Statement by Birgiur isl. Gunnarsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Chairman of the Board of Directors, at the Annual General Meeting on 26 March 2002 On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you all to the Bank's 41st annual meeting. The Bank's accounts for 2001 have today been confirmed by the Prime Minister. The Bank's annual report has also been published. It is customary to provide an overview of the Bank's operations and performance, as well as a report on its monetary policy and actions, on financial systems, financial stability and financial markets, as well as the main characteristic of economic developments over the past year. I will now, from the Central Bank's point of view, outline the highest level of economic policy in the past year and the prospects faced at the moment. 2001 was an eventful year in the history of the Central Bank of Iceland. The Althing passed a new law to the Bank, which became a strong consensus among members of the Althingi. Fundamental changes to monetary policy foundations that were introduced at the Bank's annual meeting a year ago had previously been undertaken. The legislation trusts the new monetary policy framework. I'm going to make these two important issues a further topic of discussion. The new Act on the Central Bank of Iceland replaced the Act of 1986. They had become obsolete in various sectors and out of context with progress in most industrialized countries of the world. The new law simplifies and clarifies the Bank's objectives. With them, the Central Bank sets similar targets that central banks have in our major trading countries. Stable prices are made the main objective of monetary policy. The Central Bank shall also work towards other objectives, such as an effective and secure financial system. The Bank shall promote the achievement of the Government's policy, provided that it does not consider it to be contrary to the main objective of stable prices. The new law gives the Central Bank much more independence than before. However, the ultimate objective of monetary policy, i.e. the numerical value of the inflation target, continues to be determined jointly by the Government and the Central Bank. The Bank is now guaranteed full independence in order to use its controls in favour of the inflation target, which is probably the most important new measure in the ACT. Similar provisions apply to the central banks of the vast majority of other industrialized countries. Furthermore, the act entails clearer provisions than before on the Bank's transparency and financial statements to the authorities and the public. The long-term objectives of monetary policy are thus formalised, and at the same time an open and effective monetary policy regime can be guaranteed. Stronger pillars are also underpinned by the Central Bank's independence in that the new law stipulates that direct government funding at the Central Bank is prohibited. An earlier law did not include this access, but an agreement was in force between the Minister of Finance and the Bank, originally concluded in 1992, that the Treasury should not exercise this authority. The Bank's financial independence was also enhanced by provisions that include the promotion of equity. With the entry into force of the new Central Bank Act, it can be said that the factors most important for the implementation of independent monetary policy have been moved to a similar level to the best of times elsewhere. There was a turning point in the history of exchange rates and the implementation of monetary policy in Iceland when the formal inflation target was adopted and the exchange rate was abandoned as the intermediate objective and anchor of monetary policy. A stable exchange rate had been the ballast of monetary policy in some way almost all the time since the krona was created as an independent currency, although the flexibility was sometimes so great that it bordered on floats. The decision to adopt an inflation target had some prelude. It was clear that the abolition of capital movements in the middle of the last decade stoked the progress of monetary policy on the basis of stable exchange rates under certain circumstances. Difficulties were also seen in the implementation of monetary policy in 1999 and 2000. At that time, the exchange rate policy appeared to have become a hindrance to the central bank's main objective of keeping rates steady. The exchange rate of the crown began to decrease on in 2000 despite extensive intervention by the Central Bank in the foreign exchange market. In the first quarter of 2001, the Bank's foreign exchange position had become weak, there was no let-up in foreign exchange outflows and the exchange rate close to the lower tolerance of the exchange rate policy, which allowed a 9% deviation to each direction from the median official exchange rate index. It was clear then that it would be difficult to defend the tolerance all the time. On March 27, the government and the Central Bank decided to follow the example of a number of countries that had in recent years adopted inflation targets, and the exchange rate was left floating. Preparations for a possible change had been going on for some time within the Central Bank, as research suggested that an inflation target would be more suitable here than a one-sided fixed-rate policy. It was decided by a joint statement by the Government and the Central Bank that the Bank's inflation target would be 21/2% and should be reached no later than 2003. Tolerances were also defined, i.e. 11/2% deviations in each direction. If inflation goes beyond the limits, the Central Bank should send a report to the Government clarifying the reasons for this and assess when the inflation target would be re-reached and to outline the necessary measures for this purpose. This statement should be published publicly. However, in light of the circumstances that prevailed when the inflation target was adopted, the upper tolerance was lower first, with inflation up to 6% for the remainder of 2001 and 41/2% in 2002 without a specific central bank report. The tolerance of the inflation target was breached already in June 2001, and the Central Bank then sent the government a report that was published publicly. Since then, the Bank has regularly outlined the progress of prices and outlook in its quarterly publication, Monetary Bulletin. The main objective of the Central Bank of Iceland is to promote stable prices as I mentioned earlier. I will therefore deviate from the price developments of the past year and the factors that had the greatest impact there. Inflation rose sharply during the year. The consumer price index rose by 9.4% from the beginning to the end of the year, and the index's 12-month rise had not been higher since August 1990. Inflation between 2000 and 2001 averaged 6.7%. That's the highest average inflation rate since 1991. However, productivity, measured as an increase in GDP above labour force growth, increased by 2.7% in 2000, but only by 1% in 2001. The krona decreased by almost 15% in 2001 and almost 17% from the previous year's average exchange rate. The krona's devaluation from mid-2000 can be attributed to a large trade deficit and net outflows due to the purchase of foreign securities and foreign direct investment. The funding of the deficit went viable until late 2000, but became more reluctant in the latter half of that year, and in 2001 the exchange rate decreased almost steadily until the end of November. The real exchange rate of the krona was then lower than it had been for decades and lower than the Central Bank believed was compatible with conditions in the economy. The currency devaluation unleashed inflationary pressures that had accumulated in recent years. For many years, labour costs in Iceland increased far beyond productivity. Between 1996 and 2001, wages per production unit increased by 11.5% in Iceland, and 2.2% in the trading countries. The high exchange rate of the krona until 2000 had provided an approach against the inflationary impact of wage increases, but this approach broke in 2001. Differences in inflation in Iceland and in the major trading countries increased as much as possible. In Iceland's main trading countries, inflation fell from an average of 2.7% in June 2001 to 1.8% in December. It is often cited that domestic industries that are competing with comparable sectors abroad cannot in the long run live with large interest rates. It can certainly be true, given that high interest rates are only intended to last for the time needed to restore satisfactory balance. However, it is equally clear that competitive sectors cannot live for years with many times higher inflation in Iceland than in the competitive countries. Therefore, it is an urgent task in economic policy to bring inflation down to the level in competitive countries. A number of indicators emerged in 2001 of the massive expansion of the economy. Tensions in the labour market were high up until the end of the year. The unemployment rate averaged just 1.3%, but was also rising in the last few months of the year. Tensions in the labour market also appeared to be rising payroll crawl. From the fourth quarter of 2000 to equal length in 2001, wages in private companies other than financial institutions increased by almost 31/2% above the provisions of collective agreements, while in the previous years wage momentum had long been between 11/2-2%. In the last few months of the year, however, we could see that wage momentum was declining. Wages in the public sector also continued to rise above the salaries of others, while new collective bargaining agreements with several groups of public sector workers led to significant pay rises. After excessive growth in lending for three years, they declined in 2001. If adjusted for the effect of the krona devaluation and an index increase in indexed loans, lending by depositors increased by 71/2% last year, but had increased by 20% the previous year. However, the lending of the credit system as a whole increased more. This is mainly due to increased loans for residential purchases. In the past year, the Central Bank was mostly committed to lowering interest rates more than it did. The Bank's policy rate was reduced by 0.5% in March and 0.8% in November. In this much debate, it was thought, among other things, that the economic downturn as it was called was soon to be behind us, ahead of a massive recession and even a crisis, and the economy was very much in the process of being protected. All of this proved to be very worded. Economic growth was strong in the past year, although it did not reach record levels, and is now expected to have been 3%. By comparison, economic growth in eurozone countries is estimated to have been 1.5% and in the world's largest industrialised countries at 1%. Economic growth in Iceland in 2001 was therefore higher than in most industrialized countries in the world. Economic growth in 2000 was found to have been much higher than thought for the longest time last year, or 51/2% according to the latest figures. Production tensions in the economy, i.e. economic growth beyond production capacity, were therefore much higher than previous forecasts had suggested. This tension played a part in the inflation trends of the past year. This also means that the production voltage has been maintained longer than previously thought. However, overheating was reduced, and it was more relevant to some industries than others. Imports of durable consumer goods such as automobiles decreased significantly, media advertising revenues shrank, and demand for commercial property declined, for example. That doesn't change the fact that adhering monetary policy continued to be needed to help balance the economy and reduce the high production tensions that were here last year. There is no question that monetary restraint contributed to the deflation of overheating and at the same time laid the foundations for a rapid reduction in inflation that followed the krona's rate cut. The Central Bank implements monetary policy not least by controlling interest rates on the money market, particularly by determining returns in its reversible transactions with credit institutions. Returns on the money market have a strong impact on foreign exchange flows, thereby on the exchange rate of the krona and in the long run of domestic demand. In a small and open economy, the exchange rate of the currency is of considerable importance to domestic price developments and the economy in general. Interest rate changes thus affect inflation both in the short and long term, in the short term through the exchange rate of the krona that is susceptible to interest rate changes and long-term by influencing demand and production tensions. Research by the Central Bank suggests that interest rates have a similar effect on long-term inflation as in other industrialized countries. High interest rates therefore do not cause inflation. They beat inflation. Central banks in large economic environments, such as the United States and the European Economic and Monetary Union, don't have to think much about the exchange rate, even if they sometimes do so in theory. This is because these economic structures are self-sufficient to a significant extent, and exchange rate changes have very little effect on inflation. The Central Bank of Iceland, however, cannot afford to ignore exchange rate developments, as much of an impact it has here on prices. The Central Bank's reluctance to cut interest rates in the past month is notably linked to concerns over the exchange rate trend. While observations show that the exchange rate will likely strengthen from the start to the end of this year, the experience in recent weeks shows that it is very sensitive to external influences and has fluctuated somewhat in the entire last few weeks. The agreements between the parties to the labour market on the red canvass in May have caused these short-term considerations to outweigh the Central Bank's position. The bank believed it. It is very important to ensure that the red canvases are maintained. It is also clear from the figures that have been coming out of the economy up to now, that the wave of expansion and tension in the economy rose higher than previously thought and has declined more slowly and less than expected. I'll then go next to the inflation outlook. The Central Bank publishes inflation forecasts four times a year, traditionally reaching two years ahead. The last inflation forecast was made at the beginning of February based on assumptions as they were before 21 January. Inflation is expected to fall below the 4% tolerance in the autumn. Inflation is forecast to reach 3% over 2003 and the first quarter of 2004. The price measurements that have since appeared confirm declining inflation. In the past 12 months, inflation has been measured at 8.7%, but in the past three months 4.7% on an annual basis, if adjusted for seasonal fluctuations. All predictions rest on specific assumptions. The Central Bank has so far expected unchanged rates in inflation forecasts. Last year's massive rate cuts put the Bank's inflation forecasts somewhat out of reach, and inflation has not fallen as fast as the Bank's forecasts. Now exchange rate trends have reversed, so the likelihood of the last inflation forecast has increased. The fact that the exchange rate Icelandic the krona has increased by 2.32% since the forecast increases the likelihood that the target of 21/2% inflation will be achieved in 2003. I was able to say before that the overheating that had been going on here for a while. Undoubtedly, the national economy is now heading for a more balanced economy. In recent years, there was a huge deficit in Iceland's trade with other nations. The trade deficit peaked in 2000 and amounted to ISK 67.6 billion, which corresponds to 10.1% of GDP. Last year's trade deficit was much smaller than ISK 33 billion, which is 4.4% of GDP. This improvement can mainly be attributed to greater parity of trade in goods with foreign countries, reduced imports and greatly increased exports of seafood and industrial products. The recovery in service trade also suffered greatly last year. This year looks set to see a further recovery in the balance of trade, although there is a long way to go before there will be a surplus on trade with foreign countries. This is mostly due to high interest payments, as the foreign debt position of the economy has deteriorated due to the trade deficit and the outflow of foreign currency to foreign securities purchases and direct investments abroad. When you consider the turmoil that was in the Icelandic economic crisis last year, there is no choice but to say that there is brightness ahead and the economy has shown its strength in the rapid adjustment that has occurred here. Under the new Act on the Central Bank, one of its main functions is to promote an active and secure financial system, including payment systems in the country and abroad. This challenge has become increasingly extensive in the operations of many central banks in recent years, as it was considered necessary as a result of the lifting of restrictions on the movements of capital movements between countries. The focus on an active and secure financial system is in line with the policy. Among the roles of central banks in most countries is to promote a secure financial system, i.e. to ensure financial stability. The Central Bank seeks to promote a secure financial system by closely monitoring its macroeconomic environment, relations between financial institutions and capital markets, the progress of the system both in Iceland and abroad, its strength and efficiency and the impact of economic factors on the system as a whole. Twice a year, the Central Bank publishes an assessment of financial stability in Iceland in its quarterly publication, Monetary Bulletin. This project is different from traditional financial supervision. Instead of monitoring the status of individual credit institutions, emphasis is placed on what might pose a risk to the financial system as a whole. In order to promote a healthy financial system and to trust its foundations, the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority cooperate closely. In the middle of last year, the International Monetary Fund published its assessment of the Icelandic financial system, but the Fund is now increasingly focused on such withdrawals. The results of the delegation of the Fund said that it was her overall assessment that certain vulnerabilities were found in Icelandic financial system. A specific explanation for this would be the rapid progression in financial markets over the last few years. In some ways, it would have exceeded the rules governing the markets. There would also be imbalances in the national economy, particularly the large and growing trade deficit and low savings rates. At the same time, it would be important to note that the financial sector is dynamic and responds quickly to the market's message and changes in the legal framework. It would have to be believed that the financial supervisory authority in this country would have a good position to handle its task. On this basis, the government seemed to be doing well, they could respond to potential vulnerabilities and would have the will to do so. Since this was written, various improvements have been made to laws and regulations on the financial system, and the state of the economy has blurred to a better state. If you look at the 2001 financial institutions' account results and look at the account results of financial institutions, it is clear that Icelandic financial system has as a whole passed the auras it suffered in the past year with a sharp devaluation of the krona. It can also be argued that there are no major setbacks over the financial system as a whole, although individual institutions may be affected by booze. In the past year, reforms in the field of payment processing were continued in accordance with the increased emphasis placed on it in the new Act on the Central Bank. The main emphasis has been placed on the development of a multipayment system, which is a balancing system for payments that are below the large payment limit. The large-scale payment limit is now based on ISK 25 million. The multipayment system is formally managed by a special limited liability company, Fjolgreioslumiolunar hf., which is owned by Icelandic commercial banks, credit card companies and the Central Bank. The Central Bank has initiated the formulation of the multi-payment system. At the same time, a large payment system has been put into operation, but it definitively settles individual payment instructions as soon as the deposit of the payer's account allows. The large payment system thus transfers payment instructions over large payment limits directly to the trading accounts of participants at the Central Bank or of them. These issues are continuing to work, and the aim is to ensure that payment processing in Iceland in the near future meets all the main requirements for such systems at international level. Good attendees. In situations such as those that have prevailed here, it is a matter of time when it is appropriate to take action on monetary policy. At the beginning of February, the Central Bank considered the situation "not an occasion to cut interest rates for the time being" as it was put. Assumptions could change relatively quickly, however, and there the development of exchange rates and prices in the coming months would have a lot to say. The exchange rate trend has been favourable as I mentioned earlier, and the last two price measures point to low underlying inflation. There seems to be an increased likelihood that the Bank's inflation forecast for the year will go ahead. In addition, the latest information from the National Bureau of Statistics confirms that production tensions are disappearing this year. For these reasons, the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland decided today to reduce interest rates in reversible transactions with credit institutions by 0.5%. Monetary restraint, however, is still high, as it is necessary to ensure satisfactory inflation. I would like to finally appreciate the pleasing cooperation with the governments, financial institutions and the organisations with which the Central Bank has engaged during the year.

Title: Household Overdraft Loans
text: 26.03.2014 Krist97fer Gunnlaugsson: Household Overdraft Loans There have been regular reports of the development of home overdraft loans in the media in recent years, detailing how much these loans have increased since the collapse of the financial system. It has even been concluded that the increase explains a large part of the country's private consumption and thus economic growth. It is true that the numbers of overdraft loans by depositors to households have risen. Thus, the book value of the stock was nearly 37 ma.kr. more on average in 2013 compared to the average position in 2009 and about 27 ma.kr. More taking into account price changes. The bulk of the increase, however, is due to the accounting reclassification of these loans in the books of credit institutions and therefore not the actual increase in overdraft loans. B97khaldsleg endurflokkun yfirdr87ttarl87na In the autumn of 2009, the Central Bank of Iceland established new rules, No. 849/2009, on payment settlement of card transactions. This was done, inter alia, to reduce settlement risk and ensure the security of card issuer payments to the transaction handler and on to the merchant. According to the rules, payments that transaction handlers receive from card issuers should be preserved at least risk and not paid immediately to the merchant, for example as deposits. Concurrently, the change was made that card issuers do away more quickly with transactional care than before. Following the regulation, depositors changed their settlement methods with credit card companies so that daily customer credit card withdrawals were transferred as overdraft loans. A customer's overdraft loan thus piles up alongside card usage until an invoice has been paid. The dramatic increase in overdraft loans to households towards the end of 2009, by 20.3 ma.kr., is almost wholly the result of this accounting reclassification of card transaction settlements and is thus not a real increase. The development of overdraft loans has also been tainted by the merger of financial institutions. Thus, the loans increased by the merger of easlandsbanki hf. and Byr hf. due to different methods of sorting out loans used by these financial undertakings. In addition, credit card liabilities were reclassified as overdraft loans by the merger of Kreditkorta hf. and easlandsbanki hf. in the spring of 2012. Development of overdraft loans taking into account the reclassifications Taking into account the above reclassifications, the actual development of overdraft loans is considerably different from the figures that come straight out of the accounting. Instead of 37 ma.kr. increase in the average balance of the stock of overdraft loans of depositors, the stock has increased by 10.5 ma.kr. from 2009 to 2013. Taking into account price movements, however, the increase is just under 1 ma.kr. or by 1.4%. During the same period, private national consumption has increased by 193 ma.kr. nominal value, but nearly 43 ma.kr. in real terms. Accounting reclassification thus accounts for the vast majority of the increase in the total population of overdraft credit to households in recent years. The actual change in the loans is much smaller and only a fraction of the growth in private consumption. To argue that the private consumption of the population in recent years has been funded in large part by overdrafts therefore does not add up to scrutiny.

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Address Jon Helgi Egilsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the 54th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 26 March 2015. Delivered at the 54th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 26 March 2015. The President of Iceland, the President of the Althing, the Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, the Minister of the Interior, governors, ambassadors of foreign countries and other good guests. I welcome you and sit here with the 50th and fourth annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. The current Board of Directors was elected by the Althingi on 5 July 2013. The Board of Directors elected olof Nordal as chairman and the person standing here as vice-chairman. Since last August, I have given leadership to the Board of Directors but took over the presidency of the Council when olof resigned last December when she took up the post of Minister of the Interior. On behalf of the Board of Directors, I would like to extend my special thanks to olof for her cooperation in the Board of Directors and wish her well in her new job. One of the main roles of central banks in the world is monetary policy. The Central Bank of Iceland is no exception, as its main objective is to promote stable prices. By applying its controls, it is tempted to keep inflation as close as possible to the inflation target, which is believed to be able to promote long-term steady economic growth. The monetary policy is therefore inherently a long-term perspective that can potentially be contrary to the views of politics in the short term. In the last twenty years, the independence of the world's central banks has increased considerably while setting clearly specific tasks and objectives. In 2001, the Central Bank of Iceland's independence was transferred to coincide with the countries that went the longest in this regard. The Central Bank was then given full independence to use the tools it possessed to "promote stable prices". In 2013, the Central Bank of Iceland Act was amended to ensure that the Bank's other main objective was to promote financial stability. This is in line with global trends among central banks where it was believed that before the 2008 financial crisis, there was too much emphasis on inflation targets and that financial stability needs a boost. Along with that, the debate over central bank independence continued, as independence was primarily confined to full custody of the implementation of monetary policy. Such situations that call for independence are not necessarily considered to apply to a number of issues relating to financial stability, as a central bank may to a greater extent have to cooperate with governments or other public institutions. The theory of central bank independence therefore applies primarily to monetary policy management and inflation targets. After the collapse of the banks in the autumn of 2008, the Central Bank's projects increased, with both the processing of assets and requirements and foreign exchange controls. The Bank shall, by law, be a government to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on all matters relating to foreign exchange. The Central Bank is therefore naturally involved in the abolition process of capital controls with the government. But the attitudes and perspectives that effectively determine the paths chosen in the abolition process can have a significant impact on our society for the long term and are therefore inherently political. The ultimate responsibility for the abolition process must therefore always be a democratically elected government. As mentioned here, the Central Bank of Iceland has two main objectives, that is, to promote price stability and financial stability on the one hand. The Bank also has a number of other important tasks, such as financial infrastructure, the preservation of foreign exchange reserves and promoting the government's economic policy if the Bank considers it not to be contrary to its main objective of stable prices. All we can say is that the Bank has been successful in working towards its main objectives in the past year. Inflation rebounded and, more importantly, inflation expectations were towards the end of the year in line with the target. The Central Bank imposed new precautionary measures aimed at preparing the banks for the disposal of capital controls. A new Act on the Financial Stability Council was passed and the Central Bank plays a major role in its operations and the Systemic Risk Committee acting on its behalf. The Bank's annual report, published today, briefly describes the Central Bank's diverse operations. Various publications of publications in the field of economic affairs and statistics are, as before, an important part of the operation. The Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs today confirmed the Bank's consolidated financial statements for 2014 with its signature. I will now briefly describe the financial performance and economy of the Central Bank of Iceland and its members. According to the operating accounts, profit for 2014 was ISK 11.2 billion, compared with a loss of ISK 8.3 billion in the previous year. Currency movements have a considerable impact on the Bank's performance. Exchange rate gain for the year amounted to ISK 6.2 billion, compared with an exchange rate loss in the amount of ISK 12.3 billion in 2013. The exchange rate gains in 2014 can be attributed in large part to the strengthening of the US dollar, but the majority of the Bank's assets in excess of foreign currency liabilities are in US dollars. The Central Bank's assets amounted to ISK 954 billion at year-end 2014, up from ISK 1,002 billion in the previous year. The majority of the Central Bank's assets are foreign assets in foreign reserves, with reserves amounting to ISK 530 billion at year-end. The Central Bank of Iceland's portfolio ehf. has maintained assets due to mortgages and claims on the estates of financial undertakings that fell into the central bank's favour following the collapse of the banks. This year, however, further steps were taken to free up the company's assets. Since 2009, the portfolio has decreased from ISK 490 billion to ISK 209 billion at the end of 2014. At the same time, equity has increased from ISK 1 million to about ISK 29 billion. With a new agreement on recallable equity, the Treasury undertakes, on the basis of the budget authorization, to contribute ISK 52 billion to the Central Bank in the form of marketable assets if the Bank calls for it to meet minimum requirements for deposited equity. At the same time, an agreement was reached on changes to the terms of the bond issued by the Treasury at the end of 2008 due to the Government's takeover of part of the Bank's mortgages and day loans. The Bank's initial capital was reduced by ISK 26 billion during the year and these funds were allocated to a reduction in the principal of the bond. The bond's principal has now fallen by almost half since its issuance, or from ISK 270 billion to ISK 145 billion at the end of December. The Bank's profits, after transactions in the Reserve Bank, shall be allocated to the Treasury if equity exceeds the Central Bank's capital objective. The Board of Directors now confirms each year the Central Bank's decision on capital objectives, reflecting its need for equity and interest-bearing assets. In 2015, the Bank meets its capital objective, which is why all profits in excess of reserves are allocated to the Treasury, totalling ISK 1.9 billion. The Bank's dividend payment to the Treasury for 2014 is lower than in recent years. It must, however, be put in context that the Bank's deposited initial capital was reduced by ISK 26 billion at the end of the year, which is a kind of dividend payment. Following the collapse of the banks and financial restructuring at the end of 2008/2009, the Central Bank has paid a total of dividends, profits from foreign exchange transactions and auctions, and tax to the Treasury for companies owned by the Bank by ISK 30 billion and ISK 56 billion if the aforementioned reduction in initial capital is included. This is not a small amount, as it corresponds to 2.8% of GDP in 2014. Internal controls at the Bank have in recent years been strengthened. Audits have been carried out on various activities and units of work and their results presented to the Board of Directors. This kind of surveillance is part of the increased transparency and accountability that offsets the increased independence that central banks have received. At the end of 2014, the Central Bank's employees totalled 177. During the year, 12 employees were hired and 14 retired. I would like to thank the bank's employees for their good cooperation during the year. Dear attendees, I would like to finally thank the Board of Directors, the Governor and the Deputy Governor for their excellent cooperation during the year. We will now listen to Bjarni Benediktsson's address to the Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, and after that, Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, will take over the case.

Title: Talks from the Central Bank's foreign exchange auctions
text: 28.01.2014 orgeir Eyjolfsson: From the Central Bank's foreign exchange auctions orgeir Eyjolfsson, Project Manager at the Central Bank of Iceland: This article appeared in Morgunblaoio on January 27, 2014: Iceland faces the problem of foreign entities having a significant amount of liquidity in Icelandic kronas that are likely to convert them into foreign currency at the earliest opportunity if there were no capital controls. It is necessary to solve this problem before the controls are resolved. In 2011, the Central Bank formulated a plan, which received government approval, to work systematically to bring this liquidity asset into the hands of long-term investors, thereby generating the benefit of capital controls disposal. The policy is carried out with foreign exchange auctions whose primary objective is to reduce the position size of dynamic krona assets, which amounted to ISK 605 billion after the collapse of the banks at the end of 2008 but are estimated to have amounted to ISK 327 billion at the end of last year. The foreign exchange auction of treasury bonds began in the summer of 2011, but the first auction under the investment plan was held in February 2012. A total of seventeen auctions of treasury bonds have been held and fifteen auctions have been held in connection with the investment scheme. On the basis of the auction price in each case and the central bank's registered average rate on the same day, investors have brought a total of approximately ISK 51.3 billion into the country through auctions under the Treasury bond route and 147.4 billion under the investment plan. Almost a third of this has passed through the domestic foreign exchange market, where 50% of the amount invested under the investment plan must be converted to Icelandic kronor in the domestic foreign exchange market. At the beginning of December 2013, the foreign exchange auctions had provided foreign investments to Iceland, equivalent to approximately 11.6% of GDP in 2012. About 45.5% of the capital inflows caused by the investment plan have been pegged in bonds, about 41.5% in equities, 12% in real estate and about 1% in mutual funds. Funds coming to the country under an investment plan are wholly tied to reprisals for a five-year dispensary. When it is reported between domestic and foreign parties participating in the auctions, it is found that 37% of the total amount comes from domestic and 63% from foreign investors. At this analysis, foreign companies owned by Icelandic entities are classified as domestic investors. Foreign currency, which the Central Bank acquires in the aforementioned auctions according to the Treasury securities and investment plan, is spent on buying kronur (sometimes called offshore kronur) in tenders by investors who wish to release their krona investment in Iceland in such a manner. Sixteen tenders have been held seeking bids from parties wishing to sell their krona assets in exchange for foreign currency that is exempt from return obligations. In 2011, two such auctions were held at a price of ISK 210 per euro. The price remained fairly stable in 2012, or 240 kronor per euro, which has fallen in 2013. In the last auction, held in December 2013, the auction price was ISK 216 per euro. In the sixteen auctions, a total of ISK 342.8 billion has been offered for sale, of which the Central Bank has purchased ISK 117.8 billion. The auction price is decided after the completion of the three tenders on the day of the auction. The amount of krona that the Central Bank buys for foreign currency is determined by the amount of foreign currency offered for sale for the purchase of long treasury bonds and for investment through the investment route. Thus, the impact of the auctions on the foreign exchange reserves is kept to a minimum. Tender dates are announced in advance and will be the next auctions on 4 February and 18 March 2014. There may be occasional misconceptions that the Central Bank has the authority to limit who is involved in the investment scheme on the grounds that the person or persons close to them are under investigation by a special prosecutor. The Central Bank has no qualms about knowing who is under investigation by a special prosecutor, any more than others outside that office. However, investors' participation in the tenders of an investment plan is subject to the condition that they are not subject to reasonable suspicion by the Central Bank's Foreign Exchange Authority of alleged violations, have not been indicted by the holder of a prosecution or appealed to the police by the Central Bank for alleged violations of the Foreign Exchange Act, No. 87/1992, and rules established on their basis. (Published in Morgunblaoio, January 27, 2014).

Veri hlst nokku stugt ri 2012, ea 240 krnur  evru, en a hefur lkka  rinu 2013.  sasta tboinu, sem var haldi  desember 2013, var tbosveri 216 krnur  evru.  tbounum sextn hafa alls 342,8 milljarar kr. veri bonir til slu, en ar af hefur Selabankinn keypt 117,8 milljara kr. tbosver er kvei a afloknum tbounum remur  tbosdegi. Magn eirra krna sem Selabankinn kaupir fyrir erlendan gjaldeyri rst af magni ess erlenda gjaldeyris sem boinn er til slu til kaupa  lngum rkisskuldabrfum og til fjrfestinga  gegnum fjrfestingaleiina. annig er hrifum tboanna  gjaldeyrisforann haldi  lgmarki. tbosdagsetningar eru tilkynntar me fyrirvara og vera nstu tbo 4. febrar og 18. mars 2014. ess misskilnings gtir  stundum a Selabankinn hafi heimildir til a takmarka hverjir taki tt  fjrfestingarleiinni  eim forsendum a vikomandi ea ailar nkomnir eim sti rannskn hj srstkum saksknara. Selabankinn hefur ekki tk  v a vita hverjir sta rannskn hj srstkum saksknara, frekar en arir utan ess embttis. Hins vegar er tttaka fjrfesta  tboum fjrfestingarleiar h v skilyri a eir liggi ekki undir rkstuddum grun hj gjaldeyriseftirliti Selabankans um meint brot, hafi ekki veri krir af handhafa kruvalds ea krir til lgreglu af Selabankanum vegna meintra brota  lgum um gjaldeyrisml, nr. 87/1992, og reglum settum  grundvelli eirra. Title: Speech on monetary policy
text: January 29, 2018 Arnor Sighvatsson Tri-clamp, double clamp or compromise between angle solutions1 Monetary policy problems in a small, open economy with unrestricted capital movements Talk delivered at a meeting of the Rotary Society of Reykjavik/Austurbaer 27 March 2018 After a period of instability in Iceland's monetary policy following the financial and currency crisis in the autumn of 2008, recent years have been characterised by considerable stability, but in some respects under the cover of capital controls. The monetary union is now at a crossroads that the last steps towards unrestricted capital movements are being taken again. On this occasion, and also because almost a century has passed since the disappearance of the Iceland disappeared from a currency union with Denmark, it is appropriate to look back and wonder what has dictated the decisions on the arrangements of this century's monetary policy, what the results have been, why it has been as it was and what is to be expected in the near future. The history of monetary policy in Iceland is sprinkled with thorns. It has often been pointed out that the Icelandic kronor has lost almost all of its initial purchasing power to its Danish mother in the century that has soon passed since the umbilical cord broke down between them. The real exchange rate of the krona, i.e. relative prices or purchase fees compared to major trading countries in the same currency measured, has also fluctuated in a wide range. The highest real exchange rate value in the period is 166% higher than the lowest value. Volatility in the real economy has also, for a number of reasons, been significant. It is speculative that during this period, the arrangement of exchange rates and monetary policy has spanned almost all the flora of possible varieties (except perhaps the monetary union). It is also concerning how the success of different policymakers has proved fleeting, at least if the constant value of the currency is the measure. Perhaps this fleetingness reflects the unstable resource base of the Icelandic national economy on the one hand, and the continual pursuit of the government's Icelandic for a monetary policy solution to that problem on the other. It should not be forgotten, however, that despite this instability, the country's standard of living has advanced. 1 The author is deputy governor. The views expressed here are the authors and do not have to reflect the views of other members of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee. In its quest for the most appropriate arrangements for exchange rate and monetary policy, the government faces a certain tension between the dual role of exchange rate policy: on the one hand, the flexible exchange rate of the currency can be used as a tool for adaptation when a country's economy is hit by shocks or buoys, with the aim of promoting a balanced real economy, e.g. inhibiting external shocks leading to economic recession and increased unemployment. However, a stable currency exchange rate can be an important tool for providing restraint in economic management and negotiation in the labour market, thereby contributing to price stability. Frequent devaluations in the 1980s and 1990s are examples of the former, but the exchange rate-settling policies following the so-called national reconciliation treaties in the early 1990s are examples of the latter. The government's choice between inclusion and restraint is neither a recent phenomenon nor confined to Iceland. The framework for that has been shaped by the development of trade liberalisation in the world, whether through goods and services or capital. The global monetary system that was shaped in the years after World War II, and often blamed on Bretton-Woods in New Hampshire, was essentially a flexible fixed-rate system, in which the US dollar was a golden ballast, ensuring monetary stability, while smaller nation states tried to gain a share of that stability by tying their currency exchange rates to the US dollar, but with a certain scope for adjustment - where the International Monetary Fund played the role of the ruling party on whether the exchange rate of its currencies was exchange rate registration would be adjusted or temporarily balanced balance of payments funded by the Fund and its member countries. The general sentiment among economists was, and largely still is, that the government was faced with a certain amount of choice: i.e. that it would not be possible in the long run to meet the following three criteria simultaneously: 1. that monetary policy is independent (note here is not to be talked about central bank independence but the ability to influence domestic monetary conditions), 2. that the exchange rate of the currency is stable, 3. that capital movements are unrestricted. The two of the above factors could go together, but not all three. This has been called a "trim" on English, which translates badly, but I prefer to call 2 the problem is simply "trilem".2 As a result, since capital movements are unrestricted, governments must, in theory, choose either monetary independence or stability in exchange rate issues. Capital controls were therefore, in some ways a prerequisite for a flexible fixed-rate system of the kind identified by Bretton-Woods to be credible, without implying a complete transfer of monetary sovereignty. The end of the Bretton-Woods system and the development of the European monetary system After the dollar-oriented Bretton-Woods fixed-rate system fell apart in the early 1980s, for reasons that won't be tracked here, the world's government took different paths. Some chose to sacrifice currency stability for monetary independence through unrestricted capital movements, others tried to hold on to a fixed rate of any kind by maintaining capital controls or taking some middle ground. In Europe, the European Union's intermediate and smaller member states (EU) adopted a coalition of exchange rates with a fixed-rate link to the German target instead of the US dollar. The German mark, however, was left floating against the US dollar. Thus, decisions in the monetary policy of most European countries were largely delegated to the German of the Central Bank, which was more independent and therefore enjoyed more confidence than other European central banks. European economic and monetary co-operation became steadily closer and capital controls were gradually lifted. This led to the fact that the foundations were pulled away from the independent monetary policy of the European nation states. It can therefore be said that most European countries have given up monetary independence for stability in exchange rates and freedom of movement across borders, but as trade liberalisation grew fished around the spine, exchange rate instability and capital controls became more of a problem. However, the transfer of monetary powers to the German central bank, which determined interest rates taking into account economic developments in Germany regardless of the needs of the countries associated with German target, was not problematic, either economically or politically. The economic problem with this arrangement was evident as a result of the german reunification. The central bank's German monetary policy aimed to hold down inflation in Germany following the merger. However, the rise in the German target resulting from the policy was badly affected by exports by other European countries that had tied their currencies to the German target but were in a completely different position than Germany.
