With the establishment of the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the countries shared monetary sovereignty, instead of delegitimizing it to the central bank's German. The new independent central bank (ECB) was entrusted with the implementation of monetary policy taking into account economic developments in the region as a whole, and not only in Germany, as it had been. Thus, the European countries involved (i.e. other than Germany) regained some degree of monetary sovereignty. Those who did not participate took different routes, some temporarily but others in the long run, including the Nordic countries. The Nordic Region's selection threshold In the first half of the 1990s, the Nordic countries loosened capital controls. It soon became clear that it would be difficult to maintain a stable exchange rate through some form of fixed-rate policy, as had been tried in Iceland and the rest of the Nordic countries in the first decade (and from the mid-1980s in Denmark), with an increased emphasis on stability towards the German limit or the European Currency Unit (ECU), the forerunner of the euro. All the Nordic countries, with the exception of Denmark, had to leave after a period of economic inequality, capital exodus and speculation. Iceland, Norway and Sweden chose to let their currencies float but adopted inflation targets to give monetary policy the ballast necessary across all currency systems. Denmark continued its fixed-rate policy, with the ECB's backing involved in membership of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) after the EMU was established, and the Finland (and later the three Baltic states) adopted the euro. Increased freedom of movement of capital therefore forced the Nordic countries to abdicate from time to time, independent monetary policy (Denmark, Finland) or exchange rate (Sweden, Norway and Iceland). With the exception of Iceland, the Nordic countries have all managed to preserve the stability and purchasing power of their currencies fairly well despite the different exchange rate frameworks. The exchange rate of the Danish krone has fluctuated within narrow tolerances against the euro, and previously German the target (or ECU), since the mid-1980s. The success of Norway and Sweden, which sacrificed the goal of monetary independence after their attempts to run a similar fixed-rate policy slipped into the sand in the 1990s, have also been quite good, although Sweden have faced a certain deflationary crisis and both countries with imbalances in the real estate market that do not see an end. 4 Iceland's selection throng  what explains the sluggish results? Around the turn of the last century, after Iceland had committed under Article 40 EEA to honor the freedom of movement of capital within the EEA, the Icelandic authorities took a fairly firm position on the choice between exchange rate stability and independent monetary policy, which the trilemity proclaims. Soon after capital movements had been freely given, the government Icelandic independent monetary policy over currency stability, first by increasing the flexibility of the exchange rate listing in stages, until the krona was floated as soon as the formal inflation target was adopted in 2001.3 On this choice, however, there is no unanimity, either among economists, politicians, business or the public. Now let's go back to Iceland's sluggish monetary success in the last century. Looking at Iceland's changing position in the heavy tide of international stirrings, there is an intricate picture: International policies and trends in economic and monetary policy have traditionally arrived soon in Iceland, although it can be said that Iceland has sometimes been a hesitant participant in the global economy and financial markets. Over the near-century as the history of the Icelandic krona spans, capital controls of some kind have most often been present and probably wider than in many places. World War II, World War II, and postwar instability led to instability that was difficult to cope with without restrictions on capital movements of any kind, but often also went much further than was urgently necessary. Only for 13 years, between 1995 and 2008, can it be said that cross-border capital movements have been totally unrestricted. Capital controls were reintroduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis in 2008, and it can be said that Iceland one European country implemented such broad controls, although certain restrictions have also been temporarily adopted in Greece and Cyprus. Over the past year, capital movements have been largely unrestricted again, although minor barriers, which I will devise later, are still in place. The tendency to solve economic problems in Iceland through restrictions on capital movements or at the expense of exchange rate stability, unless both are, raises the question of whether this is the result of sluggish economic management, a flawed monetary policy framework, or whether the problem is slashed deeper and can be attributed to some degree of shallow markets or other shortcomings in the infrastructure of the Icelandic economy, which causes it to be difficult to handle the turbulence of global capital markets. Iceland's experience shows that volatile capital movements can distort the functioning of the interest rate instrument and lead to monetary policy trading primarily in the path of exchange rate changes, which are ill-predictable and sometimes so high and faster in shallow markets that damage is caused by the operations of companies and households. Then lending growth and asset price bubbles may 3 However, the Central Bank took considerable intervention in 2001 when the krona fell sharply after it floated. 5 as the capital inflow pushes to negatively affect productivity.4 Triple or double-clamp? Iceland's problems bring to mind that in recent years the debate over the incompatible Trinity, the tri-clamp, has taken a new direction. Various people have argued that the so-called trilem is in fact a dilemma, i.e. that unrestricted movements of capital between countries are in fact compatible with neither monetary independence nor fixed exchange rates  not only from time to time. Some form of capital controls are in fact a prerequisite whether independence in monetary policy or stable exchange rates. The most energetic advocate of this view has been the French economist Helene Rey (2015).5 While this view is highly controversial and most economists do not want to go as far as Helene Rey, the view enjoys a growing following among economists that completely free capital movements can put monetary and exchange rate policy unwantedly severe constraints, if it is the policy to hold on to monetary independence. Some kind of restrictions on capital movements may therefore increase the scope for prudent economic management and are even a prerequisite for satisfactory stability in exchange rates and the functioning of monetary controls.6 Recent research on the Icelandic financial volatility underscores the limits that international financial conditions set for government efforts to tailor domestic monetary conditions to domestic conditions.7 These studies show that the Icelandic financial volatility has followed the global very closely for a century, regardless of monetary arrangements in This country. Independent monetary policy and flexible exchange rates have not been able to break these ties, but indeed neither has capital controls, which is interesting in light of Helene Rey's theories. 4 Sja t.d. agaeta umfjollun um ahrif fjarmalasveiflunnar a framleioni i Claudio Borio (2018). Proceedings of the 6th Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas International Research Conference, mai 2017. 6 There are three types of responses to this problem: First, you could seek the help of more controls to control the formation of instability in the national economy. Second, compromises that include apostasy from the tri-clamp's corner solutions could be sought. Thus, one can think of monetary arrangements where capital movements are mostly free, but not entirely, the exchange rate floats but with considerable central bank interventions in the foreign exchange market, resulting in some monetary autonomy, but not perfect. Third, it could be concluded from the close relationship between the domestic financial volatility and the international one that it is more promising to seek refuge in the co-insurance of a currency union and adapt to the financial conditions that prevail in the outside world rather than try to influence domestic financial conditions, which history seems to show infecting the Icelandic economy regardless of monetary arrangements; even in times of capital controls. Can aids help? In the wake of the financial and currency crisis, which began in Iceland in full force in the autumn of 2008, a reassessment of the implementation of monetary policy under the conditions of unrestricted capital movements has been carried out and various lessons have been drawn. The Central Bank has published its views in various publications in recent years.8 It seeks, among other things, answers to the question of whether other controls can be applied in addition to central bank interest rates, which is the main monetary policy instrument, so that they are enshrined in monetary policy. If they do, interest rates need to be raised so much, in order to hold back domestic demand, that it leads to a large interest rate differential with foreign countries, thereby implying unwanted strong incentives for short-term capital movements to the country, with the associated risk of instability. The hope is that by applying such so-called macroeconomic instruments, e.g. limiting mortgages for residential housing, limiting leverage relative to income or assets, or by financial volatility-related capital buffers on financial institutions, so-called countercyclical capital buffers, the volatility of volatility will be able to reduce volatility, or at least soften downturns. In general, stricter requirements currently being made on equity, liquidity and financing, stricter rules on foreign exchange balances and the Central Bank's authority to restrict the granting of foreign exchange loans to unprotected entities should reduce the undesirable side effect of independent monetary policy when domestic economic development is out of line with the environment. A fiscal policy that lags on the same volatility as monetary policy could certainly also contribute to greater stability. There, however, you must set 8 Central Bank of Iceland (2010). Monetary policy after the caps. Central Bank of Iceland, Special Publication No. 4. See also The Central Bank of Iceland (2017). Monetary policy based on inflation target: The experience in Iceland since 2001 and changes following the financial crisis, Special Publication No. 11. 7 expectations in moderation, although provisions in the Act on Public Finances on Financial Policy and the Financial Council look to progress. However, fiscal policy can be expected not to fluctuate with the economic fluctuation and volume, but so far the trend in this country has unfortunately been that public finances are relaxed during the boom as revenues rise and tighten during the downturn as incomes fall. None of the above measures, however, are likely to fully prevent the impact of flooding and tides on the global capital markets could, to such an extent, cause instability in the domestic economy. Therefore, there is every reason to consider whether there are other ways to prevent an unwanted heavy burden from falling on the Central Bank's interest rate policy in the implementation of economic management. Angle solutions or compromises? More solutions can be found in the policy makers' ransomware than the trident solutions in question, as well as aids. Does flexible exchange rates mean, for example, that interventions in the foreign exchange market with the aim of balancing short-term fluctuations or preventing too much deviation from the projected long-term balance should be abolished altogether? It doesn't have to be as if the central bank's intervention policy in recent years is an example. The crown floats, but not without interference.9 Within the framework of generally unrestricted capital movements, it is also possible to think of measures that can subside the greatest fury in capital movements without directly hindering them. Since 2016, the Central Bank has, according to the provisions of the current Foreign Exchange Act, established rules on special reserve requirements against new inflows of foreign currency for the purchase of bonds and high-interest deposits in isk. The rules underscore that the intermediate between the triangle solutions can be many. The special reserve requirement is a much milder measure than the broad controls on capital movements implemented after the banking collapse. Instead of allowing totally unrestricted capital movements to drive the government into the corner of monetary independence on the one hand or exchange rate stability on the other, the Central Bank has applied restrictions that reduce the benefits (mainly) of foreign entities from investing in kronas, but without stopping it completely. The problem, however, is that it is not fully clear whether the Central Bank's regulatory authority, currently based on the Foreign Exchange Act, complies with Article 40 eea agreement in the long term, which provides for unrestricted capital movements. However, the Central Bank is assessing whether this can be done 9 Um au sjonarmio sem haft geta ahrif a inngrip a gjaldeyrismarkaoi fjallao hofundur um i pallboroio a nylegri raostefnu i Jerusalem. Sja Arnor Sighvatsson (2017). Foreign Exchange Market Intervention in Iceland, Introductory remarks for a panel debate at conference organised by the Bank of Israel, Swiss National Bank, and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) in Jerusalem on 7  8 December 2017: Foreign Exchange Market intervention: Conventional or Unconventional Policy. 8 Been. Therefore, it can be argued that it would be desirable to allow such rules under certain circumstances, as this could reduce the likelihood that much more drastic restrictions on capital movements, based on the provisions of Article 43 EEA, would be made, as they did in the wake of the financial crisis in the autumn of 2008. The duty of binding therefore bears the characteristic of a national security control to be preventive. Among the things that need to be assessed before deciding whether it is promising to test the legitimacy of a special reserve under the EES Agreement is whether the format of the reserve requirement can be avoided when restrictions in existing foreign exchange laws on the conclusion of derivatives contracts not concluded on the occasion of hedging are cancelled after a full review of the Foreign Exchange Act. Before the financial crash, capital inflows were largely carried out through foreign issuers of high credit rating (AAA), but the impact on the economy, including the impact of the issue on monetary policy trading, was observed through Icelandic commercial banks, which entered into swaps with foreign intermediaries in this transaction, with the associated impact on domestic lending growth. It can be argued that this type of capital inflow is particularly damaging because the issue of these powerful foreign entities (with an AAA credit rating) of bonds in isk opens the door to the investment of entities that are totally unaware of the risks posed when investment has become unreasonably high relative to the national economy and external parity has become unsustainable, as happened before the financial crisis. Before the financial crisis, the bond stock accounted for more than a third of GDP. When inertia began to persist in foreign credit markets at the same time as large bond classes came due, assumptions for reinvestment broke abruptly and a military of ill-informed investors rushed to the exit at the same time. The impact on the domestic foreign exchange market was unmanageable. A special reserve requirement aims to prevent these situations from resurfacing. The middle ground most effective? In recent years, the government has considered it the most intriguingly looking for ways to support monetary policy with more tools rather than relying on tri-tier corner solutions. It's probably best to continue to follow that path in the coming years. This means that active currency artefacts will continue to be applied in order to promote exchange rate stability, to the extent that this is compatible with the inflation target, but without declaring the official exchange rate target, macroeconomic instruments will be applied in order to increase the resilience of the financial system during the downturn and balance volatility. Under certain circumstances, a reserve requirement could then be applied against foreign exchange inflows, along with stricter currency balance rules. As mentioned earlier, however, the resilience of the EEA Agreement in terms of the reserve requirement is not fully clear. 9 It is premature to make a judgment on the effectiveness of the policies that have been followed. Price stability has been higher in recent years than ever before in Iceland's recent monetary history. Inflation expectations have also been closer to the Central Bank's inflation target.10 Favourable external conditions in the economy, however, in addition to monetary policy, play a major role in these results, so it is uncertain how lasting the results will be under less favourable external conditions. Regardless of the monetary framework, monetary policy is implemented in a very small and open economy, such as the Icelandic, where the domestic financial system is integrated into the global economy, in many ways more problematic than in larger currency areas. The problem lies, among other things, in how the economy is susceptible to exchange rate changes, while domestic foreign exchange and financial markets are shallow and therefore susceptible to disruption. If other economic policies are at odds with monetary policy objectives, this problem is intensified. Thus, the debate about the best measure of serenity, courage, and judgment in the face of this problem will no doubt continue for a long time. 10 See Thorarinn G. Petursson (2018). Title: Address to the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland at the Bank's annual meeting
text: Address Gylfa Magn9csson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at the 58th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland on 28 March 2019. The Honorable President of the Althing, the Prime Minister, other ministers, governors, delegates of foreign countries and other good guests. I welcome you and sit here with the 50th and eighth annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. As previously stated on this occasion, the statutory role of the Board of Directors is to monitor that the Central Bank of Iceland operates in accordance with the laws applicable to its operations. In addition, the Board of Directors confirms various decisions and rules set by the Governor. At the beginning of 2018, the Board of Directors was appointed so that the chairman was ?97runn Gu?mundsd97ttir. Other members were Sveinn Agnarsson, Bj9arn Valur G92slason, Sigur?ur K87ri Kristj87nsson, ?97r Saari, Frosti Sigurj97nsson and Au?ur Hermannsd97ttir. A new board of directors was elected on 18 April 2018. The elected members of the Board of Directors were Gylfi Magn9csson, who was elected chairman at the first meeting of the newly elected Council, ?97runn Gu?mundsd97ttir, Bolli H8e?insson, Una Mar92a eeskarsd97ttir, Sigur?ur K87ri Kristj87nsson, Jacqueline Clare Mallett and Frosti Sigurj97nsson. The Board of Directors held 15 meetings during the year. As stated in the annual report presented here, the Central Bank carries out regular tasks in relation to the Bank's objectives, as well as various initiatives. The main focus of the Central Bank's work was, as before, related to the management of monetary policy and financial stability. At that time, the transition process towards unrestricted capital movements was a major task. This was accompanied by increased oversight and the preparation of a precautionary policy under new conditions. Other major projects include a review of monetary policy frameworks and controls, administration of large foreign exchange reserves and related work to ensure the Bank's performance, work to maintain security, efficiency and efficiency in payment processing and the renewal of financial infrastructure. In addition, projects related to the forthcoming merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority called for some work, part of which was to restructure the Bank's IT services. Other projects include work on equal pay policy and equal pay certification achieved at the end of the year, and a special project in a summary of economic logic and historical time series from the beginning of Iceland's sovereignty published on the Bank's website towards the end of the year. 1 During the year, an extensive project was continued to be carried out on the renewal of the Bank's interbank systems, the so-called balancing system and a large payment system. During the year, an analysis of domestic small payment services was also carried out from the point of view of preparedness and financial stability, citing the changes that are taking place in the arrangements and settlement procedures of credit cards. According to the law, the central bank's main objective is to promote stable prices. At the same time, the Central Bank shall promote financial stability. Inflation was close to the inflation target of 2.5 percent, at the beginning of the year, but then growing, averaging 2.7 percent and 3.7 percent at the end of the year, which is still below the four percent calling for reporting to the government. The Monetary Policy Committee kept the Bank's main interest rate unchanged for the majority of the year, up until November, when interest rates were raised by 0.25 percentage points. At the time, the Monetary Policy Committee decided to change the arrangements for reserve credit institutions so that it would be less costly to the Bank, but this change was not intended to affect the level of monetary policy restraint. This is further explained in the second chapter of the Bank's annual report presented here. In 2018, there was increased uncertainty about economic developments, although economic growth was considerable, and risks in the financial system increased even though it was still considered modest. The increased risk was mainly attributable to tourism and the real estate market. The profitability of the banks decreased, lending growth was considerable, but despite increased customer debt, credit risk decreased along with improved their asset position. A stress test for the big commercial banks carried out during the year indicated that the banks would face a significant setback caused by a significant decline in exports and revenues from tourists, along with higher bank financing costs. The position of the big commercial banks at the end of the year was solid; capital ratios were high and liquidity was well above the minimum. This is discussed in the third chapter of the annual report. One of the main functions of the Central Bank is to preserve the foreign exchange reserves of the population. The stock market has been quite large in recent years. Last year it increased by almost ISK 50 billion and amounted to ISK 736 billion at year-end. Exchange rate changes largely explained the expansion of the resource in Icelandic ISK calculated. The Central Bank handles professional and financial relations with international institutions in its field of work, such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, foreign central banks and financial supervision. 2 According to a special agreement with the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs, the Central Bank handles foreign borrowing by the Treasury, as well as the execution of domestic tenders, the purchase and redemption of Treasury securities securities, the conclusion of main broker contracts and the management of securities loans to the main brokers. The Bank is responsible for risk and credit management of the Treasury's loan portfolio, performs tasks regarding government guarantees and more related to it. Furthermore, the Bank has carried out projects relating to communications with international rating agencies on behalf of the Treasury, which have now been transferred to the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs. As noted, the Central Bank has carried out foreign exchange controls, i.e. supervision of the implementation of Act No. 87/1992 on Foreign Exchange and the Implementation of the Act on the Treatment of Kr97na-Denominated Assets Subject to Special Restrictions or the So-Called Offshore Kr97na Act. Projects in the field have fallen dramatically, as capital controls have almost fully been released, although guidance, supervision and research still need to be carried out. The Board of Directors worked last year and at the beginning of this year a report on the activities of the Foreign Exchange Supervisory Authority which was submitted to the Prime Minister and has been made public. The Central Bank of Iceland ehf.'s portfolio, which was established to manage the Central Bank's requirements for the estate of domestic financial undertakings, decreased sharply last year. ESea's balance sheet amounted to 4.4 ma.kr. at the end of the year, but its operations were so permanently terminated a few weeks ago. According to the income statement, profit from the Bank's operations was just over ISK 35 billion in 2018, while the previous year the loss was just over ISK 23 billion. Positive developments in the Bank's performance are mainly explained by large foreign exchange reserves and positive exchange rate differences, as can be seen in the accounts presented here. Net interest expenses amounted to more than 13 ma.kr. Wages and related expenses increased by 2.8% during the year after decreasing the previous year by 3%. The Bank's total operating expenses increased by 2.2% during the year. The Bank's assets amounted to ISK 754 billion at the end of the year and 98% of the Bank's assets were foreign. Equity increased from ISK 22 billion to ISK 58 billion. The Bank's capital ratio was 7.7% at year-end, compared with 2.9% at year-end 2017. Profits are not available as contributions to reserves for unrealised profits are higher. At the end of 2018, there were a total of 181 employees at the Central Bank, four fewer than the previous year. The gender ratio remained fairly even, with 92 men and 89 women employed at the bank at the end of the year. The executive group consisted of six men and six women before the end of the year, but that changed at the beginning of the year so that women in that position had grown to seven and the five men. 3 Although the Central Bank of Iceland's core tasks have not undergone drastic changes since the Bank's establishment in 1961, i.e. to promote stability in prices and to rely on the foundations and functions of the financial system, the implementation and organisation has changed at certain intervals, e.g. with legislative amendments in 1986, 2001, 2009 and 2013 related to interest rate liberalisation, inflation targets, the establishment of the Monetary Policy Committee and increased emphasis on financial stability. There is still a significant change in the central bank's projects and structures with the government's plans to merge the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority. It will therefore not affect the Board of Directors and employees of the Bank in the coming years than it has done recently in the event of a similar situation. There will continue to be a need for reliable framework and efficient operations. In this work, it is important that the Bank has adequate tools and tools to handle the transactions and communications that can be required of central banking in modern society. But most importantly, the work is that skilled workers are selected so that they can achieve set goals. The Bank also needs to have financial strength to fulfil its statutory role. I would like to finally take this opportunity to thank the Bank's employees for their good cooperation in 2018. I would like to thank the members of the Board of Directors, the two deputy governors who held that position during the year, the Secretary of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their good cooperation. In particular, I would like to thank Governor M87r Gu?mundsson for his cooperation this year, he took the job in unprecedented circumstances and has been at the helm of the bridge for a decade. M87r leaves office later this year, making this his last annual meeting as Governor of the Central Bank. M87r Gu?mundsson will then cross the road and look a little ahead, but first we will listen to the address of Prime Minister Katr92n Jakobsd97ttir. 4

Title: Talks from a conference in honor of Jhannes Nordal
text: Johannes Nordal and monetary policy in the second half of the twentieth century Statement by Governor Mar Gudmundsson at a conference celebrating johannes Nordal's 90th birthday, University of Iceland Festival Hall, 9 May 2014. This conference on monetary and financial systems is held in honour of Johannes Nordal, who turns 90 in two days. In the meantime, Jon Sigurdsson will talk about Johannes' career. Then asgeir Jonsson, Unnur Gunnarsdottir and Friorik Mar Baldursson will give a talk on certain aspects relating to monetary and financial systems. In this short sentence address, I am keen to discuss what I stand next for, i.e. on exchange rate policy and monetary policy in Iceland at the time of Johannes's tenure. It's actually the lung of the second half of the twentieth century. Johannes was Governor of the Central Bank from 1961 to 1993 and was therefore a leading figure in monetary policy at the time. In 1959 he became GOVERNOR of Landsbankinn, which then took on the central bank role and previously the Bank's economist from 1954, who would now be called chief economist. Presumably, however, his influence was not decisive until the great systemic changes that occurred at the beginning of the resurgence regime (1959-1971). At the other end, the influence of John and co-workers actually extends throughout the century, even though he quit as governor in 1993. This is because in the early 1990s, there were major changes in monetary policy that then remained largely unbalanced throughout the century. The monetary policy in Iceland has traditionally been shaped by international trends and the development stages of the domestic financial system. In connection with the establishment of the International Monetary Fund after World War II, arrangements were established for a fixed but convertible exchange rate of member countries against the US dollar. This system, along with agreements to reduce customs protection and other trade barriers, created good assumptions for the strong growth of international trade, which was one of the reasons for strong growth in the global economy in the 1950s and 1960s. Financial markets, on the other hand, were widely staple, as were capital movements across countries. As is often the case, Iceland was shaped by these international circumstances, but with its own characteristics and time delays. Until the reform of the reforms, foreign trade was marked by a complex system of export benefits, direct import controls and an opaque multi-rate system. In the year 1960 was 1 the exchange rate of the krona decreased by 30-57% depending on the exchange rate of the multi-exchange rate system compared to which was at the same time abolished. It marked a pathway for further freedom of movement in foreign trade. Measurements indicate that the real exchange rate of the krona fell by over 50% between 1959 and 1962, which contributed to the turn of the trade deficit into a surplus. This, along with domestic expansion in the years that followed, were the main reasons why inflation went for a while far beyond that of trading countries. However, it erupted as the inflation effect of the devaluation dwindled and domestic expansion subsided. Today, it is accepted that central banks should have the primary objective of promoting price stability, which is often further defined as the numbered inflation target. When considering the history of inflation, it must be borne in mind that when the Central Bank of Iceland was established it set many and in some respects opposing objectives and it was not independent regarding monetary policy decisions in the way it is now. The prevailing attitudes in economics towards inflation and monetary policy were also different from what they are now. The question remains valid, however, what role monetary policy played in inflation during this period and whether history supports the assertion that persistent inflation is, after all, a monetary phenomenon, but it is of course a prerequisite for setting central bank targets for inflation. Heimild: Mar Guomundsson og Palle Andersen, Inflation and disinflation in Iceland, BIS Working Paper No. 52 og Central Bank of Iceland Working Paper No.1, 1998 This figure shows inflation in Iceland from 1945 to 1996. In comparison, inflation is shown on average in OECD countries that we can see as a measure of inflation in trading countries. We see that until the early 1970s, inflation occasionally fluctuated above what is in the trading countries but always comes back. This inflation is linked to currency devaluation due to external shocks. When the exchange rate of the krona is subsequently stable, the 2 inflation again. The nominal exchange rate plays a big role here, but of course it's a monetary phenomenon. This pattern is disrupted between 1972 and 1983, as inflation consistently deviates more from that of trading countries and seems towards the end to be getting out of every way as the vicious cycle of wage and price increases due to wage indexation intensified inflationary declines rooted in external shocks and overly expansionary exchange rate and monetary policy. There were many reasons for this, such as larger and more frequent economic shocks, more rate cut-offs in response to them, wildly negative real interest rates and overly sluggish fiscal policies. Again, monetary factors play a big role. Inflation then reaches a similar level to that of trading countries in two phases. The first was related to measures in 1983, in which the abolition of indexation of wages and exchange rate fixes in the near term played a central role. The second one was reached towards the end of the 1980s and is in people's minds often associated with the so-called national treaties. Did they disprove monetary policy's role in the development of inflation? When you look closely, it's not. The indexation of financial obligations and later the abolition of wage indexation had reduced the supposed benefits of inflation for indebted households. A significant rise in interest rates after the mid-1990s then cooled the national economy. In addition, the exchange rate hike at a realistic exchange rate played a major role in further deflation after the national reconciliation agreements. The contribution of the social partners through the national reconciliation agreements consisted mainly of changing labour market inflation expectations from retrospectives to forward-looking, which reduced the cost of inflation deflationary degradation regarding employment levels. Monetary factors were therefore also here in the main role1. After the reforms at the beginning of the 1950s, formal exchange rate changes became the most powerful instrument of governance that the Central Bank handled and was so until the formation of the monetary and foreign exchange markets in the early 1990s. Monetary management, now known as the Central Bank's transactions in monetary and foreign exchange markets indirectly affect financial conditions, thus on the question of goods and services and then on inflation, was not possible before that time. Various markets did not exist or were significant staples. Capital movements between Iceland and the rest of the world were also staples. The monetary policy was therefore largely based on bulk control, either directly or indirectly through devices such as reserve requirements. I'll talk more about how it went at the time. 1 The above discussion on inflation in Iceland is based on a research paper by the author and Palle S. Andersen, written towards the late 1990s. See more: "Inflation and disinflation in Iceland", BIS-Working Paper, No. 52 and Central Bank of Iceland Working Paper No. 1, 1998. 3 The reforms made during the resurgence regime, including monetary policy, marked the beginning of the path of opening-up and marketization that was Iceland, with intermittent and occasional setbacks, on until the financial crisis this century. As for monetary policy, the biggest milestones on that journey were, on the one hand, the interest rate liberalisation in the mid-1980s and the release of capital movements in the early 1990s. But before those changes could be undertaken, the woes faced had to be dealt with when the nation's financial savings burned up in the combination of very high inflation and stifling interest rates in the 1970s. As a result, real interest rates were substantially negative and pension funds and other national financial savings burned up and the dissemination of funds through the banking system decreased significantly, causing problems. The solution was the adoption of extensive indexation of financial obligations created by law in 1979. The Central Bank of Iceland, led by Johannes, played an important role in this work. This change then played a significant role in rebuilding financial savings, and a wide amount of money, which had fallen from about 40% of GDP in the 1950s, reached a near-previous partial fall in the early 1990s. In the early 1990s, major changes were made to financial markets and the implementation of monetary policy aimed at ensuring the effectiveness of money management in the environment of free markets and unrestricted capital movements that were around the corner, first on the basis of regulation, then the law and the EEA Agreement3. The money market was evolving and the agreement to close the government's overdraft allowance at the Central Bank between 1992 and 1993 was a very important part of that. Title: Speech at a breakfast meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce 5 December 2005
text: 28.12.2005 Speech by Davio Oddsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland at a breakfast meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce 5 December 2005 The Fed raised its policy rate by 25 points for the weekend. I don't think that decision was a surprise. It may well be that some may have read from the Bank's writings in connection with the decision of interest rates in September that the interest rate increase would be greater now, 50 points or even 75 points. No such decisions were recorded in those writings, but on the other hand there were clear vows on the bank's part that it took its statutory role very seriously and would not hesitate to use his full-time efforts to follow through on it. These statements remain unbalanced. Monetary Bulletin, published on the Central Bank's website on Friday, provides a thorough account of the Bank's assessment of the state and outlook for economic and monetary policy and the arguments behind the Bank's decision to raise interest rates now. The film we faced on September 27th has undergone some changes. Uncertainty over collective bargaining has been eroded, albeit at considerable cost. The consumer price index fell somewhat at the last measurement. The increase in the price of real estate has decreased, and all indications are that there has been a watershed. Credit institutions are now a little more cautious than before in lending to this factor, and interest rates are changing. Oil prices appear to be more stable now than ever before, and despite rising labor market tensions, wage momentum is not out of hand. The increase in the Central Bank's policy rate is beginning to pass more widely across the economy, but there is a built-in delay in all circumstances and even increased delay due to the uniqueness of the Icelandic economy at the moment. The most important change following the increase in the rate of control in September was that yields on indexed bonds finally began to rise. It was very important that the impact of monetary policy was to be felt on the part of the economy where the expansion signals were the most clear, i.e. on the extremely rapid growth of private consumption. While all of these factors are interesting and positive, they alone do not give rise to changes in the direction that the Bank has followed. Tensions in the economy remain significant, demand high and undeniably considerable imbalance. These factors are inevitable to look at in context. As soon as it is self-evident to look at newly acquired information and short-term prospects, it is even more necessary to look at indicators of evolution in the slightly longer term. In fact, a central bank has no choice, as its instruments have in common with God's mills that they grind slowly, but they can grind well, if patience and foresight prevail. The Central Bank has not disguised the fact that the high exchange rate of the krona can hardly pass in the long run. An important change this autumn and so far this winter is a major issue of bonds in Icelandic kronas in the international market. This version feeds mainly on large interest rates between Iceland and other developed countries. Monetary Bulletin seeks to analyse the impact of the issue, including in a separate article. The effect can be positive. For example, they can lead to more active foreign exchange and securities markets in Iceland, thus having a positive impact on Icelandic economic development. However, the issue can also  temporarily at least  create uncertainty about monetary policy dissemination and even direct its impact rather than it would otherwise be on the exchange rate path. Such trading comes down export sectors but does little to restrain the growth of private consumption. Among the assumptions behind the inflation forecast, published in Monetary Bulletin now, are the usual control rates as they were on the forecast day. On the basis of this, the Board of Directors decided to raise the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points. In the near term, the Central Bank will have to act on monetary policy so that the adjustment of exchange rates, which in the long run seems inevitable, will not lead to higher inflation than conforms to the inflation target. To do so will require strict restraint as long as a significant production tensions and labour market tensions are causing pressure on prices. Interest rates abroad must also be sufficient to contribute to the slow adjustment of the exchange rate. The house price hike wave has peaked. If the exchange rate of the krona remains relatively high and stable, there is also a considerable likelihood of deterioration in commodity prices. Therefore, the prospect of inflation falling in the coming months, not least in the clear that this year's exchange rate hike has only to a small extent returned to domestic prices. If the housing market cools faster than expected in the Central Bank's forecasts, it is likely to lead to an even faster decline in house inflation than is currently projected. However, the outlook for exchange rate trends, continued rapid growth in private consumption and a higher increase in labour costs beyond productivity changes than previously expected outweighs the prospects of further ahead. The Central Bank has repeatedly warned against the notion that difficulties inevitably accompanied by adherent monetary policy can be avoided by temporarily deviating from the inflation target, or "letting inflation through," as it has been put through. This is an unrealistic option. Such a change in policy would immediately result in higher inflation expectations, push for even greater wage increases and lead to rate cuts and increased inflation. In the end, it would take an even bigger increase in the rate of control to quell inflation. The difficulties associated with such policies for households and businesses would therefore be greater than not less. It should also not be forgotten that a large part of the debt owed by individuals and companies is either indexed or exchange rate indexed. These peculiarities of financial market Icelandic imply that even the short-term benefits of households and businesses of less monetary restraint may be smaller and perhaps less than none at all. However, the public sector can contribute to less conflict-less integration by maintaining strict fiscal restraint. Strong growth in demand and corporate profits have generated government revenue this year far beyond what estimates. A similar situation may be raised next year. It is imperative that the governments, both state and local, do not respond to such revenue increases through succession on the fee side, but with plans for an increased revenue surplus as seemingly aimed at handling the budget. As recently announced recently, the implementation of monetary policy will be amended so that next year the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland will decide on the policy rate in six days that have already been announced. Three of them will be monetary policy release dates. In all these days, the Board of Directors will present its decision at a news conference, whether interest rates will be changed or not, and the rationale behind it. With this change, the transparency of monetary policy is further strengthened. It can be said that the number of formal interest rate decision days has been increased from four to six, because the Monetary Bulletin's issuance dates had in fact been recognised as such. Despite this, the Board of Directors may of course decide to change interest rates between pre-announced interest rate decision days if warranted. The first formal interest rate decision date for next year will be Thursday, January 26. Icelandic economics at any given time have some match in the world. However, a unique subject can have different tricks and call for special remedies. This is true, if you look at the central bank's policy rate at the moment. They can't look at themselves. The explanation is that in Iceland the picture is unique, and even most people would find an ambitious goal to maintain balanced inflation under our circumstances. First, the largest single construction phase in the nation's history is currently underway, and at the same time many other than Landsvirkjun and its foreign trading institutions are in great construction. Second, we, meanwhile, experience the greatest expansion of the Icelandic banking system with by far its largest debt accumulation abroad and associated inflows of funds. Third, in the same glide is established to reform the nation's credit market, where everyone who can move is invited to dance. Fourth, taxes are reduced or such reductions are offered in the coming months. And so like cocktail berries on the cake, workers are compensated for inflation caused by the fact that most of their real estate has risen in price, without them bearing off that cost. It is in these circumstances that we intend to ensure that inflation is long-term subject to the laws it has been established in the Act on the Central Bank of Iceland and its statement and that of the Government. This must be considered ambitious. When we look at the world economy, we face considerable imbalances. America's massive trade deficit eats up a substantial portion of the world's savings at the moment. Hand-managed exchange rates elsewhere, for example in China, will cause the market principles to respond later to this problem, but materials exist. However, economists say there must be a change there, and the later it came about, the more turmoil it will cause when it finally arrives. Towards us, however, external circumstances have been favourable so far. Credit is huge and our access to markets is wide open. Interest rates have been low and product prices have been favourable, making the strong position of the non-perpetual phenomenon much more bearable for many than it would otherwise be. But we need to be careful that favorable external terms in most areas will not be an inconclusive prerequisite for our success. It is my opinion, after just a few weeks at the Fed, that its management is not least paid to pay special attention to the risk factors of the economy. In that light, I'll mention the following. It is, of course, perfectly normal for progressive banks to grow rapidly, who sense that the small Icelandic market narrows them down, are seeking foreign capital in their efforts for expansion and gain. The internal strength of the banking system and all the indices that regulators and rating agencies look to are more than in good shape. Therefore, all markets should remain Icelandic banks open as far as they can see into the future. But the only problem is that it's not necessarily certain that at any given time these important assumptions will dictate one trip. They do so only when everything is on the market. But the market can be dynamic, not least when there is an imbalance in the global economy. There is a lot of growth and movement in the U.S. economy at the moment. It's a celebration. Other signs, however, are less, savings to a minimum, a budget deficit high and a trade deficit breaking new and new records. Europe has not recovered so far, and the continent's central bank's recent interest rate hike is heavily criticised by those worried about numbness and rising unemployment. All of these factors in our environment call for reasonable caution, not least when issuing bonds Icelandic financial institutions has grown so rapidly and become so cumbersome in the market. In such circumstances, the words of my colleague, the governor's Danish, who said a few days ago, it is no less important to respect the rules on the speed limit in the economy than in traffic. Let me tell you a few words about housing. It is surely easy to make a reasonable argument that the government could have thought its way better when radical changes were made to the government's housing policy at the start of the 2003 boom, and it would have been wiser to keep them until the end of the economic cycle. (I'm sure you'll know which prime minister this is going to be.) But it can even be said with better arguments that, despite the controversial timing, a very positive transition to the housing system framework has been created, of which the government can be proud. The reaction of the banking system, however, certainly came as a shock to the government. It is, from what has come, become secondary. After that reaction, the housing system in the old picture has almost become obsolete in an instant, whether one likes it or defends. Interest rates on housing loans are certainly still high in Iceland. But it's not the most interesting topic at the moment, it's the opposite. Access to credit and terms relating to housing purchases or Buildings have never been better in this country before. But the other is not to conceal that a large part of the banking system is probably paying down its mortgages at the moment. Of course, there may be a conscious risk taken in its confidence, as it is a long-term loan, that when interest rates become similar to what elsewhere happens, the lender ultimately profits well. If we put such speculation aside, we are faced with the fact that a competitive position in the housing market does not work, when one party enjoys government credit, does not pay a guarantee fee and is exempt from various fees carried by its competitors. It is true that this was known to credit institutions when they opened up a portal. But that, as mentioned earlier, has become secondary now, and the task must be to restore this order to normal as soon as possible. I am now located at that end of national life, which attracts words of concern and warning from all directions. And I'm not saying that it's a sensible order for one person to be entrusted with such an object. He must then have the capacity to weigh and assess the situation and act correctly. I hope Icelandic the bank has such a position. It is definitely true that the Fed is as acting as an air traffic controller in economic volatility, because it certainly has his mind more on the landing than the takeoff. However, it is not true, as is sometimes implied, that the bank does not care whether that landing will be soft or hard.

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 29. March 2012 Address Lara V. Juliusdottir, Chairman of the Board of Directors. Delivered at the 51st Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland, 29 March 2012. Honorary Prime Ministers, Ministers, Governors, Ambassadors of Foreign Countries and Other Good Guests! Today marks the 51st anniversary of the establishment of the Central Bank of Iceland and in just a few days it has been 25 years since the move to this building was moved to this building. All I can say is that this house is well-rounded. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 50th and first annual meeting of the Bank and say that the meeting is set. A lot has changed in the 25 years since we moved to this house. One of the most pleasing things to consider is the increased share of women in the Bank and increased levels of education. When the bank moved into the house, women accounted for nearly half of the staff. Fifty employees were college graduates, including five women. There wasn't much going on for women in managerial positions at the time. At the end of this year, women still accounted for nearly half of the bank's employees. However, they now make up about half of the Bank's university-educated employees and the number of university-educated employees has increased by half, representing almost 100. In terms of management positions, women today make up half of the Bank's managing directors, 6 out of 11. At the conclusion of my introductory remarks, a recording of the address by Steingrimur J. Sigfusson, Minister of Economic Affairs and Commerce, will be played at the moment in Toronto, Canada to take part in discussions on the state of the world's economy. After the minister's address, Governor Mar Guomundsson will give his annual meeting speech. After the meeting, I invite attendees to accept refreshments in the Lobby of the Central Bank. The Minister of Economic Affairs and Commerce has confirmed the Bank's consolidated financial statements for 2011 with its endorsement. The Bank's annual report for 2011 is published today and is due at the end of the meeting. 1 The annual report usually describes the varied activities that take place within the walls of the Central Bank. There have been a number of changes in the Bank's management team over the past year. asta H. Bragadottir was appointed Chief Operating Officer from Ingvar A. Sigfusson in February. Tryggvi Palsson resigned as Managing Director of Finance at the end of August and the division was divided into two units, Greioslukerfi and Financial Stability. Guomundur Kr. Tomasson took over as Managing Director of Payment Systems in September and Sigriour Benediktsdottir took over as Managing Director of Financial Stability at the turn of the year. The number of employees was 148 at the end of last year, an increase of three employees during the year. The bank worked well this year. The most diverse issues concerning the Bank and its operations were regularly discussed. Much can change in one year, and although the economy still does not navigate calm waters, positive developments have taken place during the year. There has also been a significant turnaround in the Central Bank's performance. I will now briefly trace the Bank's performance and economy including its subsidiaries. This time, you set up invoices in a modified format to give a better picture of the state of affairs. An annex has also been added showing the operations and balance sheet of the Bank's subsidiaries. According to the operating accounts, profit for the year 2011 was just over ISK 14 billion. In comparison, the 2010 results were negative by more than ISK 13 billion. This change is mainly explained by increased interest income, reduced interest expenses and positive exchange rate differences. Thus, interest income increased by more than ISK 12 billion, or 25%. Interest expenses also decreased by more than ISK 8 billion, or 23.4% from the previous year. The exchange rate difference was positive by ISK 7.5 billion. Other operating income changed little between years, while other operating expenses increased by almost ISK 4 billion, or 16% from the previous year. This is mostly due to impairment of claims of more than two and a half billion and other operating expenses, which increase by almost half a billion due to the cost of operating payment systems owned by subsidiaries of the Central Bank of Iceland. The Central Bank's balance sheet grew by over 23% year-on-year last year. Assets increased by ISK 303 billion in 2011, while debt levels increased by ISK 289 billion at the same time. Assets in excess of liabilities, the Bank's equity, amounted to just over ISK 83 billion at year-end. The increased scope of the balance sheet is devoted primarily to two things; increased borrowing and deposits of parties other than financial institutions at the Bank. In 2011, the loan deduction at the International Monetary Fund and the Norwegian central bank amounted to ISK 148 billion. The loans are preserved as part of the foreign exchange reserves held by the Central Bank. Other parties' deposits increased by more than ISK 246 billion, 2 which is an increase of almost 40%. The increase in the Foreign Exchange Accounts of the Treasury is mainly explained by the bond issue of the Treasury in June 2011 and also by the intrusion of Nordic loans that were deposited into foreign exchange accounts by the Central Bank. The Central Bank pays substantial amounts of money to the Treasury for its operations in 2011. First in the form of income tax for subsidiaries of about ISK 5 billion. Dividend payments according to the rules on contributions to the Treasury amount to three and a half billion. That's about eight and a half billion bucks. In addition, the Bank pays profits from foreign exchange auctions, which amounted to ISK 1 billion, including an auction in February. According to the agenda, more tenders will be held this year. In total, the Central Bank will therefore pay about ISK 9.5 billion to the Treasury. arni Pall arnason, Minister of Economy and Commerce, resigned on the last day of the year and on behalf of the Bank I would like to thank the Bank for its cooperation with him. At the same time, the Central Bank wishes Steingrimur J. Sigfusson good luck in his work. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the Board of Directors and the Bank's employees for their excellent cooperation during the year. We are now listening to the address of the Minister of Economy and Commerce, after which Mar Guomundsson, Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, will take over the case. 3

Title: Inflation is the worst enemy,' says in a speech at a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce
text: 29.08.2001 'Inflation is the worst enemy,' says Birgir isl. Gunnarsson in a speech at a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce Good attendees. I'm going to start this discussion today by talking about inflation. Both the main task of the Central Bank of Iceland is to control inflation and ensure stable prices, and the other that I have felt that in the recent debate about interest rates and monetary policy of the Central Bank of Iceland, people have covered inflation little, skated over lightly and even pretended that it does not exist and at least does not pose any danger. On 27 March, the monetary policy framework in Iceland was amended in such a way that instead of the objective of keeping exchange rates within certain limits, the Central Bank of Iceland set an inflation target, published in a joint statement by the Government and the Central Bank of Iceland. Accordingly, inflation, measured as an increase in the consumer price index in 12 months, shall be as close as possible to 21/2%. Tolerance was defined as allowing 11/2% deviations in each direction from the inflation target since 2003. Until the end of this year and next year, however, the upper tolerance will be clearer. This year, it's 6% and 4 1/2% next. If inflation exceeds its limits, the Central Bank shall report to the Government on why this happened, how the Bank intends to respond and how long it believes it will take to regain inflation below the limit. At the time of the price measurement in June, inflation had exceeded this year's tolerance and it turned out to be 6.8% in 12 months. The report was therefore drafted and sent to the government and published publicly. Its main findings were as follows: 1. In order for the target of 21/2% inflation in 2003 to be achieved, interchangeable increases in prices, wages and foreign currency must be prevented. In the absence of changes in the current collective agreements, the prospect of inflation would be close to 21/2% in mid-2003, even if the exchange rate did not rise from what it was in mid-June. 2. Monthly increases in the consumer price index had likely reached their peak in the event of no further decrease in the exchange rate of the krona. However, 12-month increases would continue to increase at least until the autumn. 3. Wages have risen far beyond productivity growth and acceptable inflation in recent years. This trend is the most important factor behind rising inflation. It is rooted in high domestic demand. Large wage increases contributed - along with tax cuts and lending expansion - to a trade deficit. 4 The decline in the exchange rate in recent months is the most immediate explanation that inflation is now above the tolerance of the inflation target. This decline, however, is rooted in the massive imbalance that has intensified in Icelandic the economy and is reflected, among other things, in excessive trade deficits. 5. The change made to the monetary policy framework towards the end of March does not explain the rate cut and rising inflation that has taken place of late. The change was made given that the new system was more suitable for Icelandic conditions permanently and that independent fixed-rate policies are very difficult to implement when capital movements are unrestricted. Pressure on the exchange rate had persisted for a while and it would have been almost impossible for the Fed to keep it much longer within tolerance with interventions in the foreign exchange market. It was also made clear that the Central Bank had decided to keep its interest rates unchanged, although increased inflation and inflation expectations gave rise to interest rate hikes. At the same time, the Central Bank directed the government that it was not time to take demand-stimulating action. Measures that strengthened the supply side of the economy, i.e. the availability of production factors or labor and capital, increased productivity and boosted savings, would simultaneously create assumptions of permanent economic growth and support the inflation target. Since the paper was drafted, two price measures have appeared, in July and August, supporting, among other things, the Central Bank's conclusion that monthly price increases had peaked but that the 12-month rhythm of inflation would continue to rise for a while. It is now 7.9%. At the beginning of this month, the Central Bank presented a new inflation forecast, but the Bank publicly publishes inflation forecasts on a quarterly basis. Inflation is now expected to reach 8.1% from the start to the end of 2001 and 2.9% over next year. The inflation target will be reached in mid-2003. It is expected that by the beginning of next year, increases due to a rate cut will be substantially overdue. Accordingly, inflation will rapidly decrease next year provided there is no further rate cut, that collective bargaining agreements are maintained and that domestic demand growth is slowing. The increase in the exchange rate from mid-June and more modest inflation expectations are the main explanations for the inflation outlook that the inflation outlook improved since the report to the government was drafted in June. The Central Bank's forecast of inflation from the beginning to the end of this year and year-on-year is now similar to that of various market participants but lower than that of the National Institute of Economic Affairs from July. In May, the public's inflation expectations were 6%, which is somewhat in line with the experience of previous surveys. Public inflation expectations typically appear a little higher than the Central Bank's inflation forecast. The inflation rate on government bonds also appears to be somewhat in line with the Bank's forecast. The developments in the near term are largely determined by three factors, namely the development of the exchange rate, whether collective agreements will be revised for an increase next year and how rapidly demand expansion will subside in the near future. I'm going to talk about this one in more detail. A very important uncertainty is facing wage increases and a possible review of collective bargaining agreements next year. Wages have risen far beyond productivity growth and acceptable inflation in recent years, which can be attributed, among other things, to very high demand for the workforce due to the overheating that has prevailed. Contractual wages in the general market have increased by 24% since 1997 and by over 31% with wage momentum. This increase in labour costs plays a significant part in the exchange rate cut in the krona and increased inflation in the past. Real wages have risen significantly in recent years, and last year the share of wages in national income had become almost as high as in the overheating years of 1987 and 1988. The Central Bank therefore does not consider economic assumptions for wage increases next year beyond the already concluded collective agreements, and indeed it can be said that if wage increases are increased in the first half of next year, the likelihood of a new inflation rate will increase considerably. The exchange rate of the krona was floated last March. In June, the exchange rate was on average 13% lower than in March. In August, the exchange rate has been 10.4% lower on average than in March compared to yesterday. In other words, the exchange rate dropped quite a bit in the spring, but has pretty right out of the way and is strengthening now in the summer months. The Central Bank believes that there is little evidence that the real exchange rate of the krona in the first half of this year has deviated considerably from the long-term balance position. In June 1983, the real exchange rate on the price scale was at its lowest level since June 1983. In light of historical experience, it must therefore be considered likely that real exchange rates will rise again, either through a rate hike or increased inflation, unless both occur. The Central Bank considers the outlook for exchange rates in the coming months uncertain, although strengthening is likely in the long term. If you look across the field at the moment, you can see that conditions that could either lead to an increase or further decrease are pulling on. These include the trade deficit, which still has a considerable need for foreign capital, although the need for credit has decreased significantly in the first quarter of the year due to reduced purchases of foreign securities, and this trend has continued this summer months. Then there are indications that this year's trade deficit will be lower than predicted at the beginning of the summer. In contrast, there is an increased short-term interest rate difference with foreign countries, which in the past has been just under 7% compared to three-month Treasury bills, but somewhat greater when compared to money market growth. This interest rate differential gives investors considerable incentives to buy rather Icelandic securities. The stock of Iceland's foreign securities assets has become quite large. If those who dispose of these assets go to the island of the strengthening of the krona, they have every reason to increase the weight of domestic assets in their portfolios. It is clear that the Central Bank's will represents a strengthening of the exchange rate from the current exchange rate, although the Bank will only intervene in the market when there is an urgent reason or when it considers that interventions are likely to produce lasting results. So let's take a look at the tensions and activity in the economy, but it's an important assumption that the Central Bank's inflation forecast is resisting the decline of production tensions as I've been before. The latest figures suggest that activity in the economy was much higher in the first half of the year, but the recent economic debate could give rise to the plan. Economic growth in the first half of the year has probably not fallen below production capacity growth, so production tensions may not have eased at all. The National Bureau of Statistics did not publish long-quarterly national accounts from 1997 to the first quarter this year. According to that statement, gdp in the first quarter was more than 71/2% higher than at the same time last year, mainly due to strong exports and a sharp increase in capital formation, while private consumption decreased slightly. These figures must be subject to certain reservations, however, it is clear that activity has still been on the rise in the first few months of the year. The figures for turnover by sector based on VAT collection support this resolution. In the first four months of the year, total turnover was nearly 7% higher in real terms than at the same time last year. As mentioned earlier, exports were very robust in the first five months of the year, mainly due to aluminium and seafood products. However, domestic non-fuel sales were about 3% higher in real terms than at the same time last year, which is a similar increase to the previous year. This is largely rooted in a sharp increase in turnover in construction and services, but retail sales remained virtually unchanged in real terms. Real turnover in industry without heavy industry and fisheries was 41/2% higher than at the same time last year, which is a greater turnover increase than was then measured. It is also worth noting in this regard that sales in March ' April had increased in domestic sectors rather more from the previous year than the turnover in January and February. The real turnover increase in credit cards in the first six months of the year is around 5.8%, i.e. 3.7% in debit cards and 10.6% in credit cards No signs are yet found in these figures of a decline in economic life, and this is well aligned with indicators of the labour market that I will discuss in more detail below. The progress so far this year does not confirm what was often claimed in a public debate earlier this year that activity in the economy was significantly reduced. The Bank's surveys of likely construction and activity in the coming winter do not indicate that a rapid transition is coming in the coming months. Unemployment figures for July have recently been published. The unemployment rate averaged 1.1% compared to 1.2% in June. In July last year, unemployment was also 1.1%, i.e. no year-on-year easing. Over the past 12 months, unemployment has averaged 1.3%. Far more work permits were issued to foreigners in the first half of the year than at the same time last year. These figures suggest that there is still a lot of tension in the labour market, which increases the risk of wage momentum. In the general labour market, wage momentum was more than twice as high between the first quarters of 2000 and 2001, taking into account the paired sample of the Wage Research Committee and not the increase in the wage index. In the second quarter of the year, wages in the general labour market had increased by 8.1% in one year according to the Wage Index, which includes a 2.1% increase in excess of collective wage agreements, assuming contracts of the largest workers' groups. Wage momentum was therefore measured the same as in the first quarter of the year on the measure of the wage index. According to the Collective Bargaining Committee's sample, however, there was 41/2% wage momentum in the first quarter. According to that sample, real wages in the general labour market had increased by 9.3%. High tensions in the labour market, of course, increase the risk of increased wage momentum, which is likely to fuel rising inflation. The pleasing development in recent months is that the growth rate of lending by depositors has unequivocally decreased. New figures on the expected change in lending by depositors between June and July indicate that lending decreased by 1.12% between months when adjusted for changes in exchange rates and prices. This is the first time such figures have been seen in a very long time. The increase over the last twelve months was 10.6% with corresponding adjustments and the corresponding increase over the last six months was 5%. However, this is not corrected for loans to foreign parties. By the end of July, M3's money and savings had grown by 12% in 12 months, and its growth has changed little in the full year. Discussions on interest rates in Iceland have often referred to what happens in other countries, both in general in our trading countries and also developments in the United States in particular have been on the agenda. In the debate on interest rates, it has been understood that such high interest rates in Iceland and for such a long time would be a totally special Icelandic phenomenon. It is true that at the moment interest rates are much higher here than in major trading countries, as the economic challenges are quite different from those of our trading nations due to the failure of the economic cycle. However, it is interesting to look at what other nations feel compelled to do when there is a great deal of tension. Short-term interest rates in the UK, i.e. real interest rates, averaged 7.1% for twenty-nine months in 1990' 1992, actually rising to a high of 9.2%. In Germany, short-term interest rates were 7% on average for 11 months from 1990 to 1991. In Sweden, such interest rates averaged 7.7% for twenty-six months, from February 1985 to March 1987, reaching their highest level at 11% in that year. These are just a few examples, but similar cases from the United States, France, Italy, Canada and other countries could be mentioned. In Iceland, the Central Bank of Iceland's real interest rates exceeded 51/2% in early 2000, but fell below again in the spring due to an inflation shot. They then went up at the end of July and are now about 61/2%. If you look past the dip in the spring, the period is just over a year and a half or eighteen months in this country. In any case, it is based on real interest rates that are calculated using inflation figures six months back and six months forward. These high interest rates temporarily in Iceland are therefore not unique when nations feel compelled to deal with overheating in the economy. Many have compared the implementation of monetary policy in Iceland and in the United States in the past. The U.S. Federal Reserve has cut interest rates many times in the past, and many have cited it as a precedent for the Federal Reserve to go the same way. There is a lot going on in the U.S. economy and Iceland. This table shows a comparison of the economic situation in the UNITED STATES and Iceland as it was towards the end of July, and I will review history quickly. The latest figures on inflation in the US are 3.6% and 7.9% in Iceland. In the United States, inflation between 2000 and 2001 is 3.1% and 6.4% in Iceland. The increase in wages between 1996 and 2000 has been 12.7% in the UNITED STATES and 31.4% in Iceland when wage momentum has been included. The average growth rate between 1996 and 2000 has been 3.4% in the US and 4.5% in Iceland. Growth is forecast to be 0.7% this year in the US and just under 2% in Iceland. U.S. lending growth has been fairly rapid in recent years. In 1998 and 1999, the 12-month growth in U.S. credit lending to domestic companies ranged from 6.5' 7%. Growth has decreased considerably in the past year and has recently been in the range of 4.5' 5%. In comparison, the Icelandic loan increase has amounted to approximately 20% over the past year and lending by depositors increased by almost 35% when growth peaked in 1999. Since then, the lending rate of deposit institutions in Iceland has not fallen significantly below 25%, but part of the growth over the past year can actually be attributed to the automatic upgrading of exchange rate indexed and indexed loans. If they are taken into account, the lending increase has been 12' 13% which is a much higher figure than in the US. From the above, it can be clear that conditions in Icelandic economic policy are very different from those of the United States. It's good to look for role models. other nations, but this must not be done at all to lead people off the road. Good attendees, The reason why the Central Bank is set the goal of promoting low inflation ' in fact, regardless of other objectives' is that the experience of both Icelanders and other nations shows that in the long run it is best for economic growth and living standards that inflation is low. Inflation is the worst enemy for businesses and households. This is an internationally recognised policy, so central banks around the world have been set the goal of keeping inflation under control. For these reasons, the Central Bank of Iceland has now for quite some time run a restrained monetary policy. I can well agree that there are a number of signs that the overheating in this country is being reduced. This film is far from clear and unambiguous. Keep in mind that it is very important when relaxation measures are timed. Precociousness in this regard can make matters worse. Therefore, the Central Bank concluded in its analysis in early August that there was no reason to lower interest rates any further anytime soon. In this analysis, both looked backwards and forwards. That conclusion still stands. Statement by Birgiur isl. Gunnarsson at a meeting of the Icelandic Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday 29 August 2001
