Title: Open meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee with the Parliamentary Economic and Business Committee
text: August 29, 2016 Governor's introductory remarks at an open meeting of the Economic and Trade Committee on the work of the Monetary Policy Committee Members of the Monetary Policy Committee last attended a meeting of the Economic and Trade Committee on 25 April. Since then, there has been considerable news as far as monetary policy is concerned. First, in June, a special reserve requirement was placed on the influx of capital from abroad into the bond market and into deposits. As a result, this influx has almost stopped. The deterioration in the monetary policy trading process that followed has almost disappeared. Second, inflation has continued to decline and remained lower than the Central Bank's last forecast since May, which was based, as in recent forecasts, on a technical assumption of the unchanged exchange rate from the forecast date. However, the exchange rate had risen by 61/2% since May, when an interest rate decision was taken last week. According to the newly published CONSUMER PRICE INDEX this month, inflation is now 0.9% and therefore fall below the lower tolerance of the inflation target. On this occasion, the Central Bank will in the near future send a report to the Government as required by the Bank's laws. In addition, the growth in money supply and lending overall has been very modest in the past. Third, inflation expectations have continued to approach inflation targets, and they were before last week's interest rate decision on most scales at or very close to the target, both in the short and long term. Fourth, the Central Bank's interest rate was cut by 0.5 percentage points last week. This decision was taken in reference to the developments I have traced here, the increase in real interest rates that have resulted from it and the assessment of the state and outlook of the economic situation presented to the MPC meeting and published in Monetary Bulletin published last week. A key factor in this regard is the Committee's view that it looks like inflation can be kept at targets in the medium term with lower interest rates than previously thought. How much lower, of course, is uncertain and will be revealed in the coming months. This also calls for the likelihood of rising tensions in the national economy and plans for major steps in the release of capital controls in the coming months on a cautious basis for determining interest rates in the near future. The next interest rate decisions will therefore depend on the economic progress and how to deal with the release of capital controls. Of course, this trend involves very satisfying news. It is understood that we are making more lasting progress on the inflation target than ever before in its history. The credibility of monetary policy has become greater than it has been, as inflation expectations at targets are evidenced. In this regard, it was pleasing to see that long-term inflation expectations declined further as a result of last week's interest rate decision. Thus, the difference between interest rates on non-indexed and indexed bonds decreased to five and nine years in both cases by 0.3 percentage points on Wednesday and Thursday, with the first case 2.4% and 2.6% in the second. Since these differences in interest rates involve both inflation expectations and risk loads, long-term market expectations after the interest rate cut are likely to be in good harmony with the inflation target. That's not to say that the bear is gone. According to the inflation forecast published by the Central Bank last week, inflation looks set to remain below target until next year if the exchange rate remains unchanged but will then increase and for a while exceed the target when import prices stop falling and the impact of a rate hike will fade away. It is, however, our task to work towards the fact that this forecast does not come true and that the ballast of inflation expectations at targets will remain, even if there will be fluctuations in exchange rates and inflation in the future. Favourable external conditions that appear, among other things, in a significant improvement in business rates, high tourist flows and low global inflation certainly play a very big part in the positive developments I have made here a topic of discussion. Inflation, however, has been below target for a high third year. It has become too long for it to be explained without reference to the impact of monetary policy. In more than two years, a less conservative monetary policy would have skeptically delivered higher inflation. An analysis of the impact of inflation in the past supports this conclusion. In addition, the increase in the exchange rate of the krona in the past is not independent of monetary policy. Monetary policy has a stake in this success, and probably far greater than many believe. Higher interest rates have, among other things, contributed to lower domestic demand than otherwise, contributing in part to a sharp increase in disposable income allocated to savings. As a result, trade surpluses and foreign exchange inflows will be more than otherwise pushing for the strengthening of the krona. In addition, relatively high interest rates and credible statements by the Monetary Policy Committee that everything needed to keep inflation at targets may have led companies to be more arrogant about rolling out expenses for wage increases to prices. I'm going to stop here and look forward to having an interesting discussion with you hereafter about a variety of issues relating to monetary policy.

Title: Responsible and high-quality implementation of monetary policy most likely to be successful
text: Responsible and high-quality implementation of monetary policy most likely to be successful In recent months, there have been proposals for changes to the implementation of the Central Bank of Iceland's Monetary Policy (Sea), which involve the widespread use of interest-free reserve requirements in order to increase dividend payments to the Treasury. There will be an argument here that an interest-free reserve requirement is an ineffective monetary policy instrument, its extensive use can therefore jeopardise the success of monetary policy, and it is really nothing more than a latent tax credit on domestic savings. The proposals also appear to be based on a misunderstanding of the role of tie-ups with modern monetary policy, a narrow view of efficiency and an underestimate of the importance of predictable and systematic implementation of monetary policy. Work to improve the implementation of monetary policy is desirable and is ongoing within s92. It is natural to consider feasibility in this regard, but the most important thing is that improvements to the implementation are based on quality assessments and that there is no way to deviate from the assumption that the retention of price stability is the main function of an independent central bank. Vague expectations of short-term government gains due to the abandonment of recognised and effective practices may not prevail. Clear and effective controls are crucial To the influence of monetary policy, rooted in the monetary authority's control over the supply of central bank funds, i.e. banknotes, coins and deposits of financial institutions at the Central Bank. By controlling the supply of central bank funds (and affecting the demand of financial institutions for it), central banks can have a significant impact on the short-term interest rates that ensure a balanced money market at any given time. Significant secrecy surrounded central banks' actions in the past, but in recent decades they have sought to make the implementation of monetary policy clearer to further increase its influence. The transparency has reduced the need of central banks to change the supply of central bank funds to produce the desired change in interest rates. It happens almost automatically as market participants know that if necessary, central banks in the most successful cases can ensure the short-term interest rate level that is aimed at. Today, the implementation of monetary policy of developed countries is therefore based primarily on transparent communication on interest rates, emphasising that the effect is mediated in a predictable and efficient manner (see Disyatat, 2008, Friedman and Kuttner, 2011, Borio, 1997, 2001). The policy of obliging banks to own liquid assets in a certain percentage of their obligations has a long history. In some U.S. states, tie-ups were first established after the financial crisis in 1837, but after it had proved incapable of preventing yet another financial shock 70 years later, it was decided to establish a central bank (Carlson 2015). In the aftermath of the Great Depression and back to the mid-century, changes in reserve requirements for a while were used in support of interest rate policies to counteract lending expansion but without much success (Feinman, 1993, Gray, 2011). The widespread use of reserve requirements as a monetary policy control has in many places gone to the skin. Experience shows that market activity is a much more efficient way to manage short-term interest rates than quantitative actions of this kind (Gray, 2011). Nowadays, the reserve requirement is therefore primarily used to ensure the relatively stable demand of financial institutions for central bank funds, thereby preventing demand from fluctuating too much with deprivation in the liquidity of individual institutions, resulting in interest rates in the money market deviating from what is expected at any given time (Friedman and Kuttner, 2011). Since there is no reserve requirement, such as in Canada, Sweden and Australia, central banks usually need to intervene more often in the money market to keep interest rates at the desired level. The reserve requirement therefore plays primarily a supporting role in modern monetary policy and in Iceland the arrangement of the reserve requirement is based on the model of the European Central Bank. The impact of the financial crisis on the implementation of monetary policy the financial crisis had many impacts on the implementation of monetary policy. As major central bank operations during the crisis were financed by increased central bank funds, liquidity for financial institutions became accommodating, trading in the interbank market was similarly low, and central bank deposit rates became widely the active control rates instead of mortgage interest rates before. Similar developments took place in Iceland and the SI's deposit rates have for this reason played a key role in the implementation of monetary policy in the wake of the crisis. Nevertheless, the exchange of monetary policy seems to have been fairly effective in Iceland, as interest rates in the market have essentially changed in line with the changes in interest rates. Finally, the results show that the Bank's objective of price stability has been achieved and that inflation expectations are at the inflation target. Monetary policy controls have therefore produced the desired results, but in support of interest rate policy, s92 has increasingly applied interventions in the foreign exchange market. It can be argued that s92 is easier to combine the interest rate policy and efforts to expand the part of the foreign exchange reserves that are financed in ISK precisely because it pays interest on all deposits of financial undertakings at the Bank, including those deposits that exceed that required by the reserve requirement. Under such circumstances, doors open for more controls and the more targets central banks can achieve (see Goodfriend, 2002, and Friedman and Kuttner, 2011). That interest rates on deposits of financial institutions at Sea play a key role in the implementation of monetary policy certainly come with some costs, but the gains of effective monetary policy are likewise significant for households and businesses, and it must offset the costs. The increased use of reserve requirements reduces the predictability of monetary policy Increased use of reserve requirements could result in complicating the implementation of monetary policy by making the application of the controls more blurred and tortuous. In addition, it would be more difficult to assess monetary policy's dissemination of financial markets as its impact is primarily conveyed on the interest margin on deposits and lending rates for financial institutions. The increase in interest rate-free reserve requirements thus reduces the returns on the assets of financial undertakings that are in the form of deposits at Sea and in doing so they can respond by increasing the returns of other assets (i.e. raising the lending rate) and/or reducing their financing costs through a reduction in deposit rates. The increase in lending rates increases monetary restraint, but the reduction in deposit rates reduces this in return, making it difficult to estimate to what extent the increase in reserve requirements increases monetary restraint. Frequent changes in reserve requirements can also create problems with liquidity management and the operation of financial institutions, which can undermine financial stability. Incentives would also be created for financial institutions to dodge the tie-up, cf. the U.S. experience (see Feinman, 1993, and Borio, 2001), and it is likely that the transfer of credit would increasingly shift to the shadow banking system (i.e. to financial institutions less dependent on supervision and regulation) that could also undermine financial stability. These costs must be offset by possible short-term gains from increased government revenues due to the increased use of interest-free reserves. Interest-free reserve requirement is an inefficient taxation Interest-free reserve requirement is the equivalent of taxation on the brokerage of credit as it compels financial institutions to increase interest rates on their out and deposits, as described above. It thus increases the cost of credit brokerage and undermines the assumptions of financing some profitable investment projects. It also reduces important incentives for savings, but low savings levels have been cited many times as an urgent problem in Iceland. This inefficiency of interest-free reserves increases in proportion to its scope and nominal interest rate increase (Hardy, 1993, Gray, 2011). These costs must therefore also be offset by possible increased government revenues due to the use of interest-free reserve requirements. It is primarily underdeveloped countries that exercise high and interest-free reserve requirements for the purpose of monetizing the Treasury, In many cases, they find it difficult to monetize through the tax system and therefore take these measures (see Ag8enor and Montiel, 1999). Safeguarding the independence of monetary policy Sea has clear instructions in law that the main objective of monetary policy is to ensure price stability. The law gives the Bank full independence to achieve this goal. At the same time, transparency and high-quality practices are required to characterise decision-making and the Bank publicly delivers on its actions. This kind of framework is designed to establish long-term perspectives on the importance of price stability in the mix and to promote the systematic, transparent and credible implementation of monetary policy. In the aftermath of the financial crisis, important steps have been taken towards greater independence and transparency in implementing monetary policy that have produced the desired results. The task now is to establish price stability. Everyone needs to step up their efforts and safeguard the statutory independence of the MONETARY POLICY Committee to make decisions on monetary policy measures and assess to what extent other objectives are compatible with the inflation target. In this way, we ensure that long-term views on price stability are the guiding principles of the implementation of monetary policy. Hopes of uncertain short-term gains due to increased dividend payments to the Treasury may not result in the deviation of recognised and effective practices to unchecked matters. ?orvar?ur Tj9arvi eelafsson, economist at the Central Bank of Iceland. Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: Statement by olafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 30 March 2005 Prime Minister, Honorable Ministers, President of the Althing, other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 44th annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. After my introductory remarks, chairman of the Board of Directors Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson will discuss the progress of the economy and monetary policy, the Bank's monetary policy and its implementation and the prospects ahead. After his speech, Prime Minister Halldor asgrimsson addresses the meeting. At the end of the meeting, I invite the attendees to accept refreshments. At a meeting of the Board of Directors today, the Prime Minister confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2004 with his signature. The Bank's annual report for 2004 is published today and is due at the end of the meeting. The Act on the Central Bank of Iceland states that the preparation of the annual accounts is governed by law, rules and good accounting practice. The Prime Minister lays down further rules on the Bank's financial statements and annual accounts. An internal audit at the Central Bank is carried out by the Central Auditor, which is appointed by the Board of Directors and is directly subject to it. The National Audit Office also reviews the Bank every year. According to the income statement, losses on the Central Bank's operations in 2004 amounted to ISK 6 billion. The book value loss resulting from the effect of an increase in the exchange rate of the Icelandic of the krona on the amount of the foreign exchange reserves in ISK amounted to ISK 61/2 billion. After the losses were released, profits from the Bank's operations amounted to more than ISK 500 million. Interest income from foreign assets increased by ISK 400 million from the year before, but decreased by ISK 1.8 billion of domestic assets, as the Central Bank's claims on domestic credit institutions decreased on average from the previous year. It was most likely that the Central Bank's reversal of transactions with credit institutions decreased significantly from the previous year. Interest expenses increased little from the previous year and net interest income to excluding exchange rate losses decreased by ISK 1.5 billion. The Bank's operating expenses amounted to ISK 1.3 billion. It should be noted that the central banks of various neighbouring countries suffered significant accounting losses last year for the same main reason as the Central Bank of Iceland. Their currencies rose against currencies that are cumbersome in their foreign exchange reserves. The Central Bank's total assets amounted to nearly ISK 107 billion at the end of 2004 and had increased by more than ISK 19 billion since the end of 2003. Foreign assets increased by ISK 7.4 billion and domestic assets increased by almost ISK 12 billion, solely due to higher demands from the Bank on domestic credit institutions at the end of 2004 than at the end of the previous year. On average, however, they were smaller in 2004 than in the previous year. The Bank's domestic liabilities, including banknotes and coins, increased by more than ISK 25 billion, while posted foreign debt remained virtually unchanged, amounting to just ISK 1.7 billion at the end of 2004. The Bank's equity was scrapped by ISK 6 billion during the year and amounted to ISK 34.2 billion at the end of the year. At year-end 2004, the Bank's equity accounted for 32.1% of the balance sheet results, compared with 46.6% at the end of 2003. According to the law, the Central Bank of Iceland is required to preserve foreign exchange reserves. There are no absolute rules on how much foreign exchange reserves should be. This depends, among other things, on the size of the economy in question, the scope of foreign trade and capital movements, and most importantly, foreign debt and their composition. The Central Bank's foreign exchange position had become too diminished in 2002 and it became urgent to strengthen it in order to rely on the foreign liquidity of the national economy, thereby strengthening the foundations of the credit rating of the state's Icelandic and other domestic borrowers in foreign credit markets. By keeping foreign exchange reserves, the Central Bank is sold under exchange rate risk caused by changes in the exchange rate of the Icelandic the krona, which it cannot forfeit and the more the reserves are higher. Changes in the exchange rate of the krona have no effect on the value of the reserves in foreign currency or its purchasing power abroad. It serves its purpose regardless of changes in the exchange rate of the krona. However, the Central Bank's financial statements rules allow changes in the exchange rate to directly affect the Bank's calculated profits. From the end of 2003 to the end of 2004, the exchange rate of the krona, according to the official exchange rate index, increased by 9.2%, resulting in the Central Bank's ISK 6.5 billion exchange rate loss in 2004, as previously reported. Move the exchange rate loss SI-21508 - Statement by olafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of si 2 fully to the Bank's income statement and fully impair its calculated performance. From autumn 2002 to the end of 2004, the Central Bank steadily strengthened its foreign position through regular purchases of foreign currency in the domestic interbank market. At the end of 2004, the foreign exchange reserves amounted to ISK 65.6 billion and the Bank's foreign short-term liabilities were nonexistent. In mid-2002, the Bank's net foreign assets amounted to only ISK 7 billion. As a result of the strengthening of the reserves and the decrease in the reversal of credit institutions' transactions since their highest level in 2003, the share of foreign assets in the Bank's total assets increased from 32% at the end of 2002 to over 60% at the end of 2004. At the same time, the Bank's foreign debt decreased from less than 16% of total liabilities and equity to about 11/2%. The Central Bank's performance was therefore much more susceptible to changes in the exchange rate Icelandic the krona than before. Interest rates in international markets have been historically low in the past and were still in 2004, reflected in the returns of the majority of the Central Bank's assets, i.e. foreign exchange reserves, and at the same time in the Bank's performance. Nevertheless, returns on the reserves were relatively good in foreign currencies compared to international bond indices held by the Bank. At the same time, interest rates on the Bank's domestic debt have increased, as the vast majority of them are in ISK Icelandic. From this it is clear that the rising exchange rate of the krona, historically low interest rates in foreign markets and rising interest rates in Iceland all had a negative impact on the Bank's performance in 2004. In the same way, the Treasury benefited from this situation where its foreign loans declined measured in Icelandic kronas and the interest rate burden was relatively light. The same was true in 2004 for other domestic entities that owed in foreign currencies. As a consequence, the Bank's operating expenses amounted to ISK 1.3 billion during the year, compared with just over ISK 1.1 billion in 2003, assuming a special charge in that year for the retirement obligations of former employees of the National Statistical Institute. The Bank's financial statements are published in its entirety in the annual report as well as detailed explanations of individual items. There were major changes in the Central Bank's workforce in 2004. Fourteen employees quit or retired, while 11 employees were hired. However, four of them did not start work until this year. These included 115 employees at the end of 2004, three fewer than at the end of 2003. The job value was 107.3 at the end of the year. Among those who retired during the year were Mar Guomundsson, chief economist who was hired by the International Payment- SI-21508 - Statement by olafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of si 3 The Bank of Basel. Mar had worked at the Central Bank since 1980 and had been the Bank's chief economist since 1994. Instead of Mar, Arnor Sighvatsson was appointed chief economist at the Bank. Sveinbjorn Haflioason, chief legal officer, retired at the end of the year and retired. He joined the Bank in 1965 as a lawyer, was director of the legal department for many years and the Bank's chief legal officer from 1994. In his place was hired by Sigriour Logadottir. olafur Palmason, director of the Bank's museum department, retired this year. He had been director of the Bank's museum department since 1984. During the year, documents were separated from the museum department and transferred to a document centre in the Bank's operations department. The director of the museum department was appointed Valborg Stefansdottir and director of the document centre Eva Soley Siguroardottir. I would like to thank all those who retired from the Central Bank in the past year for their dedicated service to the Bank and welcome new employees to work. Last autumn Halldor asgrimsson took over as Prime Minister from David Oddsson. I would like to thank David for his very pleasant relations during the years he was Minister of the Central Bank. In those years, the Central Bank was enacted new and modern laws, and the monetary policy framework was changed. I'm looking forward to the charm of all my career and I look forward to a successful relationship with him. He is no stranger to central bank infrastructure because he served on the Board of Directors from 1977 to 1983 and was in fact its chairman from 1980. There was no change in the structure of the Board of Directors in 2004. The Board of Directors held 22 meetings during the year. I thank the members of the Board of Directors for their very enjoyable cooperation and well-done work. I also thank the Board of Directors and the Bank's employees for their very good work over the past year and a successful cooperation with the Board of Directors. SI-21508 - Statement by olafur G. Title: Address at the Bank's annual meeting
text: 30. March 2017 Address orunnar Guomundsdottir, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at the 56th Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland on 30 March 2017. Honorable Prime Minister, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, Governors, Delegates of Foreign Countries and other good guests. I welcome you and sit here with the 50th and sixth annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. This year marks 60 years since the first steps towards independent central bank operations were taken with the separation that occurred within Landsbanki islands when it was divided into two independent units, a central bank and a commercial bank. It is therefore particularly pleasing to see that at today's meeting there are individuals who took part in these first steps with the Bank, including Johannes Nordal, who was then chief economist at Landsbanki islands and later governor of the Central Bank, but here are also Sigurour orn Einarsson and Petur Urbancic who worked at the Bank at the time, But Peter still does a certain job for the bank. The role of the Board of Directors is in particular to monitor the Central Bank's activities and to confirm the rules and recommendations of the Governor. The Council consists of seven members elected after each parliamentary election. Sometimes changes occur during the term, but the general representatives have been the same since the last annual meeting. The Board of Directors held 14 meetings in 2016. As stated in the annual report presented here, the Central Bank carries out regular tasks as well as larger initiatives. As in the previous year, last year's largest initiatives were linked to the government's plan for the release of capital controls based on the plan presented in 2015. The first phase was the resolution of the winding-up of fallen commercial banks and savings banks, the second phase was the delimitation and resolution of offshore krona assets, and the third general disposal of capital controls on households and businesses. From the end of March 2016 until the end of the year, assets in offshore krona decreased from ISK 320 billion to ISK 191 billion, but the main decrease occurred at auction in June. With the entry into force of the act at the end of October, steps were taken to almost full release controls last year that laid the groundwork for the pleasing announcement of the elimination of capital controls on individuals, companies and pension funds published earlier this month. Extensive preparatory work for the second two phases was carried out at the Central Bank last year in cooperation with other authorities. The same can be said of the setting of rules in June in order to affect capital inflows that had been observed due to interest rate differentials abroad. According to the law, the central bank's main objective is to promote stable prices. At the same time, the Central Bank shall promote financial stability. Inflation remained below the inflation target throughout last year. The Monetary Policy Committee cut interest rates in August and again in December, a total of 0.75 percentage points, which is further reported in the second chapter of the Bank's annual report. In 2016, economic conditions were essentially favourable to the financial system. The leverage of households and businesses was relatively low historically and their scope to meet Trauma was more than for a long time. The results of stress tests showed that the big commercial banks, on the whole, were quite well equipped to deal with shocks, and the position of commercial banks was solid at the end of the year, the terms of the banks in foreign markets improved and access to foreign markets became more favourable with rising government credit ratings. During the year, however, there were signs of upticks in the labour market and housing markets, as well as strong growth in tourism, as stated in the third chapter of the Bank's annual report. The Central Bank works specifically to promote the security, functionality and viability of the core infrastructure of the financial system in Iceland. The so-called bulk payment systems and balancing systems are of great importance, and their full renewal was carried out during the year. The operation of the systems went well. During the year, the implementation of a new trading system for the Bank was underway. The electrification of cash has been debated and the Central Bank has been closely monitoring what happens at that level. However, traditional cash remained at ease during the year in the sense that the proportion of banknotes and coins of GDP rose slightly and was 2.3%, which is still low in international comparisons. The central bank's role in this regard is to meet the demand for cash. The share of the 10,000 ISK note was growing and was at more than 47% of the value of issued banknotes as a whole by the end of the year. The foreign exchange reserves held by the Central Bank expanded substantially to ISK 815 billion at year-end. The Governor will further outline the cost and profit analysis of the reservoir for the national economy as a whole. As it shows, the gains are spread across society, but the costs are mostly seen in the Central Bank's accounts. According to the income statement, losses from the Bank's operations amounted to just under ISK 35 billion in 2016, while in the previous year profit was ISK 5.6 billion and in 2014 profit was ISK 11.2 billion. The Bank's negative performance is, as mentioned earlier, mainly due to the foreign exchange reserves and is explained by negative exchange rate differences as can be seen in the accounts that are available here. It is one of the Bank's roles to preserve foreign exchange reserves and the larger it is, the greater the impact on exchange rate changes in its performance. Wages and related expenses increased by 9% between years, mainly attributable to contractual increases and high workload during the year. The Bank's assets amounted to ISK 876 billion at the end of the year, while equity decreased from ISK 79 billion at the end of 2015 to ISK 44 billion at year-end 2016. The Bank's capital ratio was 5% at year-end, compared with 8.6% at year-end 2015. Profits are not available and the Bank considers it not time to decide on the withdrawal of equity on the basis of Article 34 of Act No. 36/2001, as set out in the annual report. At the end of 2016, there were a total of 180 employees at the Central Bank. The gender ratio remained fairly even, rising to 51% men and just under 49% women. The ratio became a bit more unequal among managers and middle managers during the year, with second-in-line members at the Bank at the end of the year 61% men and 39% women. The executive group now includes six men and four women, while two women retired from the executive group this year. I would like to finally take this opportunity to thank the Bank's employees for their exceptionally good cooperation in 2016. In particular, I would like to thank the members of the Board of Directors, the Governor, the Deputy Governor, the Secretary of the Board of Directors and the Internal Auditor for their good cooperation. We are now listening to Prime Minister Bjarni Benediktsson's address and after that, the governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Mar Guomundsson, will take over the case.

Title: Introductory remarks by Director General of the Financial Supervisory Authority, at this morning's press and news conference
text: 30.06.2010 Introductory remarks by Gunnar ?. Andersen, Director General of the Financial Supervisory Authority, at this morning's press and news conference Recommendations of the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank of Iceland to financial undertakings regarding non-binding exchange rate guarantee provisions We are faced with the fact that there has been a great deal of uncertainty following a Supreme Court ruling that interferes with the stability of the financial system. It is the duty of the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank to create a firmness in financial market transactions and to promote an active and secure financial system. When there is a public interest inherent in the above objectives set by the Legislature to these institutions, they come across the special interests of certain groups, they are obliged to act in the public interest. With these recommendations presented here today, the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank of Iceland are not grouping themselves with one party d0 or group of parties d0 against another, but rather playing their role as regulators and responding to the uncertainty that has arisen. First, we direct financial undertakings that in loan agreements which, in their opinion, contain non-binding exchange rate guarantee clauses, as compared to the recent judgments of the Supreme Court, they are based on interest rates that the Central Bank decides on the lowest interest rates on new general non-indexed or indexed loans by credit institutions and applied when there is uncertainty about credit terms. Second, we request that these assumptions be considered as soon as possible. Third, we ask the companies to reassess their capital needs in light of the circumstances. And fourth, we advise them that reporting on foreign exchange balances, liquidity and capital positions to the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Central Bank of Iceland be based on these assumptions. Now it is clear that each financial undertaking must carefully review its portfolio and make a cold assessment of whether the various types of contracts are likely to be judged unlawful. If they consider it a high probability that certain contracts will be judged unlawful or if more judgments are disadvantaged at a later date, it is recommended that the aforementioned legal provisions be complied with in determining interest rates. However, it is up to the financial institutions themselves to decide in which cases they want to defend themselves in court and in which cases they do not want it. In many cases, they will no doubt choose to give it a try in the courts whether certain types of contracts are legitimate or not. Regulators can't take that right from them. Of course, financial institutions are also free to negotiate alternative solutions with their customers d0 their freedom of contract has not been compromised d0 but they must ensure that such solutions do not cut the credit institutions' equity out of whack. Over the next few weeks and months, intelligence will continue. There have been calls for detailed information from financial institutions, aimed at mapping the complexity of contracts the companies have entered into and could prove to contain unlawful contractual clauses. The companies are then asked to reassess their capital needs in light of that information. When detailed information is available, the government should have a solid basis for assessing whether further action is needed. When the Financial Supervisory Authority assessed the business plans of the new banks last year, taking into account, among other things, risk management and management, a 16% CAD ratio was required for all of them. This was done to have a table for boars due to possible future setbacks. Furthermore, we demanded to the owners of the banks that they demonstrate a grant in the form of a contingency fund that they could take to meet setbacks. These decisions have proved to be correct in light of what has now happened. The problem is so large that, given the darkest scenarios, this percentage could fall below the minimum we set, i.e. 16%. It is difficult to say at this time whether it could fall below the statutory 8% minimum. The need for d0 and size d0 additional ownership of the owners' contributions will not be revealed until the analysis Which the Financial Supervisory Authority has launched is over. It has been asked whether it would be possible to review capital requirements to the credit institutions to which this might apply. The answer to that, of course, depends on what the future will be and how uncertainty will be eradicated, whether by a new judgment or otherwise. I just want to say in the end that the Financial Supervisory Authority has focused on responding to the situation based on a professional assessment of the situation. Our role is to promote firmness and security in Icelandic financial life and work in the public interest d0 regardless of popularity. We will continue to do so.

Title: Statement at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland
text: 31.03.2006 Statement by eelafur G. Einarsson, Chairman of the Board of Directors at the Annual General Meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland 31 March 2006 Prime Minister, Honorable Ministers, President of the Althing, other good guests. On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland, I welcome you to this 45th annual meeting of the Bank and say the meeting is set. At the conclusion of my introductory remarks, chairman of the Board of Directors of The Board of Directors of The Board of Directors Dav92? Oddsson will discuss the progress of economic and monetary policy, the Bank's monetary policy and its implementation, as well as discussing aspects relating to the position of financial undertakings. After his speech, Prime Minister Halld97r e7sgr92msson addresses the meeting. At the end of the meeting, I invite the attendees to accept refreshments. Attendees will notice that the Central Bank and the National Museum of Iceland's coin collection, formerly housed in Einholt 4, has now been moved to the Bank's main building on Kalkofnsvegur. The exhibition has pretty much been permanently arranged and will be officially opened in due course. Guests have the opportunity to respect her as she is now. At a meeting of the Board of Directors earlier today, the Prime Minister confirmed the Bank's financial statements for 2005 with his signature. The Bank's annual report for 2005 is published today and is due at the end of the meeting. The Central Bank of Iceland's financial statements are settled on the basis of rules established by the Prime Minister. They stipulate, among other things, that it should be settled in accordance with the provisions of the Act on Annual Accounts, on Financial Undertakings and on Accounting, and in good accounting and accounting practices. Important changes were made to the rules last year and were implemented in the Bank's financial statements for 2005. First, the changes mean that the Bank's fixed assets should be transferred to its balance sheet. Previously, they were charged at the time of purchase and mentioned in the notes to the annual accounts. During this change, the Bank's balance sheet increased by ISK 4.9 billion. It followed the example of the central banks of most industrialized countries. The second major change in the Rules was that before calculating the contribution to the Treasury under Article 34 of the Act on the Bank, profit for the year shall be deducted according to the income statement calculated revenues and expenses due to changes in the exchange rate of the Icelandic the kr97na. By keeping foreign exchange reserves, the Central Bank is sold under exchange rate risk caused by changes in the exchange rate of the Icelandic the kr97na, changes that it cannot forfeit and the greater the reserves. Changes in the exchange rate of the kr97na, however, have no effect on the value of the reserves in foreign currency or its purchasing power abroad. The Bank's foreign assets and liabilities are recognised at the market value converted at the exchange rate Icelandic isk at the end of the year. Changes in the exchange rate of the kr97na directly affect the Bank's performance, as exchange rate losses and exchange rate gains are both fully recognised in the income statement. According to the income statement, losses on the Central Bank's operations in 2005 amounted to ISK 2.8 billion, compared with a loss of ISK 6 billion in the previous year. The book value loss resulting from the effect of an increase in the exchange rate of the Icelandic of the kr97na on the amount of the foreign exchange reserves in ISK amounted to ISK 2.6 billion. Interest income from domestic assets increased by ISK 1.7 billion and from foreign assets by ISK 51 million. Interest expenses on domestic liabilities increased by ISK 2.5 billion, while foreign liabilities increased by ISK 13 million. Depreciation in the amount of ISK 90 million was transferred for the first time to charges in the income statement. The Bank's operating expenses, including depreciation, amounted to nearly ISK 1.3 billion, down somewhat from the previous year. In 2005, the Central Bank's balance sheet results figure increased by nearly ISK 56 billion to ISK 162 billion at the end of the year. On the asset side, in particular, the Bank's reversal of transactions with credit institutions increased, and on the debt side, mainly government deposits increased. As a result, considerable changes were made to the composition of the Bank's balance sheet in 2005. In 2003 and 2004, there were the Bank's assets were much smaller than foreign ones, accounting for 33 and 39% of total assets. This happened in 2005. At the end of this, domestic assets accounted for more than 58% of the Bank's total assets. The reason for this change is not least that the Treasury placed part of the sales value of S92minn paid in the autumn to an account at the Central Bank. In doing so, the liquidity of credit institutions narrowed and the central bank's reversal business increased considerably. They were nearly ISK 38 billion at the beginning of the year, but almost ISK 88 billion at the end of the year. Since 2004, the Central Bank has significantly narrowed its interest rate gap, i.e. the difference between its highest and lowest interest rates. In mid-2004, the Bank's highest and lowest interest rates were 5 percent different, but by the end of 2005, this difference had reached 3 percent. The purpose of this change was to strengthen the bank's monetary policy actions and to reduce fluctuations in interest rates in the interbank market. A smaller interest rate differential also means that the Bank's performance will be inferior to otherwise unchanged. The Bank's annual report publishes the annual accounts in its entirety along with notes. In addition, the report provides a more detailed account of the Bank's performance during the year and changes in the balance sheet. In September, the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Birgir easleifur Gunnarsson announced that he had decided to resign at the end of that month. Birgir easleifur Gunnarsson was appointed CEO of the Central Bank of Iceland from 1 February 1991. He was elected chairman of the Board of Directors in early May 1994. Birgir easleifur had therefore been CEO for over fifteen years and chairman of the Board of Directors for somewhat in his twelfth year. During Birgiur easleifur's time as chairman of the Board of Directors, there were drastic changes in the Icelandic financial system. Restraints and restrictions a week for freedom in all kinds of business, domestic financial markets developed rapidly, and most importantly, the monetary policy framework was transformed and the Central Bank was granted more independence for action and its own decisions than it enjoyed before. No one who watched the Central Bank in recent years disguised the fact that it was managed with determination and professionalism, and its credibility strengthened. Such success can only be achieved under strong control. Birgir easleifur earned respect and trust inside and outside the Bank. Professionalism, modesty, fixation, and dignity all characterized his phase of dealings with the Board of Directors, whether at its meetings or at other times. On behalf of the Board of Directors, I thank Birgi easleifur for his cooperation and successful leadership at the Bank. Dav92? Oddsson was appointed Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Iceland from 20 October 2018. he is known for his work in other venues, as mayor of Reykjav92k, prime minister for more than 13 years and most recently foreign minister. I formally welcome David Oddsson to work and bring him all the good work at the Central Bank. There have been a number of changes in the Bank's workforce over the past year. A total of 13 employees retired, while 14 joined the Bank, so the number of employees increased by 1 since 2004. At the end of the year, the Central Bank had 116 employees, while the number of employees was more than 107. In 2005, the board of directors changed the structure of the Board of Directors that Ingibj9arg S97lr9cn G92slad97ttir disappeared at her own request. I thank You for your cooperation in the Board of Directors. In her place, the Althing elected J97n ?97r Sturluson to the Board of Directors, having previously been an alternate. He was replaced by Ellert B. Schram. The Board of Directors held 22 meetings during the year. I thank the members of the Board of Directors for their very enjoyable cooperation and well-done work. I also thank the Board of Directors and the Bank's employees for their very good work over the past year and a successful cooperation with the Board of Directors. The past year was an eventful year for the Central Bank of Iceland and the current year is expected to be the same. I am confident that the Bank will continue to perform its role professionally and firmly.

Title: Address by the Chairman of the Supervisory Board of the Central Bank of Iceland at the Annual Meeting
text: 30. March 2023 Address by Gylfi Magnusson, Chair of the Central Bank of Iceland Supervisory Board, at the 62nd Annual Meet- ing of the Central Bank, 30 March 2023 Madame Prime Minister, honourable Ministers, Speaker of Parliament, for- eign ambassadors, honourable Governor(s), Governor, Central Bank officials and staff members, ladies and gentlemen: I hereby call to order the sixty- second annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. The Central Bank's activities gradually returned to normal early last year, after the pandemic and the challenges and disruptions it brought with it. The domestic economy continued to right itself after a sharp contraction, and the Central Bank tightened its monetary and macroprudential policy stance in order to curb rising inflation and support financial stability. Now, more than three years after the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority, the activities of the merged institution have settled into their routine. As is provided for in Article 36 of the Central Bank Act, an appraisal of the Bank's performance in fulfilling its monetary policy, financial stability, and financial supervision objectives was conducted last year, together with an examination of other aspects of the Bank's opera- tions. The appraisal was carried out by three foreign experts with long- standing experience from the central banks of their own countries. In their report, published in January, the appraisal committee concluded that the merger had been executed quickly and effectively, and that the Bank had performed very well in all three of its main policy areas. By law, the Central Bank of Iceland is required to promote price stability, financial stability, and sound and secure financial activities. Three standing committees comprising Bank officers and outside experts and officials are tasked with taking decisions on the application of policy instruments. The Governor is responsible for the Bank's operations and is authorised to take decisions on all matters not entrusted to others by law. The appraisal com- mittee points out that this new organisational structure featuring three standing committees needs to be evaluated in light of experience, and that there is particular reason to re-examine the mandate of the Financial Super- vision Committee. The appraisal committee's report includes a discussion of the Bank's governance structure and the experience gained from it to date. It also contains several recommendations that the Bank and other parties, as applicable, intend to consider. Asgeir Jonsson has served as Governor of the Central Bank since 2019. The Bank's Deputy Governors, who have held these positions since 2020, when the new Central Bank Act entered into force, are Gunnar Jakobsson, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability; Rannveig Sigurdardottir, Deputy Governor for Monetary Policy; and Unnur Gunnarsdottir, Deputy Governor for Finan- cial Supervision. As is well known by now, it was decided that all of the Central Bank's activi- ties should be located under one roof, in the Bank's headquarters at Kalkof- nsvegur 1. In order to bring this about, major modifications and renovations were launched, including the introduction of more open workspace. Not only did the building need modifications in order to accommodate all of the Bank's employees, but the need for renovations was urgent as well - cabi- netry and fixtures, plumbing and wiring, and many other parts of the build- ing's infrastructure needed work after thirty-five years of use. It is efficient and economical to carry out modifications and renovation work simultane- ously, and the project has been ongoing more or less since the merger took effect. The work is well advanced in the main building but is still underway in the annex, with completion expected in 2024. The Supervisory Board monitors the Bank's compliance with the statutory provisions applying to its activities. In other respects, the Board undertakes such tasks as are outlined explicitly in the Central Bank Act. The Supervisory Board held 13 meetings in 2022. A new Supervisory Board was elected during the year. At the beginning of 2022, the principal members of the Board were Bolli Hedinsson, Frosti Sig- urjonsson, Jacqueline Clare Mallett, Sigurdur Kari Kristjansson, Una Maria Oskarsdottir, and Thorunn Gudmundsdottir, while I served as chair. Sitting on the new Supervisory Board, elected on 24 March 2022, are Arnar Bjarnason, Kirstfn Flygenring, Sigridur Andersen, Sigurjon Arnorsson, Thor- steinn Viglundsson, and vice-chair Thorunn Gudmundsdottir, in addition to myself. According to the profit and loss account, the Bank recorded a loss of just over 18 b.kr. in 2022, as opposed to a loss of just under 16 b.kr. in 2021. The loss on the Bank's activities during the year is largely attributable to asset valuation adjustments, which in turn are due to steep policy rate increases in the US, and interest expense. The Bank's operating expenses totalled just over 8 b.kr., some 12% more than in the prior year. Operating revenues came to nearly 3.5 b.kr. and were marginally higher than in 2021. The Bank's assets amounted to nearly 875 b.kr. at the year-end, or 90 b.kr. less than at the end of 2021. Its capital declined by 19 b.kr., to 115 b.kr. at the year-end. The Bank's capital adequacy benchmark, which has been en- dorsed by the Supervisory Board, is 150 b.kr. Because of the operating loss and capital below the benchmark, no dividend will be paid to the Treasury for 2022. The Central Bank employed 296 members of staff at the end of 2022. The gender ratio remains relatively equal, and an equal pay analysis conducted within the Bank showed that there was no unexplained statistically signifi- cant wage gap between the sexes. The Bank continued to work systemati- cally on climate and sustainability issues during the year, both in its profes- sional capacity and in its operations. More detailed information on the Bank's operations and operating results can be found in the Annual Report, published today. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all staff members for fruitful cooperation and a job well done in 2022. I would also like to extend special thanks to my colleagues on the Supervisory Board, the Deputy Governors, the Board secretary, and the Internal Auditor for smooth collaboration. And I would like to thank Governor Asgeir Jonsson for our work together during the year. Unnur Gunnarsdottir, Deputy Governor for Financial Supervision, has stepped down from her position at her own request and is leaving the Bank in April. I would like to thank her most particularly for her long and successful service in the public sector, which ends where it began: in the Central Bank. The Governor will address the meeting later, but first I would like to turn the podium over to Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir.

Title: Speech by Deputy Governor for Monetary Policy: Monetary and Fiscal Dimensions of Responding to Multiple Global Shocks
text: 13 April 2023 Monetary and Fiscal Dimensions of Responding to Multiple Global Shocks Presentation at the 15th Annual Meeting of the OECD Working Party of Parlia- mentary Budget Officials and Independent Fiscal Institutions by Rannveig Sig- urdardottir, Deputy Governor for Monetary Policy, Central Bank of Iceland It is a pleasure to join you here to discuss the role and interaction of monetary and fiscal policy - a topic that deserves our full attention today in times of high inflation. The global economy had barely recovered from the financial crisis when it was hit again by two subsequent shocks that have had enormous impact on both mone- tary and fiscal conditions around the globe. I want to give you a snapshot of how the Icelandic economy has weathered these shocks relative to other OECD econo- mies, firstly, during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent supply-chain disrup- tions, and then, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the ensuing energy and food crises. Finally, I will discuss the role played by monetary and fiscal policies in re- sponse to these shocks. Iceland was among the countries most severely hit by the global financial crisis (GFC). Prior to the crisis, the country was uniquely vulnerable due to macroeco- nomic imbalances, including a large current account deficit, unfavourable net in- ternational investment position, highly indebted households and business sector, inflated asset prices, and an oversized and undercapitalized banking sector. Ice- land's strength, on the other hand, was the relatively strong position of its public finances. This set Iceland apart from several other countries that also suffered badly from the GFC, mainly because of vulnerability of public finances. In the aftermath of the crisis, the economy was rebalanced; the current account transformed from a deficit to a surplus; the international investment position changed from large net debt to significant net assets; a major share of private debt was wiped out; the banking system recapitalized; and asset prices deflated. 1 The economic consequence of the pandemic As a result of the rebalancing of the economy following the financial crisis, Iceland's economy was in a position of relative strength when the pandemic struck. The mac- roeconomy remained broadly balanced, despite a negative shock to exports in 2019. Unemployment was low, private sector indebtedness relatively benign, infla- tion moderate and public finances had recovered significantly from the turmoil fol- lowing the GFC. The human suffering from the pandemic was also less pronounced than in many advanced economies. Iceland's relatively young population, strong health care system, low population density and the relatively well-balanced man- agement of the outbreak, are all likely positive contributing factors. Measures taken to slow the spread of the disease were relatively successful and the Icelandic authorities did not need to impose exceedingly stringent and protracted restrictions, as was required in many other countries. As a result, the impact of the pandemic on households' willingness and opportunity to spend and on corporate operations was milder than in countries where stricter measures had to be adopted. Thus, the impact of the pandemic on domestic demand was less pronounced. Despite relatively successful public health measures, the large share of tourism ser- vices in Iceland's GDP made the economy quite vulnerable to the economic con- sequences of global restrictions on travel and tourism services. In 2019 tourism and tourism-related services amounted to about 8% of Iceland's GDP, a proportion sec- ond only to that of Portugal and Spain in the OECD. Reflecting the weight of tour- ism in exports, Iceland's exports contracted by 31%, more than in any other OECD country, and service exports shrank by 54% in the wake of restrictive measures taken by all major trading partners. Other tourism-dependent countries such as Greece, Spain and Portugal also suffered severe export shocks. The smaller than expected effect of the pandemic on Iceland's economy can there- fore be attributed to rather agile expenditure switching, helped by a 12% depreci- ation of the krona relative to the trading partner currencies from end-February until early May 2020. Local consumers and firms transferred their expenditures during the pandemic from imported consumer durables, investment goods and tourism- related services to domestic services and housing. As in other countries, they also ramped up their savings. Iceland's imports contracted by 21%, more than else- where in the OECD. The contribution of net trade to output growth was still nega- tive by 5.5 percentage points. The combination of agile expenditure switching, and fiscal and monetary stimulus, considerably softened the shock to household finances and corporate profitability. After a short pause, the housing market recovered, as households took advantage of record low interest rates. The impact of the pandemic on the economy was therefore not as strong as expected. Recovery amidst a war in Europe The global recovery turned out to be stronger than expected and rekindled infla- tion in most parts of the world. In Iceland, the recovery was particularly strong, driven by a sharp reversal of the contraction in services exports. Like other coun- tries, Iceland suffered from the inflationary impact of global bottlenecks as the structure of global demand changed and expanded post-COVID, but a significant share of the increasing inflation in Iceland can be attributed to excess demand for housing and faster wage growth than in most other OECD countries. As in other parts of the world, the recovery has been complicated by the impact of the Russian war against Ukraine, which in many countries has been simultaneously inflationary and contractionary - threatening stagflation. In the case of Iceland, the impact of the war has been mostly inflationary, initially, much less so than in coun- tries which before the war relied on imported gas from Russia and on fossil fuels for heating and electricity generation. As electricity generation and heating in Ice- land is based on domestic renewable energy, its economy has not been directly affected by the spike in gas and electricity prices which most European countries have suffered greatly from. Firstly, the share of exports to Russia, Belarus and Ukraine, the three countries most affected by either the war or sanctions, is relatively small compared to many European countries. Only 1.7% of Iceland's goods exports went to these countries in 2020. The weight of imports from these countries in Iceland's value chain is most likely insignificant and can easily be replaced by imports from other countries. Because Iceland is a very small economy and price taker in most export markets, the loss of one market can easily be replaced by shifting to other markets. Although the war in Ukraine has affected Iceland's terms of trade, the net effect is ambiguous, with the prices of both imports and exports rising. Iceland is an ex- porter of both metals (mainly aluminium) and food products and thus has both gained and suffered from rising raw material and food prices. Terms of trade have remained favourable, although they have declined from their recent peak. Despite access to abundant domestic renewable energy, imported fossil fuels im- pact the Icelandic value chain both through the price of imported fuels, various imported goods and generally the cost of transportation, which is high given Ice- land's remoteness from major markets. Fuel is also an important cost item in fish- eries. Rising import prices, however, result not only from the war in Ukraine, but can be partly explained by supply-chain disruptions and the container cost crisis triggered by a reallocation of resources in the global economy as it recovered from the pandemic. The cost increases seep into the global value chain and affect infla- tion globally. Eventually those mismatches are being resolved from the supply side, as firms respond to price signals, and from the demand side, with global tightening of monetary conditions and the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus. The post-pandemic recovery in Iceland has two distinguishing features that set it apart from the recovery in most other OECD economies. Firstly, the expansion of the tourism sector and the associated construction boom have relied quite strongly on imported labour. Because of net migration the average rate of population growth since 2016 has been 2%, far higher than in other advanced countries. The rate of population growth has also been quite variable. To some extent, cyclical expansion has been facilitated by variability in the net migration rate rather than the domestic unemployment rate. Population growth fell into negative territory following the GFC, but has twice peaked at 3% during periods of tourism sector expansion, before and after the pandemic. While the variability of net migration can be a useful shock absorber, helping to keep unemployment low and relatively stable during downturns and make the la- bour market less overheated during expansions, variable population growth cre- ates problems in the housing market. The most recent surge in net migration has amplified the impact of COVID-related expenditure switching on housing prices. The demand for housing fluctuates in line with migration; however, the character- istically inelastic supply of housing may become even more inflexible if volatile mi- gration makes future housing demand more uncertain. As a result, what is gained in terms of a more flexible labour market may be lost due to a more volatile hous- ing market. Finland, Norway and Sweden. Iceland's tourism and construction sectors typically attract workers from other EEA countries during expansions. This time around, there has been an additional push effect from the war in Ukraine as Iceland has received a significant number of Ukrainian war refugees. The number of asylum seekers from other parts of the world has also risen. Many refugees and asylum seekers have already found work, but finding permanent housing has been a challenge. This may have contributed somewhat to higher housing prices recently and thus higher inflation in Iceland. Iceland's strong economy and relatively good employment prospects will likely continue to attract migrants and asylum seekers even after the war ends. The strong link between net migration and house price inflation suggests that policy- makers need to pay attention to the role of the housing market in Iceland's inflation dynamics. There are two roads to a more balanced outcome. Firstly, better demand management could make the demand for foreign labour and hence immigration more stable. Secondly, if the supply of housing could be made more elastic, hous- ing price volatility would diminish. In the face of the large external shocks the econ- omy has suffered in the past few years, both will be needed, but these are chal- lenging tasks with no easy solution. Due to the strong recovery of tourism, the output gap returned to positive territory at an earlier stage than in most other OECD economies. In addition to the housing market, emerging overheating has become most visible in the labour market. Wage growth in Iceland averaged above 7% during the pandemic, a somewhat faster pace than over the preceding decade and much faster than in main trading partner countries. Recently, short-term wage settlements have been concluded that imply that the fast pace of wage growth will continue at least for the coming year. This is worrisome for medium-term inflation prospects, since the buffers that ex- isted in the decade prior to the pandemic, and allowed faster wage growth for several years without commensurate inflationary consequences, have been de- pleted. The depressed level of relative unit labour costs following the GFC, fast expansion of tourism services exports in 2015 - 2017 and a current account surplus had allowed the krona to appreciate, with moderating impact on inflation. As the buffers are depleted, the relationship between wage growth and inflation is likely to be much less benign in the period ahead than during the pre-pandemic period. The fiscal and monetary dimension of the response to pandemic and war Three factors are likely to have determined the fiscal and monetary response of different countries to the pandemic: i) fiscal and monetary space at the outset, ii) the severity of the outbreak and iii) structural factors that affected the economic impact of the outbreak and restrictions imposed to contain it. On the first two ac- counts, Iceland was in a relatively good position. Modest public debt gave the gov- ernment significant fiscal space, and the outbreak and restrictive measures were moderate. The structure of the economy, on the other hand, with tourism-related services being the largest sector, created a large potential demand for fiscal ac- commodation to compensate affected firms and households, as discussed above. As in other countries, both fiscal and monetary policy were applied to respond to the pandemic with substantial easing, and the size of the fiscal measures taken were close to the average in OECD countries. Fiscal measures in response to the pandemic Sources: IMF Fiscal Monitor October 2021 database, Macrobond. COVID-19 measures * of 2020 GDP Italy United States Greece Iceland New Zealand Sweden Fiscal Measures in Response to the COVID-19 Pandemic since January 2020 % of 2020 GDP Iceland's monetary space was also substantial, with domestic interest rates being significantly above zero at the outset of the pandemic. However, the size of Ice- land's monetary space should not be overestimated. The combination of relatively illiquid currency markets, fairly strong exchange rate pass-through to prices and a long history of monetary instability limit how much the interest rate differential vis- a-vis abroad can narrow without a risk to inflation. Nevertheless, the Central Bank of Iceland's policy rate was reduced to a historical low, greatly softening the blow to the domestic economy, especially the construction sector. As it turned out, the economy recovered very strongly as COVID restrictions were lifted and the Central Bank needed to withdraw the monetary stimulus and start raising interest rates earlier and at a faster pace than most advanced countries. Sources: Statistics Iceland, Central Bank of Iceland. Reversing the stance of fiscal policy has been a more gradual process. As tempo- rary support measures have expired, the fiscal stimulus has gradually petered out and, with the economy expanding faster than previously forecast, public finances have also recovered faster than expected. The accelerated pace of the economy provides an opportunity to reach a structurally adjusted fiscal balance at an ear- lier stage than expected. However, although the current fiscal policy framework may be relatively transparent and predictable, it does not seem to provide a suffi- ciently strong incentive to take advantage of unexpected fiscal windfalls in a counter-cyclical fashion. Consequently, monetary policy has been forced to carry a larger share of the burden of adjustment than would be desirable from the standpoint of an optimal policy mix. As inflation hits social groups differently, fiscal policy can be effectively used to support the most vulnerable groups in the economy. However, as the immediate impact of inflation on the fiscal balance is positive - as revenues are in practical terms price-indexed during times of high inflation - it is important that fiscal policy resist the temptation to allow increased revenues to feed into expenditures more than is necessary. From the standpoint of the monetary authorities, while providing support to vulnerable groups, the fiscal authorities could prioritise tightening the fiscal stance and take advantage of the strong economic growth to close the budget deficit. The war in Ukraine still poses significant risks to the global economy. However, as the global energy and food crisis is resolved and monetary and fiscal stimulus is withdrawn, the prospects for global disinflation improve. Recent financial market turmoil may complicate the transmission of monetary policy in some countries. If it amplifies the downturn in economic activity, it may accelerate disinflation from what is currently projected, although so far this appears unlikely to fundamentally change the outcome. Inflation and inflation expectations have started to decline in Europe and the US. Disinflation may take somewhat longer in the case of Iceland, given the still strong economic momentum and prospects for higher wage growth than in trading partner countries. Much will depend on the interaction between three markets: the labour market, the housing market, and the foreign exchange market Monetary policy will have to remain tight until the relationship between the three markets has been stabilized. Stronger counter-cyclical fiscal policies would shorten the time needed to reach the balance and bring inflation to target.

Title: Address by the Chairman of the Supervisory Board of the Central Bank of Iceland at the Annual Meeting
text: 7 c/T 7* MN 31. March 2022 Gylfi Magnusson, Chair of the Central Bank of Iceland Su- pervisory Board, at the 61st Annual Meeting of the Central Bank, 31 March 2022 Madame Prime Minister, Governor, and other guests: I hereby call to order the sixty-first annual meeting of the Central Bank of Iceland. The pandemic continued to affect the Central Bank in 2021, although in different ways than in the year beforehand. When COVID-19 struck, the Bank applied its policy instruments decisively, in order to cushion against the economic impact of the pandemic. It is beyond doubt that those measures delivered the intended results. The economy began to rebound in 2021, and the Bank started to unwind the previ- ous years accommodative measures and take steps to tighten policy where neces- sary. But the pandemic continued to have a significant impact on the Banks day- to-day activities through the public health measures that were in place for most of the year, forcing Bank staff to work from home for long periods of time. Fortu- nately, that has changed, and employees are back at the Bank. When the end of the pandemic was finally in sight, war broke out in Eastern Europe. This could have profound repercussions, economic and otherwise, and it is vital to address them calmly, and by strengthening contingency measures in important areas such as fi- nancial market infrastructure and cybersecurity. The Central Bank will do its part in this effort. By now, just over two years since the merger of the Central Bank and the Financial Supervisory Authority, the activities of the merged institution have settled into their new routine. According to the report submitted late last year by the committee ap- pointed to appraise the experience gained from the work of the Monetary Policy Committee, Financial Stability Committee, and Financial Supervision Committee, all indicators suggested that the merger between the Bank and the Financial Super- visory Authority had been undertaken decisively and successfully. As has been stated previously, it was decided that all of the Central Banks activities should be located under one roof, in the Banks headquarters at Kalkofnsvegur 1. In order to bring this about, major modifications and renovations were launched. Work on the main building, which will house most of the Banks employees, is well advanced, and preparations are underway for the renovation of the ground floor and the annex. By law, the Central Bank of Iceland is required to promote price stability, financial stability, and sound and secure financial activities. Three committees comprising Bank officers and outside experts and officials are tasked with taking decisions on the application of policy instruments and other important matters. The Governor is responsible for the Bank's operations and is authorised to take decisions on all mat- ters not entrusted to others by law. Asgeir Jonsson has served as Governor of the Central Bank since 2019. The Banks Deputy Governors, who have held these po- sitions since the beginning of 2020, when the new Central Bank Act entered into force, are Rannveig Sigurdardottir, Deputy Governor for Monetary Policy; Gunnar Jakobsson, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability; and Unnur Gunnarsdottir, Deputy Governor for Financial Supervision. The Banks organisational structure is unchanged since the merger. The Bank has seven core departments and four support departments, plus the centralised General Secretariat. Information on the Banks operations and operating results can be found in the Annual Report, published to- day. The Supervisory Board monitors the Banks compliance with the statutory provi- sions applying to its activities. In other respects, the Board undertakes such tasks as are outlined explicitly in the Central Bank Act. Members of the Supervisory Board were the same as in 2020. I served as Board chairman, and other members were Thorunn Gudmundsdottir, Sigurdur Kari Kris- tjansson, Frosti Sigurjonsson, Bolli Hedinsson, Una Maria Oskarsdottir, and Jacqueline Clare Mallett. The Supervisory Board held 12 meetings over the course of2021. The new Supervisory Board, appointed on 24 March, held its first meeting today. Its members, apart from myself, are vice-chair Thorunn Gudmundsdottir, Amar Bjamason, Kirstin Flygenring, Sigridur Andersen, Sigurjon Arnorsson, and Thor- steinn Viglundsson. I would like to welcome them all. According to the profit and loss account, the Central Bank recorded a loss of just under 16 b.kr. in 2021, as opposed to a profit of just over 68 b.kr. in 2020. The loss on the Banks activities during the year is largely attributable to exchange rate- driven changes in foreign asset values. The Banks operating expenses totalled 7.8 b.kr., about 5% higher than in the prior year. Operating revenues totalled nearly 4.7 b.kr., about 9% higher than in the prior year. The Banks assets amounted to nearly 964 b.kr. at the year-end, or 121 b.kr. more than at the end of 2020. Its capital declined by 17 b.kr., to 134 b.kr. at the year-end. The Banks capital adequacy benchmark, which has been endorsed by the Supervi- sory Board, is 150 b.kr. Because of the operating loss and capital below the bench- mark, no dividend will be paid to the Treasury for 2021. At the end of 2021, the Bank employed 294 members of staff, a reduction of 9 relative to the prior year. The gender ratio remains relatively equal, and an equal pay analysis conducted within the Bank showed that there was no unexplained sta- tistically significant wage gap between the sexes. It is worth adding that during the year, the Bank began working systematically in areas relating to sustainability and climate issues, and has taken a number of steps and decisions in this regard, includ- ing setting a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions from its activities by 40% between 2019 and 2030. In pursuit of this goal, the Bank will switch to electric vehicles, cut back on air travel, and increase recycling. Furthermore, the Bank no longer maintains conventional accounts only; it now practises green accounting as well. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all staff members for fruitful cooper- ation and a job well done during the year. I would also like to extend special thanks to my colleagues on the Supervisory Board, the Deputy Governors, the Board secretary, and the Internal Auditor for smooth collaboration. And I would like to thank Governor Asgeir Jonsson in particular for our work together during the year. The Governor will address the meeting later, but first I would like to turn the podium over to Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir.

Title: Update on Iceland's economy
Subtitle: Address by Birgir sleifur Gunnarsson, Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at its Annual General Meeting, Reykjavk, 27 March 2001
text: Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson: Update on Icelands economy Address by Birgir isleifur Gunnarsson, Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Central Bank of Iceland, at its Annual General Meeting, Reykjavik, 27 March 2001. * * * On behalf of the Board of Governors of the Central Bank of Iceland I welcome you all to the Bank's 40th annual meeting.
